Step two: which line? (the CPU one)
Going from the function to the line
Step three: the one the profiler will never find
Step four: the same thing, under load
What the run knows that k6 does not
One bug I hit wiring this up
What I would actually tell you to do
pages.text: Every Grit project ships with Pulse mounted at `/pulse/ui`. People see the dashboard, nod, and never open it again, because when everything is fine a monitoring tool is a wall of green. So let me make something not fine. I am going to build a shop, write two slow endpoints into it deliberately, and then find them. Not by remembering where I put them. By starting from "something is slow" and following the tooling until it names a file and a line number. The two endpoints are slow in completely different ways, which is the point: one of them is invisible to the screen that catches the other. Then I am going to put twenty concurrent users on both and get a CPU profile of exactly those fifty seconds. Everything below is a real run. Every number is copied out of the terminal or read off a screenshot taken while it was happening. 200 products, 2000 reviews, a working admin panel and API. Now the two bad endpoints. These are not strawmen. I wrote each one the way the ticket would have described it, and neither looks wrong when you read it. The merchandising team wants related products, and the only data we have is names. So: score every product against every other product by name similarity, keep the best three. If you are already pointing at the nested loop, hold that thought. You are about to be half right, and the half you are wrong about is the interesting half. Every product, with how many reviews it has and their average rating. That is a textbook N+1: one query for the products, then one more per product. 201 queries to answer one request. Two switches, and deliberately two. In `.env`: and `PULSE_PROFILE_ENABLED=true` in the environment the server actually runs in. Why two? A profile is an unauthenticated description of your program's internals, and a thirty-second CPU profile that anyone can request repeatedly is a denial of service. One forgotten setting should not be enough to expose that, so it takes a config value *and* an environment variable, and the endpoints sit behind the Pulse dashboard credentials on top. Mutex and block profiling cost the runtime something merely to be switched on, so they are separate numbers you set deliberately. Leave `PULSE_BLOCK_PROFILE_RATE=0` and ask for a block profile, and you get a `409` that names the option to add rather than an empty profile that reads as "nothing is blocking". That distinction matters more than it sounds: an empty profile is a wrong answer that looks like a right one. Drive some traffic, open `/pulse/ui`, go to **Routes**. ![The Pulse Routes page: a table of method, path, requests, error rate, avg, p95, p99, rpm. /api/v1/reports/suggestions shows 356ms avg and 419ms p95, against 2ms for /api/v1/products](/blog/profiling/routes.png) There it is, in ten seconds. `/products` is a generated list endpoint doing real work with pagination and filtering, and it answers in 2ms. `suggestions` takes 178 times longer. Note the two columns on the right, **VS USUAL** and **TREND**, both showing `—`. Those are the per-route baselines added in Pulse v1.3.0: once there is a week of history they show the current p95 as a ratio against what the route normally does. That is the difference between "this route is slow" and "this route *got* slow", and only the second one tells you to go looking at a recent deploy. On a six-minute-old process there is nothing to compare against yet, and the dashboard says so rather than inventing a number. So: `suggestions` is slow. Pulse has taken me as far as the route. Now I need the line. The dashboard has a **Flame Graph** page. Click it, pick **CPU**, hit Sample: ![The Pulse Flame Graph page in CPU mode. The stack reads bottom-up through the gin middleware into handlers.CatalogReportHandler.Suggestions, services.similarity, and a wide tower of services.normalise into runtime.concatstrings](/blog/profiling/flame.png) Read it bottom-up and the whole chain is there: the gin middleware, then `handlers.(*CatalogReportHandler).Suggestions`, then `services.(*CatalogReportService).Suggestions`, then `services.similarity`, and then the widest tower on the page, `services.normalise` opening into `runtime.concatstrings` and `runtime.concatstring2`. That is the answer, and the page tells you how to read it: *"Width is CPU time, so the widest frame is the one burning the machine."* > **This page was useless a day before I wrote this.** It sampled **goroutine stacks** rather than CPU time, so a goroutine parked in a network read counted on every tick while using no CPU at all, and the widest towers were `runtime.netpollblock` and `net.(*conn).Read`. The hot code was a sliver you had to hunt for. [I filed it](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/pulse/issues/10) and Pulse v1.5.0 added the CPU/Goroutines toggle with **CPU as the default**. Goroutine mode kept its own job, finding leaks and stuck workers, and now folds away parked stacks unless you ask for them. The flame graph names the function. For the line, pull the profile and open it in the tool Go ships with: Read the `cum` column, not `flat`. `normalise` is **38.17% of all CPU in the process**. The Levenshtein distance, the thing that looks expensive, is 18.48%. A function whose job is to lowercase a string and drop punctuation costs twice what the actual algorithm costs. And `runtime.concatstrings` at 19.19% is the confession. Now the move that ends the investigation: **Line 92. `out += string(r)`. 2.82 seconds of a 9.85 second profile. One line, 28.6% of everything the process did.** That is the answer to "how would I discover which file is burning CPU". A file name, a line number, and a share of total CPU, from a running process, without a debugger and without adding a single line of instrumentation. Strings are immutable in Go, so `out += string(r)` allocates a brand new string and copies the old one on every kept character. For a 30-character product name that is 30 allocations and 465 bytes copied, and the nested loop calls it 40,000 times per request. Which brings us to
pages.title: Finding the line that is burning your CPU

headings: The writer count is a property of the database
The batch size is computed, not chosen
It resumes, which changes what the index means
The first error stops everything, carefully
The idea Grit does not use, and where it should
What transfers to your own code
pages.text: Somebody sent me [Kennedy Karoko's two-part series on processing a million transactions in under a second](https://blog.karoko.dev/processing-1-million-transactions-in-under-a-second-using-go-part-1-98c9079375ac) and asked whether it is the same thing Grit does when you run `grit seed Product --count 1000000`. It is the same family, and the differences are the interesting part. So here is the honest comparison, followed by the parts of Grit's seeder that go further, and the one idea in that article that Grit does not use anywhere and probably should. First, the number, because a post about performance that does not measure anything is an opinion: Sixty seconds, on SQLite, on a laptop. The number that matters is not 16,742 rows per second. **It is the 10 MB.** Because there are two obvious ways to write this and they fail in opposite directions. Insert one row per statement and memory is perfect, flat and tiny, while the job takes an afternoon: you are paying query parsing, a transaction and a round trip a million times over. Build all million rows into a slice first and insert them in one go, and the throughput is fine right up until the process is holding a million structs plus the driver's copy of them, at which point it either swaps or the OOM killer takes it. The pipeline below is how you get neither. The rows are built in chunks, written in batches, and the number of chunks in flight is capped by a channel, so the memory ceiling is a property of the data structure rather than of how many rows you asked for. Ask for ten thousand or ten million: the heap looks the same. Karoko's article builds up to it from the naive version, which is the right way to teach it. The naive version reads a file line by line and writes each row as it goes, and gets about 350 transactions per second. The final version: 1. One goroutine reads, pushing into a buffered channel. 2. A worker pool consumes, parsing concurrently. 3. Each worker batches, and aggregates into its own private map. 4. The maps merge at the end, and the result is flushed in bulk. Grit's seeder, in `internal/database/seedbatch.go`, has the same skeleton. A bounded channel, producers on one end, consumers on the other, batched writes: And the two headline conclusions are identical, so let me state them plainly because they are the whole lesson: **Batching the writes is the win, not the goroutines.** Going from one insert per row to one insert per batch is the change that moves the number by an order of magnitude. Parallelism on top of that is worth maybe five times. Parallelism without batching is worth almost nothing, because a million round trips is a million round trips no matter how many goroutines are waiting on them. **Bounded memory is a property of the channel, not of discipline.** A buffered channel of fixed capacity means a fast producer blocks when consumers fall behind. That backpressure is what keeps the heap flat. It is not something you remember to do; it is something the data structure does whether you remember or not. The article has one worker pool that parses *and* writes. Grit has two pools with the channel between them: The reason is that building a row and writing a row are different kinds of work, and the right number of goroutines for each is different. Building rows is CPU-bound: `gofakeit.ProductName()`, a money value, a random number. More than a few cores of that is wasted, so makers cap at four. Writing is I/O-bound and bounded by what the database will accept concurrently, which is a completely different number. Fuse them into one pool and you have to pick a single worker count that is wrong for one half of the job. Split them and each side gets sized on its own terms, with the channel absorbing the mismatch. SQLite takes a single writer lock. Pointing eight goroutines at it does not produce eight times the throughput; it produces eight goroutines taking turns, plus lock contention and `SQLITE_BUSY` retries. One writer is not a limitation being worked around, it is the correct number for that engine. This is the general form of the article's own closing observation, that pushing the worker count higher stops helping past a point. The point is not a universal constant. It is a property of what sits at the end of the pipeline, and the code should know which one it is talking to. The article suggests 500 to 1,000 and says to benchmark. Reasonable advice. Grit computes it: There is a hard ceiling here that benchmarking will not reveal gently. Postgres and MySQL accept 65,535 bind parameters in one statement; SQLite accepts 32,766. A multi-row insert uses one parameter per column per row, so the real limit is `65535 / columns`. A model with 12 columns tops out at 5,461 rows per insert; a wide model with 60 columns tops out at 1,092. Pick 1,000 by benchmarking on a narrow table and it works. Add columns to the model over the next year and one day the insert fails with a parameter-limit error that has nothing obviously to do with the column you added. Deriving it means the ceiling moves when the model does. The `if size > 1000` cap on top is the benchmarking answer: past about a thousand rows the gains flatten and the cost of a failed batch grows, so there is no reason to go near the ceiling even when it is allowed. The article's producer pushes each line into the channel and the workers pull. Grit's makers pull their own work from a counter: `next.Add(1)` is a single atomic increment. There is no dispatcher goroutine, no mutex, and no coordination between makers beyond that one instruction. Each maker computes which rows it owns from the index it claimed, which means it can build its chunk without reading any shared state at all. This is the same insight as the article's worker-local maps, applied to work distribution instead of to aggregation: **the fastest synchronisation is the synchronisation you do not perform.** The article removes lock contention from the aggregation hot path. This removes it from the sched
pages.title: How to Bulk Insert a Million Rows in Go Without Running Out of Memory

headings: The relay, and the part people get wrong
Retries that do not hammer a dead endpoint
When you need it and when you do not
pages.text: Here is a bug that is almost impossible to reproduce and very easy to write. An order is placed. You save it, then fire a webhook so the warehouse starts picking. Two lines of code, in the obvious order: That is wrong, and swapping the lines is also wrong. There is no third option. This post is about why, and about the thing you have to build instead. **Publish first, then commit.** The webhook goes out, the commit fails on a constraint or a dropped connection, and the warehouse is now picking an order that does not exist in your database. There is nothing to reconcile against, because the row was never written. Downstream systems have acted on a fact you do not have. **Commit first, then publish.** The commit succeeds, the process is killed between the two lines, and the order exists with nobody told. The warehouse never picks it. No error is logged anywhere, because from the process's point of view nothing failed. You find out when the customer emails. Neither is a rare race. A deploy restarts every process, by design, continuously. If you ship often enough, that gap gets hit. The usual instinct is to make the gap smaller: retry the publish, defer it, wrap it in a goroutine with a timeout. All of that makes the window narrower and none of it closes it, because the problem is not the size of the window. The problem is that you are performing two operations that must either both happen or neither happen, and you have no mechanism that makes them atomic. You do have exactly one such mechanism: the database transaction. So use it. Write the message to a table in the same transaction as the business data. One commit. Both rows or neither. There is no window, because there is no second operation to fail. A separate relay then reads committed messages and delivers them. If delivery fails, the message is still sitting in the table and gets tried again. If the process dies mid-delivery, the message is still sitting in the table and gets tried again. The package comment in `internal/outbox/outbox.go` puts the trade in one line, and it is worth being blunt about it because this is where people get surprised: > The cost is delivery semantics: at-least-once, not exactly-once. A message can be delivered twice if the process dies between the send and the status update. Consumers have to be idempotent, which is what a dedup key on the receiving end is for. **At-least-once is not a flaw in the design, it is the design.** You have moved the hard problem from "did this get sent at all" to "might this arrive twice", and the second problem has a cheap, local, verifiable answer: the receiver records message IDs it has processed and ignores repeats. The first problem has no answer at all. Anyone who tells you their queue is exactly-once is describing at-least-once delivery plus deduplication, which is the same thing with the dedup hidden somewhere you cannot inspect. A naive relay is a loop: select pending messages, send each one, mark it sent. That works on one process. Run two replicas and both select the same rows, and every message goes out twice. Not occasionally. Every time. The fix is to claim work rather than read it. Here is the query the relay actually runs, lifted from a running project's query log: Two conditions joined by OR, and the second one is the one that matters. The first clause is ordinary pending work: messages whose status is pending and whose `available_at` has arrived. The `available_at` column is what makes backoff possible, which we will get to. The second clause picks up messages that are marked *claimed* but whose `claimed_at` is older than some threshold. That is a **lease**. A relay claims a message by stamping `claimed_at` and marking it in-flight. If it delivers successfully, the message is marked sent. If the process dies holding the claim, nobody marks anything, and after the lease expires another relay sees a claim older than the threshold and takes it over. Without a lease, a process that dies mid-delivery strands its claimed messages forever. They are not pending, so nobody picks them up, and they sit in the table looking fine. The lease is what turns "claimed" from a permanent state into a temporary one. The lease duration is the usual availability-versus-duplication dial. Short, and a slow delivery gets taken over by a second relay while the first is still working, producing a duplicate. Long, and a crashed process's messages sit idle for that long. Since consumers must be idempotent anyway, erring short is usually right. Exponential backoff from five seconds, doubling, capped at thirty minutes, twelve attempts before the message is parked. Those three numbers say something specific. Twelve attempts with doubling backoff capped at half an hour covers roughly five hours of a downstream system being unavailable. That is a deliberate statement: a webhook endpoint that has been down for five hours is not having a blip, and continuing to retry is not helping anybody. The message is parked for a human rather than retried forever. Parked, and specifically not deleted: > MaxAttempts is how many times to try before parking a message at "failed". Parked rather than deleted: a message nobody can deliver is evidence of a bug, and deleting the evidence is how the bug survives. A dead-letter row is the only artefact that says what was supposed to happen and did not. Delete it and the system looks healthy while silently dropping work, which is the worst of both outcomes: no delivery and no trace. The cap matters as much as the doubling. Uncapped exponential backoff reaches days between attempts surprisingly fast, which means a system that recovers at hour three waits until hour nine to find out. The cap bounds the detection delay at thirty minutes. `available_at` is how backoff is stored. Rather than keeping a retry schedule in memory, which a restart loses, the next attempt time is written on the row. The relay's query only picks up messages whose `available_at` has passed. Restart

headings: Why this is not a bug you can fix with care
The textbook answer, and its bill
Put the fact on the person
Three details that are each a bug if you get them wrong
Only on a write that worked
Check the method, not the route
Five seconds, and why it is not fifty
It is not a security boundary, and does not need to be
And it is free when you have no replicas
pages.text: You add a read replica. Reads go to the replica, writes go to the primary, and the primary stops being the bottleneck. Everything is faster and nothing breaks. Except one thing, and it is the single most reported bug of that change: **somebody posts, the page reloads, and their own post is not there.** So they post it again. It is maddening to debug because it does not reproduce. You post, you reload, it is there. The replica caught up in the time it took you to move your hand to the keyboard. It happens to a fraction of users, for a fraction of a second, and only to the person who wrote. Everyone else sees exactly what they expect, which is the list as it was a moment ago, and a moment ago is fine for them. The sequence is just what replication is: There is no mistake in that trace. The write went to the right place, the read went to the right place, and the replica is doing exactly what an asynchronous replica does. The data is not lost; it is in flight. What is wrong is the expectation. Eventual consistency is fine for reading other people's data, where "a moment ago" is indistinguishable from "now". It is not fine for reading your own, because you have a memory of what you just did, and a system that contradicts it looks broken. The property you want has a name: **read-your-own-writes consistency**. Not global consistency, which is expensive and which you do not need. Just the guarantee that one person's reads reflect that person's writes. The standard solution is a sticky-write store. When a user writes, record "user X wrote at T" in Redis. On every read, look up that user, and if they wrote within the replication window, read from the primary. It works. It also means: - **A Redis round trip on every read.** Not on the writes, which are rare. On the reads, which are everything. You have added a network hop to the hot path of your entire application to fix a one-second edge case. - **Redis is now on the critical path for reading.** If Redis is down, every read either fails or silently loses the guarantee. You have taken a cache, which is supposed to be optional, and made it load-bearing. - **It is one more thing to run**, size, monitor and pay for. There is a reflex in systems work that reaches for shared state whenever two requests need to agree about something. Sometimes that is right. It is worth asking first whether the two requests have anything in common that could carry the fact for you. Here they do. **They are the same browser.** The whole mechanism, from `internal/middleware/read_your_writes.go`: A successful write sets a cookie holding the current timestamp. A read that arrives with a recent timestamp in that cookie is flagged, and the flag tells the database layer to use the primary for this one request. That is it. No store, no lookup, no new dependency. The properties fall out of where the fact lives: **It cannot be stale.** The cookie travels with the browser that did the write. There is no replication delay on the thing that measures replication delay, which is the circularity a shared store has to work around. **It costs nothing on the read path.** Reading a cookie that is already on the request is free. Compare that with a Redis round trip per read. **It fails in the right direction.** No cookie, expired cookie, nonsense cookie: you read from the replica, which is the normal path. The failure mode of the mechanism is the behaviour you had before the mechanism. **It is per-browser, which is per-person in practice.** Exactly the scope the guarantee needs. A `POST` that returned 422 changed nothing. Setting the cookie for it pins that user's next five seconds of reads to the primary to protect a write that never happened. On a form people fill in badly a few times before getting it right, those are the reads you least want on the primary. A `GET` never sets the cookie, however it is spelled. Routes with names like `/items/:id/archive` that are secretly writes are a different problem, and the honest fix is to make them a `POST`. Deciding by HTTP method keeps the rule mechanical. This is the only real dial, and it is a direct trade. Too short and the bug comes back for the tail of your replication distribution. Too long and every user who writes once sends all their reads to the primary for that long, which on a write-heavy application is most of your traffic, and you have quietly undone the reason you added the replica. Five seconds is roughly five to ten times typical sub-second replication lag, which covers the tail without being generous. The number to tune it against is your actual lag metric, not a guess, which is why the comment says so. A cookie the client can forge decides which database a read goes to. That sounds alarming for about ten seconds, until you ask what forging it achieves. > The worst a forged cookie achieves is reading from the primary, which is the correct answer served by a more expensive machine. There is no privilege here. The flag does not change *what* you can read, only *which replica answers*. Both hold the same data. A user who forges the cookie permanently has opted themselves out of the read replica and is getting slightly fresher data at slightly higher cost to you. The only abuse worth a thought is a client forging it at scale to push load onto the primary, and that is a rate-limiting problem, not an authentication one. If someone can send you enough traffic for that to matter, they can hurt you without the cookie. Not every mechanism needs integrity. The question is what an attacker gains, and here the answer is a marginally slower response for themselves. > It does no work on a project with no replicas: the flag is read by `database.ForRequest`, which returns the same handle either way when nothing is configured. The middleware is always mounted. With one database, `ForRequest` returns that database whether the flag is set or not, so the whole thing is a cookie read and a map write. When you add a replica later, the consistency bug y

headings: Why the obvious handler has this bug
Pessimistic locking, and why it is not the answer here
A version column, and the WHERE clause that gives it meaning
The client has to say what it is overwriting
409 is only useful if it says what happened
Why this is in the framework and not in your handler
pages.text: Two support agents open the same customer record. One fixes the phone number. The other, a minute later, fixes the address. Both press Save. The phone number is gone. Nobody is told. No error, no log line, no conflict. The second save wrote the whole record from a form that was loaded before the first save happened, so it wrote back the old phone number along with the new address. From the database's point of view, two perfectly valid updates were applied in order. From the first agent's point of view, their work silently evaporated. This is the **lost update** problem, and it is the most common data-integrity bug in CRUD applications, because the obvious implementation has it and it takes real work to even notice. That is correct in the sense of doing what it says. The problem is what the client sent: a complete record, read at some earlier moment, with one field changed. `Updates` writes all of it. Note that a transaction does not help. Both updates are individually atomic; the agents are minutes apart, not microseconds. Neither does a stricter isolation level, because there is no concurrent transaction to serialise against. The first write committed long before the second began. This is not a race in the database. It is a race between two humans and a stale form. The ingredient missing is that the second request never says what it thinks it is overwriting. The heavyweight fix is to lock the record when someone opens it. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or an application-level "Alice is editing this" flag. It works, and it is the wrong tool for a web application: - **A lock has to be released by someone.** A user who opens a record and closes their laptop holds it until a timeout. Now you need the timeout, and a way to break a stale lock, and a story for what happens when the timeout is wrong. - **It holds a database transaction open for human time.** Seconds to minutes, across a think-time pause, consuming a connection the whole while. - **It is pessimistic in the literal sense.** It pays the cost on every edit to prevent a conflict that is rare. Most records are edited by one person at a time. Optimistic locking inverts it: let everyone write, detect the collision, and make the loser deal with it. You pay only when it actually happens. Every model Grit generates carries one: Every update increments it, in the database, as part of the same statement. There is no read-then-write, so two concurrent updates cannot both compute version 8 from version 7. On its own a version column does nothing. It is a number that goes up. As the package comment says: > Generated models already carry a version column that every update increments; this is the WHERE clause that makes it mean something. The clause is this: If the record is still at version 7, one row is affected and the write lands. If somebody else got there first, it is at 8, **zero rows are affected**, and nothing is overwritten. The database tells you about the conflict by doing nothing, and the number of affected rows is how you hear about it. The server cannot infer the version the client read. The client has to send it, and HTTP has had the header for this since 1999: `If-Match`. `IfMatch` reads the header and turns it into the WHERE clause: Three things in that small function are deliberate. **No header means no change in behaviour.** An existing client that knows nothing about any of this keeps working exactly as before, last-write-wins. That is what makes this shippable into an API with clients you do not control. The guarantee is opt-in per request, and a client opts in by being able to lose. **`*` is also a pass.** `If-Match: *` means "as long as it exists", which is the HTTP spec's meaning, and it is the right escape hatch for a client that wants to force a write. **It accepts three spellings.** A bare `7`, a quoted `"7"`, and the weak ETag form `W/"7"` the API sends back. Clients echo back what they were given, and ETags are quoted by the spec, so an implementation accepting only bare integers rejects every well-behaved HTTP client. Accepting the form you emit is the minimum bar. And a value that parses as none of those matches nothing, so a malformed header fails closed. The write does not land. Given the alternative is silently overwriting with an unverified assumption, refusing is correct. A bare 409 is nearly useless to a client: it knows it lost and nothing else. Returning the current version lets the client re-fetch, show a real diff, and offer "keep mine / keep theirs / merge", which is the interface users deserve for this. The response also carries the new `ETag`, so a client that wants to retry already has the value to send back. There is a comment above that function worth repeating, because it is the kind of detail that only shows up after it has bitten someone: > Built by hand rather than through `respond.Fail`: Fail's details are strings, and `current_version` is a number on the wire. v3.285.0 sent it as `"2"`, which broke every client comparing it with the version it holds. A generic error helper that stringifies everything is fine until one of the fields is meant to be compared rather than displayed. `"9" !== 9` in JavaScript, so a client doing the obvious check against the version it holds silently never matches, and the retry logic quietly never fires. Worth knowing if your error envelope has a `details` map typed as `map[string]string`. **It is per-record.** Two edits to the same record conflict. Two edits to related records that are only valid together will not. That needs a transaction with both rows, or a version on the aggregate. **The window is the client's.** The guarantee holds from the version the client read. A client that reads, waits an hour, and sends `If-Match: 7` gets a conflict, which is right. A client that reads twice and sends the version from the first read has lied to you, and nothing can catch that. **It only covers writes that go through it.** A background job, an admin script or a bulk import th

headings: The three paths worth a budget
pages.text: Most projects have benchmarks nobody runs. The reason is structural rather than lazy. You write `BenchmarkVerifyToken`, it reports 1.2µs, and you think: good, now let me fail the build if it goes above 2µs. Then CI runs it on a shared runner next to three other jobs and it reports 3.1µs. You raise the threshold. It reports 0.9µs on a quiet afternoon and 4µs on a busy one. Within a week the threshold is so loose it would not catch a tenfold regression, and shortly after that the benchmarks stop being run at all. A wall-clock benchmark measures your code *and the machine it ran on*. On a shared CI runner the second term dominates, so the measurement cannot be an assertion. There is a number right next to it that does not have that problem. `AllocsPerRun` runs the function N times and returns the average number of heap allocations per run. It does not measure time. It counts events. And the count does not move with the machine. A loaded runner does not make your code allocate more. Four other jobs on the same box do not change how many times `make` is called. Run it on a laptop, run it on CI, run it at 3am or during a deploy storm: the same code allocates the same number of times. That makes it the thing a benchmark cannot be: **an assertion with a stable expected value.** It is also not a proxy for a thing nobody cares about. Most Go performance work is allocation work. Allocations are what produce garbage, garbage is what produces collection pauses, and collection pauses are what produce the p99 that wakes someone up. A change that doubles allocations on a hot path will not fail any test you have, and it will show up in your garbage collector. Every project Grit generates ships `internal/handlers/perf_test.go` with budgets on three paths, chosen because they run on every request or every list request: The `why` field is not decoration. It is printed in the failure message, because the person who trips this budget is usually not the person who set it, and "this allocates more than it used to" is not actionable without "and here is why anyone cared about this path". Two details in the harness matter more than they look: First-call costs are real but they are not per-request costs. Including them makes the number higher and noisier, which is the worst combination: a budget you have to set loose *and* that still flakes. The token verification case also runs with a nil database on purpose, so it measures the cryptography and the parsing rather than a session lookup. A budget is only useful if you know what is inside it. And CI runs these without `-race`, because the race detector allocates on its own account and the resulting counts are not the ones your users get. The first version of that file shipped with this comment: > An allocation count does not: the same code allocates the same number of times on every machine, every run. The first half is true. The second half is not, and CI told me so within a day. Token verification allocates **56 times under go1.26.9 and 41 under go1.27.2.** Same code, same machine, same test. The newer runtime does the same work with fifteen fewer allocations. I had set the budget to 50 from a local run on Go 1.27. CI pins 1.26.9. So it passed on the machine that wrote it and failed on the machine that judges it, which is the oldest mistake in performance work: measuring somewhere other than where the number is enforced. The fix is a rule rather than a bigger number: **Budget from the oldest supported toolchain**, because it allocates the most and is the binding constraint. **Record every figure you measured**, so the next person can tell a real regression from a toolchain difference. And check with the version CI actually uses: The failure message now says this out loud, because the right response to a failing budget is frequently "your Go version is different", not "your code got worse": Note the last line. **A budget you are allowed to raise is the point, not a loophole.** Sometimes the extra allocations buy something worth having. The test is not there to forbid that, it is there to make the new number a decision somebody recorded rather than a drift nobody saw. Not by taste. By profiling a generated API under load and reading what the profile said. `runtime.mallocgc` and friends sitting that high in a profile is the signal that a workload is allocation-bound rather than compute-bound. When the garbage collector is a visible fraction of your CPU, the useful lever is allocating less, and the useful test is one that notices when you start allocating more. Which is a general point about performance work: **profile first to find out which resource you are short of, then write the test that guards that resource.** Writing a latency assertion for an allocation-bound workload gives you a flaky test guarding the wrong thing. The trick generalises past Go. When you want CI to enforce a performance property, look for a metric with three properties: **It counts events rather than measuring duration.** Counts are deterministic; durations include every other process on the box. **It is a property of the code, not of the environment.** Ask what else could change it. Machine load, no. Go version, yes, which is why that one has to be pinned and recorded. **It moves when the thing you care about moves.** Allocations correlate with GC pressure and tail latency. A metric that is stable but unrelated is a test that always passes. Other metrics that qualify: query count per request (which is the N+1 detector as an assertion), bytes allocated per operation, goroutines spawned per request, and output size for a serialiser. Each is a count. Each moves when the code changes and holds still when it does not. The ones that do not qualify are the obvious ones: wall time, CPU time, requests per second, p95. Those are worth measuring, worth graphing, and worth alerting on in production against a baseline. They are not worth failing a pull request over, because the number they report is par
pages.title: Go Benchmarks Are Too Flaky to Fail a Build: Use Allocation Budgets Instead

headings: The mental model: a branch, not a cache
The two tables on the device
Squashing: why the outbox is keyed, not appended
Pull: the cursor is the hard part
The N+1 that would have been
Three conflict policies, and the one that must be the default
Policies, and the fields that never leave the device
Two more things the server will not take from you
What you actually have to build
pages.text: A field engineer drives into a basement car park to inspect a building. No signal for forty minutes. She updates eleven records. Meanwhile her colleague, above ground, edits one of the same eleven. She comes back up. Now what? That question is the whole of offline sync, and almost none of it is about networking. It is about what you do with two versions of the truth and no authority to pick between them. This post walks through the engine Grit generates for that, both halves, with the code. The most common mistake is to think of offline data as a **cache**. A cache is a copy of someone else's truth that you throw away when it goes stale. If that were what this is, the problem would be easy: refetch and move on. It is not a cache. It is a **branch**. The moment the device goes offline and somebody edits a row, that device has forked. It has its own commits. The server has carried on and may have its own. When the network returns you are not refreshing a cache, you are **merging two branches**, and every hard part of offline sync is a hard part of merging: what changed, in what order, and what do we do when both sides touched the same line. Hold that analogy. Everything below is a piece of machinery that a version control system also needs, and the resemblance is not a coincidence. **`records` is the working copy.** Every read in the app comes from here, always, even when online. That single decision is what makes the app feel instant and is what "offline-first" actually means: the network is never on the path between a user and their data. It is a background process that reconciles. **`outbox` is the stack of unpushed commits.** A local write does two things, and the order matters: Write the mirror so the UI updates instantly. Write the outbox so the change survives the app being closed, the battery dying, or the user not reconnecting until Tuesday. An outbox that lives in memory is not an outbox; it is a plan to lose data at the first crash. Here is the first design decision that is not obvious. The outbox is not a log of every change. It holds **at most one row per record**: That unique index on `(Model, EntityID)` is the whole policy. A user who edits the same inspection note nine times offline does not produce nine pushes. They produce one, holding the final state. The merge rules are small enough to read in full: Two of those are worth stopping on. **`update` on top of an existing `create` keeps the op as `create`.** The server has never heard of this row. Sending it an update for a row it does not have would 404. The change of state is real but the *operation* is still "this row is new to you". **`delete` on top of a `create` deletes the outbox row entirely.** The user made something offline and then changed their mind. The server never knew. There is nothing to tell it. Sending a create followed by a delete would be two round trips to arrive at the state of having done nothing. This is `git rebase -i` with every commit on a file squashed into one. You lose the intermediate history, and for a sync protocol that is a feature: nobody wants the server's audit log to record eight keystrokes-worth of saves from a train. Pull first and some of your conflicts evaporate before they exist. If a colleague edited row 7 and you did not touch row 7, pulling takes their change quietly. If you *did* touch row 7, you now know you are in conflict before you push, which means the conflict can be presented while the user is still in the app, rather than as a failed push. Push first and you are writing to a version of the server you have not looked at since yesterday. Every conflict that was going to happen still happens, and you find out about all of them afterwards. Fetch before you merge. It is the same instinct. Pull asks "what changed since I last looked", which needs a bookmark. The obvious bookmark is a timestamp, and the obvious bookmark is wrong. Here is the bug that clause exists to prevent, and it is a data-loss bug that looks like nothing. Say 600 rows share a millisecond, because a batch import wrote them. The page size is 500. With a cursor of time alone, you send 500 rows and the cursor becomes that timestamp. Next page asks for `updated_at > T`. **The other 100 rows are at exactly `T`.** They are not greater than `T`. They are skipped, silently, forever. The client's mirror is missing a hundred rows and nothing anywhere reports an error. The fix is to make the cursor a **compound key**: the timestamp *and* the last ID seen. `(updated_at = T AND id > lastID)` picks up the stragglers in the same millisecond, then `updated_at > T` moves on. The wire format is unglamorous and good: `2026-10-22T09:14:03.123456789Z~01a1...`. Nanosecond precision because millisecond precision creates more ties, and ties are what the ID half is there to break. There is a second reason for keyset over `OFFSET`: rows are moving. A row edited during your paging gets a new `updated_at` and jumps to the end of the ordering. With `OFFSET 500` the rows behind it shift up by one and you skip one. Keyset pagination reads a stable window because it asks "after this key" rather than "skip this many". If a row is deleted on the server, the next pull returns everything that changed. A hard-deleted row does not appear in that list. It does not appear in *any* list. There is no way for the client to distinguish "deleted" from "unchanged", so the client keeps it. Forever. So deletes must leave something behind to travel. A **tombstone**: and pull reads **unscoped**, which is the line that makes it work: Normally you work hard to make soft-deleted rows invisible. Here you work hard to make sure they are visible to exactly one reader. This one is my favourite thing in the package, because it is subtle, it is a performance bug and a correctness bug at once, and it took a production failure on MySQL to find: GORM's soft delete sets `deleted_at` and leaves `updated_at` alone. So a deleted row's "change time" was `deleted_at`, while

headings: Auto-Generated API Docs: Scalar & Swagger in Grit
pages.text: Every API needs documentation. Other developers (and your future self) need to know what endpoints exist, what parameters they accept, and what they return. In this course, you will learn how Grit auto-generates interactive API documentation using gin-docs , no annotations required. You ll explore the Scalar UI, test endpoints live, and export the OpenAPI spec. Reference docs: API Documentation → Imagine you inherit a project with 50 API endpoints. No documentation. No comments. You have to read every handler, every route, every model to figure out what the API does. That s a nightmare , and it s surprisingly common. API documentation solves this by providing a clear, browsable reference of every endpoint your API offers. Why does documentation matter? Three reasons: • For other developers: Frontend developers, mobile developers, and third-party integrators need to know your API s contract without reading Go code • For your future self: You will forget what endpoints exist, what parameters are required, and what the response looks like. Documentation is your memory • For testing: Interactive docs let you test endpoints directly in the browser , no Postman, no curl, no frontend needed Have you ever used an API without documentation? How was the experience? Think about how you figured out what endpoints existed, what parameters to send, and what the response looked like. Write down 3 problems you encountered (or would encounter) when using an undocumented API. Most API documentation tools require you to write annotations , special comments above every handler function describing the endpoint. That s tedious and error-prone because the annotations can drift out of sync with the actual code. Grit takes a different approach. Grit uses gin-docs to auto-generate OpenAPI 3.1 specifications. No annotations needed. It works by introspecting your Gin routes and GORM models at startup. Here s what gin-docs does when your API starts: 1. Scans your Gin router. It reads every registered route , the HTTP method, the URL path, the middleware chain, and the handler function. 2. Reads your GORM models. It inspects the struct fields, their types, JSON tags, and GORM tags to generate request/response schemas. 3. Generates the OpenAPI 3.1 spec. A complete JSON specification describing every endpoint, parameter, request body, and response schema. 4. Serves the Scalar UI. The interactive documentation is available at /docs in your browser. Open http://localhost:8080/docs in your browser. How many endpoint groups do you see? List the group names (e.g., Auth, Users, etc.). How many total endpoints are documented? When you open /docs , you see the Scalar UI , a modern, interactive documentation interface. Let s walk through its key features. The left sidebar shows all your endpoint groups , organized by route prefix. Click a group to expand it and see individual endpoints. Each endpoint shows: • HTTP method badge , color-coded: green for GET, blue for POST, orange for PUT, red for DELETE • URL path , the full endpoint path including path parameters like /api/users/:id • Description , auto-generated from the handler name and route • Request builder , fill in parameters and body, then click Send to test the endpoint live • Response preview , shows the actual response with syntax highlighting • Authentication indicator , shows whether the endpoint requires a JWT token Find the POST /api/auth/login endpoint in the Scalar UI. Fill in the email and password fields in the request builder. Click Send. Does it return a token? What other fields are in the response? One of gin-docs most powerful features is automatic schema generation. It reads your GORM models and generates JSON schemas that describe the shape of request bodies and response payloads. For example, consider a simple User model: From this model, gin-docs automatically generates: • A request schema for POST/PUT , includes name, email, role (excludes id, password, timestamps) • A response schema for GET , includes id, name, email, role, timestamps (excludes password) • Required field markers , from the binding: required tag • Type information , string, integer, boolean, datetime for each field Fields with json: - (like Password and DeletedAt) are excluded from the documentation entirely. This is important , your docs never expose sensitive fields. Generate a new resource with several fields: Restart your API and refresh /docs . Does the Product schema appear? Can you see which fields are marked as required vs optional? Many endpoints require authentication , they expect a JWT token in the request headers. When you try to call a protected endpoint without a token, you get a 401 Unauthorized error. The Scalar UI lets you set your authentication token so you can test protected endpoints directly. Here s the workflow: 1. Login via the docs. Find POST /api/auth/login , enter your email and password, click Send. Copy the access_token from the response. 2. Set the token. Look for the Authentication or Auth section in Scalar. Select Bearer Token and paste your access token. 3. Test protected endpoints. Now every request you send from the docs will include the Authorization: Bearer <token> header automatically. Login via /docs using POST /api/auth/login . Copy the access token from the response. Set it in the Scalar authentication section. Then call GET /api/users . Do you get a list of users? What happens if you remove the token and try again? The Scalar UI is a complete API testing tool. Let s walk through testing all five CRUD operations for a resource. Find the POST endpoint for your resource (e.g., POST /api/products ). The request builder shows the JSON body schema with all required fields. Fill in the values and click Send. A successful creation returns a 201 Created status with the new resource in the response body. The list endpoint supports pagination. Use query parameters ?page=1&page_size=10 to control which page of results you see. The response includes a me

headings: Build & Deploy a REST API with Go (API-Only Masterclass)
pages.text: Build a complete REST API from scratch using grit new myapi --api . No frontend, no admin panel , pure Go API. You ll scaffold, generate resources, test with API docs, add authentication and roles, and deploy to production. Reference docs: API-Only Architecture → Not every project needs a frontend. Sometimes you just need a clean, fast API that other services or apps consume. Grit s --api flag gives you exactly that , a lean Go API with no frontend overhead. When does API-only make sense? • Mobile app backend , your iOS/Android app needs an API, but the frontend is native code, not React • Microservice , one service in a larger architecture that handles a specific domain (payments, notifications, search) • Third-party integrations , building a public API that other developers consume (like Stripe or Twilio) • Separate frontend team , the frontend is built by a different team using their own stack (Vue, Svelte, Flutter) • Data pipeline , an API that ingests, transforms, and serves data with no user-facing UI Think of 3 real-world projects where API-only is the right choice. For each one, explain why a frontend would be built separately (or not at all). Example: a weather data service that mobile apps and websites consume. Let s build a task management API. One command gives you the full project: The --api flag tells Grit to skip the frontend entirely. No apps/web , no apps/admin , no turbo.json , no pnpm-workspace.yaml . What you get is a clean Go API project: Compare this to a triple project (the default): no apps/web , no apps/admin , no packages/shared . The API stands alone. Run grit new taskapi --api . Open the project in your editor. How many folders are inside apps/api/internal/ ? List them. Compare the folder count to what a grit new myapp (triple) project would create. Let s walk through each folder in the API and understand what it does: The pattern is simple: handlers receive HTTP requests, validate input, and call services . Services contain business logic, call the database through models , and return results. Handlers format the results as JSON responses. This separation keeps your code testable and organized. Open apps/api/internal/ . How many folders are there? List each one and write a one-sentence description of what it does. Which folder contains the most files? Starting an API-only project requires two steps: start the infrastructure services (database, Redis, etc.) and then start the Go API itself. You should see output like: Verify everything is working: Start the infrastructure and API. Verify the health check at localhost:8080/pulse/health . Are both database and Redis connected? Open GORM Studio at localhost:8080/studio , how many tables exist in the fresh database? This is where the code generator shines. Instead of manually creating models, handlers, services, and routes for each entity, you describe the resource and Grit generates everything. Let s generate two resources for our task API: For each resource, Grit generates: • Model , internal/model/task.go with GORM struct and field tags • Service , internal/service/task_service.go with CRUD operations + pagination + filtering • Handler , internal/handlers/task_handler.go with HTTP endpoints • Routes , injected into internal/router/router.go • Migration , auto-migrated by GORM on startup The field type syntax is name:type with optional modifiers: Generate both the Task and Category resources. Then run grit routes to see all registered API endpoints. How many new endpoints were created? List them. Restart the API and check GORM Studio , are the new tables there? Grit s auto-generated API docs at /docs are not just documentation , they re an interactive testing tool. You can send real requests, see real responses, and explore every endpoint without writing a single curl command. Let s create some test data through the API: Once you have data, test the list endpoint with pagination and filtering: Open /docs and create 3 categories (Work, Personal, Learning) and 10 tasks spread across them. Test pagination with ?page=1&page_size=5 , do you get 5 results on page 1 and 5 on page 2? Sort by priority descending. Does the highest priority appear first? Real APIs have relationships between resources. A Task belongs to a Category. An Order has many OrderItems. Grit handles relationships with the belongs_to field type. To add a relationship, regenerate the Task resource with a category_id field: The category_id:belongs_to:Category field tells Grit: • Add a category_id column (foreign key) to the tasks table • Add a Category field to the Task struct for preloading • Include the Category data when fetching Tasks (GORM Preload) Now when you create a task, you include the category_id : And when you fetch the task, the category data comes along: Regenerate the Task resource with the category_id:belongs_to:Category field. Create 3 categories and 5 tasks, each assigned to a category. Fetch a single task , does the response include the full category object? Fetch the task list , does every task show its category? Every Grit API ships with JWT authentication. Users register, log in, receive a token, and send that token with every request to access protected endpoints. The authentication flow: The Authorization header uses the Bearer scheme: the word Bearer followed by a space and then the token. This is the industry standard for JWT authentication. Using curl or the API docs: Register a user with your name and email Log in and copy the JWT token Call GET /api/tasks without a token , what error do you get? Call GET /api/tasks with the token , does it work? Try creating a task with the token , does it associate with your user? Authentication answers who are you? Authorization answers what can you do? Grit supports role-based access control (RBAC) with two built-in roles: USER and ADMIN . By default, all generated resource routes require authentication but allow any role. You can restrict routes to admin-only by adding the --roles flag

pages.text: Every Grit project records who did what , automatically. Each authenticated mutation is appended to a SHA-256 hash chain that makes the log tamper-evident: change one row in the database and the chain no longer verifies. This is the audit trail auditors actually trust. Reference docs: Security Guide → An audit log is an append-only record of meaningful changes in your system. Unlike application logs (which are for debugging), an audit log is for accountability , it answers "who created this invoice," "who deleted that user," and "when did the price change." In Grit, audit logging is automatic. A middleware records every authenticated mutating request (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) into an activity_logs table , no per-handler code required. Each log entry stores a hash computed from the entry's contents plus the previous entry's hash . That links every row to the one before it, like blocks in a blockchain. Recompute the chain and a single altered row invalidates every hash after it. The admin panel exposes the activity log with filters for user, action, and resource. Each row captures the actor, the HTTP method + path, the target resource, the timestamp, and the request's public IP. Log in to the admin panel and create, update, then delete a record. Open the Activity page. Do you see three new entries? What actor, action, and resource does each show? Verification re-walks the chain from the beginning, recomputing each hash and comparing it to what's stored. If every entry matches, the log is intact. If one doesn't, you get the exact entry where the chain broke. Open GORM Studio at localhost:8080/studio and edit a single field on an old activity_logs row. Now call /admin/activity/integrity . Does it report the tampering? Which entry id does it flag? Add a cron entry that hits the integrity endpoint every night. Where would you send an alert if it fails? Sketch the flow. Pick SOC 2, HIPAA, or PCI-DSS. Name one specific control the hash-chained audit log helps you satisfy, and explain why "tamper-evident" matters for it.
pages.title: Audit Log + Hash Chain

headings: Batteries Included: Every Feature That Ships with Grit
pages.text: Every Grit project ships with 17 production-ready features pre-configured and wired together. This course walks through every single one , what it is, why it matters, how it s configured, and how to use it. By the end, you ll know your project inside and out. Reference docs: Batteries → Most frameworks give you a foundation and tell you to install plugins for everything else. Need caching? Find a Redis library, wire it up, write middleware. Need email? Pick a service, install an SDK, build templates. Need file uploads? Choose between S3, Cloudflare, or local storage, configure presigned URLs, handle multipart forms. Every feature is a research project. Grit ships 17 features pre-configured and wired together in every project. They work on day one , no setup required. And because they re modular, you can remove any feature you don t need without breaking the others. Here s the full list of what ships with every Grit project: Look at the table above. Pick any 5 features and estimate how long it would take you to set up each one from scratch in a new Go project (finding the library, reading docs, writing code, testing). Add up the total hours. That s the Setup Tax Grit eliminates. Caching is one of the most impactful performance optimizations you can make. Instead of querying the database every time a user requests the same data, you store the result in memory and serve it instantly. Grit s cache service wraps Redis with a clean Go API. Grit s cache service exposes three methods , Set , Get , and Delete : On top of the service, Grit includes cache middleware that automatically caches GET responses. When a GET request comes in, the middleware checks Redis first. If the response is cached, it returns it instantly without hitting your handler. If not, it calls your handler, caches the response, and returns it. Open the file internal/service/cache_service.go in your Grit project. What methods does it expose? What parameters does Set accept? What does Get return when the key doesn t exist? Every real application needs file uploads , profile pictures, documents, images, attachments. Grit s file storage service works with any S3-compatible provider: MinIO for local development, AWS S3 for production, or Cloudflare R2 for edge storage. The upload flow in Grit works like this: Configuration uses environment variables: Start your Grit project with Docker Compose. Open the admin panel and upload a file (any image will do). Then open the MinIO Console at localhost:9003 . Can you find the file in the uploads bucket? What is the full path of the file? Transactional email is essential for any application , welcome emails, password resets, verification codes, notifications. Grit includes a complete email service powered by Resend with 4 pre-built HTML templates. Grit ships 4 HTML email templates: • Welcome , sent when a user registers • Password Reset , sent when a user requests a password reset • Email Verification , sent to verify a user s email address • Notification , a generic template for system notifications In development, emails are captured by Mailhog instead of being sent to real inboxes. This means you can test every email flow without configuring a real email provider. Start your Grit project. Open Mailhog at localhost:8025 . Now register a new user through the web app or API. Go back to Mailhog , do you see the welcome email? Open it and look at the HTML template. What information does it include? Some tasks are too slow or too resource-intensive to run inside an HTTP request. Sending an email takes 200-500ms. Processing an image takes 1-2 seconds. Generating a report takes 5-10 seconds. You don t want users waiting for these. Background jobs let you offload work to a separate process that runs asynchronously. Grit uses asynq , a Redis-backed job queue for Go. It ships with 3 built-in workers: • Email Worker , sends transactional emails asynchronously • Image Worker , processes uploaded images (resize, thumbnails) • Cleanup Worker , removes expired tokens, old sessions, temp files Dispatching a job is a single function call: The admin panel includes a Jobs dashboard where you can monitor queued, active, completed, and failed jobs in real time. Open the admin panel and navigate to the Jobs page. Are there any queued or completed jobs? Try registering a new user , the welcome email is sent as a background job. Go back to the Jobs page. Do you see the email job in the completed list? Background jobs handle one-off tasks. Cron jobs handle recurring tasks , things that need to happen on a schedule. Clean up expired tokens every hour. Send a weekly digest every Monday. Generate reports every night at midnight. Grit s cron scheduler uses the same worker pool as background jobs, so you don t need a separate process. Here s the cron expression format: Common examples: Write the cron expression for each schedule: Every hour on the hour Every day at midnight Every Monday at 9:00 AM Every 15 minutes The first of every month at 3:00 AM Check your answers against the table above. The last two are not in the table , you ll need to figure them out yourself. Every Grit project ships with AI integration powered by Vercel AI Gateway . One API key gives you access to hundreds of models from dozens of providers , Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, and more. No provider-specific code required. Grit exposes 3 AI endpoints: • POST /api/ai/complete , single prompt in, single response out • POST /api/ai/chat , multi-turn conversation with message history • POST /api/ai/stream , streaming response (tokens arrive in real-time) If you have an AI Gateway API key, add it to your .env file. Start the API, get a JWT token by logging in, then test the /api/ai/complete endpoint with a prompt of your choice. What model did the response come from? (Check the response headers or body for provider information.) Passwords alone are not enough. If someone steals a user s password (phishing, data breach, reuse), they can access the
