headings: What about setup that shouldn't count?
pages.text: Go's benchmarking is built in and small. Write a function whose name starts Benchmark , loop over b.N , run go test -bench=. . This lesson is that whole loop, end to end. Your project already has some: Grit scaffolds apps/api/internal/handlers/bench_test.go with benchmarks for the health check, login and registration, and perf_test.go beside it with allocation budgets. The example below is a pure function, because that is the simplest thing to measure and the easiest to get wrong. Three things to absorb: Name starts with Benchmark , Go test tool finds it. Takes *testing.B . Loops b.N times . Go decides b.N at runtime , it ramps until the benchmark runs long enough to be statistically meaningful (usually a second). Three flags worth knowing: -bench=BenchmarkXxx , which benchmarks to run. =. matches all. -benchmem , also report bytes/op and allocs/op. Use it every time. -count=3 , run each benchmark 3 times. You want this , single runs are noisy. Decode each column: BenchmarkPluralize-10 , the -10 is GOMAXPROCS (cores). Same number across runs means same machine. 5012461 , the b.N Go settled on. ~5 million iterations. 228.4 ns/op , average nanoseconds per operation. THIS is the headline metric. 64 B/op , bytes allocated per op. Lower = less GC pressure. 2 allocs/op , number of heap allocations per op. Lower = even less GC pressure. b.N changes between runs (or even between machines), so absolute total time is meaningless. What matters is the per-op average, which IS comparable across runs and machines (with caveats , see "noise" below). Compare different input shapes side by side. Often the revelation: "long words are 3x slower", "irregular words trigger a fallback path". b.ResetTimer() says "everything before this is setup; start measuring now". Critical for benchmarks where the setup is expensive. Output shows each as its own line: One file, comprehensive coverage of the function's input space. The Go convention for serious benchmarking. Write your first three benchmarks: Pick a function in your service layer. Anything pure and side-effect-free is easiest (a parser, a formatter). Add func BenchmarkX(b *testing.B) { for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { X() } } to the test file. Run with go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=3 ./your/pkg/ . Make a 3-input table-driven version (sub-benchmarks). Paste the output in notes.md . Circle the most interesting line , the one that's slower than you expected. You should have 3 working benchmarks and a feel for the output. Next lesson: how to read ns/op, B/op, allocs/op for what they really tell you about your code. Next lesson , Reading the output . The numbers tell a story. After this lesson you'll be fluent enough to spot "there's a hidden allocation" or "this function is O(n²) and we didn't notice".
pages.title: The shape of a benchmark

headings: What ns/op alone can't tell you
pages.text: You wrote a benchmark and got numbers. Now make them mean something. This lesson is fluency with ns/op , B/op , and allocs/op , what each tells you, when each matters, and what red flags to look for. Nanoseconds per operation. The number you optimise for, most of the time. Under 100ns , fast. Probably a pure function with no syscalls. 100ns - 1µs (1000ns) , typical for string ops, simple JSON marshal, small loops. 1µs - 100µs , non-trivial work. Allocation, regex, complex parsing. 100µs - 1ms , usually some I/O or a big loop. If you didn't expect this, investigate. 1ms+ , likely the wrong target for microbenchmarking. Profile the broader system instead. How many bytes of heap memory the operation allocates per iteration. 0 B/op , zero allocations. Often achievable for pure ops with stack-only data. The dream for hot paths. 16-64 B/op , typical for ops that build a small string, return a struct on the heap, or take a slice. 1KB+ /op , large; either you copied data or allocated a buffer. Usually a flag for optimisation. Sometimes more important than bytes. Each allocation: Costs CPU to satisfy. Increases the work the GC has to do later. Causes a tiny pause when the GC runs. For libraries used a million times per second (logging, request routing), driving allocs/op to 0 or 1 is a common target. Two red flags worth noting: BenchmarkZodType at 1.3µs with 8 allocs. Likely building intermediate strings. strings.Builder would drop both numbers. BenchmarkInjectBefore at 2.4µs with 12 allocs. 12 allocations PER OP is a lot , almost certainly a string search-and-replace with many intermediate values. A scanner or single buffer would help. Same logical work, ~3x faster + 6x fewer allocations. The benchmark numbers told you exactly where the inefficiency was. Noise. Your laptop is doing something else under load (browser, Spotlight, antivirus). Don't trust these numbers. Fix by: Closing background apps. Running on a quiet machine (CI, dedicated box). Using -count=10 + benchstat (chapter 3). Avoiding battery / thermal throttling. Benchmarks measure ONE thing in isolation. They don't tell you: How often this function is called. A 5µs function called 10× a day is fine. A 50ns function called a million times per request matters. What the rest of the system is doing while it runs. Lock contention, GC pauses, network jitter all dwarf microbenchmark differences. Real-world data shapes. Your benchmark hits one input; production hits a distribution. Profiling (next chapter) helps with the "how often" question. Load testing (the K6 course) helps with the "real world" question. Use the right tool for the right question. Interpret real numbers: Take the benchmarks you wrote last lesson. Look at each B/op number. Find the benchmark with the highest allocs/op . Read the source. Make ONE hypothesis about why it allocates that much. Try one quick change (use strings.Builder , pre-allocate a slice with make([]T, 0, cap) , or avoid an intermediate string). Re-run. Did the numbers move? Write down: how much, in which direction, and your guess at why. Paste before / after in notes.md. You should have moved at least one number. The important part is the DISCIPLINE: hypothesis → measurement → conclusion. Most performance work is vibes; you're doing it the legit way. Chapter 2 , Profiling with pprof . Benchmarks tell you ONE function's cost; pprof tells you where a whole program spends its time. The CPU + heap flame graph is the highest-bandwidth tool in Go.
pages.title: ns/op , the headline

headings: Why CI does not do this
pages.text: Run the same benchmark twice and you get two different numbers. Run it before and after a change and you get two different numbers, which may or may not be about the change. benchstat is the tool that tells the difference, and it is the one thing standing between performance work and a vibe. -count=10 is the point of the exercise. One run gives benchstat nothing to work with: with a single sample there is no spread, so there is no way to say whether a difference is larger than the noise. Ten is the usual minimum, and more for a benchmark that is naturally variable. ± 3% is the spread across the ten runs. A large spread means the measurement is unstable, and the first thing to fix is the measurement. p=0.000 is the probability of seeing this difference if the change did nothing. Below 0.05 it is reported; above it, benchstat prints ~ . n=10 is how many samples survived. If benchstat discarded some as outliers it says so, and that is worth reading. A ~ in the vs base column means "no difference was detected". It does not mean the change is free and it does not mean it helped by a small amount. It means this experiment cannot tell, and the honest responses are more samples or a revert, not a sentence in the pull request saying it is slightly faster. A ± of 15% makes any change under 15% unmeasurable, so it is worth spending a minute on: Two benchmarks in the same package also interfere: one leaves the caches warm and the allocator in a different state for the next. Use -bench with an exact name when the number matters. Grit's scaffolded ci.yml runs the benchmarks with -benchtime 1x and asserts nothing about their timing, with a comment saying why: timing a shared CI runner tells you about the runner. What CI asserts instead is the allocation budgets, which do not move with the machine. Timing comparisons belong on a machine you control, run deliberately, with the result written down. One. Run a benchmark with -count=10 twice, changing nothing, into a.txt and b.txt . Run benchstat a.txt b.txt . Two. Note the ± figure and whether benchstat reports a difference between two identical versions. Three. Repeat with a browser and a dev server running. Compare the ± figures. Step two should print ~ . If it reports a significant difference between two runs of identical code, your measurement environment is the thing you are measuring. Step one is a calibration: it tells you what "no change" looks like on your machine, so you can recognise it later. Step three usually doubles or triples the ±, and that is the argument for closing things. A noisy machine does not add noise evenly, it adds occasional very slow iterations, which is also why benchstat works on the distribution rather than the mean.
pages.title: Install it, then use counts

headings: Pick the thing that is worth it
Then write it down, and move the budget
pages.text: Everything in this course has been instruments. This lesson is the whole loop once, end to end, on one real change, with the parts people skip left in. Two questions before any measurement, and they rule out most candidates: In a Grit API the per request hot path is the place to look, because everything there is multiplied by your whole traffic. That is the argument internal/handlers/perf_test.go makes for the paths it budgets: token verification, parameter binding, the list envelope. Step three is one change. Two at once gives one number and no attribution, and the usual outcome is that both get kept: the one that helped and the one that quietly cost something. Baseline 14790 ns/op, 11390 B/op, 36 allocs/op . The alloc_space profile points at the slice the handler builds, grown one row at a time: A one line change, and the kind that is worth the ceremony only because the loop runs on every list request in the application. Lowering the budget in the same commit is the part that makes the work stick. Left at 36, the next change can put fourteen allocations back and nothing will say so. If a change raises a budget, that can be correct: a feature costs what it costs. Raise it in the same commit, with the reason in the comment, so the next person sees the new number was a decision and not a drift. The change is within the noise floor. Revert it. An unmeasurable gain is a maintenance cost with no benefit. The code got significantly harder to read. A 3% win for an unreadable function is a bad trade, and most of the time somebody undoes it later without knowing why it was there. You are optimising something that is not the bottleneck. A function at 2% of the time cannot give you more than 2%. The real fix is elsewhere. Shaving allocations off a handler that issues 21 queries per request is polishing the wrong surface. Fix the N+1 first. One. Run the whole loop above on one function in your own project, start to finish, including the two baseline runs. Two. Write the notes entry: before, change, after, p value, and kept or reverted. Three. If you kept it and the function has a budget in perf_test.go , lower it and confirm the test still passes. If the change is not significant, write the entry anyway and revert. A recorded null result is worth more than an unrecorded win, because it stops the next person repeating it. The deliverable is the notes entry, not the speedup. A change with a number, a p value and a date can be defended, reproduced and reversed. A change without one is a thing in the codebase that nobody can evaluate. With the budget lowered, the improvement is defended by CI: the allocation test fails if it comes back. That is the difference between making something faster once and keeping it fast.
pages.title: Pick the thing that is worth it

headings: What a CPU profile cannot see
pages.text: A benchmark says a function takes 14790 nanoseconds. A CPU profile says which of the fifty functions it calls spent them. You need both, and you need them in that order: profiling without a benchmark gives you a profile of whatever the process happened to be doing. -benchtime 5s matters more than it looks. A profile is a sample taken roughly a hundred times a second, so a benchmark that runs for 200 milliseconds gives you about twenty samples and a graph made of noise. Five seconds is five hundred, which is enough for the shape to be real. -run XXX is there to match no test. Without it you profile the test suite as well as the benchmark, and the test suite is usually the larger half. flat is time inside that function itself. cum is time inside it and everything it called. The handler has 92% cumulative and 2% flat, which is exactly what you expect: it is a handler, it does nothing but call things. Sort by flat to find the work, and read cum to find which path led there. A function with high cum and low flat is a signpost, not a destination. In the web view, the Flame Graph is the fastest way in, and Source is the most convincing: it shows per-line timings in your own code, which usually ends an argument about whether a loop is the problem. A benchmark profiles one function. Sometimes the question is what the whole API is doing under load, and for that Pulse serves standard pprof: This is off by default, and it takes two switches rather than one: PULSE_PROFILING=true in .env , and PULSE_PROFILE_ENABLED=true in the environment. A profile leaks the shape of your code, so one forgotten setting is not enough to expose it. It samples goroutines that are running . A request that spends 900 milliseconds waiting for a database, a lock or an HTTP call appears nowhere, because nothing was on CPU. This is the single most common way a profile misleads: a handler that is slow for waiting reasons looks cheap. One. Profile BenchmarkListEnvelope for five seconds and open it. Note the top three functions by flat time. Two. Run the same benchmark with -benchtime 100ms and profile that. Compare the top three. Three. Add time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond) inside the function, re-run the five second profile, and find the sleep. For step three, look at the wall clock the benchmark reports first, and then try to find those milliseconds in the profile. Step two usually disagrees with step one, sometimes completely. That is the lesson: a short profile is not a smaller version of a long one, it is a different and mostly fictional picture. In step three the benchmark's ns/op jumps by ten million and the sleep is not in the profile at all . A sleeping goroutine is not running, so it is never sampled. Every kind of waiting looks like this, which is why the question "is CPU actually high?" comes before opening a profiler.
pages.title: From a benchmark

headings: Start with the numbers you already have
pages.text: Most Go performance work is allocation work. The collector is fast, but it is not free, and the cheapest way to spend less time in it is to give it less to do. A heap profile says where the allocations come from. alloc_space is everything allocated over the run, including what was freed immediately. This is the one for garbage pressure: a function allocating a megabyte per request and freeing it still costs you collector time. inuse_space is what is still reachable at the sample. This is the one for leaks: memory that should have gone and did not. Picking the wrong one is the usual mistake. Hunting a leak in alloc_space shows you your busiest function, which is almost never the leak. -benchmem is free and often enough. From a scaffolded Grit API: Note that verifying a token allocates more times than building a list envelope while allocating a third of the bytes. Count and size are different costs: many small allocations are mostly collector bookkeeping, one large one is mostly the copy. The profile tells you which you have. Grit scaffolds internal/handlers/perf_test.go , and the reasoning in it is worth more than the numbers: That is why the budgets exist and the timings do not get asserted. CI runs the benchmarks with -benchtime 1x , purely to prove they still compile and run, and the allocation budgets are the part that can actually fail. Allocation counts move with the Go toolchain, by more than you would guess. Token verification allocates 56 times under go1.26.9 and 41 under go1.27.2: the same code, a newer runtime. So a budget is set from the oldest toolchain the project supports, because that is the one that allocates most. Set from whatever is on your laptop, a budget passes locally and fails in CI. Growing a slice in a loop. Each growth copies. make([]T, 0, n) when you know n turns many allocations into one. String concatenation in a loop. Every += allocates a new string. strings.Builder does not. interface{} and any . Putting a value in an interface usually heap allocates it. A response built as map[string]any allocates once per value. Taking the address of a local. If a pointer escapes the function, the value moves to the heap. go build -gcflags=-m prints every such decision. -diff_base is the most useful flag in pprof and the least used. Two captures, one graph, showing only what moved between them. One. Run the handler benchmarks with -benchmem and write down allocs/op for each. Two. Take a memory profile of the one with the most allocations and find the top three sources by alloc_space. Three. Change one of them: preallocate a slice, or swap a concatenation for a strings.Builder . Re-run and compare allocs/op. In step three, watch ns/op as well. Fewer allocations usually means less time, and when it does not, that is a result worth keeping too. A preallocated slice typically removes several allocations and a proportional slice of the time. If allocs/op falls and ns/op does not, the allocations were not the bottleneck in that function, which is a real finding and the reason to measure rather than assume. Whatever the result, if the function has an entry in perf_test.go , lower its budget in the same commit. A budget left at the old number is a regression nobody will catch.
pages.title: Two different questions

headings: CI/CD with GitHub Actions: Automated Testing & Deployment
pages.text: Set up automated testing and deployment for your Grit projects. You ll understand the CI/CD workflows Grit scaffolds, extend them with frontend tests, configure automated deployments, and set up branch protection for a professional development workflow. Reference docs: Deployment → Without CI/CD, shipping code looks like this: you write code, run tests manually (maybe), build the project, SSH into a server, pull the code, restart services, and pray nothing breaks. With CI/CD, you push code and everything else happens automatically. A typical CI/CD pipeline: 1. Developer pushes code to GitHub 2. CI runs Go tests ( go test -race ./... ) 3. CI runs frontend tests ( pnpm test ) 4. If all tests pass, CD deploys to staging 5. On tag push (v1.0.0), CD deploys to production Explain CI/CD in your own words. Why is it important? What happens when a team doesn t use CI/CD? Think about: how bugs reach production, how long deployments take, and how confident developers feel pushing code on a Friday afternoon. When you run grit new , it scaffolds a .github/workflows/ci.yml file. This is a complete CI workflow that runs automatically on every push and pull request. This workflow does 3 things: • Checks out your code , downloads the repo to the runner • Sets up Go , installs the specified Go version • Runs tests , executes all Go tests with race detection enabled Find the .github/workflows/ directory in your Grit project. What workflow files exist? Open ci.yml and read through it. What triggers the workflow? What Go version does it use? YAML workflows can look intimidating. Let s break down every section so you can read and write them confidently. Key concepts: • Jobs run in parallel by default , unless you use needs to create dependencies • Steps run sequentially within a job , if one fails, the rest are skipped • Each job gets a fresh VM , nothing persists between jobs unless you use artifacts • Actions are reusable , actions/checkout@v4 is maintained by GitHub Read your ci.yml file carefully. Answer these questions: (1) What Go version does it use? (2) What test flags are set? (3) What events trigger it? (4) What operating system does the runner use? (5) How many jobs are defined? The scaffolded CI only tests the Go API. For a complete pipeline, add a separate job that tests the frontend , Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for end-to-end tests. This job runs in parallel with the Go test job. Both must pass for the overall CI to be green. If either fails, the PR gets a red X. For end-to-end tests with Playwright, you need a running API. Use a service container: Add a test-frontend job to your CI workflow. It should set up Node.js 20, install pnpm, install dependencies, and run pnpm test . Push the change and check the Actions tab , do both jobs run? Grit also scaffolds a release.yml workflow. Unlike CI (which runs on every push), the release workflow only triggers when you push a version tag like v1.0.0 . It builds cross-platform binaries and creates a GitHub Release with downloadable files. To create a release: Open release.yml and answer: (1) What event triggers it? (2) What platforms does it build for? (3) How would you create a release? Write the git commands you d run to release version 1.0.0. The most powerful CI/CD feature: automatic deployment. After tests pass, the deploy job ships your code to production. No SSH, no manual steps, no forgetting to restart the service. Key parts of the deploy job: • needs: [test] , only runs after tests pass • if: github.ref == refs/heads/main , only deploys from the main branch (not PRs or feature branches) • Secrets store sensitive values like server addresses and SSH keys What secrets would you need for automated deployment? List them all. Think about: server address, domain name, SSH credentials, database connection, and any API keys your app needs in production. CI is only useful if you enforce it. Branch protection rules prevent merging code that fails CI. No green checkmark, no merge , period. To set up branch protection: 1. Go to Repository Settings 2. Click Branches in the sidebar 3. Add a branch protection rule for main 4. Enable Require status checks to pass before merging 5. Select the CI jobs (test, test-frontend) as required checks 6. Optionally require pull request reviews With this setup, the development workflow becomes: Set up branch protection on your main branch. Require the CI test job to pass before merging. Create a feature branch, make a change, push it, and open a PR. Does CI run? Can you merge before CI passes? Production apps need a staging environment , a copy of production where you test changes before they go live. Different branches deploy to different environments: The branching strategy: • Feature branches , where you write code. CI runs tests. • staging branch , merge features here first. Auto-deploys to staging.myapp.com for testing. • main branch , merge from staging when ready. Auto-deploys to myapp.com (production). Design a branching strategy for your project. Which branch deploys where? How does code flow from feature to staging to production? Draw the flow: feature branch, then PR to staging, then test, then PR to main, then production deploy. When CI fails at 2 AM, you want to know. When a deployment succeeds, the team should celebrate. Notifications close the feedback loop , the pipeline tells you what happened. Common notification patterns: • Test failure , urgent notification to Slack/Discord with the failing branch and commit • Successful deploy , info notification: v1.2.0 deployed to production • New release , announcement: Release v1.2.0 published with 5 new features • Deploy failure , critical alert: Production deploy failed , rollback may be needed What notifications would you want for these events? (1) Test failure on a PR, (2) Successful deploy to staging, (3) Successful deploy to production, (4) New GitHub Release created. For each, specify: who should be notified, how (Slack, email, Discord), and what the m
pages.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions: Automated Testing & Deployment

pages.text: You've seen every mode. Now the framework for picking , a decision tree you can run any new idea through and land on the right command without memorizing the table. Default to triple. When in doubt, use --triple . You can ignore the admin app if you don't need it today, and it's already wired when you do. Skip the admin only when you're sure. Most products eventually need one , support staff, ops, finance. Pre-wiring it beats retrofitting. Mobile + desktop are surfaces, not modes. Add --mobile or --desktop to triple if you need both. Don't treat them as exclusive picks. Don't want to memorize the tree? Use the Stack Selector on the docs site. Answer 4 questions, get the exact command. Same logic as the decision tree above, in a UI. The chapter assignment is waiting , "Pick the right kit for three ideas." Open it from the sidebar and tackle it now. Pick three real product ideas (yours, your friend's, anything from HN), trace each through the decision tree, and write one paragraph justifying your pick. The trick: try to pick three DIFFERENT modes. That forces you to find ideas that genuinely justify different shapes. No solution here , the assignment page on the sidebar evaluates your three picks. Common pitfalls: Picking triple for everything (over-engineering) Picking single for something that needs an admin (under-engineering) Picking desktop for a product that doesn't need offline (over-spec) If your three are genuinely different shapes, you've internalised the kit choices. That's the goal. Five chapters, ~20 lessons, five assignments. You can now: Explain what Grit is in 30 seconds Install + verify the CLI and keep it updated Scaffold a project, navigate every folder, run the dev servers Recognise the naming conventions and API response shapes Generate a resource end-to-end and keep types in sync Pick the right architecture mode for any product idea Next, pick one of the specialist courses based on the kit you want to dive deeper into: Building a Go API , Web with Next.js , Mobile , or Desktop . All assume the foundation you just finished.
pages.title: The decision tree

pages.text: Single mode is the smallest possible Grit deploy: one Go binary with the React frontend embedded inside it. No separate frontend server, no reverse proxy juggling , drop the binary on a VPS and run it. You get ONE directory (not apps/ ). The Go code lives at the root; the React app lives in frontend/ and gets compiled into the Go binary at build time via go:embed . One file deploy. scp myapp user@host: + ./myapp on the box. Done. No CORS. The frontend is served by the same Go process as the API , same origin, no preflight requests. No reverse proxy required. Optional, of course , Caddy / Traefik for TLS , but not architecturally needed. Smallest infra surface. Postgres + one binary. That's it. Solo / indie products Internal tools deployed to a single VPS Self-hosted apps you ship to customers (one binary they can run) MVPs you want to iterate on without infra complexity You need a separate admin panel for non-engineers (no admin surface in single mode by default , use triple) The web and the API will be deployed independently (different regions, different scaling) You're scaling to multiple frontend regions but one backend In notes.md , list three real apps you'd ship as single mode. For each, write one sentence on why single beats triple for that case. Examples: A LAN-only POS for a coffee shop , single binary on their router box, no separate admin needed. A personal Read-It-Later clone , solo project, you're the only user, no admin needed. A self-hosted feature-flag service for a small team , one binary on a tiny VPS. Single is the smallest. Next is its opposite , triple : the kitchen-sink SaaS shape with web + admin + API.
pages.title: The shape

pages.text: Three modes for when you want one slice instead of the full triple: API-only, Mobile, and Desktop. Each has its own course in the Learning Paths section. Pure Gin + GORM Go backend. No frontend. Auto-served OpenAPI docs at /docs . Ships every battery (auth, jobs, mail, storage, AI, Sentinel + Pulse) , just no UI. When to use: Backend for a mobile-only product (bring your own iOS / Android client) Backend for a Discord / Slack / Telegram bot Backend for a native desktop app you're building separately Microservice in a larger system (a Grit project consumed by other services) A monorepo with apps/api (Go) and apps/mobile (Expo). Shared types via grit sync . Mobile-friendly auth (refresh tokens in SecureStore), EAS Build configured, push-notification scaffolding. When to use: Mobile-first product where the web is secondary or absent Field-service apps (drivers, technicians, sales reps) Consumer apps for iOS + Android Standalone Wails v2 app , Go bound to React via Wails. Local SQLite (offline-first), local auth, in-app auto-updater, NSIS installers (full + slim), branded MUI. Different command ( new-desktop instead of new ) because it's structurally different from the rest. When to use: POS systems / kiosks that need to work offline Field service tools that go to areas with no internet Single-user apps where the data should stay on the user's machine Tools that need access to OS-level features (filesystem, native dialogs) For each of these ideas, write down the right command in notes.md : Open-source feature-flag service (one binary, web UI to toggle flags, no admin staff) Restaurant POS that runs on a tablet without internet Discord bot that watches GitHub repos for new issues Fitness tracker with iPhone + Android app grit new flagd --single , one binary, no staff/admin, web UI embedded. grit new-desktop restaurant-pos , Wails, local SQLite, offline-first. grit new gh-watcher --api , no UI, just a backend the bot calls. grit new fitness-app --mobile , Expo mobile + Go API. Final lesson , a decision tree to pick the right kit for any idea without having to memorize the table. After that, the chapter assignment is "match 3 of your own product ideas to the right kits."
pages.title: API-only

pages.text: Triple is the SaaS shape , three apps in one monorepo. It's the most common mode you'll use, the one this course's scaffolded project is built in, and the recommended starting point for almost every multi-tenant product. web , your customers. Marketing pages + the logged-in dashboard. admin , your staff. Sales sees customers, support edits orders, ops triggers refunds. api , both of the above + future mobile + desktop. One backend, multiple surfaces. Separate domains, separate concerns: Different auth scopes. Customers can't log into the admin panel; staff doesn't need to sign up for customer accounts. Different SEO needs. The public site is marketing-optimized; the admin is behind auth, no SEO. Different shipping cadence. Marketing changes weekly; admin features change on a different rhythm. Different attack surface. Admin can sit behind a VPN or IP allow-list; the public site can't. One thing matters most: packages/shared . Both Next.js apps import @workspace/shared and they always agree on schemas + types. No drift. You can ship triple in two ways: All three on one box with a reverse proxy (Traefik) routing web.example.com → apps/web, admin.example.com → apps/admin, api.example.com → apps/api. Simplest for small teams. Apps deployed independently. apps/web on Vercel, apps/admin on a private box, apps/api on a VPS. Most flexible. Look at your scaffolded triple project. Pick one feature (signup, login, the admin's users page) and trace it across all three apps. In notes.md , list: Where in apps/web is the UI? Where in apps/admin is the matching admin view? Where in apps/api is the handler + service? Where in packages/shared is the Zod schema? For signup: apps/web/app/(auth)/signup/page.tsx apps/admin/app/resources/users/page.tsx (admin lists users) apps/api/internal/handlers/auth.go + internal/services/auth.go packages/shared/src/schemas/user.ts (SignupSchema) Four files, three apps, one Zod schema validating signup in all of them. That's the triple mode flow. Single and triple cover the two extremes. Next we cover the three specialized modes , API-only, Mobile, Desktop , for when you want one slice instead of the full triple.
pages.title: The three apps

pages.text: Last battery: AI. Grit ships a unified client for Claude (Anthropic) and OpenAI , same interface, swap with one env var. Streaming chat, embeddings, structured output, all behind a small Go service. Provider switching , one SDK per provider gets you locked in. A common interface lets you A/B Claude vs. GPT vs. Llama-on-OpenRouter without rewriting features. Streaming , both APIs use SSE differently. The wrapper normalises so your handler always emits the same shape to the frontend. Cost tracking , every call logs tokens in, tokens out, cost (rate × tokens). Admin dashboard shows weekly spend. The unified interface Three operations: blocking chat, streaming chat, embeddings. Same shape regardless of provider. Pick which provider via: Notice: each chunk gets flushed immediately. The frontend reads the SSE stream and appends each delta to the UI as it arrives , that's the "typing" effect users expect from a modern AI app. Browser-native streaming. No special SDK. Works on every modern browser; works in React Native via the same fetch + reader pattern. Embeddings enable "find me docs that MEAN this", not just "match these words". The vector is dense , far better than keyword search for question-answering, support bots, and recommendations. Admin page /admin/system/ai shows: Today / week / month spend by model. Top users by token consumption. Average cost per request. When the bill arrives at end of month, you can correlate it to product usage. Without this, AI costs are a mystery. Add a new provider (Llama via OpenRouter, Mistral, Gemini) , implement the Provider interface in a new file. Wire it in New() . Done. Change the default model , edit the handler's Model: string. Or pull from config so it's env-driven. Add prompt logging , for debugging or audit trail. Store the user's prompt + the assistant's reply in a table. Be aware of privacy implications; redact PII if your domain demands it. Per-user budget , sum usage.cost_cents for the user this month. Reject if over. No mock; you need real keys for local dev. Use the cheapest model in dev ( claude-haiku-4-5 or gpt-4o-mini ) so accidental loops don't burn money. Switch to the big model only when shipping. Build a real AI feature: Add an endpoint: POST /api/notes/:id/summarise that loads a Note from the DB and asks the AI to summarise the body into 2 sentences. Save the summary to a new field note.summary string . Render the summary in the notes list. Try with both providers. Set AI_PROVIDER=openai , restart, hit the endpoint again. Same code path, different model. Confirm token + cost logging in the usage table. You should have a working AI feature you can swap models for, and cost data per call. That's the foundation for any AI-powered SaaS feature: drafting copy, summarising threads, generating images, code review bots. Five batteries: Cache, Storage, Mail, Jobs, AI. You know what each does, where the code lives, how to call it from a service, and how to modify it. That's the entire surface of the Grit batteries-included offering. Chapter 7 , Architecture Modes . With all the Grit fundamentals in place, the last orientation chapter: which architecture mode (kit) is right for which kind of product.
pages.title: Why we need a wrapper

headings: How you call it from a service
Idempotency keys , the safety net for retries
Retry backoff , what actually happens on failure
pages.text: Some work shouldn't happen inside a request: sending emails, resizing images, generating PDFs, syncing third-party data. Background jobs handle it asynchronously , your handler enqueues, returns instantly, a worker processes later. Grit ships asynq as the job engine. Three reasons to push work to a job: Speed up requests. Sending email = 200ms; the user shouldn't wait. Enqueue, return in 5ms. Retries on failure. External API hiccupped? The job retries automatically with backoff. The handler would have just 500'd. Scheduled work. Cron-like , nightly digest, hourly cleanup, weekly report. Without a job system, you spawn a cron container that's hard to monitor. The API enqueues; the worker dequeues. They're separate Go processes. Both connect to Redis. You can scale workers independently , 10x more worker pods if your queue grows without touching the API. How it's implemented Two operations: enqueue now, enqueue in delay (great for "send reminder in 24h"). Each task name maps to a handler function. Return nil for success; return an error to trigger retry. asynq re-runs the job up to N times with exponential backoff, then dead-letters it. Run this as a separate process: go run cmd/worker/main.go in dev, or a separate deploy unit in prod. Two processes, one DB, one Redis. Standard cron syntax. The scheduler runs as part of the worker; it enqueues the task at the right time, the same workers process it. Grit's admin panel at /admin/system/jobs shows: Queue depth per queue (active, pending, retry, dead). Recent runs with status + duration. Failed jobs , click to inspect payload + error, re-queue. Throughput chart (jobs/min). When something's wrong, this is the first place to look. Receipt: now. Inventory update: now. Review request: in 7 days. Customer's checkout response still returns in 50ms , and none of these jobs fire twice for the same order. Retries cause duplicates. The most common production incident: a payment job fires, the worker crashes mid-flight, the next worker picks it up and charges the customer twice. Idempotency keys fix this at the queue level. Pass an IdempotencyKey in EnqueueOption and the queue refuses to enqueue a second task with the same key during the window (default 24h). The first call wins; the second silently returns success (the operation is already on its way, which is what the caller wanted). The key should be a natural business identifier for the action , not the payload, not a timestamp, not random bytes: "receipt:" + order.ID , one receipt per order. "welcome:" + user.ID , one welcome email per user. "charge:" + invoice.ID , one charge per invoice. "digest:" + user.ID + ":" + today , one digest per user per day. Return an error from a job handler and asynq re-runs it with exponential backoff. Grit's explicit schedule (set via ExponentialBackoff in workers.go ): The total budget at default settings is ~16 minutes , long enough to ride out a typical downstream outage, short enough that the dead queue doesn't fill with hours-old work. Tune MaxRetries per-task when the failure mode warrants it (e.g., a webhook delivery to a flaky third party might want MaxRetries: 25 ). Add a new task , register the handler in handlers.go , enqueue it from a service. That's it. Add a queue priority , edit the Queues map in server.go . Higher weight = more worker attention. Increase concurrency , bump Concurrency: 10 to 50. Watch DB connection pool , if you exhaust it, raise the pool too. Change retry policy , pass asynq.MaxRetry(3) at enqueue, or set a default in the server config. Wire your first custom job: Define a task: "send_birthday_email" that takes a user_id payload. Register the handler , it loads the user, sends an email via the mail service. Enqueue it from a test endpoint POST /api/dev/send-birthday/:user_id . Boot the worker: go run cmd/worker/main.go in a second terminal. Hit the endpoint. Watch the worker logs , should see the job processed. Mailhog should show the email. Bonus: make the handler return an error on purpose once. Confirm it retries (asynq logs retry attempts). You should have an end-to-end job flow: enqueue → Redis → worker → email. The admin page should show the job; re-queueing a failed one should work. This pattern unlocks every "don't block the request" feature you'll ever build. Last battery , AI (Claude + OpenAI) . Streaming chat, embeddings, and how Grit lets you swap providers without touching feature code.
pages.title: Why we need it

headings: Where the batteries live in the code
The admin dashboard for each battery
What this chapter covers, in order
pages.text: Grit ships with five "batteries" , pre-wired services that solve real production problems. Cache, file storage, email, background jobs, AI. You don't have to choose, install, or configure them from scratch , they're there, ready, in the right shape. This chapter walks through each one in turn. A battery is an included service that: Is enabled in docker-compose.yml for local dev. Has a Go client / service initialized in main.go . Is exposed to your code via a clean interface (e.g., s.cache.Get(key) , s.mail.Send(to, ...) ). Has an admin page in the dashboard so non-devs can poke at it (Jobs dashboard, Mail preview, etc.). Without batteries, the "day-1" experience of a new API looks like this: Pick a Redis client library (3 choices, vibes-based decision). Wire connection pool, retry, env config. Decide on cache key naming convention. Wrap GET/SET in a service so you can test it. ... and you haven't written any product code yet. Multiply that by five (S3, mail, jobs, AI). Grit makes the decisions for you , opinionated, but the opinions are defensible. You can replace any battery later, but you don't have to choose to get started. Same shape: one package per battery, exposing a thin Go interface. Tests can swap in a fake; production wires the real thing. When you run grit new , the CLI asks which batteries you want. You can include everything (default for triple kit) or skip some for a minimal API. You can also add a battery later by running grit add battery <name> . Every battery gets a page in the admin panel under /admin/system : Jobs , live queue depth, running jobs, retry attempts, failed jobs you can re-queue. Mail Preview , render templates with sample data without sending. Files , browse + delete uploads. Cron , see scheduled jobs, last/next run. AI , usage stats, token spend. Redis cache , speed up reads, throttle, store ephemeral state. S3 storage , uploads, signed URLs, image processing. Mail (Resend) , transactional + marketing email with editable templates. Jobs (asynq) , background work, retries, cron. AI (Claude + OpenAI) , chat, embeddings, provider swap. Each lesson follows the same template: what it does, how it's implemented, where the file lives, how to modify it, and a small exercise. Next lesson , Redis cache . Speed up reads, cache list endpoints, throttle expensive calls. The most common production performance win.
pages.title: What is a "battery"?

headings: How you call it from a service
pages.text: Every product sends email: welcome, password reset, receipt, notification. Grit's mail battery wraps Resend with editable HTML templates and a preview page in the admin panel. Type-safe, testable, swappable. Three reasons SMTP is a bad direct dependency: Deliverability , random SMTP servers land in spam. Resend, SendGrid, Postmark handle SPF/DKIM/DMARC for you. Templates , building HTML email from string concat is suffering. Templates separate copy from code. Preview + test , Mailhog locally, --preview mode in admin, no accidental sends to real customers. How it's implemented Notice: templates are parsed ONCE at startup. Calling Send is fast , just execute the pre-parsed template and hand off to Resend. Go's standard html/template , auto-escapes every variable to prevent XSS. {{.Name}} injects safely; an attacker who controls Name can't inject HTML. Critical: email is async . The user gets their token in 50ms; the email goes through a background job. If Resend is slow or down, the user's registration still succeeds. Grit's admin panel includes /admin/system/mail , a page that renders every template with sample data so you can iterate copy / styles without sending. Add a new template, it shows up automatically; edit copy, refresh, see the result. Implementation: a Go endpoint reads template files, executes them with seed data, returns the HTML. The admin page embeds it in an iframe. For local dev, Grit defaults to Mailhog , an in-memory SMTP server with a web UI at localhost:8025 . Sending an email shows it in the Mailhog inbox; nothing leaves your machine. When RESEND_API_KEY is empty, the mail service routes through Mailhog automatically. Set the key for staging to test real deliverability. Add a new template , drop an HTML file in mail/templates/ . It's auto-loaded on startup. Reference it by filename in Send(ctx, to, "new_template.html", ...) . Swap Resend for Postmark / SES , implement the same Send method. The service interface is tiny , one function. Add Markdown templates , parse .md + Go template, render through Markdown lib, send as HTML. Useful for content-heavy emails. Per-user opt-out , add an email_opt_out field on User. Check it in the service before calling client.Send . Transactional (welcome, receipt, password reset) is what we just covered. Marketing (newsletter, drip, broadcast) is a different beast: Higher volume , needs batching. List management , segments, opt-ins. Open / click tracking , pixel + tracked links. Grit's admin panel has a marketing email module that uses the same Resend backbone but adds list management. Out of scope for this lesson; covered in the SaaS-with-AI course. Send your first email through Grit: Sign up for a Resend account (free tier). Set RESEND_API_KEY in your .env . For dev, use Resend's test-mode key , it doesn't actually deliver. Trigger registration on your local API. Watch the Jobs admin page , you should see send_welcome appear and complete. Check the Resend dashboard for the test email. Now create a NEW template , "Account suspended" or "Password changed" , and call it from a handler. You should have a working welcome email landing in Resend for every registration, and confidence to add new templates. Email is one of the highest-leverage UX touches , abandoned carts, re-engagement, receipts all start with this lesson. Next lesson , Background jobs (asynq) . The engine that runs the "send welcome" you just queued. Retries, cron, dashboards, all baked in.
pages.title: Why we need it

headings: How you call it from a service
How to modify the cache battery
pages.text: Redis is an in-memory key-value store. In Grit, it's the cache that sits between your handler and the database , saving you a query on hot paths. This lesson is what it does, where the code lives, and how to add caching to your own endpoint. A list endpoint that runs the same query 1000 times per minute wastes the DB. With a 60-second cache, that's 1 DB query per minute instead of 1000. The DB is happier, p95 latency drops, and you don't need a bigger DB to scale. How it's implemented Three operations, JSON serialization baked in, cache-miss treated as "not an error, just no data". That last detail matters: a cache miss is a normal case, not an exception. Three lines you'll see in every cached-read service: Try cache. If hit, return immediately. The DB never gets touched. Hit DB. Normal query. Populate cache. So the NEXT request is a hit. Versioned ( :v1 ). When you change the value shape, bump the version. Old keys expire naturally; no manual invalidation. Hierarchical with : . Lets you group + scan keys for debugging in redis-cli . Deterministic. Same input → same key. Otherwise you never hit. "There are only two hard problems in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things." Three patterns to know: Set a short TTL (30s, 60s, 5m) and accept stale data for that long. Simple, robust, hides bugs. Right answer for most cases. After a write, blow away the cached read. Next read repopulates. Works well when you know exactly which keys are stale. For broader invalidation (delete every product cache for a user), use SCAN + DEL in a loop. Avoid in production at scale , keep keys scoped instead. Wire this on any GET endpoint where the response is identical for the same URL across users. The X-Cache: HIT/MISS header lets you verify in the browser DevTools. Change the default TTL , find the service or middleware that sets time.Minute and adjust. Swap Redis for an alternative (Dragonfly, KeyDB) , they speak the Redis protocol, so just change REDIS_URL . Add metrics , wrap Get / Set with a Prometheus counter for hit ratio. One of the highest-signal metrics you can add. Disable in dev , set REDIS_URL="" and Grit's service falls through to no-op (always returns miss). Useful when debugging stale-data bugs. In production, point REDIS_URL at Upstash, Redis Cloud, ElastiCache, or self-hosted. Same code, no change. Add a cache to a real endpoint: Pick a GET endpoint with no per-user data (e.g., the products list). In the service, wrap the DB call with Get / Set / 30s TTL. In the Update + Delete services for the same model, add a cache.Del . Test: hit the list endpoint twice with -v via curl. Second request should be faster. (You can also add a temporary log line in the service to confirm cache hit / miss.) Test invalidation: edit a row, immediately re-fetch the list, confirm the change shows up. You should see ~10x speedup on a cache hit and an instantly-updating list after a write. That's the cache pattern at its best. Next lesson , S3 file storage . Uploads, signed URLs, image processing , without taking on AWS' whole learning curve.
pages.title: Why we need it

headings: Signed URLs , when you need access control
pages.text: Files don't belong in your database (rows balloon, backups get expensive). They belong in object storage , S3 or S3-compatible. Grit ships a storage battery that abstracts the provider, so MinIO locally and R2 or AWS in production feels the same to your code. Three jobs object storage handles better than a DB: Big binary data , images, PDFs, videos. Cheap per-GB, infinite scale, no DB bloat. Direct serving , clients fetch files via CDN-backed URLs, not through your API. Signed URLs , give time-limited download access without sharing credentials. How it's implemented Same interface, three deploy targets: Local dev: MinIO (via docker-compose ) , set STORAGE_DRIVER=minio . Big prod (default for most teams): AWS S3 , set STORAGE_DRIVER=s3 . Leave S3_ENDPOINT empty so the SDK uses the regional default. If your API runs on EC2/ECS/Lambda with an IAM role, leave the access/secret keys empty too , the SDK auto-discovers role credentials. Cheap prod (zero egress fees): Cloudflare R2 , set STORAGE_DRIVER=r2 and the R2_* block. Cheapest per-GB: Backblaze B2 , set STORAGE_DRIVER=b2 and the B2_* block. Same code; only the env vars change. Three details worth absorbing: Random key ( uuid + ext ) , never trust the client filename. ../../../etc/passwd is a real attack. Size cap upfront. Otherwise a malicious user can DOS your storage budget. DB record . The S3 object is the bytes; the uploads table is the metadata. You need both to let users list / delete. Critical gotcha: don't set Content-Type manually . The browser must set it with the correct boundary string for multipart parsing. Override it and Gin can't read the file. Cheap thumbnails: resize once on upload, serve thumbs in lists, full size on detail pages. Saves the user's bandwidth. Public files (avatars, blog images): just use storage.URL(key) . No auth, served via CDN. Private files (user's personal documents): the bucket should reject anonymous access. Use storage.SignedURL(key, 5*time.Minute) , that returns a long URL with a query-string signature. Valid for 5 minutes, then dies. Hand the URL to the frontend; the user's browser fetches the file directly without going through your API. Increase the size cap , edit the fh.Size check in handler.go . Restrict MIME types , add an allow-list: allowedMimes := map[string]bool{"image/jpeg": true, ...} . Add virus scanning , pipe the upload through ClamAV before saving. Heavier; only do it if your threat model requires it. Per-user quota , sum uploads.size by user_id, reject if over. For prod, swap to STORAGE_ENDPOINT=<account-id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com + Cloudflare R2 credentials. Zero code changes. Add file upload to the User profile (avatar): Add an AvatarKey string field to the User model. Add a route: POST /api/me/avatar that accepts a multipart file, uploads via the storage service, sets user.AvatarKey , deletes the old one if present. Return the URL via storage.URL(user.AvatarKey) . Display it in the admin user list. Try uploading a 20MB file , confirm you get 400 due to size cap. You should have a working avatar upload that displays in the admin panel and cleans up old files. That's the storage battery doing what every SaaS needs. Next lesson , Mail (Resend) . Transactional email with editable templates , the most-needed external service after the DB.
pages.title: Why we need it

pages.text: Every Grit API endpoint returns one of three shapes. Memorise these and you can read any response without looking up the schema. Used for GET /api/users/123 , POST /api/users , PUT /api/users/123 . message is human-readable; the UI shows it as a toast. Used for GET /api/users and any list endpoint. meta drives pagination UI. Any 4xx or 5xx response. code is machine-readable (used for branching in the UI); message is human-readable; details is per-field for form validation errors. With the API running, hit three endpoints from your browser or curl and paste the JSON in notes.md : GET /api/health , see Shape 1 GET /api/users with a fresh JWT (admin) , see Shape 2 (paginated list) GET /api/users/nonexistent-id , see Shape 3 (404 error) You should see: {` `} , bare health response (not the full envelope; /api/health is the one exception). A list response with data + meta . {`{ "error": }`} Three shapes, predictable structure, easy to read. You know what success and failure look like. Next , how Grit handles errors internally: explicit on the Go side, error boundary + toast on the React side.
pages.title: Shape 1 , Single item

headings: Go side , explicit, wrapped, never ignored
pages.text: Errors are normal; how you handle them is what makes the code production-ready. Grit has one pattern for Go (explicit + wrapped) and one for React (error boundary + toast). Both close the loop so no error is silently swallowed. The three rules: Every error is checked. Never _ := someFunc() . Errors are wrapped with context. fmt.Errorf("doing X: %w", err) . The %w makes it unwrappable upstream (with errors.Is / errors.As ). Handlers convert errors to HTTP responses. Services return errors; handlers map them to status codes via a tiny helper. respond is a tiny package that shapes the envelope you learned in the last lesson. Above the page, an <ErrorBoundary> catches anything the mutations / queries don't , including render-time crashes. Users see a friendly fallback, not a white screen. Trigger every error path in a real request. With the API running, use curl or the OpenAPI docs to hit: POST /api/auth/login with no body , capture the 422 response in notes.md . POST /api/auth/login with valid email + wrong password , capture the 401. GET /api/users/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 , capture the 404. You should see Shape 3 in all three cases. Each response follows Shape 3 with a different code: {`{ "error": { "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "message": "...", "details": } }`} {`{ "error": }`} {`{ "error": }`} That's the convention surface end-to-end , same shape for every error, code + message + optional details. Chapter 4 , Code generation . The most fun command in Grit. grit generate resource Product writes 7 files and wires them all together. We tour them line by line.
pages.title: Go side , explicit, wrapped, never ignored

headings: internal/ , the seven sub-folders that matter
What does NOT go in internal/
pages.text: Grit has one place for everything. That sounds like a constraint , it's actually a superpower. Every team member, every AI agent, every future-you knows where to look without thinking. This lesson covers the rules. apps/api/cmd/ , entry points (just server/main.go usually) apps/api/internal/ , everything that's not exported. The actual code lives here. apps/web/ + apps/admin/ , Next.js apps. Standard App Router shape. packages/shared/ , Zod + TS types. Imported by web and admin. Tests , they live alongside the file they test: handlers/user.go → handlers/user_test.go . Migrations , Grit uses GORM AutoMigrate by default. No internal/migrations/ folder. Static assets , frontend assets live in apps/web/public/ or apps/admin/public/ . You need to add a NotificationService that sends push notifications when a user's order ships. Decide where each piece goes , write it in notes.md : The struct + methods that talk to Expo Push? The DB row that tracks "was this notification sent?" The HTTP endpoint to trigger a test push from the admin panel? The TypeScript type for the admin form's payload? apps/api/internal/services/notification.go apps/api/internal/models/notification.go apps/api/internal/handlers/notification.go (calls the service) packages/shared/src/schemas/notification.ts (Zod schema) Four files, four homes, no decisions needed. That's the point. Folders sorted. Next , naming. snake_case for Go files, kebab-case for TS, plural for routes. Same logic: one rule, applied everywhere.
pages.title: The four big places

pages.text: Grit names things consistently so you never have to guess what to call your new file. This is a 5-minute lesson , but it's the one that makes your future code look like it belongs. Three principles cover everything: Go uses snake_case for filenames + PascalCase for types and exported funcs. That's the Go community convention. Grit doesn't fight it. TS uses kebab-case for filenames + PascalCase for components. The kebab-case convention is from React Router / Next.js , readable in URLs. API routes and DB tables are plural. /api/users , users table , a user is a single resource; the collection is plural. Avoids the "is it /user or /users?" debate. Look at your scaffolded project. Find three files across web, admin, and api , pick one from each. In notes.md , write the filename + which convention it follows. Example picks: apps/api/internal/handlers/user.go , snake_case (Go file) apps/web/components/landing-hero.tsx , kebab-case (TS file) apps/admin/app/resources/users/page.tsx , plural lowercase URL segment (resource name) + kebab-case files Files are named. Next , how Grit's API responses are shaped. One envelope every endpoint follows. Memorise it once, use it forever.
pages.title: The full table

pages.text: Time to start everything. By the end of this lesson, Postgres, the API, the web app, and the admin panel will all be running together and you'll have URLs to open in your browser. Brings up Postgres (host 5434), Redis (host 6380), MinIO (host 9002 + 9003), and Mailhog (1025 + 8025) in the background , the host ports are intentionally offset from the canonical defaults so a native install of Postgres / Redis / MinIO on your machine doesn't collide. Wait ~5 seconds for them to be ready. Installs everything for web, admin, and the shared package , all in one pnpm workspace. The seed creates an admin@example.com user with password admin123 . We'll log in with that in the next lesson. One command, three apps: Hot reload is on for all three. Edit a file, the page reloads. Run the full boot sequence on your machine. When all four steps have run successfully, paste the grit start output into notes.md . You should see the three checkmarks: If one of them is red instead of green, scroll up , the error message tells you what's wrong (usually a port conflict or a missing dep). Everything's running. Next lesson , open the URLs, log into the admin panel, and click around so you understand what each surface looks like.
pages.title: 1. Start the infrastructure

headings: 1. The API , the smallest possible win
pages.text: Everything is running. This is the "see what you have" lesson , open each URL, recognise what it is, log in to the admin panel, and read the JSON the API returns. Open http://localhost:8080/api/health . You should see: That's the API alive and responding. Tiny but important. Open http://localhost:8080/docs . You see Scalar UI , an auto-generated, interactive docs surface for every endpoint. Click any endpoint to see the schema, try it out, see the response. No OpenAPI YAML to maintain , Grit generates it from the Go code. Open http://localhost:3001 . Log in with: You land on the admin dashboard. Click Users in the sidebar , you'll see a table with sortable columns, a filter bar, and pagination. That's the DataTable primitive doing the work. Click a user to edit them , that's the FormBuilder . Open http://localhost:3000 . The public Next.js site , scaffolded with a landing page, signup, login, and a basic dashboard. We won't touch this much in the concepts course; the Building Web with Next.js course goes deep here. http://localhost:8080/studio opens GORM Studio , a visual DB browser. Click users in the left rail. You see the seeded admin row, schema, indexes. Run ad-hoc SQL from the query tab. Useful when you're debugging "is this row really in the DB?". Take a tour. Open each URL and capture three screenshots for your notes.md : The JSON response from /api/health The admin dashboard after you log in The users table in GORM Studio That's the chapter 2 assignment done. Open the assignment page in the sidebar to tick off the success criteria. No exact solution , the screenshots are the proof. If you can see live API JSON + the admin panel logged in + the users table in Studio, chapter 2 is done. You now have a working Grit project in your browser. Chapter 3 , The Convention Surface . Now that you can see the project running, we get into the rules every file follows and why. Once you internalise these, you can write code that fits the codebase before you've even read it.
