Two patterns to control spend: Per-user rate limits in Sentinel (covered in next chapter): "max 100 AI calls per user per day". Token budgets : track input + output tokens per user in a ai_usage table, cap based on subscription tier. For agentic workflows , "Claude, look up this user's recent orders" , Grit's AI module supports tool definitions: The model decides whether to call the tool; Grit dispatches the handler and feeds the result back. Multi-turn tool use just works. Call the AI Gateway directly from your bench-api: Get a Vercel AI Gateway key (free tier works) at vercel.com/ai-gateway . Set it in your .env . Add a debug handler that calls h.ai.Chat with the prompt "Write me a one-line haiku about Go programming." Hit the handler and paste the result in notes.md . One example response: You've made an AI call from your Grit API. From here: streaming for chat UIs, tools for agentic flows, per-user budgets for cost control. Chapter 4 done. Chapter 5 , Security + Observability . Sentinel WAF, Pulse dashboards, the tamper-evident audit log. The trio that keeps production alive.
pages.title: The Gateway shape

headings: Handling the task in the worker
pages.text: Some work shouldn't block the HTTP request , sending an email, resizing an image, calling an LLM. Grit uses Asynq for background jobs: enqueue from anywhere, a worker process consumes them. This lesson covers the pattern + the four primitives you'll actually use. Two processes , the API and the worker , share Redis as the queue. Both run from the same binary; you start the worker with ./api worker instead of ./api server . Return nil = task completed. Return an error = Asynq retries with exponential backoff up to MaxRetry , then moves it to the dead-letter queue. Notice , enqueue failure doesn't fail the request. The user's account exists; the welcome email is best-effort. Different behaviour for critical paths (payments, audit) where you'd return the error. For recurring work (daily digests, hourly metrics roll-up): Same handler signature as one-off tasks. The scheduler runs as part of the worker process , no separate cron daemon. Grit's scaffold includes /admin/jobs in the admin app , visual dashboard for active/pending/failed/dead jobs, with retry + delete buttons. For the API-only kit, expose Asynq's web UI on a dedicated port; password-protected via the Sentinel dashboard credentials. Wire your first job. Register a new task type: Define TaskTypeLogHello + a handler that just log.Println("hello from a job!") . Add an enqueue call to your /api/health handler. Start the worker: go run ./cmd/server worker (or whatever the scaffolded subcommand is). Hit /api/health , you should see "hello from a job!" in the worker's output. You should see two log streams , your API logs the request, the worker logs the job: That's producer + consumer working. Now you can offload anything heavy from the request path. Transactional email is the most common job. Next lesson , how to send it via Resend and watch it land in Mailhog during dev.
pages.title: How it's shaped

pages.text: Transactional email is plumbing every product needs. Grit uses Resend in production and Mailhog in dev , same code path, different backend. This lesson covers sending your first templated email and the patterns you'll repeat. Same mailer.Send() call everywhere. Grit picks the backend based on env. You never have to write in your handler. The mailer loads the welcome template, fills in the data, and dispatches. Grit ships four templates by default: Go template syntax , simple, no learning curve: The scaffolded templates are intentionally simple. Most teams swap in a designer's HTML once they ship. While the API runs locally, every mailer.Send call delivers to Mailhog. Open http://localhost:8025 and you see the inbox , including the rendered HTML, the headers, and the raw source. For high-volume products, hook the Resend webhook into your API: When a user's email hard-bounces, stop sending them mail. Grit gives you the webhook receiver; you decide the policy. Don't call mailer.Send from inside an HTTP handler. Mail is slow (~200ms), can fail, and shouldn't block the user's request. Enqueue an Asynq job (from the previous lesson) and let the worker send it. Send your first email through Mailhog: Add a temporary debug handler that calls h.mailer.Send with the welcome template and your own email address. Hit the handler. Open Mailhog at http://localhost:8025 . The email should be sitting there. Click it, view the rendered HTML. Paste a screenshot or the email subject + body in notes.md . You should see in Mailhog: Same Send() call works in production via Resend. Same templates. Same code path. The only thing that changes is the env vars. Email + jobs. Next , file storage . Uploading avatars, attachments, and the S3-compatible interface that swaps between MinIO (dev), R2, and AWS S3 (prod).
pages.title: Two backends, one API

headings: Direct uploads (presigned URLs) , when files get large
pages.text: File uploads , avatars, attachments, exports. Grit's storage package abstracts S3-compatible backends: MinIO in dev (ships with docker-compose), Cloudflare R2 or AWS S3 in production. One interface, swap the backend via env. Same four operations regardless of backend. The handler doesn't know if it's talking to MinIO or R2. Change STORAGE_DRIVER , restart. Same handler code, different bucket. Grit ships a generic upload handler at POST /api/uploads : Behind the scenes: file goes into the storage backend keyed by its SHA-256 hash (deduplication by content), an Upload row is created in the DB. The returned URL is a Grit proxy URL that streams the file with auth + access checks. For files >5 MB, you don't want them to pass through your API process. Use presigned URLs: Bandwidth doesn't hit your API. Useful for image uploads, video, backups, exports. The handler validates content-type from the uploaded bytes (sniffing), not from the user-supplied Content-Type header. An attacker who renames shell.php to image.png gets caught , the sniffer sees PHP source, the handler rejects. For avatars and thumbnails, Grit ships an image processing pipeline: Upload a real file and read it back: With your access token, POST a file (a small PNG) to /api/uploads with curl: Note the url in the response. Open MinIO console ( http://localhost:9001 , login minioadmin/minioadmin ) , you should see the file in the bucket. Fetch the file via the API URL with your token , should stream the PNG back. The upload response shape: File is in MinIO under the content-hashed key, indexed in the DB by ID, accessible via a clean Grit URL. Last battery , AI Gateway . Stream from Claude, GPT-4, and ~98 other models with one API key. Built for products that wrap AI as a feature.
pages.title: The Storage interface

headings: You finished Building a Go API 🎉
pages.text: Last lesson , the pre-launch env vars checklist. Miss one of these and prod either won't boot or will boot in an insecure state. Five minutes to read, save hours of debugging. v3.25.1+ of Grit auto-generates these at scaffold time. If you scaffolded older, regenerate before going to prod. Each OAuth provider needs your production callback URL added to its allow list: Google: https://api.acme.com/api/auth/google/callback GitHub: https://api.acme.com/api/auth/github/callback Both providers let you list multiple URLs , keep your localhost dev URLs too so dev still works. Not strictly an env var, but: set up daily backups before going to prod. Five-minute setup, prevents catastrophic data loss. Options: pg_dump + cron , simplest. Dumps DB nightly, ships to S3 / R2. Backrest / pgBackRest , production-grade PITR (point-in-time recovery). Managed Postgres (Neon, Supabase) , backups are automatic. Skip the self-host. Before grit deploy --domain ... in production: ☐ .env.production exists and has every required var ☐ All passwords are random (not change-me ) ☐ APP_ENV=production ☐ CORS_ORIGINS only lists real frontend domains ☐ GORM_STUDIO_ENABLED=false ☐ OAuth callback URLs are added to provider allow lists ☐ DNS A record points to VPS IP ☐ DB backup plan exists ☐ You can SSH to the VPS Build the pre-flight checklist for your bench-api's production env. In notes.md : List every env var your .env.production sets For each, write "random", "copied from dev", or "from a service dashboard" Confirm no value is change-me , your-super-secret-jwt-key , or similar template text That's the chapter 6 assignment partially done , the second half is the actual deploy + HTTPS verification. A healthy .env.production looks like (abbreviated): Six chapters, 19 lessons. You can now scaffold a Go API, model the data layer, add auth with JWT + OAuth + 2FA + RBAC, integrate background jobs / mail / storage / AI, run a real WAF + observability + audit log, and deploy to a VPS with HTTPS. Next: pick the frontend that fits your product , Mobile (Expo) , Web (Next.js) , Web (TanStack) , Desktop (Wails) , or Multi-platform . All assume the API you just built.
pages.title: The must-set list

pages.text: Time to ship. grit deploy takes your local project and runs it on a VPS , Docker, Traefik for HTTPS, your domain, a functioning Postgres. One command. This lesson covers what it does and the prerequisites. It runs (in this order): SSH's to the host, installs Docker + Docker Compose if missing Builds your project locally + ships the image to the host Copies docker-compose.prod.yml + your .env.production Provisions Traefik with Let's Encrypt for HTTPS Starts Postgres + Redis + your API behind Traefik with the domain you specified Health-checks the deployment Prints the URL , typically https://api.acme.com/api/health A VPS (Hetzner / DigitalOcean / Linode / Vultr , anywhere with SSH + a public IP). $4/month tier works. SSH key access (no password auth) A domain you control + DNS access An .env.production in your project with real secrets Point an A record at your VPS IP before running deploy. Otherwise Let's Encrypt can't verify domain ownership and HTTPS provisioning fails. Your dev .env uses localhost services + Mailhog + MinIO. Production uses real services: Docker Compose handles all process management. systemd is optional; the compose stack starts on boot via restart: unless-stopped . Grit rebuilds the image, ships it, restarts the API container with a rolling update. Zero downtime if you wire health checks (see next lesson). Dokploy , UI for the same docker-compose deploys. Worth a look if you want a dashboard. Fly.io / Railway / Render , managed PaaS. More expensive than a VPS but zero config. Kubernetes , for products at scale. Grit ships example manifests; for <10K users you don't need it. Spin up a $4 VPS (Hetzner / DigitalOcean / etc) and deploy your bench-api to it. Create the VPS, note its IP. Point an A record at it. Wait ~5 minutes for DNS to propagate. Create .env.production with your real secrets. Run grit deploy --host root@<IP> --domain api.<your-domain> Hit https://api.<your-domain>/api/health from your phone (not localhost!) to confirm. Paste the response (with the real domain) in notes.md . You should see the same envelope you saw locally , now over HTTPS: With a green padlock in the address bar. You have a real production API. That's chapter 6's assignment done. Last lesson , the env vars checklist . What MUST be set in production before you ship to real users.
pages.title: What the command does

headings: A model is a Go struct + tags
pages.text: GORM is the ORM that ships with Grit. It speaks Postgres and SQLite out of the box; you write Go structs, it writes SQL. This lesson is the 7-minute crash course you need to read every Grit model. gorm:"primaryKey" , this field is the PK gorm:"type:uuid" , column type (use uuid for IDs; Grit defaults to UUID PKs) gorm:"not null" , DB-level NOT NULL constraint gorm:"uniqueIndex" , unique index on this column gorm:"default:value" , column default gorm:"-" , skip this field entirely (never write to DB) json:"snake_name" , how it appears in the API response Grit uses UUIDs for primary keys, not uint auto-increment. Two reasons: (1) IDOR defence , attackers can't guess the next ID; (2) globally unique , you can generate them client-side and merge across DBs without conflict. You don't need to write this hook yourself if you use grit generate resource , it's already in the template. GORM auto-sets CreatedAt on insert and UpdatedAt on every save. No work on your part , just declare them with the right names and types. Always pass arguments as the second+ parameter , never concatenate strings (covered as SQLi defence in the Concepts course). Add a Customer model to your bench-api. Then write three lines of code in main.go (or a temporary debug handler) that create one and read it back. Paste the log output in notes.md . You should see something like: UUID + name printed. GORM did the table creation, the insert, and the read for you. Single tables are easy. Real apps have relations , Customer has many Invoices; an Invoice belongs to a Customer. Next lesson: the three relation kinds and how Grit defines each.
pages.title: A model is a Go struct + tags

headings: When to switch to explicit migrations
The pragmatic middle: AutoMigrate + occasional raw SQL
pages.text: Grit's default migration strategy is GORM AutoMigrate : run it on boot, GORM reconciles the schema with your struct definitions. Magical when it works. This lesson covers when to keep it and when to switch. For each struct, GORM: Creates the table if it doesn't exist Adds new columns when you add struct fields Adds new indexes when you add new gorm:"index" tags Adds new foreign keys when you add relations Remove columns , you can delete a struct field but the column lingers. Manual ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN . Rename columns , it would see the rename as "drop A, add B" and lose data. Use raw SQL with a manual rename. Change column types , only certain narrowings work; widening usually does, narrowing rarely does. Data migrations , backfilling values when a new column lands. AutoMigrate handles schema; YOU handle data. Grit ships grit migrate as a CLI command that calls AutoMigrate on the same model list. In production: This way the migration only runs once per release (not per worker on boot), and a failed migration aborts the deploy before serving traffic. You need to do data migrations (backfills, splits, joins) You need to rename columns without dropping data You ship to customers who self-host (they need versioned migrations they can roll back) You need a review trail , explicit SQL files in git that's reviewable The graduation path: add golang-migrate/migrate or pressly/goose , put SQL files in internal/database/migrations/ , run them from a CLI. Grit doesn't prescribe one , pick what fits your team. Most Grit projects start with AutoMigrate, then run an occasional manual ALTER TABLE for renames + drops. That's fine for teams of 1-5 with a clear deploy process. Trigger the rename gotcha on your bench-api: In your Invoice model, rename a field , e.g., Total → TotalAmount . Run grit migrate . Open GORM Studio and look at the invoices table. You'll see both columns. In notes.md , write the SQL you'd run to consolidate: copy data + drop old column. Run via psql or GORM Studio's Query tab. Future boots see one column, with the correct data. This is the kind of manual step you graduate from when you switch to explicit migrations. Chapter 3 , Auth + RBAC . JWT, OAuth2, TOTP 2FA, and role-based gating. The heaviest chapter, the highest leverage.
pages.title: What AutoMigrate does

headings: 1. BelongsTo (the foreign key sits on this row)
2. HasMany (the other table owns the FK)
pages.text: Real domains have shapes , a customer has many invoices, an invoice belongs to a customer, a tag belongs to many products. GORM has one struct tag per relation kind. This lesson covers all three. Two pieces , the FK column ( CustomerID ) and the relation field ( Customer Customer ). Use Preload to eager-load: Invoices []Invoice means "this customer has many invoices". The FK lives on the Invoice row. Eager-load the same way: GORM creates the product_tags join table for you. Add a tag: What happens when you delete a customer with invoices? Three choices: Production-grade Grit projects tend to use RESTRICT + soft-delete the parent. Cascade is irreversible , pick it consciously. Add the invoice domain to your bench-api: Customer (HasMany Invoices) Invoice (BelongsTo Customer, HasMany LineItems) LineItem (BelongsTo Invoice) Wire each with the right FK + relation fields. Run grit migrate and confirm via GORM Studio that the FK columns exist. Paste the schema in notes.md . Three models, six fields each (PK, FK, parent, plus domain-specific): That's chapter 2's assignment done. AutoMigrate creates the tables + FK columns + indexes on boot. Models compile, AutoMigrate runs. But should you use AutoMigrate forever? Last lesson of this chapter: when AutoMigrate is fine and when to switch to explicit migrations.
pages.title: 1. BelongsTo (the foreign key sits on this row)

headings: 2. Run the API from the project root
The other URLs you can poke
pages.text: Time to bring the API up. Four commands. By the end you'll have a live JSON response in your terminal. Brings up Postgres, Redis, MinIO, and Mailhog in the background. The -d means "detached"; check status with docker compose ps . Important: run from project root, not from inside apps/api/cmd/server/ . The config loader looks for ./.env relative to your working directory, and .env lives at project root. Wait , that's also a non-root cwd. The trick: run from apps/api/ (because that's where go.mod lives), and the loader will find the project-root .env via the ../../.env path it tries. Every battery wired in five lines. If any of these say "failed", scroll up , the error message tells you exactly what's missing (usually a env value or Docker service that didn't come up). You should see: That's success. The API connected to every service it needs and is ready to handle requests. http://localhost:8080/docs , auto-generated OpenAPI documentation http://localhost:8080/studio , GORM Studio (DB browser) http://localhost:8080/sentinel/ui , Sentinel WAF dashboard http://localhost:8080/pulse/ui , Pulse observability http://localhost:8025 , Mailhog (captures all dev email) Get the API running end-to-end. From your scaffolded project: docker compose up -d cd apps/api && go run ./cmd/server In another terminal: curl http://localhost:8080/api/health Paste the curl response in notes.md . That completes chapter 1's assignment , the criteria are in the sidebar. Final response: Congrats , you have a Grit Go API running locally. Chapter 2 opens with modelling the data layer. Chapter 2 , Modeling with GORM . You'll define your first model, see how AutoMigrate handles tables, and learn the GORM tags Grit assumes.
pages.title: 1. Start Postgres + friends

pages.text: Let's walk every folder inside apps/api/ . By the end you'll know what each file does and where to put new code without thinking. This is where Gin starts. The full flow: Roughly 30 lines. main.go is intentionally tiny , its job is to wire dependencies, not to contain logic. Every external dependency (Redis, S3, Resend, AI Gateway) is wrapped in a tiny service. Those services compose into a single routes.Services struct that's passed to routes.Setup() . Handlers get the services they need by reference; nothing is global. You met this folder in Grit Concepts ch.3. Quick refresher of the hot path: jobs/ , Asynq integration. Enqueue from anywhere; the worker (separate process) consumes them. mail/ , Resend client + HTML templates. In dev, all mail goes to Mailhog. storage/ , S3-compatible (R2, MinIO, B2). One interface, swap the backend via env. ai/ , AI Gateway client. Stream from Claude, OpenAI, and ~98 other models. totp/ , 2FA: TOTP seeds encrypted at rest via AES-GCM. Open apps/api/internal/routes/routes.go . Count how many route groups are registered (look for r.Group(...) or api.Group(...) ). For each, write one line in notes.md describing what it serves. You should find something like: /api/health , public, returns the version envelope /api/auth/* , login / register / refresh , public /api/users/* , protected, requires JWT /api/uploads/* , protected, file upload + serve Each group is registered with its own middleware stack , that's how Grit applies auth selectively without per-handler boilerplate. You know the layout. Last lesson of this chapter , start everything up, make a request, prove the API works.
pages.title: The full tree

headings: The kit's shape at a glance
pages.text: Welcome to Building a Go API . Goal of this chapter: scaffold an API-only project, identify every file, get it serving requests. This first lesson is the scaffold itself , 5 minutes, one command, you're ready. Pick the project name (anything kebab-case works). The --api flag tells Grit you want the headless Go backend kit , no apps/web , no apps/admin , just the Go API. You'll see the standard checklist run: No apps/web/ , no public Next.js site No apps/admin/ , no Filament-style admin panel No packages/shared/ , no Zod schemas + TS types No turbo.json , pnpm-workspace.yaml , Go-only deps Everything else from the Concepts course , random JWT secret, Sentinel + Pulse pre-configured, SQLite support out of the box , still ships. Scaffold bench-api with the API-only kit. Then run ls -la bench-api (Mac/Linux) or dir bench-api (Windows) and paste the output in notes.md . Note: do not use cd apps/api yet , we'll tour the structure in the next lesson before running anything. You should see (Mac / Linux): No package.json , no turbo.json , that's the difference from triple. Tiny and focused. Files are on disk. Next lesson , the tour . We open apps/api/internal/ and walk every folder, naming the responsibility of each.
pages.title: The command

pages.text: "Who changed this and when?" is a question every production app eventually answers. Grit's audit log answers it tamper-evidently , each row stores a SHA-256 hash of the previous row + its canonical fields. Delete a row, the chain breaks at verify time. Two hash columns. PrevHash chains back to the previous row; CanonicalHash is this row's identity. Hash construction: Suppose an attacker has DB access and tries to hide their actions: Delete a row , the next row's PrevHash doesn't match any existing row. Chain broken. Edit a row's fields , the row's CanonicalHash no longer matches what its content hashes to. Chain broken. Edit and recompute , possible, but every row AFTER the edit has stale PrevHash values that no longer match. To stay consistent, they'd have to rebuild every subsequent row's hash , and the verifier still notices the mismatch with a hash you exported earlier. Same pattern as git commits and blockchain blocks. Cryptographic chaining, no central authority. The middleware grabs user_id from context, computes the PrevHash from the last row, computes the new CanonicalHash , writes the row. user.login , user.logout user.register , user.role_changed user.password_changed , user.totp_enabled account.locked (AuthShield triggered) authz.denied (RequireRoles rejected) sentinel.suspicious (WAF / Anomaly fired) Add your domain events alongside: order.created , refund.issued , invoice.voided . Anything material to your business. Run periodically (cron job, weekly batch): Alert / page when this returns an error. Now you're informed about DB-level tampering. Audit writes are synchronous (you don't want to lose audit events in a worker queue). Each write is one SQL INSERT + one SHA-256 hash , sub-millisecond on modern hardware. For very high-write systems, you can move this to the worker queue with an idempotency key, at the cost of weakened guarantees. Trigger an audit event and inspect the chain: Log into your API , that fires user.login . Open GORM Studio & look at the activity_logs table. Find the most recent row. Note its PrevHash and CanonicalHash . In notes.md : paste them, and explain what would happen if you edited Event from user.login to user.logout . Two columns you should capture: An edit to Event would change the inputs to CanonicalHash . The stored hash ( abcd... ) would no longer match the recomputed hash. Verify job raises an alert. That completes chapter 5's assignment. Final chapter , Deploy . Take what you built to a VPS with one command and a domain name.
pages.title: The audit log model

headings: Prometheus export , when you grow up
pages.text: You can't fix what you can't see. Pulse is Grit's observability dashboard , p50/p95/p99 latency, RPS per route, per-handler timings, slow-query log. No Datadog bill, no separate infra. Mounted at /pulse/ui in every Grit API. Live request rate (last 1 min / hour / day) Latency percentiles per route , p50, p95, p99 Error rates per route (4xx / 5xx breakdown) Slow query log (queries >100ms) System metrics , Go runtime, goroutine count, GC stats An average hides outliers. If your endpoint serves 99 fast requests (10ms each) and 1 slow one (2,000ms), the average is 30ms , looks fine. But for that 1% of users, the experience is unusable. p99 catches it. p50 , typical experience. Should be 100ms for most CRUD endpoints. p95 , almost everyone. 500ms is a healthy ceiling. p99 , the worst 1%. 2s; over that, something is wrong. Error rate , should be 0% for healthy endpoints. A spike means a regression. Queries that take >100ms get logged. Grit's Pulse dashboard groups them by SQL signature so you see which query is slow, not just that something is . The most common fix is an index. Add gorm:"index" to the field, run grit migrate , problem solved. Pulse is in-process , same binary as your API. That has trade-offs: No cross-service tracing. If you have multiple Grit APIs talking to each other, you can't follow a request across them. Use OpenTelemetry for that. Metrics are per-replica. If you run 3 API containers, each has its own Pulse view. The Postgres backend can merge if you point all 3 at the same DB. Last 24 hours by default. Older data ages out. For long-term retention, export to Prometheus / Datadog. For most products, single-binary Pulse is enough. You can always graduate. Pulse exposes /pulse/metrics in Prometheus format. Add Prometheus + Grafana, scrape this endpoint, and you have proper long-term metrics. Use the Pulse UI for day-to-day; Prometheus for historical analysis. Load-test your API to populate Pulse: Make sure Pulse is on ( PULSE_ENABLED=true ). Run ab or wrk for 30 seconds against /api/health : Open /pulse/ui . You should see the spike + the p50/p95/p99 numbers. Screenshot the route view and paste it in notes.md . Healthy Pulse output for /api/health: Health checks are designed to be 10ms , anything else indicates middleware bloat or contention. Last lesson of the chapter , the tamper-evident audit log . Every mutation is hashed into a chain so retroactive tampering breaks verification. The compliance team will love you.
pages.title: What you see

pages.text: Sentinel is Grit's in-process Web Application Firewall (WAF). It does rate limiting, AuthShield (brute-force lockouts), Anomaly detection, and Geo blocking , all in middleware that runs in sub-millisecond time. This lesson covers what it ships and how to configure it. Open http://localhost:8080/sentinel/ui . Log in with SENTINEL_USERNAME / SENTINEL_PASSWORD from your .env . You'll see: Live request rate + p95 latency Blocked requests (by reason: WAF rule, rate limit, AuthShield) Recent suspicious IPs Per-route rate-limit counters OWASP CRS-lite ruleset embedded. Blocks: SQLi probes ( ' OR 1=1-- , UNION SELECT, time-based) XSS payloads in query / body Path traversal ( ../../etc/passwd ) Dotfile probes ( .git , .env , .bak ) Two modes: ModeBlock (return 403 + record) or ModeLog (record but pass through , useful during rollout). The default config: 100 req/min per IP across all routes 5 req/15min per IP on /api/auth/login Custom rates per route via the ByRoute map Exceeded → 429 Too Many Requests. Counters live in Redis (shared across API replicas). After N failed logins for an email, the account enters a cool-down regardless of source IP. This defends against distributed credential-stuffing where every attempt comes from a different IP. Anomaly: behavioural rules , rapid 4xx bursts, suspicious user-agent strings, scanner signatures. Bots get throttled before they exhaust your rate-limit budget. Geo: country-level allow/block list. "Block everything outside the US" or "flag high-fraud-rate countries for manual review" , both are config flags. Sentinel refuses to mount in production with the default password sentinel . v3.25.1 of Grit fixes this by generating a random password at scaffold time, but if you somehow kept the default, the API won't start in APP_ENV=production . Set strong credentials or set DEMO_MODE=true for the public-demo carve-out. Trip the rate limit: Run 6 login attempts in quick succession with curl: You should see five 401s, then a 429. Open the Sentinel dashboard and look at the rate-limit page. Paste the curl output and a dashboard screenshot in notes.md . You should see: Sentinel did its job. The 6th request hit the per-route rate limit. The audit log records the event; the dashboard shows the IP. Security on. Now to see what's actually happening , Pulse's p50/p95/p99 dashboards, per-route metrics, slow-query visibility.
pages.title: The Sentinel dashboard

headings: The problem, in the framework's own history
Three deliveries, and choosing between them
The outbox, and the choice it removes
pages.text: An application grows a particular kind of mess: one thing happens, and five systems have to hear about it. An order is placed, so write the audit record, push to the open dashboard, send the webhook, queue the receipt, update the cache. Every one of those is a line in the handler, and the sixth is the one somebody forgets. This chapter is the alternative: the handler says what happened, once, and anything interested listens. Before the bus existed, a generated handler called the audit logger and nothing else. Webhooks, realtime and background jobs all existed, and *none of them was ever fired by generated code*. Dispatching a webhook meant hand-writing the call in every handler, for every operation, on every resource. Forgetting one produced no error at all. Just a subscriber that never heard anything, which is the worst failure mode there is: silent, and only noticed by the customer whose integration stopped working. One line in the handler. The audit log, outbound webhooks and realtime clients are now subscribers rather than things somebody has to remember to call. Sync Runs inline, before the handler responds. For work that must be part of the request Async Runs on the bus's worker pool after the response. For anything with a network call Durable Through the transactional outbox: at least once, retried, surviving restarts Sync is for the audit record: it needs the request context and should be written before the caller is told the write succeeded. A slow Sync subscriber is a slow endpoint, and that is the whole cost model. Async is for the webhook endpoint that takes four seconds. The API must not take four seconds because somebody else's server is slow. Durable is for work another module depends on . If losing the event would leave two systems disagreeing, it is durable. Watch out The async queue is bounded, and that is deliberate. An unbounded queue turns one slow subscriber into memory exhaustion, which fails later and worse than dropping events and saying so. When you see events being dropped in the logs, the fix is not a bigger queue. It is finding the subscriber that is slow, and usually moving it to Durable where retrying is the design rather than an accident. Durable delivery exists because of a problem with two halves, and doing the obvious thing gets one of them wrong whichever order you pick. Publish, then commit. The publish succeeds, the commit fails, and a webhook has announced an order that does not exist. Downstream systems act on it, and there is nothing to reconcile against because the row was never written. Commit, then publish. The commit succeeds, the process is killed before the publish, and the order exists with nobody told. Nothing is logged anywhere, because from the process's point of view nothing failed. The outbox removes the choice: The message is written in the same transaction as the business data, so it commits or rolls back with it. A relay reads committed messages and delivers them afterwards. Either both happened or neither did. If you know JavaScript This pattern is worth carrying with you whatever you build next, because it is not a framework feature. It is the standard answer to "I need to update my database and tell somebody else, atomically", and it works in any language against any queue. The name to look up is transactional outbox . Once you have seen it, you start noticing the places you got away without it. The cost is honest and must be stated: delivery is at least once , not exactly once. A message can be delivered twice if the process dies between the send and the status update. Consumers have to be idempotent, which is what a dedup key on the receiving end is for, and which is the same discipline chapter forty three asked for. The hub can address a user, everybody, or a named channel. Channels are the one that makes a real interface possible: The server answers subscribed , subscription_error or unsubscribed , each naming the channel, and server code publishes to the name: Every subscriber on every replica receives it, which is the part that is tedious to build: a second instance of your API has to reach clients connected to the first, so the hub has a backplane. Watch out A channel name is a permission question, and it must be answered server side. invoice.42 means "whoever may read invoice 42", not "whoever can type that string". The hub has a registry of authorizers per channel pattern for this reason. A realtime layer where the client picks what it hears is an API with no access control, reachable from a browser console. Without channels, a page showing one invoice had no way to hear about that invoice without every event for that user being pushed at it, which is a real cost on a busy account. Some platforms do not pass a WebSocket upgrade through to the application. One managed host strips Connection: upgrade before the container, and it is not alone: a corporate proxy, an older load balancer, or an API gateway configured for plain HTTP all do the same. The failure is unpleasant: the handshake fails, the client's reconnect loop retries forever, and live updates silently never arrive. Nothing errors in a way anybody sees. So there is a Server-Sent Events fallback. SSE is plain HTTP with a response that never ends, so it survives all of that. WebSocket Two-way, lower latency, needs the upgrade to survive the network SSE Server to client only, plain HTTP, reconnects by itself For dashboards, notifications and live lists, which is most of what an application needs, SSE is enough. Reach for WebSockets when the client needs to send continuously: a cursor position, a drawing, a chat typing indicator. That wires outbound, Standard-Webhooks-signed deliveries with retries, a delivery log and manual replay. Core already verifies incoming webhooks; this sends outgoing ones, which is the opposite direction and a different problem. What matters when you are the one sending: Sign every delivery. The receiver has to know it was you. Standard Webho

headings: What makes this harder than CRUD
Numbering, which is a concurrency problem in disguise
Immutability, and why an edit is the wrong verb
The state machine, written as methods
Payments, and the status you should not store twice
Reminders, in one line for now
pages.text: An invoice is not a record. It is a document somebody can be held to, and that changes what the software has to guarantee: the number must be unique and gap-free, the document must not change after it is sent, the arithmetic must be exact, and every change must leave a trace. Chapter forty did the arithmetic. This chapter is the rest, and most of it is about refusing to do things. Numbering INV-202610-0003 must be unique, sequential and gap-free, under concurrent creates Immutability A sent invoice is evidence. You correct it with another document, not with an edit State Draft, sent, part paid, paid, void, and the transitions that are not allowed Money Totals, tax, partial payments, in a currency that is not always yours Trace Who changed what, when, kept in something nobody can quietly rewrite The naive version is SELECT MAX(number) + 1 , and it is wrong the first time two people create an invoice in the same second. Both read the same maximum, both write the same number, and one of them wins depending on your unique index. That creates a counter package backed by a table, and a typed wrapper: Bucket is the period key: 202610 for a monthly reset, 2026 for yearly, empty for never. The increment runs inside a transaction holding a row-level lock: so concurrent callers serialise on that row rather than racing. Watch out Call the sequence from the model's BeforeCreate , and call sequence.Next directly rather than the generated services.Next... wrapper. Services already import models. A model importing services is an import cycle, and Go refuses to compile it. The error names two packages and not the line you are thinking about, so it is worth knowing before you meet it: The wrapper exists for handlers and jobs. The hook, which lives in the model package, uses the generic function. If you know JavaScript The honest limit, stated in the package's own comment: one counter row serialises its writers, so beyond roughly a hundred invoices a second on a single counter you need a different design. That number is far above what an invoicing application does and far below what an event stream does. Knowing which side of it you are on is the useful part. Most business documents are rare events; telemetry is not. A draft is yours to change. A sent invoice is not, because a copy exists outside your database, in somebody's inbox and somebody else's accounts. So the model has two regimes: and a correction is a second document: Watch out The pressure to allow "just a small edit" on a sent invoice will come from the client, and it will sound reasonable, because the mistake is small. It is still wrong, and the argument that works is not technical: the number on the document in their customer's hand no longer matches the number in the system, and the first person to notice is an auditor. Offer a credit note and a reissue, which is what accountants already expect. The ledger of what actually happened goes in a resource nobody can rewrite: --append-only means no update and no delete routes, a GORM guard, and a database trigger installed by grit migrate . Three layers, because the one that matters is the one that still holds when somebody writes a quick script against the database directly. Statuses in a dropdown are a suggestion. Statuses as methods are a rule: The transitions worth refusing, in any document workflow: Send an empty invoice A document with no lines is a mistake, not a zero bill Void a paid invoice Money moved. Refund it, do not pretend Pay a draft The customer has not been asked yet Edit after sending Covered above A payment is its own record, because partial payments exist and because a payment has a date and a method that the invoice does not: The balance is arithmetic over payments, not a column somebody updates: Watch out Storing paid_amount on the invoice as well as storing payments is two sources of truth, and they will disagree. They always disagree after the first deleted payment, the first failed transaction, or the first manual correction in the database. Derive it. If the derivation is too slow at scale, that is a caching decision made later with measurements, and a cached value is clearly labelled as one. It is not the same as two columns that both claim to be the truth. The admin gives you two ways out of the screen: Print and PDF. The detail page has a print action, and PDF rendering uses @react-pdf/renderer in the browser, lazy loaded so it is not in the first load of every list page. Excel. The list exports with the current filters applied, through xlsx , also lazy loaded. If you know JavaScript Client-side PDF is right until it is not. It is free, it uses the layout you can see, and it needs no fonts installed on a server. It stops being right when the PDF must exist without a browser: attached to an automated email, archived nightly, generated by a webhook. At that point the job moves server side and becomes a real project with fonts, page breaks and a rendering budget. Start with the browser. Move it when a background job needs the document, not before. Overdue invoices should chase themselves: That writes a job that runs at nine every morning. Chapter forty three is about what makes a job safe to run unattended: retries, idempotency, and what happens when it fails at three in the morning. For now, note the shape: the job calls the same service method a human would, so the rules cannot be bypassed by automation. Project 38: build the invoicing application One: numbering under pressure. Wire the sequence into BeforeCreate . Then create fifty invoices concurrently: Assert fifty distinct numbers with no gaps. Run it with -race . Two: the state machine. Send , Pay , Void and CreditNote as service methods, each refusing the transitions in the table above, each idempotent where that makes sense. Tests for every refusal, not just the happy paths. Three: immutability. Prove that updating a sent invoice fails through the API and through the admin. Then try it in /studio and notice that

headings: Return an error to retry, return nil to stop
The two kinds of "it ran twice"
pages.text: Some work must not happen inside a request. Resizing twelve images, emailing four hundred people, reconciling yesterday's payments: if the user is waiting for it, you have built a timeout. This chapter is the queue, the scheduler and the mailer, and most of it is about the two questions that separate a job system from a go func() : what happens when it fails, and what happens when it runs twice. Three things are wrong with it, and the third is the one that hurts. It dies with the process. A deploy, a crash, a scale-down, and the work is gone with no record that it existed. It cannot be retried. The error goes to a log, if anywhere. It cannot be seen. Nobody can answer "did the invoice reminders run last night", which is the question you will actually be asked. If you know JavaScript This is the same reason a Node application reaches for BullMQ rather than setTimeout . The difference in Go is that the goroutine is so cheap and so easy that the temptation is stronger, and it works in development every single time. The framework does keep a small escape hatch for genuinely minor work: a detached task with its own context and a hard cap of thirty two concurrent slots, deliberately small, because *anything needing more than thirty two workers is a job*. That writes three things: the job file, a handler registration in the worker's mux, and, with --cron , a schedule entry that the admin's cron page lists. The job file is yours from the moment it is written, and a second generate refuses rather than overwrites. Two conventions in that template are the whole discipline. The payload is IDs and small values. It is serialised into Redis, and a retry sees exactly what the first attempt saw. Putting a whole struct in the payload means a retry works from a snapshot that may now be stale. *An undecodable payload is wrapped with asynq.SkipRetry .* A payload that does not parse now will not parse in four minutes either. Retrying a permanent failure is how a queue fills up with work that can never succeed. That is the entire protocol, and the second half of the first line is the part people get wrong. A task that fails for a reason that will never change, a deleted record, a malformed input, a file that is not an image, should return nil and log loudly, or wrap with SkipRetry . Returning the error buys you the same failure five more times with exponential backoff. Watch out The practical rule: *retry anything that is about the world, do not retry anything that is about the data*. A network timeout, a rate limit, a database that is briefly down: retry. Invalid JSON, a missing user, an unsupported format: do not. If you cannot tell which one you have, you can log it and return nil , and the work stays visible in the logs rather than invisible in a retry loop. A queue guarantees at least once , not exactly once. The retry that happens after a worker was killed mid-task is the normal case, not the pathological one. So every job has to answer: what if this runs again? Idempotency at the enqueue. The same work queued twice is refused: A second enqueue inside the window returns ErrDuplicateTask rather than running. This is how a nightly job that is triggered twice, by a scheduler and by an impatient human, stays a single run. Idempotency in the work. Even one enqueue can execute twice. So the work itself should be safe to repeat: mark the invoice as reminded in the same transaction that records the send, and skip the ones already marked. Watch out The order matters, and the wrong order is the one that feels natural. Send the email, then mark it sent: a crash between the two sends it again tomorrow. Mark it sent, then send: a crash between them means nobody is ever reminded. Neither is free, so choose the failure you prefer. For a reminder, a duplicate is better than a silence. For a payout, a silence is very much better than a duplicate, and the answer is usually a record written first with a status that a later pass reconciles. The spec is validated when you generate, not at three in the morning: Scheduled runs arrive with an empty payload, which is why the template handles that case. The schedule is registered with a retry limit, and every registered task appears on the admin's cron page with its name, its spec and its type, so "did it run last night" is a screen rather than a grep. Watch out Cron runs in the server's timezone. A daily report at 0 9 * * * lands at nine in UTC, which is not nine for anybody you are reporting to. Set the timezone deliberately and write it down. And for anything that must happen on a date rather than at an hour, a daily job that checks for the date beats a schedule that tries to express it. Three behaviours in the configuration are worth copying into whatever you build next. An unset driver does something sensible. In development the mail goes to Mailhog from Docker Compose, falling back to the log when Mailhog is not running, so a password reset link is never lost. A named but misconfigured driver is an error, not a fallback. An application that believes it sends through SES must not quietly write to a log instead. Production with no mailer configured returns nothing , and the code that sends says so, rather than pretending. Your turn Set MAIL_MAILER=log , trigger a password reset, and read the link out of your terminal. It is the fastest way to work on an auth flow, and it is the setting to reach for whenever an email is in the way of what you are actually testing. Transactional mail goes through one function, and the decision is made there: With Redis, the mail is queued and retried. Without it, the mail is sent inline with a timeout. The caller does not care, which is why a project can start without Redis and gain it later without touching the sending code. context.WithoutCancel is the detail worth stealing. The send is allowed to finish after the request it came from has been answered, but not to run forever: the request's context is cancelled the moment the response is writ
pages.title: Why not just a goroutine

headings: Why a float is the wrong type for money
Money: an integer and a currency
The operations, and which ones can fail
Not every currency has two decimal places
Dates: the type that exists because of one error message
date against datetime, and how to choose
The same move, in smaller places
pages.text: There is a class of bug you cannot test your way out of, because the test and the code share the same wrong assumption. A total that is a cent off. A birthday that is a day early for half your users. A currency conversion that is a hundred times too large and looks plausible. The defence is not care. It is a type that cannot hold the wrong thing. This chapter is the two the framework ships, and the general move behind both. This is not a Go problem. It is binary floating point, and JavaScript does the same thing, which is why you have seen toFixed(2) sprinkled through every invoice page you have ever worked on. If you know JavaScript toFixed(2) is a display fix applied to a storage problem. The error is already in the number; rounding it at the end hides one cent per operation and accumulates in the direction nobody notices until a month-end total is off by four pounds and somebody has to explain it. The fix is the same in both languages: store integers of the smallest unit, and keep the decimal point as a rendering concern. Amount is in minor units : 2800 is twenty eight dollars. The currency rides with it, because an amount without one is not a quantity of anything. A money field embeds this as two columns with the field name as prefix: gives total_amount and total_currency . Watch out Two columns rather than one string, for a reason you feel at the first report: a column holding "19.99 USD" is not something you can SUM , index or compare in SQL. The amount stays an integer the database understands, and the currency is queryable, so "total revenue by currency this quarter" is one query rather than a loop in application code. Three of these are worth stopping on. * FromMajor is the one place a float is allowed near money*, because a person typed 28.00 into a form. It is converted immediately rather than carried, and Major() goes the other way for display. Feeding Major() back into arithmetic is how the cent you were protecting gets lost. * Add returns an error*, and the error is a currency mismatch. Watch out You will be tempted to ignore that error, because your application has one currency. Do not. The day it has two, an ignored error is not a crash and not a validation message. It is a total that is silently wrong, computed from amounts that were never comparable, and it will be wrong in reports that have already been sent. This is the clearest case in the book for chapter four's rule: the error exists because the operation genuinely cannot be defined, and _ is a decision to produce nonsense. * Allocate is the one people write by hand and get wrong.* Splitting 10.00 three ways gives 3.34, 3.33, 3.33. Three lots of 3.33 loses a cent, and in accounting a lost cent is not a rounding detail, it is a reconciliation that fails. The remainder goes to the earliest parts, which is the convention accounting systems expect. Yen and Ugandan shillings have no minor unit. Kuwaiti dinars have three. Every other currency is assumed to have two, which is true of most of ISO 4217. Watch out A hardcoded amount / 100 anywhere in your frontend is a bug waiting for its first international customer. Dividing a UGX amount by a hundred turns fifty thousand shillings into five hundred, on the invoice, in the email, in the report. Format through the shared helper, which knows the exponent. This is a one-line habit that saves an embarrassing afternoon. Conversion handles it too, which is the subtle part: Multiplying the amount by the rate and relabelling the currency would give 148200: a hundred times too much, silently, because USD has two decimals and JPY has none. The rate is a decimal string rather than a float, and that is deliberate: 1.005 is 1.00499999999999989 in binary, and an exchange rate multiplies the largest amounts in the system, which is exactly where that error stops being invisible. The string is parsed as an exact fraction, multiplied once, and rounded once. A date field used to be a *time.Time , and time.Time accepts RFC 3339 and nothing else. The admin's date picker sends "2001-08-06" . So every date field failed to save with this: The fix was not to make the browser send a timezone it does not have. It was two wire types that accept what a browser actually sends: The accepted layouts, widest first: The middle two are what <input type="datetime-local"> produces: no zone, and often no seconds. Neither is RFC 3339, and both are what you get from a real browser. If you know JavaScript The JavaScript habit that causes the worst version of this is building a Date from a date string and sending that. new Date("2001-08-06") is parsed as UTC midnight, so a user west of Greenwich sees the fifth of August. A date of birth that is a day early for everybody in the Americas is a bug that survives for years, because it is correct in the office where it was written. A date is not a timestamp. Send the string. date A day that is the same day everywhere: a birthday, an invoice date, a public holiday, a due date datetime A moment on the clock: a login, an appointment, a reading from a sensor The test: *would two people in different countries disagree about what day it is?* A birthday is the sixth of August in Kampala and in Lima. A meeting at 14:00 is not the same moment in both. Store timestamps in UTC and render them local. Store dates as dates, with no zone at all, because a zone on a birthday is a question nobody asked. Watch out Date sorting failed silently once, and the way it failed is worth knowing because it will happen to you with some other column. The sortable-column check tested the Go type for string , int or uint . A date is *jsontime.Date , so it matched none of them and was never added to the whitelist. The pagination layer drops a sort it does not recognise rather than rejecting it, so the request succeeded, the rows came back in whatever order the database felt like, and an invoice list could not be sorted by its issue date. Nothing errored. Nothing logged. The general lesson: *a whitelist
pages.title: Why a float is the wrong type for money

headings: Studio: the database, as it is
Sentinel: the attacks you were not watching
Health: the one endpoint a load balancer reads
The logs, and the ID that joins everything
pages.text: B11 was "when something goes wrong, nobody can tell me what happened". The honest version of that problem is that the information existed, in a log file, on a server, in a format nobody could search, during an hour when the person who could read it was asleep. A generated project mounts three dashboards and a health endpoint. This chapter is what each one answers, and the discipline that makes them useful rather than decorative. /studio What is actually in the database? /pulse What is this request doing, and why is it slow? /sentinel Who is attacking us, and what did we do about it? /health Is everything this process depends on alive? They answer different questions, and reaching for the wrong one is how a debugging session takes three hours. "The invoice shows the wrong total" is Studio. "The invoice page takes four seconds" is Pulse. The embedded database browser at /studio lists tables, browses rows, follows foreign keys and runs queries. It is the fastest way to answer a question of the form "did that actually save". The habit worth forming: before debugging the code, look at the row . Half of all "the API is broken" reports are a row that is exactly what the code wrote, and the bug is upstream in what was sent. Watch out Studio sees everything, which is the point and also the risk. The scoping that makes a user's query return only their rows is in the service layer, and Studio is underneath it. So a row you can see in Studio and cannot fetch through the API is usually ownership scoping doing its job rather than a bug. Chapter thirty five's 404 is the same observation from the other side. Pulse mounts at /pulse and records request traces, database queries, runtime metrics and errors. It is the tool for the question "why is this slow", and it answers it in the only way that helps: by showing which part took the time. The three views that earn their keep: The request trace. One request, with its queries listed and timed. An endpoint taking 800ms turns out to be forty queries of 20ms, which is the N+1 from chapter twenty two, now visible rather than suspected. The slow query list. Sorted by total time rather than by worst case, because a 5ms query run ten thousand times costs more than a 2 second report nobody runs. Errors with their context. Not just the stack, but the request that caused it. The dashboards exclude each other, which sounds obvious and is a real bug otherwise: an observability tool observing its own polling fills itself with its own traffic. Watch out A story worth carrying, because the shape of it is common. An earlier version of the request-body capture read the body to record it and put back only the first four kilobytes. Every request carrying a Content-Length reached the handler truncated. Uploads from a phone and from curl failed; uploads from a browser worked, because browsers send chunked bodies with no Content-Length . So the bug report was "uploads fail on mobile", and nothing in the upload code was wrong. *Middleware that reads a request body and puts it back is a place to look* whenever a request behaves differently depending on who sent it. Pulse can keep its data in SQLite so traces survive a restart, or stay in an in-memory ring buffer for peak throughput. The trade is the usual one: the ring buffer costs nothing and forgets, the file costs writes and remembers. Sentinel is the security suite: a web application firewall, rate limiting, an auth shield and anomaly detection, with a dashboard at /sentinel . What it changes is not that you are attacked. It is that you can see it. A login endpoint takes credential stuffing from the day it is public, and without a dashboard the only evidence is a slightly busier log. Two configuration details are worth knowing before you meet them. Development gets relaxed limits. A rate limit tight enough for production blocks you while you are testing, and a developer who has been blocked by their own firewall usually turns the whole thing off. Its storage is its own. Sentinel persists the threat log, blocked IPs and audit trail through its own adapter, not the application's database handle. Left unset it falls back to a local SQLite file, which is ephemeral inside a container, so every redeploy drops the threat log and the blocked-IP list. Point it at the real database in production. Watch out A mount failure is logged rather than fatal. Sentinel refuses to start on a misconfiguration, and in development that should not take the API down with it. The consequence to watch for: *a security layer that failed to start looks exactly like one that is running, unless you read the log line*. Check the dashboard after a configuration change rather than assuming. The distinction that makes this endpoint useful is between off and broken . Redis absent because nobody configured it is a working project without caching. Redis configured and unreachable is an incident. A health check that reports both as "red" gets ignored within a week, and a health check that reports both as "green" is worse. If you know JavaScript The equivalent in most Node projects is app.get('/health', () => res.send('ok')) , which answers "is the process running" and nothing else. The process is almost never the thing that broke. The database connection pool is exhausted, Redis went away, the disk is full. A health check that cannot say which is a status page that is always green during an outage. Every request carries a request ID, returned in a header and attached to every log line it produces. That is what turns "it failed around two o'clock" into one search. grit start records everything the API and the frontends print into .grit/logs/dev.log and keeps the previous run beside it, which matters more than it sounds: the interesting output is usually from the run that just crashed and scrolled away. Watch out Log the error and return a generic message, as chapter forty eight's handler did. The log gets the table name, the query and the stack. The client gets a code
pages.title: Four questions, four tools

headings: The one that is not optional: sanitising HTML
Draft and published, as a service rule
The cache, and the one rule about it
Rendering it in the web app
The things a publication needs that nothing generates
pages.text: Every project in Part V so far has been behind a login. This one is not, and that changes almost everything: the audience is the internet, the content is written by people rather than generated, and the pages have to be fast for somebody who has never signed in and never will. We are building a publication: posts with a rich text body, images, a draft and published workflow, a public API and a web front end that renders it. A new project ships with a Blog model, and it is worth reading before replacing it, because it is a worked example of several chapters at once: Five decisions in one struct: uniqueIndex on slug The URL is a key, and the database enforces it sanitize:"html" The body is cleaned on every write. See below Published plus PublishedAt State and the moment it changed Version Optimistic locking, from chapter thirty three DeletedAt Soft delete, so an unpublish is never a loss The slug is generated in a BeforeCreate hook, which is the right place for it: a title is typed once and the slug must exist whichever surface created the row, including a seeder and an import. A rich text editor produces HTML, and HTML from a user is an attack surface with a text box attached. The tag says what to do about it: Every write that has a model passes through the sanitiser, so a <script> in a draft does not survive being saved. Not on render, on write , which matters because the content will be read by more things than your web page: an RSS feed, a mobile app, a newsletter. Watch out Sanitising on render rather than on write is the mistake that keeps coming back, because it works perfectly until the second reader exists. The database holds the attack, and every new consumer has to remember to defuse it. Sanitise once, at the boundary where the data arrives. Then the thing in the database is safe, and the number of places that have to be careful is one rather than one per feature. Publishing is not a column edit. It is a transition with consequences: Three things in that function are worth copying into whatever you build next. It refuses an empty post. The rule lives here, so the admin, the API and a scheduled publish all obey it. It is idempotent. Publishing something already published returns it rather than erroring. Retries happen, double clicks happen, and a second publish should not move PublishedAt . It emits an event rather than doing the downstream work inline. Chapter forty four is about the bus; what matters here is that "tell the newsletter" is not the publishing function's business. The generated endpoints are behind authentication, which is right for an admin and useless for readers. A public-facing resource asks for a second, narrower surface: That adds a list and a get-by-slug under /api/v1/public/ , mounted outside the auth middleware. The protected routes are untouched, because the admin still calls those. Two properties of that surface are the whole design. The response is an allowlist, not the model. A public response is its own struct, built from the fields that are publishable by default: names, slugs, descriptions, images. Anything whose name contains cost , margin , profit , internal , note , secret , token , supplier or wholesale is excluded whatever its type, and foreign keys and stock counts are left out too. A column added next month is private until somebody says otherwise. That is the opposite default to the admin surface, and it is the right one when the audience is the internet: the alternative, publishing everything and trusting the developer to remove what should not be there, puts a cost_price column on the web the first time somebody adds one in a hurry. To publish a field that was excluded, you edit one struct, deliberately, in a diff somebody can review. Watch out The public group is guarded by an API key, which is not secrecy: a publishable key ships inside your app where anybody can read it. What it buys is identification, a rate limit bucket per key, per-endpoint and per-origin narrowing, and the ability to turn one client off without a deploy. Treat it as a name badge rather than a password. Responses on the public group are cached, and nowhere else. The cache key is the URL and nothing else: On a public endpoint that is exactly right. Every caller gets the same answer, so one cached copy serves all of them and an article page stops hitting the database on every visit. Watch out *Never mount a writing endpoint on the public group, and never move this cache onto an authenticated one.* The second is the dangerous one: with the URL as the key, GET /api/v1/ invoices cached for one user is served to the next user who asks. One line of middleware in the wrong group is a data breach that passes every test, because tests usually run one user at a time. --public is read-only by design. A public write , a comment form, a newsletter signup, is a hand-written endpoint with its own rate limit and its own validation, and it does not belong on a cached group. The public list, in a server component: And the article page, by slug rather than ID, which is why the public endpoint looks up by slug: If you know JavaScript dangerouslySetInnerHTML is doing what its name says, and it is acceptable here for one reason only: the HTML was sanitised on write. If you are ever tempted to render untrusted HTML that has not been through a sanitiser, the answer is not a careful regular expression. It is a library, on the way in. Metadata comes from the same fetch, so the social preview and the page agree: Four small pieces, each about twenty lines, none of them framework specific: A sitemap. app/sitemap.ts fetching the public list and returning the URLs with their published_at as lastModified . An RSS feed. A route handler returning XML. Readers still use them, and so do aggregators that will send you traffic. Related posts. The public surface can expose a related endpoint; otherwise it is a query by tag with the current article excluded. A reading time. Word count divided by two hundred
pages.title: The model you already have

headings: The four shapes, and the question each answers
The admin dropdown, and the label it shows
one_to_one is belongs_to plus one index
A relation pointing at itself is a tree
many_to_many, and the table you did not name
Line items: a child inside its parent
What relationships cost on a list page
pages.text: A model on its own is a spreadsheet. The moment a task belongs to a project and carries tags, you have the thing that makes applications hard: two tables that must agree, a form that has to offer the right options, a query that must not run once per row, and a JSON shape the frontend can rely on. Grit has four relationship shapes. This chapter is what each one writes, and where each one bites. belongs_to This row points at one other row. A task has a project one_to_one The same, but only one row may point at each target. A user has one profile many_to_many Both sides have many. A task has tags, a tag has tasks --items A child that exists only inside its parent. An invoice has line items The fourth is not a field type, and the difference is worth naming early: an --items child has no life of its own. You do not browse line items; you edit an invoice. Everything else is a relation between two things that each exist. The related model is the third part, and it is optional when the field name already names it: project:belongs_to finds Project . Spell it out when the field is called something else, which is the usual case for people: author:belongs_to:User . In the model you get two things, not one: ProjectID is the column the database knows about, indexed because every listing filters on it. Project is the association GORM fills in when asked, and it is a *pointer with omitempty *. Watch out That pointer is not a style choice, and the version before it shipped a convincing bug. As a value, a relation that was never preloaded marshalled as a complete zero-value object: "project": {"id": 0, "name": "", "colour": ""} . To a client that reads as a real project whose every field happens to be blank, and the generated TypeScript agreed, because it said the object was always there. As a pointer with omitempty , an absent relation is absent. The frontend can tell "not loaded" from "loaded and empty", which are different facts and used to be the same one. The service preloads it, so a list of tasks arrives with its projects: That is chapter twenty two's N+1 solved by default: one query for tasks, one for the projects they reference, rather than one per row. You get it without asking, which is also why it is worth knowing it is there when a list of twelve columns suddenly reads from five tables. The form field for a belongs_to is a searchable dropdown, and the thing that makes it usable is what it displays. It is not the ID, and it is not a field called whatever came first. The generator looks for a label column on the related model, in this order: The first one that exists wins. A Project shows its name, an Invoice shows its number, and a User with none of those falls back to its email, which is the reason the fallback list ends there rather than at code . If you know JavaScript Every admin panel you have built by hand has had this bug: a select showing [object Object] , or a list of IDs, or a dropdown that loads six thousand rows to find one. The generated one searches server side and shows a human label. It is a small thing that is tedious to get right once per relation, and there are usually twenty relations. The generated code differs from belongs_to in exactly one place: the foreign key gets a unique index rather than an ordinary one. That single line is what makes the name true. Without it, "one profile per user" is a comment, because the database would happily accept a second row pointing at the same user, and the second one usually arrives from a retried request rather than from a user doing something strange. Electronics above Cameras above Lenses, in one table. Two details differ from an ordinary relation, and both were found the hard way. The association must be a pointer. Go rejects a struct that contains itself by value: invalid recursive type . A generated project with a self-reference did not compile at all before this was handled. The foreign key must be nullable. GORM creates a real foreign key constraint, and a root category has no parent, so the column has to hold something the constraint accepts. SQL has exactly one such value, and it is NULL . Watch out An earlier version used the empty string for "no parent", matching what every other belongs_to field does. It passed every test and failed on the first real project: The tests ran on SQLite, which does not enforce foreign keys unless you ask it to. Postgres does. The generated tests now switch foreign keys on for exactly this reason, and the general lesson is larger than trees: *a test database that is more permissive than production is a test database that hides this class of bug entirely*. For a real hierarchy, the flag does more than the field: That gives the self-referential parent plus a materialized path, a depth, a sibling order, the tree queries and a move endpoint. The difference matters when you need "everything under Electronics" as one query rather than as recursion in application code. The related model is required here. There is nothing to infer from, because tags is a plural of the field, not of the model. The model gets a slice and no foreign key, because the keys live in a third table: The join table is named from the owning model and the field: tasks_tags . GORM creates and maintains it, and you do not get a model for it. Watch out The moment you need a column on the relationship itself , a quantity, a role, a date added, many_to_many is the wrong shape and no flag fixes it. "A user belongs to many projects" is many-to-many. "A user belongs to many projects as owner or as member " is a Membership model with two belongs_to fields and a role , generated like any other resource. Reaching for the join table as a place to put data is the single most common modelling mistake in this chapter, and it is expensive because the migration that fixes it has to move rows. In the admin this renders as a multi-select picker, and in JSON it is an array, which means a create or update sends IDs: The child is generated fully, and t
