headings: Step three: the rule, in the only place it can live
Step five: data worth looking at
Step six: the admin screen, customised
Step seven: a page the admin cannot be
Step eight: a form for people without accounts
Step nine: the things that make it a product
pages.text: Part IV explained the pieces. This chapter uses them, in order, to build something a small team could actually run: projects, tasks with a status and an assignee, comments, a dashboard, and a web page that is not the admin panel. Everything here is a command you type and a file you open. Nothing is skipped for space, and the parts that are genuinely tedious are called tedious rather than hidden. A tracker with three models and one rule that matters: Project A name, a colour, an owner. Archived rather than deleted Task Belongs to a project, has a status, an assignee and a due date Comment Belongs to a task, written by a user The rule: a task cannot be closed while it has open subtasks , which is the kind of thing that is trivial to state, easy to enforce in one place, and impossible to enforce if it lives in a form. Three applications come up: the API on :8080 , the web app on :3000 and the admin on :3001 . Log in with the seeded admin account printed in the output, and confirm the dashboard renders before generating anything. A broken starting point is worth five minutes to rule out. Watch out If the admin loads and the lists are empty while the API logs show nothing, the usual cause is that migrations have not run. grit migrate once, then reload. The second most common cause is a port already in use from an earlier project, which shows up as a login that posts and does nothing because :8080 belongs to somebody else. grit doctor reports both. Generate the parent first, because the child refers to it: Then the task, with the relationship and a real status: And the comment: Then once: Reload the admin. Three new sections in the sidebar, each with a working list and form. The task form has two dropdowns with labels rather than raw values, a date picker, a rich text editor, and two searchable relationship pickers. If you know JavaScript Count what you did not do. No table component, no form library wiring, no <select> with hand-written options, no fetch hook, no TypeScript interface, no Zod schema, no migration file, no route registration. That is chapter twenty nine's claim arriving. The reason it is worth distrusting until you have done it is that most tools make the same claim and stop at the list page. Open apps/api/internal/services/task.go and add a method. This is chapter thirty two, applied: The subtask relationship needs a column, which is one command rather than a migration file: A self-referencing belongs_to is legal and useful: it is how a task gets subtasks without a second model. Watch out s.db(ctx) rather than s.DB . The first is scoped by the actor in the context, the second is not. On a --owned-by user resource that one difference decides whether the subtask count includes other people's tasks. It will look correct in your own testing, because you are the only user, which is exactly why this is the bug that reaches production. Register it next to the generated routes: And teach the boundary what the new error means, so the frontend gets a 409 rather than a 500: Check it is wired: That prints every registered route with its method, handler and middleware group, which is the fastest way to catch a route registered on the wrong group and therefore unauthenticated. An empty application tells you nothing about whether it works: Four hundred tasks is where the list page stops being a demo. Sort by due date, filter by status, search a title, and page through. Pagination is server side, so the browser is holding twenty rows no matter how many exist. Your turn Seed a hundred thousand tasks and try the same screen. It stays quick, because the query is doing the work rather than the client. Then sort by a column the service did not whitelist and watch nothing happen. That is chapter thirty two's whitelist, and it is also the reason the first sort you add by hand appears to be ignored. The generated list is correct and plain. Two changes make it usable, and both live in apps/admin/app/_dashboard/resources/task/index.tsx . A status badge rather than a word: And an overdue due date, because a date that is late should look late: Re-run the generator for Task afterwards and confirm these survive. They are in the file the generator writes once. An operator console is not a product. The team wants a board, so write one as an ordinary Next.js page using the generated hooks: Moving a card calls the same API the admin does: Nothing here is framework-specific. It is React against typed hooks, and the types came from the Go model through chapter thirty six's shared package, so renaming due in the model makes this page fail to compile rather than fail in front of a user. Watch out Resist putting the "cannot close with open subtasks" check in this page. It is one line of JavaScript and it is wrong, because the board is not the only caller. Call the endpoint, show the 409's message, and let the rule live once. The test is always chapter twenty eight's: would it still have to be true if a nightly job did it? Bug reports should not require an admin login. One command writes the page: That emits a Next.js page with one input per field, submitting through the authenticated create hook. For a genuinely public form, create a form share in the admin under System, then: which posts to the public submission endpoint instead, with no account required. Watch out A public write endpoint is a spam target the hour it is discovered. The share token is revocable in the admin, and the form share is rate limited, but the decision about what a stranger may create is yours. The safer shape for a bug reporter: a public form that creates a Report , and a human who turns a report into a Task . One extra model, and no stranger ever writes to the table the team works from. Four small commands, each closing something a client will ask about: A role that the sidebar, the forms and the seeded permissions all know about. A backup you have actually taken. A health check across the project. A route list you have read, looking for
pages.title: What we are building

headings: What is worth testing, and what is not
The highest-value test in the whole project
Allocation budgets, and a trap in the toolchain
pages.text: Chapter eighteen taught the mechanics. This chapter is the harder question: in an application where most of the code was generated, what is worth testing , and which tests pay for the time they cost. The short answer: do not test the generator. Test the things you wrote, the boundaries you configured, and the one property whose failure is silent. A new project comes with tests, and they are worth reading before you add any: auth_test.go Register and login, success and every failure user_test.go The auth guard, an admin list, a 404, a success bench_test.go Health check, login, register perf_test.go Allocation budgets for the per-request hot path __tests__/ Component tests with Vitest and Testing Library e2e/ Playwright: the auth flow and the admin One report, and suites that do not apply to your architecture are reported as skipped with the reason rather than quietly dropped. A test suite that silently does not run is worse than no suite, because it reports green. This one is worth the whole chapter, because it produces a test that fails six runs in ten and looks like a broken login. *Every connection to :memory: gets its own empty database.* The pool opens a second connection as soon as two queries overlap, and in this project they do, because registering a user writes an activity row on a goroutine. The login that follows lands on a fresh, empty database, finds no user, and returns 401. Watch out The failure reads as a broken login rather than a test harness problem, which is why it costs an afternoon. The tell is the flakiness: *a test that passes about six runs in ten is almost never a race in your code and almost always a race in your fixture*. One connection, and only one. If you need concurrency in a test, use a file database in a temporary directory instead. The same harness makes a second decision worth copying. The email verification token table is deliberately not migrated , because that write happens on a goroutine so a slow SMTP call cannot hold the response open. Creating the table would turn a harmless early return into a background writer racing whatever the test does next. If you are testing verification itself, migrate that table in that test and call the service directly rather than through the register handler. Do not test That a generated create returns 201. The generator's own tests cover it, and your copy adds nothing Test Every rule you wrote in a service, especially the refusals Test The whitelists, by asserting their contents Test Ownership isolation between two users Test The error boundary: each error kind maps to the status you expect Test Anything that broke once. A bug without a test comes back The whitelist one is not obvious, and chapter forty's date-sorting story is why: the pagination layer drops a sort it does not recognise rather than rejecting it, so a missing column fails silently and the endpoint still returns 200. Four lines, and they catch a class of bug that no endpoint test catches. Most of your tests belong here. The rules live in services, so testing them through HTTP adds a router, a body, a status code and a JSON decode to every assertion, for nothing. Note the assertion is on the sentinel , not on a message. The message is allowed to change; the identity of the error is the contract, which is chapter eleven's whole point arriving in a test file. Test at the HTTP level only what is about HTTP: the status code, the envelope, the headers. The decode into an int is the assertion. If the server ever regresses to sending "9" as a string, this fails, which is the bug chapter thirty three said shipped once. In a multi-user application this is the test to write first and run in CI forever. The bug it catches is silent, is not a crash, produces no error in any log, and is the one you cannot apologise your way out of. Watch out Write it once per ownership-scoped resource , not once per project. The scoping is applied per service, and the one that was added last month by somebody in a hurry is the one missing s.db(ctx) . A table-driven version over every scoped service is about thirty lines and catches the regression on the day it is introduced. perf_test.go asserts how many allocations the hot path makes: A benchmark tells you how long something took on the machine that ran it, which on a shared CI runner moves on its own. An allocation count does not move with the machine or the load, which is what makes these assertions rather than measurements, and why they can fail a build when a benchmark cannot. Watch out Allocation counts do move with the Go toolchain, by more than you would guess: fifteen fewer allocations for the same work between two releases. So a budget is set from the oldest toolchain the project supports, because that is the one that allocates most. Set it from whatever is installed on your laptop and it passes locally and fails in CI, which is how that file first failed. When a budget fails, it is telling you a change allocates more than it used to. That is not automatically wrong: read the change, decide whether the cost is worth it, and if it is, raise the budget in the same commit , so the next person can see the new number was a decision. Component tests with Vitest and Testing Library, for logic that lives in the browser: a form that disables its button, a list that shows an empty state, a hook that retries. Fast, and they run on every save. End-to-end tests with Playwright, for the three or four flows that must never break: sign in, create the central record, and whatever your application exists to do. They are slow and they are flaky in proportion to how many you have, so keep the set small and keep it meaningful. If you know JavaScript The temptation is to write end-to-end tests for everything, because they feel like proof. The cost arrives later: a suite that takes twenty minutes and fails for unrelated reasons twice a week gets marked "allowed to fail", and then it is decoration. Rule of thumb: an end-to-end test for every flo

headings: Deployment, in the order of effort
Two deployment bugs worth not repeating
The checklist before a first deploy
pages.text: Two things decide whether a framework is a help or a trap, and neither is visible on the day you start: can you take a new version without a rewrite, and can somebody else run this when you are not available. This chapter closes Part V with both, plus the handover that the last project of your career will thank you for. A framework that generates code into your project has a problem a library does not: it wrote files, you edited them, and the next version wants to write them again. There are three possible answers, and two of them are bad. Overwrite Your edits are gone. Nobody upgrades twice Never touch Framework fixes never reach existing projects. Everybody is stranded on the version they started with Know which Track what was generated, leave what changed Files Grit wrote and you have not touched are regenerated. Files you have edited are left alone and reported , because the upgrade knows the difference: each generated file was recorded when it was written, and a file whose content no longer matches is yours. Watch out --force is a real option and it is occasionally right, for instance when you edited a file by accident and want it back. Commit first. Then --force is a diff you can read and revert, rather than a decision you cannot undo. This is true of every generator command that writes into your project, and it is worth a habit rather than a rule. Three things, and the second is the one people do not expect. It regenerates framework-owned files. The admin panel's shared components, the configs, the web app shell. It repairs generated code it does not own. Your services are yours, and upgrade does not rewrite them. But a framework fix that only the generator carries reaches new resources and leaves every existing one broken, so there are targeted repairs that go and fix one specific thing in files the upgrade otherwise leaves alone. "A record with a price cannot be saved" is not something to leave broken on existing projects because of a rule about ownership. It upgrades installed plugins. Left to a command of its own, nobody runs it, and a plugin fix reaches nobody. Watch out A repair finds its target by matching an anchor in your file. If your version of that file has drifted far enough, the anchor is not found, and the repair warns and returns rather than guessing. So read the warnings from an upgrade . They are the list of places where the framework wanted to fix something and could not reach it, and each one is a manual edit somebody has to make. Releases follow channels: a plain version is stable, and a version with an -rc , -beta or -alpha suffix is not. grit update stays on stable unless you ask otherwise, which is what you want on the machine you work from. Upgrade the CLI and the project separately, in that order, and *test a fresh project after upgrading the CLI*. A scaffold template change only shows up in something newly generated. One binary go build , copy, run under systemd. Chapter twenty five grit deploy Build, upload over SSH, configure systemd, optionally Caddy with automatic TLS grit deploy --railway Link the project, push the variables from .env , upload the API, generate a URL Docker Compose docker-compose.prod.yml , for a single machine with Postgres and Redis beside it A platform Any host that runs a container. The API is one image Start at the top. A Go API on one server under systemd, with Caddy in front for TLS, serves a great deal more traffic than most applications ever see, and it is a stack you can hold in your head at three in the morning. If you know JavaScript Coming from Next.js, the thing that takes adjusting is that there is no build output to upload and no Node runtime to match. One file, built on your machine, copied to the server. The frontends are still Next.js and still need their own hosting or their own container. The simplification is on the API side, and it is the half that used to need the most care. Both of these were real, and both have the same shape: a path guessed from the wrong directory. The module is not where you are standing. In a monorepo the Go module is in apps/api , and reading go.mod from the repository root finds nothing. The deploy announced itself, named the app grit-app , and then failed on "go.mod file not found". A module's base name is not the application's name. The module is invoices/apps/api , whose base is api , so the systemd unit, the remote directory and the binary were all called api . Two Grit projects on one server would have overwritten each other. Watch out The general lesson for any deployment script you write: *derive names from something that identifies the project*, and print every derived value before acting on it. A deploy that says "deploying api to /srv/api" gives somebody the chance to stop it; one that says "deploying" does not. Run these and read the output rather than assuming: Then the environment: APP_URL Correct, and matching the real port. Uploads build their URLs from it JWT_SECRET Generated for this environment, not copied from the example file Database Postgres, with a password that was not in a repository Sentinel storage Pointed at the real database, not the SQLite file that a redeploy deletes MAIL_MAILER A real driver, configured, and tested by sending one Backups Scheduled, and restored once to prove they work Watch out The one people skip is the restore. A backup that has never been restored is a file, not a backup, and the first restore attempt is not the moment to discover it is missing the uploads or the schema. Restore into a scratch database, open the application against it, and look at a record. Then you have a backup. The last thing a project needs is for somebody else to be able to run it. Four files, none of them long: * README.md *: what this is, the three commands to run it locally, and where the environment variables come from. * ARCHITECTURE.md *: the request path from route to query, and where rules live. Chapter twenty eight's assignment, kept up to date. * RUNBO

headings: A file field, and what it stores
What happens to an image on the way in
Your own profile, when the default is wrong
The decompression bomb, which the size limit cannot see
pages.text: D9 was "a user uploads a ten megabyte photo from their phone, and it is served to every visitor at ten megabytes". It is the most predictable performance problem in web software, it is never the thing anybody plans for, and it has a second half nobody mentions: that photo arrives with the GPS coordinates of the house it was taken in. This chapter is what a file field does, what happens to an image between the form and the disk, and the two attacks that live in this feature. file is one, files is many. The column does not hold a path. It holds a structured reference: If you know JavaScript A bare URL string is what everybody stores first, and it is missing exactly the fields a page needs. Without width and height the browser cannot reserve space, so the layout jumps as images load, which is most of a bad Cumulative Layout Shift score. Without name you cannot show the user what they uploaded. Without mime you are guessing from the extension. Without thumbnail_url a list page downloads full-size images to draw at 60 pixels. optimised: false is the one people miss: it says the pipeline failed and the original was stored untouched, which is a thing you want to be able to find later. S3, R2, Spaces Production. Any S3-compatible object store MinIO The same API, in Docker, for local development Local disk STORAGE_DRIVER=local . No object store at all The local driver is the one to use while learning. It needs nothing running, and uploads land in a directory the API serves. Watch out With STORAGE_DRIVER=local , every stored file's URL is built from APP_URL . Change APP_PORT without changing APP_URL and every upload gets a URL pointing at a port nothing is listening on. The upload succeeds, the file is on disk, and the image is broken, which sends people hunting through the storage code for a bug that is in an environment variable. On a phone or another machine, the same applies to localhost : an image URL that says localhost resolves to the phone itself. Mobile clients rewrite the host for this reason, and MinIO has to be published on the LAN address rather than 127.0.0.1 . Every image field runs through a profile. The default one is a set of decisions somebody would otherwise have to research: 1600 Covers a 2x retina display at a typical content width. Storing more is paying to keep pixels no browser will draw 0.82 The point at which JPEG is visually indistinguishable from source. Below about 0.75, gradients and skin show artifacts 400 The thumbnail an admin row or a card grid needs at 2x Auto Encode to the best format the client can take, usually WebP Measured on a 5.3 MB phone photo: 147 KB out, including the thumbnail . That is D9 closed, and it happened without anybody remembering to do it. Three more things happen in the same pass, and two of them are not about size. EXIF orientation is applied. A portrait photo from a phone is usually stored landscape with a rotation flag, and a naive decode produces a sideways thumbnail. Metadata is stripped. Including GPS coordinates. A photograph taken at home and uploaded to a public listing carries the house's location in a field nobody looks at, and stripping it is not a feature request anybody files: it is something a framework should do by default. Renditions are derived. The thumbnail comes from the decoded original rather than from the resized copy, so it is not a resize of a resize. A clothing retailer wants more pixels and higher quality than a blog does. A document scan wants no lossy compression at all. The profile is the one place that decision lives, rather than being spread across the upload handler, the list page and whatever the mobile app does. The chainable API is there when you need something bespoke: An operation that fails does not panic and does not return its own error. The error travels down the chain and comes out of Encode or Store , which is what makes the chain readable. This is the line that stops a specific attack, and it is worth understanding because the obvious defence does not work. A solid-colour PNG compresses to almost nothing whatever its dimensions. *165 kilobytes on the wire can be 144 megapixels decoded.* Measured, one such upload allocated 224 MB, and ten concurrent uploads would have been 2.2 GB, which is the process gone. Your file size limit cannot see it, because on disk the file is small. The header is read first, the pixel count is computed before any pixels are allocated, and an image claiming more than the profile allows is refused without being decoded. Watch out Fifty megapixels is chosen to pass a 48 megapixel professional camera frame and refuse the bomb. If you raise it, raise it with a number in mind rather than to make one complaint go away. The same reasoning applies to the upload cap of 50 MB. Limits that exist for a reason should carry the reason in a comment, or the next person removes them during a demo. A transform that fails stores the original untouched and marks the ref optimised: false . The alternative, Reject , refuses the upload. Storing a large image is a worse outcome than storing a small one, and both are much better than losing the user's file because your encoder did not like something. The failures are findable afterwards, and a reprocess pass can retry them. Watch out DiscardOriginal is deliberately phrased in the negative, and the story is a general lesson about defaults in Go. It began as KeepOriginal , which read better. But profiles are merged with the defaults field by field, and a bool has no way to say "unset": every profile that did not mention KeepOriginal had it as false , so the original was silently discarded while the documentation promised the opposite. The rule: *in a struct that gets merged with defaults, the zero value must be the recommended behaviour*. Where it cannot be, use a pointer and treat nil as unset. The admin has a dropzone component, and the generated form uses it for any file or files field. Behind it is an ordinary multipart POST: Watch out Do no

headings: Why a tree and not a hash
Leaves hold data, internal nodes hold directions
Durability, and the page that was half written
A buffer pool, because reading the same page is silly
Testing a data structure you cannot see
pages.text: The key-value store in chapter fifty one has a limit it does not advertise: on startup it replays the whole log into a map, so the index lives in memory and the startup time grows with the data. At a few hundred megabytes that is fine. At fifty gigabytes it is not a database, it is a long wait. The answer is an index that lives on disk and is read a page at a time. That is what every real database does, and the structure is nearly always a B-tree. A hash map finds one key in constant time, and that is all it does. A database needs more: Range scan WHERE created_at > ? reads a contiguous run of keys Ordering ORDER BY with no sort step Prefix LIKE 'inv-2026%' is a range Locality Nearby keys are on the same page, so one read serves many A B-tree gives all four because it keeps keys in order, and it is shaped for disks rather than for memory: wide and shallow, so finding a key costs very few reads. If you know JavaScript The arithmetic is the whole argument. With a 4 KB page and keys around 30 bytes, one page holds roughly a hundred entries. One hundred to the power of three is a million. So a million keys is *three page reads deep*, and a hundred million is four. A binary tree with the same million keys is twenty levels, which is twenty seeks. Depth is the number of disk reads, and fanout is how you buy it down. Everything is read and written in whole pages, at offset int64(id) * PageSize . The size matches what the operating system and the disk move anyway, so a partial read costs the same as a full one. A page starts with a header, then entries: Fixed offsets, little endian, no reflection, no JSON. The point of a page format is that reading it is a few binary.LittleEndian.Uint16 calls, not a decoder. This is a B+tree, which is what databases actually use: Two properties follow, and both matter. All values are in the leaves. An internal node is only directions, so it fits more separators, so the fanout is higher and the tree is shallower. Leaves are linked. A range scan descends once and then walks sideways, reading consecutive pages without touching the tree again. search is a binary search inside the page , because the keys in a page are sorted: Note the loop in Get rather than recursion. Descending a tree iteratively costs nothing extra and removes any question about stack depth. Inserting is "find the leaf, put it in". The interesting half is what happens when the leaf is full. The split propagates: if the parent is now full, it splits too. If the root splits, a new root is made above it and the tree gets one level deeper . That is the only way a B-tree grows in height, which is why its depth is uniform and why every lookup costs the same. Watch out fits() rather than "count < max". Keys and values are variable length, so a page is full when the bytes no longer fit, not when some count is reached. Writing this as a count works perfectly until a long key arrives, and then corrupts a page by overwriting the one after it. Size the check in bytes and test it with a key that is deliberately enormous. Textbook B-trees merge underfull nodes and rebalance. It is fiddly, it is where the subtle bugs live, and many real systems do something simpler: Mark the entry deleted and leave the page alone. Space is reclaimed when the page is rewritten or during a compaction pass. The cost is pages that are emptier than they could be, which costs reads. The benefit is a much smaller surface for corruption. Start here, and implement merging only when you can measure that it matters. Pages become free when a compaction empties them. Without a list of them, the file only grows: The free list lives in a page of its own, usually near the start, and it is the second thing to write after the root pointer. A page write is not atomic. The power goes out, and 4096 bytes are partly old and partly new: a torn page . A B-tree with a torn internal node is not a tree with one bad row, it is a tree that cannot be traversed. Two defences, and real databases pick one: Write-ahead log Write the change to a log and fsync it, then update the page. Recovery replays the log. This is chapter fifty one's machinery, reused Copy on write Never overwrite a live page. Write a new one, then flip the root pointer with one small atomic write Copy on write is the one to build first here, because it fits the structure: The top two levels of the tree are read on every single lookup, so caching turns three reads into one. A few thousand pages of cache covers the internal nodes of a surprisingly large tree, and that is why databases want memory. Three techniques, in increasing order of how much they find. Differential testing against a sorted map. Any sequence of operations must produce the same answers as map plus a sort: An invariant check. Walk the tree and assert: keys sorted within each page, every key in a child within its parent's separators, all leaves at the same depth, pages at least half full except the root. Run it after every thousand inserts in a test. A crash test. Kill the process mid-write, reopen, and check the invariants plus every acknowledged key. This is the one that finds the fsync ordering bug, and nothing else will. Project 48: the index, measured In part6-from-scratch/52-btree , build it and then find out what you built. One: pages. A pager with read , write , allocate , a free list and a header page. Test that reopening finds the root. Two: the tree. Get , Put , Delete with tombstones, splits for leaves and internal nodes, and a root split that deepens the tree. Three: the invariant checker , run after every thousand operations in a test. Four: the differential test against a reference map, with fifty thousand random keys. Five: ranges. Scan(from, to) using the leaf links. Prove with a timing that scanning ten thousand consecutive keys is far cheaper than ten thousand Get calls. Six: the depth. Insert one million keys and report the tree height and the fanout you achieved. Compare it with the arithmetic at the top o

headings: Everything is an object, named by its hash
Trees, and the format that catches everybody
References, and what a branch is
The index, and why it exists
pages.text: Git is the tool you use most and understand least. Its interface is famously awkward and its data model is famously elegant, and the gap between those two facts is why most people learn commands rather than concepts. The model is small enough to implement in an afternoon: a content-addressed store with four object types. By the end of this chapter your program will write objects that the real git command reads, and git log will show commits your code created. An object is stored as: compressed with zlib, and its name is the SHA-1 of that whole thing , uncompressed, in hexadecimal. The path is the first two hex characters as a directory and the rest as the filename: Fifteen lines, and that function is the whole of Git's identity model. If you know JavaScript "Content addressed" means the name is the content, which has three consequences that explain most of Git's behaviour. Identical files are stored once , however many directories or branches contain them. Nothing can be modified. Changing a file produces a different hash, so it is a new object. The old one is still there. A commit's hash covers its entire history , because it names its tree and its parent, which name theirs. That is why rewriting one old commit changes the hash of every commit after it, and why a force push is a different history rather than an edited one. That is a valid repository. git status will run in it. HEAD is a symbolic reference : a file containing the name of another reference. That one indirection is the entire branch mechanism. Switching branches rewrites that line; a detached HEAD is the same file containing a hash instead. Two details that are not accidents. *If the file exists, you already have the content*, because the name is the content, so there is nothing to compare. And the mode is 0444 , read-only: objects are immutable, and the filesystem is told so. A tree is a sequence of entries, with no separators and no JSON: The modes are a short list: 100644 a file, 100755 an executable, 40000 a directory, 120000 a symlink, 160000 a submodule. They look like Unix permissions and are not: Git stores only whether a file is executable. Watch out Two things here will produce objects real Git rejects, and both are silent. The hash is twenty raw bytes, not forty hex characters. It is the one place in the format where the hash is not text. Entries must be sorted , and the sort is not plain byte order on the name: a directory sorts as though its name ended with / . So lib.rs comes before lib/ , which is the opposite of what a naive sort gives. Get either wrong and your objects hash differently from Git's for the same content, which means your repository and a real one disagree about history that is identical. Check with git cat-file -p early rather than after building three more layers. Plain text, which is why git cat-file -p HEAD is readable. Zero parents is the first commit. One parent is ordinary. *Two or more parents is a merge*, and that is the entire representation of merging: a commit that points at both histories. There is no other record of a merge anywhere in Git. A branch is a file containing forty one bytes. That is the whole implementation. It explains things that otherwise seem arbitrary. Creating a branch is instant because it writes one small file. Deleting a branch deletes a file and *not a single commit*, which is why the commits are still there and git reflog can find them. Moving a branch is overwriting those forty one bytes, which is what reset --hard does. git log with no flags does exactly this: follow the first parent. The difference between that and --graph is whether you also walk the other parents of merges, which needs a queue ordered by commit time and is where log's real complexity lives. The staging area is a file, .git/index , holding the paths and hashes that will go into the next tree, plus the stat information Git uses to decide whether a file changed without reading it. That last part is the real purpose. git status in a repository with a hundred thousand files is fast because it compares size and modification time from the index rather than hashing every file. For this project, a simple text index is enough: Real Git's index is binary and versioned. Replacing it is a chapter of its own, and it is the right thing to leave out. Packfiles Thousands of objects delta-compressed into one file. This is how a repository stays small, and it is the biggest omission here The network git fetch and git push speak their own protocol, with negotiation about which objects the other side lacks Merging Creating a merge commit is easy. Computing the merged content is a three-way diff algorithm Rebase Replaying commits onto a new base, which is merge plus bookkeeping Loose objects are correct and are what Git itself writes before gc runs. Your repository will simply be larger than it needs to be, which for a learning project is not a cost at all. Watch out SHA-1 is broken for collision resistance, and Git still uses it. That is survivable because Git is not using the hash as a security control against a motivated attacker with your repository, and because Git adds a collision detection step on top. The project has a SHA-256 mode and a long transition plan, because changing the hash changes every object name in every repository that exists. The lesson worth taking: an identifier is a decision you cannot reverse . If you build a content-addressed anything today, use SHA-256, and store the algorithm next to the hash so the next change is possible. Project 51: a repository real Git can read In part6-from-scratch/55-git , build it, and validate against the real thing at every step. *One: init and hash-object .* Hash a file with your tool and with real Git: The two hashes must be identical. If they are not, stop here: your header format is wrong and nothing later will work. *Two: cat-file .* Read any object back, printing its type, size and contents. Check against git cat-file -p . *Three: write-tree .
pages.title: Everything is an object, named by its hash

headings: What a good CLI does, before any code
Cancellation that is not a kill
Output humans read and machines parse
pages.text: Every tool you write grows a command line eventually, and most people reach straight for Cobra without ever knowing what it does. A command framework is about three hundred lines. Writing one makes every CLI you use afterwards legible, and it is the fastest way to learn what separates a tool people enjoy from one they tolerate. We are building: nested subcommands, per-command flags, generated help, "did you mean", correct exit codes, and cancellation on Ctrl-C. The design decisions matter more than the parser: Exit codes 0 success, 1 failure, 2 usage error. Scripts read these Streams Results to stdout, diagnostics to stderr. Always Help Generated from the commands, never written twice Errors Say what to do next, not just what went wrong Cancellation Ctrl-C stops the work, it does not kill it mid-write If you know JavaScript The stream rule is the one JavaScript developers break most, because console.log goes to stdout and it is right there. The consequence shows up the first time somebody writes mytool list > out.json and finds a progress message in the middle of their JSON. Results on stdout, everything else on stderr, and the tool becomes something people can build on. Everything else in this chapter is built from that struct. Note what it does not have: no global state, no init() registration, no singleton root. A command tree is a value you can build in a test. Walking the tree is a loop, not recursion, and it stops at the first argument that is not a known subcommand: So tool db migrate --dry-run status.json finds migrate and hands it ["--dry-run", "status.json"] . Then parse that command's own flags and run it: Watch out flag.Parse stops at the first non-flag argument. tool add file.txt -v leaves -v in the arguments rather than setting the flag, and the user sees nothing happen. Go's own tools accept this; GNU tools do not. Decide which you are, say so in the help, and if you want flags anywhere, sort the arguments before parsing rather than writing your own parser. This is the design decision that most improves a CLI, and almost nobody makes it deliberately. A usage error means the command was typed wrong: an unknown flag, a missing argument. Print the error, then the usage, and exit 2. The flag list is exactly what the user needs. Every other error means the command was fine and the work failed: a file was missing, the server refused, the database was down. Print the error and exit 1, without the usage . Watch out Printing the flag list under "connection refused" is the most common CLI mistake there is. It buries the one sentence that matters under forty lines of options, and it implies the user typed something wrong when they did not. Grit's own CLI sets SilenceUsage the moment it knows the flags parsed and the project was found, for exactly this reason. If you take one thing from this chapter into a tool you already maintain, take this one. 130 is the conventional code for "killed by Ctrl-C", and scripts do check it. Help that is written by hand goes stale on the first new flag. Generate it: The io.Writer parameter is not decoration. It is what makes the help testable without capturing os.Stdout, which is chapter twenty's lesson applied to a command line. A typo should not produce a wall of help. It should produce one suggestion: Edit distance, bounded so nonsense suggests nothing: distance is Levenshtein, about twenty lines with two rows rather than a full matrix. Writing it once is worth it: the same function powers "did you mean" in every tool you will ever write, and in your API's error messages for an unknown field. The first interrupt cancels the context, so the command can finish writing the file it is in the middle of and exit cleanly. The second one exits immediately, because a user pressing Ctrl-C twice has stopped asking politely. Every long-running command then has one obligation, from chapter sixteen: *check ctx.Done() *. A command that ignores it is a command Ctrl-C cannot stop. The same command often has two audiences: Two rules make this work. The JSON goes to stdout and nothing else does , or piping it breaks. And colour is disabled when stdout is not a terminal , or your pipeline fills with escape codes: NO_COLOR is an agreed convention. Honour it, and the people who need it will never have to ask you to. Because nothing is global, a test builds a tree and runs it: If you know JavaScript Compare this with testing a CLI built on package-level variables and init() registration, which is the shape most tutorials teach. There, every test shares one root, flags keep values between tests, and the only way to assert on output is to swap os.Stdout . The design in this chapter is not cleverer; it just passes its dependencies in, which is the same argument chapter ten made about interfaces. Project 45: build the framework, then a real tool with it In part6-from-scratch/49-cli , build the framework above as a package, and then a tool that uses it. One: the framework. Command , Add , find , Execute , PrintUsage , Main , suggestions, signals. No global state. Two: the tool. A notes CLI with real subcommands: Store them in a JSON file under the user's config directory, found with os.UserConfigDir . Three: the exit codes. Verify with a script: Four: the pipe. notes list --json | jq '.[0].text' must work, which means no progress output on stdout and no colour codes when piped. Five: cancellation. Add notes import <big-file> that reports progress and honours ctx . Interrupt it halfway and confirm the file it was writing is not left half written. Then interrupt twice and confirm it exits immediately. Six: the typo. notes lst suggests list . notes xyzzy suggests nothing and exits 2. Seven: tests. Every exit code, the help output, the suggestion, and one test that runs the whole tree against a temporary config directory. Your turn Run --help on three tools you use daily and read them as a designer rather than a user. Which one tells you what to do next when you get it wrong? Whic
