headings: Three layers, decided before any code
Listing, which is where the work actually is
A router, written rather than imported
Testing the whole thing without a port
pages.text: Every backend job, in the end, asks for the same thing: create a record, read one, list many with a filter, change one, delete one. Parts I to III gave you every piece. This chapter assembles them into a complete API with no framework and no ORM, and then counts what it cost, because that number is the honest case both for and against the rest of this book. Nothing here imports anything outside the standard library except a database driver. A tasks API, in one binary: POST /tasks Create, with validation, returning 201 GET /tasks List, paginated, filtered, sorted, with meta GET /tasks/{id} Read one, or 404 PATCH /tasks/{id} Partial update DELETE /tasks/{id} Delete, returning 204 Plus the things that separate an API from a demo: one response envelope, real status codes, a request ID in the logs, timeouts on the server, a recover boundary, graceful shutdown and tests that run without a port. The envelope is the one from chapter thirty three, on purpose. You are about to write by hand the contract a generated handler gives you. The rule, which is the whole of chapter thirty two said again in your own project: a handler parses and responds, and decides nothing . The store talks to the database and knows no HTTP. In between sits the thing that knows the rules. If you know JavaScript In an Express application this layering is a convention you keep by discipline, and the reason it slips is that req and res are in scope everywhere, so any file can reach for them. Here, the store package cannot see an HTTP request even if it wants to: it does not import net/http . The architecture is held by the import graph rather than by review, which is why it survives a busy week. DueAt is a pointer because a task may genuinely have no due date, and chapter nineteen's lesson applies: a zero time.Time serialises as the year one, which is not "none". Validation lives with the type, returning field errors rather than one string, because the frontend needs to know which input to highlight: The schema, applied at startup. For a project this size that is enough, and chapter thirty one explains what you give up by not having real migrations: Create, returning the assigned ID: Read one, with the sentinel the rest of the program will match on: Watch out sql.ErrNoRows must not escape this package. It is a database/sql detail, and if a handler matches on it then swapping the store for an in-memory one breaks the handler, which is exactly the coupling the layering was for. Translate it once, at the edge of the package that produced it. That is chapter eleven's boundary rule, and this is the line where it is easiest to get right and easiest to skip. Create and read are five lines each. Listing is where every API grows hair: pagination, a filter, a search, a sort, and a total count that has to agree with the filter. Build the WHERE once, and use it for both queries: The count comes from the same clause, or your pagination lies: And then the page itself. Note what is concatenated and what is a placeholder: Watch out A column name cannot be a placeholder. ORDER BY ? is not valid SQL, so the sort column has to be concatenated into the string, and that is precisely how a sort parameter becomes an injection. The map is the defence, and the important part is that it is a *whitelist of allowed values*, not an escape or a check for suspicious characters. Anything not in the map is not a column, so the worst an attacker achieves is the default sort. This is the same whitelist a generated Grit service carries, and now you know why it exists rather than being a configuration chore. Finish the rows properly, because the loop is not the end: rows.Err() is the line people omit for years without noticing. A connection dropped halfway through a result set ends the loop quietly, and without that check you return half a page and call it success. Go 1.22 taught ServeMux method and wildcard patterns, so in a real project you would use it. Write one once anyway: a router is about forty lines, and knowing that number changes how you think about frameworks. Matching is a comparison, segment by segment, with the parameters collected into the request context as they are found: The 405 is the detail worth copying. A path that exists for another method is not a 404, and an API that cannot tell the difference sends every client on a debugging trip through its own URL building. And one failure path that works out the status from the error, so no handler decides it twice: Watch out The default branch logs the real error and returns a generic one. That split is deliberate: the message a stranger sees must not contain the table name, the query or the file path, and the message you see must contain all three. The request ID is what joins the two halves. Return it in a header, log it with every line, and a support message saying "it failed at 14:05" becomes a one-command search. Four steps, in the same order, in every handler in the file: parse, validate, call, respond. When a fifth thing appears in a handler it is nearly always a rule, and it belongs one layer down. The list handler is the one that parses the query, and it clamps rather than trusts: Watch out The clamp on page_size is not tidiness. Without it, ?page_size=1000000 is a one-request denial of service that your own API happily performs, and it will be found by a crawler rather than by an attacker. The recover boundary is the one that earns its place on the first bad day: Chapter twelve said recover belongs only at a boundary. This is the boundary: one panic takes down one request rather than the process, and the stack reaches the log instead of the client. serveUntilSignal is chapter twenty one's graceful shutdown, unchanged. An in-memory database per test, no fixtures to clean up, no ports to collide, and the tests run in parallel. This is the shape every API test in your career should have. When it works, count the lines: For one resource, done properly, it lands somewhere around six hundred
pages.title: What we are building

headings: The accept loop, with the timeouts that matter
Keep-alive, and the body you forgot to read
Routing, which you have already written
pages.text: Chapter twenty one used net/http , which hides the protocol so completely that most web developers have never seen a request line. This chapter removes the hiding: a TCP listener, HTTP/1.1 parsed by hand, keep-alive, chunked bodies, and the timeouts without which a server can be held open by one slow client. The payoff is not a better server. It is that the next time you read about request smuggling, a reverse proxy misbehaving or a mysterious hanging connection, you will know exactly which bytes are involved. A request line, headers, a blank line, and optionally a body. The response has the same shape with a status line instead: That is HTTP/1.1. Everything else is rules about how to know where the body ends and whether the connection stays open. If you know JavaScript This is why curl -v is such a good debugging tool: it prints exactly these lines. Once you have written the parser, curl -v stops being noise and becomes the clearest view of what your framework is actually sending. Watch out ReadHeaderTimeout is separate from ReadTimeout , and the reason has a name: Slowloris . The attack is to open a thousand connections and send one header byte every twenty seconds. Each connection is technically active, so a single overall timeout never fires, and the server runs out of connections while using almost no bandwidth. A deadline on the headers specifically is the defence, and it is why net/http grew that field. A server with no header deadline is held open by a laptop. Headers are a loop until the blank line, with two defences: Header names are case insensitive, so they are canonicalised once on the way in. Doing it at every lookup instead is both slower and a source of bugs where Content-Type and content-type are two different entries. The limits are not politeness. Without them, a client sending headers forever is an out-of-memory error with no request ever completing. This is the whole of HTTP/1.1's complexity, and there are exactly three answers: Content-Length: n Read exactly n bytes Transfer-Encoding: chunked Read chunks until a zero-length one Neither There is no body. A GET, usually Chunked is the one worth implementing, because it is how a server streams something whose size it does not know yet: Each chunk is a hexadecimal length, CRLF, that many bytes, CRLF. A zero-length chunk ends the body. Watch out That refusal is not pedantry. A message with both framing headers is the basis of HTTP request smuggling , and it is one of the highest-impact web vulnerabilities there is. The attack works when two servers disagree: a front-end proxy uses Content-Length and your back-end uses Transfer-Encoding , or the reverse. The bytes one of them considers to be the end of request A, the other considers the start of request B. An attacker appends a request that your server attributes to the next user's connection. The defence is to refuse the ambiguity rather than resolve it. If both headers are present, the message is malformed: 400, and close the connection. HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default. After responding, you loop and read the next request from the same socket. And the trap: Watch out This bug is unforgettable once seen. A handler returns 400 early without reading the body, the next loop iteration reads the unread JSON as a request line, and the error message contains fragments of the previous request. Worse, it is intermittent: it only happens when a handler returns early, so it shows up under error conditions, which is when you are least able to reason about it. Drain or close. net/http drains a limited amount and closes beyond it, which is a good policy to copy. If the handler knows the length, send Content-Length . If it does not, switch to chunked. That is the decision net/http makes for you: it buffers a little, and if the handler finishes within the buffer it sets a length, otherwise it goes chunked. Two responses have no body at all and must not have a length: 204 and 304. A server that sends Content-Length: 0 with a 304 confuses caches in ways that take a day to find. A client about to upload something large asks first. The server answers either: and the client sends the body, or it answers 413 or 401 immediately and the client never uploads a gigabyte that was going to be rejected anyway. curl sends this automatically for large bodies. A server that ignores it makes those clients wait for a timeout before uploading, which presents as "uploads are slow from curl and fine from the browser". The router from chapter forty eight drops straight in: match the method and the path segments, collect parameters, call the handler. Nothing about routing changes because you parsed the request yourself. TLS crypto/tls wraps your listener in about ten lines. Not hard, just not HTTP HTTP/2 Binary framing, HPACK header compression, multiplexed streams. A different project of a similar size HTTP/3 QUIC, over UDP. A much bigger project Compression Accept-Encoding and a gzip writer. A good exercise Against real clients, as in chapter fifty three: And against raw bytes, which is where the interesting failures live: Project 50: the server, and the attacks it survives In part6-from-scratch/54-http , build it. One: the parser. Request line, headers with limits and canonical names, and all three body framings including chunked. Two: the writer. Status line, Date , Content-Length or chunked, and correct handling of 204 and 304. Three: keep-alive. Persistent connections, the drain, and Connection: close honoured in both directions. Four: the timeouts. Separate header, read, write and idle deadlines, each configurable. Five: Slowloris. Write a client that opens 200 connections and sends one header byte every two seconds. With the header timeout off, show the server stop accepting. Turn it on and show it survive. Record both. Six: smuggling. Send a request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding and confirm a 400. Then read the two smuggling variants and write a paragraph on which one
pages.title: What a request actually is

headings: Claiming work, which is the whole problem
Failure, backoff and the dead letter
Polling, and the latency it costs
Fairness, and the queue that starves
When this is the wrong design
pages.text: Chapter forty three used a queue. This chapter builds one, on the database you already have, which for most applications is the right answer: no Redis, no second thing to operate, and jobs that can be enqueued *inside the same transaction* as the work that caused them. The hard parts are not the obvious ones. Storing a job is a row. Handing that row to exactly one worker, and getting it back when that worker dies, is the engineering. Two index decisions carry most of the performance. The partial index. Claiming only ever looks for pending rows, and a finished job is dead weight in the index. A partial index stays small even when the table holds millions of completed jobs. The partial unique index is idempotency: a job with a unique_key that is already pending or running cannot be enqueued twice, and the database enforces it rather than the application checking first and racing. If you know JavaScript That tx parameter is the whole reason to put a queue in your database. With Redis, enqueueing and committing are two systems, which is chapter forty four's publish-or-commit problem and needs an outbox. Here the job row and the business row commit together or not at all: the outbox is the queue. It is the strongest argument for a database-backed queue, and it disappears the moment your throughput needs something specialised. Several workers poll the same table. Two must never get the same row, and a worker waiting on a lock is a worker doing nothing. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is the line that makes this work, and it exists in Postgres for exactly this use case. Watch out Without SKIP LOCKED , ten workers all select the same oldest rows, nine block on the first one's lock, and your queue processes jobs one at a time with nine idle workers holding transactions open. With it, each worker takes the rows nobody else has locked and moves on. MySQL 8 has it too. SQLite does not, and serialises writers anyway, so there a single claiming goroutine handing work to a pool is the honest design. Claim a batch rather than one row. The round trip dominates at small sizes, and ten or twenty jobs per claim is usually an order of magnitude more throughput. The job is running , locked_by names a process that no longer exists, and nothing will ever finish it. The lease is what fixes this: And a worker on a long job keeps its lease alive: Watch out The lease is why delivery is at least once and can never be exactly once. A worker that finishes the work and dies before marking the job done will have that job reclaimed and run again. There is no ordering of those two steps that removes the window, which is the same impossibility chapter forty three described for mail. So the handler must be idempotent, and the lease duration must exceed your longest job. A five minute lease on a job that takes ten minutes means the job is reclaimed and run again while it is still running , which is the worst outcome available: two workers doing the same work at the same time. Watch out The jitter is the part people skip, and it is the part that matters during an incident. A downstream service goes down for a minute. Five thousand jobs fail at once. Without jitter, all five thousand retry at exactly the same instant, four seconds later, and again sixteen seconds later. The service comes back, gets hit by five thousand simultaneous requests, and goes down again. You have built a mechanism that prevents recovery. Spread the retries. Full jitter, half jitter, anything: the shape matters far more than the formula. A dead job is not deleted. It sits in the table with its error, where somebody can look at it, fix the cause and requeue it. A queue with no dead letter state loses work silently, which is the one thing a queue must never do. Polling every second means up to a second of latency for every job. For a reminder email that is irrelevant; for a user waiting on a thumbnail it is not. Postgres gives you a way out: Notifications are an optimisation, not a guarantee. Keeping the poll as a floor means a missed notification costs latency rather than a stuck job. With several queues, the naive loop takes everything from the first queue before looking at the second, so a flood of image jobs stops every email. Weighted selection, by starting from a random position in a weighted list, is enough: default weight 5, email 3, images 2. Over any reasonable window each queue gets its share, and no queue can be starved by another. Four numbers, and the second is the one to alert on: Counts by state Pending, running, dead. The shape of the backlog Oldest pending age The single best queue alert there is Duration by type Which jobs are getting slower Dead per hour A rise means something downstream broke Depth alone is misleading: ten thousand jobs enqueued a second ago is fine, and one job pending for an hour is an outage. Age catches both. That last branch is worth the few lines. A deploy that releases its leases makes the next worker pick those jobs up immediately, instead of them sitting running until the reaper notices. Be honest about the ceiling. A database-backed queue handles a few thousand jobs a second on decent hardware, which is more than most applications ever produce. Beyond that, the claim query becomes the bottleneck and the table becomes a hot spot. Database queue You already have a database, you want transactional enqueue, and volume is moderate Redis queue High throughput, low latency, jobs that are not tied to a transaction Kafka or similar Streams, many consumers, replay, retention. A different tool for a different problem Project 53: a queue you would trust In part6-from-scratch/57-queue , build it against Postgres in Docker. One: the schema and enqueue , with the partial indexes and transactional enqueue taking a *sql.Tx . Two: claiming with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED , batched. Run eight workers against ten thousand jobs and assert every job ran exactly once. *Three: prove SKIP LOCKED matters.* Remove it, run the same test, and record
pages.title: The table

headings: Numbers, and the decision JavaScript cannot make
pages.text: JSON is the smallest grammar worth parsing properly. It has five kinds of value, no ambiguity, and a specification you can read in an afternoon. Once you have written a parser for it, every other parser you meet, a config format, a query language, a template engine, is the same shape with more rules. We are building a lexer, a recursive descent parser, errors that name a line and a column, and the defences a parser needs when the input comes from strangers. That is the whole language. Strings and numbers have their own rules, which is where most of the work turns out to be. If you know JavaScript JSON.parse in the browser is roughly this, plus a reviver function and some extremely optimised string handling. The one behavioural difference worth knowing before we start: JavaScript numbers are float64, so JSON.parse('{"id": 9007199254740993}') gives you 9007199254740992. The parser is not wrong, the type is. We will hit the same decision later in this chapter, and in Go we get to choose differently. The position goes on the token, not on the parser, because the parser reports errors about tokens it has already read. Retrofitting positions later is miserable, and every parser author does it once. The dull part is advance , and it is the part to get right first: Every byte goes through it, so the line and column are always correct, and no later code has to remember to update them. Three correctness points that separate a parser from a toy. Raw control characters are illegal inside a JSON string. A literal newline in a string is a malformed document, and accepting it means your parser disagrees with everybody else's. The escapes are a fixed list : " \ / b f n r t and uXXXX . Anything else is an error, not a passthrough. Surrogate pairs are real. 😀 is one emoji expressed as two escapes, and handling each in isolation produces two broken runes: Watch out utf16.DecodeRune returns U+FFFD for a pair that does not combine, which means a lone high surrogate becomes a replacement character rather than an error. Decide deliberately which you want. Being strict is right for a validator and wrong for a parser that has to read whatever a legacy system emits, and either way it should be a decision with a comment and not an accident. Note what it does not do: it does not convert. The token carries the raw text, and the decision about what Go type to produce belongs to the caller. Watch out This is not a detail. A 64-bit ID, a currency amount in minor units, a nanosecond timestamp: all of them exceed the 53 bits a float64 can hold exactly, and converting silently changes the value. 9007199254740993 becomes 9007199254740992 , and no error is produced anywhere. If your parser is reading somebody's API responses, keeping the raw text and converting on demand is the only safe default. This is the same lesson as chapter forty's money, arrived at from the parsing side. Recursive descent means one function per production, and the structure reads like the grammar: An object is a loop over pairs: Arrays are the same shape with no keys, and that is the parser. A parser that will be fed data from outside needs both of these, and neither is obvious until you have been bitten. A depth limit. [[[[[[...]]]]]] with ten thousand levels recurses ten thousand times, and a deep enough document is a stack overflow, which in Go is a crash you cannot recover from. A size limit, upstream. Not the parser's job, but the parser is where the cost appears: a hundred megabyte document becomes several hundred megabytes of map[string]any . Cap the reader with io.LimitReader before parsing, and remember chapter forty two's decompression bomb is the same family of attack. Watch out Duplicate keys are where the specification shrugs: {"a":1,"a":2} is legal and the result is "implementation defined". Most parsers keep the last. Some keep the first. A few error. The attack this enables is real: a document parsed by two systems that disagree is a way to show one value to a validator and another to a consumer. Pick last-wins to match everybody else, and offer a strict mode that errors. Then write it down, because the next person will assume whichever one you did not choose. Three pieces: the position, what was expected, and what was found. The caret line costs about fifteen lines of code and is the difference between a parser people debug with and one they swear at. Table tests for the cases you thought of. Then two techniques that find the ones you did not. Differential fuzzing against the standard library: Sixty seconds of that finds the cases a human table never contains: a lone surrogate, a number like -0 , 1e999 , a string of nothing but escapes. The JSON test suite. There is a well-known corpus of files named y_ (must accept), n_ (must reject) and i_ (implementation defined). Running against it is how you find out your parser is not as correct as it feels. If you know JavaScript Fuzzing is built into go test , which is unusual and underused. In most languages it is a separate tool with its own configuration, so people do not bother. Here it is three lines and a flag, and for anything that parses untrusted input it finds more real bugs per minute than any other technique available to you. Benchmark against encoding/json and report the number honestly. A clean hand-written parser usually lands in the same order of magnitude for parsing into any , and loses badly to the standard library's struct decoding, which has years of optimisation in it. That is the right outcome. You did not build this to replace the standard library. You built it so that the next time you read a stack trace through encoding/json , you know what each frame is doing. Project 46: a parser that passes the suite In part6-from-scratch/50-json , build it completely. One: lexer and parser , producing any , with positions on every token. Two: errors with line, column, expected and found, plus the caret line. Three: the number decision. Implement UseNumber , and write a test with
pages.title: The grammar, in full

headings: Replay, and tolerating a torn tail
The one system call that matters
pages.text: A map in memory is a key-value store until the process restarts. This chapter builds one that survives a crash, which turns out to be a question about exactly one system call. Everything here uses only the standard library, and everything you need is in Parts I to III. The checksum is what makes a half-written record detectable. Without it a truncated write looks like a valid record with garbage in it. encoding/binary writes fixed-width integers in a defined byte order. Big-endian is conventional for file formats; the only rule that matters is that the reader and writer agree. Watch out Do not use fmt.Sprintf or JSON for a log format. Both are variable-width, so you cannot know how many bytes to read without scanning for a delimiter, and a delimiter can appear inside a value. A length prefix removes the question entirely: read the header, then read exactly that many bytes. O_APPEND matters: every write goes to the end regardless of where the file offset happens to be, which is what makes concurrent appends safe at the operating system level. The three break s are the whole crash-recovery story. A torn header, a torn body and a failed checksum all mean the same thing: *the log ends at the last good record*, and everything after it was never acknowledged to a caller, so discarding it is correct. Watch out append(header[4:], body...) is the slice trap from chapter six wearing a disguise. header[4:] has spare capacity, so append may write into header rather than allocating. It happens to be harmless here because header is re-read next iteration, but it is exactly the pattern that corrupts data elsewhere. The careful version: Which is also faster, because it allocates nothing. The ordering in Set is the correctness argument, and it is worth saying out loud: log first, then memory . If memory were updated first, a reader could observe a value that the crash removes, and the store would have lied. Two steps, and people routinely do only the first. Flush moves bytes out of Go's buffer into the operating system. At that point the data survives your process crashing, because the kernel has it. Sync is fsync , and it asks the kernel to put the bytes on the physical device. Only after this does the data survive the machine losing power. Watch out fsync is slow: on spinning disks milliseconds, on an SSD still far slower than anything else in this program. Calling it on every write makes a store that does maybe a few thousand writes a second. That is the durability dial, and every database exposes it. Postgres calls it synchronous_commit , Redis calls it appendfsync , and the options are always the same three: every write Slowest, loses nothing every N ms Fast, loses up to N milliseconds on a power cut never Fastest, the operating system decides, can lose a lot There is no correct answer, only a choice about what you can afford to lose. A store that does not tell you which one it made is the one to distrust. The log grows forever. Setting one key a million times means a million records and a one-entry map. os.Rename on the same filesystem is atomic, which is the trick that makes this safe. Write the new file completely, sync it, then swap. A crash at any point leaves either the old log or the new one, and both are valid. If you know JavaScript Write to a temp file, fsync, rename is the durable-replace pattern, and it applies far beyond databases. Any time you overwrite a file that matters, a configuration file or an export, this is the correct way to do it. Writing in place can leave a half-written file that nothing can read. Project 34: make it crash and watch it recover The tests are the chapter. Each proves a property the code was written for. TestTornTailIsDiscarded is the one to run first. It writes eight bytes of a record that should have been twenty, which is exactly what a power cut mid write leaves behind, and asserts three things: the open succeeds, the partial record is not replayed, and the store still accepts writes. A store that fails any of those will one day refuse to start, and refusing to start is how a durable store loses data. Your turn Three extensions, each teaching something different. Add a syncEvery option so a caller can choose the durability dial, and benchmark Set with sync on every write against sync every 100ms. The ratio you measure is the reason databases have that setting. Add automatic compaction when the log exceeds a multiple of the live data size, and think about what happens if the process dies during compaction. The rename makes it safe; prove it with a test that leaves a stale .compact file behind. Then replace the map with the B-tree from the next chapter and watch the store gain ordered range queries, which is the step from a key-value store to something you could call a database. Commit your work with the message Key Value Store - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Finish the store, then try to corrupt it. One. Complete the write-ahead log, the replay and the compaction as written, with tests for each. Two. Crash it for real. Write a test that starts the store in a subprocess, writes, and kills it with no chance to clean up: Reopen and confirm every acknowledged write is present. Three. Truncate the log file mid-record, on purpose, and show the store recovering to the last whole record rather than refusing to start. Four. Benchmark with and without the sync on every write, and put both numbers in NOTES.md with one sentence on which you would default to. That trade, durability against throughput, is the one every database makes. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.
pages.title: The problem, stated precisely

headings: Incrementing, which is where atomicity shows up
Persistence, which you have already built
pages.text:
Everything you have written so far has spoken HTTP, which is a protocol somebody else parsed for you. This chapter goes one layer down: a TCP listener, a wire format you implement yourself, and a server that the real redis-cli can connect to. That last part is what makes this the best protocol exercise there is. You are not testing against your own client. You are testing against a program written by people who have never heard of you, and when it works, your implementation is correct in a way no unit test proves. RESP is deliberately simple. The first byte says the type: A client sends commands as arrays of bulk strings . SET name Ada arrives as: That is the whole format. Five types, one of which is a container. If you know JavaScript Compare this with JSON, which you parsed in chapter fifty. RESP carries the length of every string before its bytes, so the reader never scans for a delimiter and never has to escape anything. That is the difference between a format designed for humans and one designed for throughput, and it is why $5
hello
 looks redundant and is not: a string containing 
 needs no special handling at all. Goroutine per connection, which in Go is the obvious design and in most languages is not. Ten thousand connections is ten thousand goroutines and a few hundred megabytes, which chapter thirteen promised and this is where you cash it in. Watch out The flush condition is the single most important line for performance. Flushing after every command turns a pipeline of a thousand commands into a thousand small writes and a thousand round trips. Flushing only when the read buffer is empty lets a client that sent a thousand commands in one packet receive one packet back. Measured with redis-benchmark -P 100 , the difference is roughly an order of magnitude. io.ReadFull is the heart of it, and it is the line that separates a working server from a mysteriously broken one. Watch out TCP is a stream, not a sequence of messages. One Read can return half a command, or two commands, or one and a half. Nothing preserves the boundaries the sender used. So a bulk string of five bytes is read with io.ReadFull , which loops until it has five, rather than with one Read that might return three. Every protocol bug that only appears over a real network and never over localhost is this, because localhost rarely splits packets and the internet does it constantly. Note n > maxBulk as well. A client claiming a 4 GB bulk string must not cause a 4 GB allocation, which is chapter forty two's bomb wearing a different hat. Expiry is lazy plus active , which is what Redis itself does: a key is dropped when somebody touches it after its deadline, and a background sweep samples random keys to catch the ones nobody asks for. Without the sweep, keys nobody reads live forever and the memory never comes back. Watch out The real Redis is single threaded for command execution, so it needs no lock at all. Your Go version has a goroutine per connection and therefore does. That is a genuine trade: the lock costs you contention on a hot key, and Redis's single thread costs it one core. Before deciding yours is better, benchmark with redis-benchmark and look at the numbers, because a global RWMutex under write-heavy load is less impressive than it sounds. Sharding the map by key hash is the usual next step. Arity checked once, in execute , rather than in every handler. And command is in the list for a practical reason: redis-cli sends COMMAND DOCS on connect, and a server that errors on it looks broken before you have typed anything. The read, the increment and the write are inside one lock. Doing Get then Set from the handler would be two operations with a window between them, and two clients incrementing at once would lose a count. This is chapter fifteen's lesson in its smallest possible form, and it is exactly why INCR exists as a command rather than being left to the client. An append-only file: every write command is appended to a log, and on startup the log is replayed. That is chapter fifty one's write-ahead log, unchanged. The questions are the same too. fsync on every write is durable and slow; once a second is fast and loses up to a second. Redis makes that a configuration option, and so should you, with the trade written down where the person choosing can see it. The benchmark with and without pipelining is the measurement that tells you whether your flush logic is right. If you know JavaScript This is the most satisfying validation in the book. redis-cli knows nothing about your code, implements the protocol strictly, and will tell you immediately when a reply type is wrong. Interoperating with somebody else's client is a different standard of correctness from passing your own tests, and it is the standard that matters when you write a protocol anybody else will speak. Be clear about the gap, because "I built Redis" is a sentence that needs qualifying: Data types Real Redis has lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams. This has strings Pub/sub A different connection mode, where the server pushes Scripting Lua, executed atomically on the server Replication A whole protocol of its own Cluster Key hashing, slots, redirects Strings plus expiry is perhaps five percent of Redis and a hundred percent of the protocol work. That is the right trade for a chapter, and the remaining list is a very good source of weekend projects. Project 49: a server redis-cli cannot tell apart In part6-from-scratch/53-redis , build it. One: the protocol. Reader and writer for all five RESP types, with io.ReadFull for bulk payloads and a cap on declared lengths. Two: the commands. PING , ECHO , SET with EX , GET , DEL , EXISTS , INCR , DECR , EXPIRE , TTL , KEYS , COMMAND . Three: expiry. Lazy on read plus an active sampler. Prove with a test that a key nobody reads is eventually reclaimed. Four: the real client. Every command above verified through redis-cli , pasted into SESSION.md . Five: the benchmark. redis-benchmar
pages.title: The protocol, in one page

headings: The core, which is shorter than you expect
Hop-by-hop headers, and why they must be removed
X-Forwarded-For, and the header that lies
Retries, and the one that corrupts data
Streaming, and the buffering that breaks it
pages.text: Every production system has one of these in front of it, and most developers treat it as a configuration file somebody else wrote. A proxy is a few hundred lines, and writing one explains a list of things that are otherwise folklore: why X-Forwarded-For can lie, why some headers must be stripped, why a retry can corrupt data, and why your streaming endpoint buffers when it goes through nginx. Four jobs, and only the first is obvious: Distribute Spread requests over healthy backends Protect Timeouts, limits, and TLS termination in one place Hide One public address for many internal services Survive Take a backend out when it fails, put it back when it recovers Everything after this is the detail, and the detail is where proxies go wrong. Some headers describe this connection , not the message. Forwarding them onward is wrong because the next connection is a different connection: And the subtle part: Connection can name other headers that are also hop-by-hop for this connection, so those must be stripped too. Watch out Forwarding Transfer-Encoding: chunked to a backend that also sets a Content-Length is the smuggling setup from chapter fifty four, built by your own proxy. Strip, then let your HTTP client decide the framing for the connection it is making. Never copy framing headers across a hop. The chain grows as the request passes each proxy, so the leftmost entry is the original client and each later one was added by a hop. Watch out *A client can send X-Forwarded-For itself.* Nothing stops it. So the leftmost value is not the client's IP; it is whatever the client claimed, followed by the truth. The consequence is real: an application that rate limits, geolocates or audits by the leftmost entry can be fooled by anybody who sends a header. Logs attribute actions to an invented address. The rule: *count from the right, and trust exactly as many entries as you have proxies you control*. One proxy means the real client IP is the last entry your proxy appended, not the first in the list. Configure the count explicitly; do not infer it. Round robin is two lines and is the right default: Least connections is better when request durations vary a lot, which is most real traffic: Round robin Even request counts. Fine when requests cost the same Least connections Even load . Better with mixed fast and slow endpoints Weighted Backends of different sizes Consistent hash The same key goes to the same backend, for cache locality or sticky sessions Round robin's failure mode is worth knowing: one slow backend keeps receiving its share, so a quarter of your users wait on the sick machine while three healthy ones idle. Least connections drains away from it automatically, because its in-flight count stays high. Active : ask each backend, on a timer. Passive : notice real traffic failing. A backend that refuses three connections in a row is out, regardless of what its health endpoint says. Recovery must be careful. A backend that has been out comes back half open : it gets one request, and only if that succeeds does it rejoin. Watch out Without the half-open step, a backend that is still broken rejoins the pool on a timer, takes its full share, fails them all, and leaves again. The pool oscillates and a steady fraction of users get errors for as long as the backend is sick. This is the circuit breaker pattern, and the half-open state is the part people leave out. Thresholds matter too: two consecutive failures to eject, three consecutive successes to restore. One failure is a blip, and treating it as an outage makes the proxy less reliable than no proxy. Retrying a failed request sounds obviously good. It is conditional: Watch out Never retry a POST that was fully sent. A connection that failed after the request reached the backend may have failed on the way back, and the work is already done. Retrying charges the card twice. A connection refused is safe to retry: nothing was delivered. A connection reset mid-response is not. And cap the total: a retry budget of ten percent of traffic. Without a cap, a failing backend turns into three times the traffic at the exact moment the system is least able to take it, which is how a small outage becomes a retry storm. This is why your streaming endpoint works locally and arrives all at once through a proxy: the default is to buffer, and a stream needs the opposite. Detect it by Content-Type: text/event-stream , or by the absence of a Content-Length , and flush. WebSockets need the connection itself, not the body: on a 101 Switching Protocols , hijack the client connection and copy bytes in both directions until either side closes. Deployment is where a proxy earns its place. Taking a backend out gracefully means: stop sending it new requests, let the in-flight ones finish, then stop the process. That loop, plus chapter twenty one's graceful shutdown in the backend, is a zero-downtime deploy. There is nothing else to it. Project 52: the proxy, measured under failure In part6-from-scratch/56-proxy , build it and then break things on purpose. One: the proxy. Header stripping, forwarded headers, round robin, and a configurable backend list. Two: three backends. Write a tiny backend that reports its own name and can be told to be slow or to fail: Three: the strategies. Round robin and least connections, both implemented. Drive 10,000 requests through each with hey or k6 and record p50, p95 and p99 for both. The difference with backend b slow is the whole lesson. Four: health. Active probes and passive ejection with thresholds, plus the half-open recovery. Kill backend a mid-load and record how many requests failed before it was ejected. Then restart it and time the recovery. Five: the oscillation. Remove the half-open step, make a backend fail its probe but fail real traffic, and watch the error rate pulse. Put it back. Six: streaming. Add an SSE endpoint to a backend and prove the events arrive one at a time through the proxy. Then set the flush interval to zero and wa

headings: The trick: it writes a program
Step three: running, in parallel, in isolation
Step four: output people can use
The features that make a runner good
What go test does that yours will not
pages.text: go test feels like magic in a way the rest of Go does not. There is no registration, no decorator, no configuration file. You write a function whose name starts with Test , and it runs. This chapter is how. By the end you will have a runner that discovers tests, builds a binary, runs them in parallel with timeouts and isolation, reports failures usefully, and emits machine-readable output. And you will know precisely which of Go's conveniences are compiler features and which are ordinary code you could have written. go test does not interpret your test files. It *generates a main package* that imports your package, lists your test functions in a slice, and calls testing.Main with them. Then it compiles that program and runs it. If you know JavaScript This is the answer to a question most Go developers never ask: how is there no registration step? In JavaScript, describe and it are function calls that push into a registry at import time. In Go there is no import-time registry, because the tooling walks the source, finds the functions and writes the list. The magic is in the build step, not the language. Which means you can build it yourself, and that is exactly what this chapter does. Parse the package with go/parser and find the functions. This is the same go/ast work grit sync does to read models, so the shape should be familiar: isTestFunc is the rule, written out: That lowercase rule is real and catches people: a function called Testing is not a test, and Testadd is not either. Write it to a temporary directory, then: Notice what this means: your test runner is a compiler front end . It produces Go source and hands it to the Go toolchain, which is how go test gets types, build tags and vet checks for free. Watch out The generated file imports your package, so a test in package foo can only see exported identifiers. That is why Go has two kinds of test file: package foo tests, compiled into the package and able to see everything, and package foo_test tests, which see only the public API. go test handles both by generating two sets of entries. It is worth supporting in your version, because the distinction is one of the better habits Go encourages: a _test package forces you to use your own API the way a caller does. Each test runs as a subprocess invocation of the built binary with -test.run=^TestName$ : A process per test is heavier than go test 's goroutine per test, and it buys two things worth having: a panic kills one test rather than the run, and a test that leaks goroutines or global state cannot affect its neighbours. Watch out Each test gets its own temporary working directory, and that is not politeness. A test that writes output.json in the current directory passes alone and fails when run next to another test that does the same. Those failures are order dependent, so they appear when somebody adds an unrelated test, and they are blamed on the new test. Isolate the filesystem and the environment, and randomise the order occasionally. A suite that passes in a random order is a suite whose tests are genuinely independent. Two audiences, as in chapter forty nine. For a human, failures only, with the file and line so an editor can jump there: For a machine, one JSON object per event, which is what go test -json produces and what every CI system consumes: Streaming the events rather than printing a report at the end matters more than it sounds: a twenty minute suite that prints nothing until it finishes is indistinguishable from a hung one. Watch out Print the failures last, or print them twice. Scrolling back through four thousand lines of passing output to find the one failure is a daily annoyance in a hundred CI systems. A summary at the end, repeating each failure with its output, costs nothing and is the single most appreciated feature of a runner. This is also why you never pipe a test log through tail : the summary survives and the context that explains it does not. Having built the core, these are each an afternoon and each one you will miss if you leave it out: Filtering -run with a regular expression. The most used flag there is Timeouts Per test and overall, with the stack dumped on timeout Retry flaky -retry 2 , and report the retry rather than hiding it Shuffle Random order with a printed seed, so a failure is reproducible Sharding -shard 2/5 , for splitting a suite across CI machines Slowest Print the ten slowest tests. The list is always surprising If you know JavaScript The retry one deserves a warning. A runner that silently retries turns a flaky test into a passing test, and the flakiness becomes invisible until it is twenty tests and nobody trusts the suite. Retry if you must, but print FLAKY: TestX passed on attempt 2 and count it in the summary. Make the flakiness visible, or you are building a machine for ignoring problems. Worth knowing, because the list is a map of the remaining depth: Caching Results keyed by the inputs: source, environment, files read. This is why an unchanged test prints (cached) Coverage Rewriting the source to add counters before compiling Benchmarks Adaptive iteration counts until the timing is stable Fuzzing Corpus management, mutation, minimisation of a failing input Subtests t.Run , with its own parallelism and naming rules Vet A subset of checks run automatically before the tests The caching one is the most interesting piece of engineering in the list: it hashes everything that could affect the outcome, including the files the test read, and that is why it is safe to trust. Project 54: a runner you would use In part6-from-scratch/58-runner , build it and then run it on real code. One: discovery. Parse a package, list its tests with file and line. Compare your list with go test -list '.*' on the same package: they must match exactly, including the Testing and Testadd edge cases. Two: generate and build the runner binary. Three: run with configurable parallelism, a per-test timeout, a temporary working directory each, and a summary
pages.title: The trick: it writes a program

pages.text: D4 was "the same UI for every table, twenty tables, twenty slightly different list pages". D11 was "the frontend is somebody else's job, and there is nobody else". This chapter is the answer to both, and the part of the framework that is easiest to undersell and easiest to oversell. Generate a resource and the admin gains a working screen: a table with pagination, sorting, search and filters, a form with the right input for every field type, a detail view, bulk actions, Excel export and CSV import. Reload the admin and Invoices is in the sidebar, listing rows. The form is the part worth looking at. total is a money input with a currency prefix and two decimals. due is a date picker rather than a text box. client is a searchable dropdown showing client names . None of that was configured; it follows from the field types, which is chapter thirty's argument arriving where you can see it. The generator writes index.tsx once . After that it is yours, and a re-generate will not touch it. Everything underneath, the table component, the form builder, the inputs, is framework code shared by every resource. Watch out That single file is the seam, and it is worth understanding before you fight it. Customising a column, adding a computed cell, changing how a row renders: all of it happens in index.tsx , and it survives regeneration. Changing how every table behaves happens in the shared components, and that is framework code which grit upgrade will want to update. The rule: per-resource changes in the resource file, cross-cutting changes in the shared components and expect to merge them on upgrade. The file is a definition rather than a page, which is why it is short: To change a cell, give the column a renderer: This is ordinary React. Everything you know applies, which is the point: the generated screen is a starting point written in the same language you would have used. If you know JavaScript If you have used Django admin or Laravel Filament, the shape is familiar: a resource definition rather than a page. The difference from Django is that this is React you can read and change, not a template system with its own idioms, and the difference from a hand-built panel is that twenty resources cost twenty definitions rather than twenty pages. What the table does for you: Pagination Server side, using the meta from the last chapter Sorting Only on columns the service whitelisted Search Across the Searchable columns, server side Filters Per column, from the Filterable map Selection With bulk delete, edit and export Import CSV, with per-row errors rather than all-or-nothing Export Excel, honouring the current filters Notice that four of those are driven by the service's configuration from chapter thirty two. The frontend does not decide what is sortable; it asks, and the server is the authority. That is why a column you added by hand without updating the maps appears in the table and refuses to sort. This is the part worth being plain about, because an admin panel demo always looks like it does more than it does. It is an operator interface, not your product. It is excellent for the screens staff use: managing records, fixing data, running an import. It is not a customer-facing experience, and trying to make it one fights the grain. A genuinely custom screen is a page, not a resource. A dashboard that joins four models with a chart and a date range is not a table of one resource. Write it as a normal Next.js page using the generated hooks, and put it in the sidebar by hand. The shared components are opinionated. They are dark-themed, dense, built for operators. Reskinning them entirely is possible and is a real project, and you will be merging your changes against upgrades afterwards. Watch out The failure mode to avoid is bending the resource definition into something it is not. If you find yourself writing a render for every column, hiding the table and nesting a custom layout inside it, you have written a page inside a resource file. Write the page. The generated hooks and types are available to it, and you lose nothing except the table you were not using. Each resource generates typed React Query hooks: These are the same hooks the generated table uses, and they are available to any page you write yourself. The types come from packages/shared , which came from the same field definitions as the Go model, so the autocomplete in your editor is describing the actual API. That chain is D3 closed end to end: change a field, run one command, and the Go struct, the validation, the TypeScript type and this hook all move together. Project 31: customise a resource screen Take the bookshop and make the Books screen genuinely useful, which means touching exactly one file. Open apps/admin/app/_dashboard/resources/book/index.tsx . One: a computed cell. Add a column that shows stock as a badge: red at zero, amber under ten, plain otherwise. Two: a thumbnail. Render cover as an image rather than a filename. Three: prove the whitelist is the authority. Make stock sortable in the definition, then try to sort by it. If you added the field with grit generate field it works. Now add a column for a field you added to the model by hand, mark it sortable, and watch it do nothing, because services/book.go never heard of it. Four: prove the seam. Re-run grit generate resource Book --fields "..." with the original fields. Your index.tsx edits survive, because that file is written once. Check the model and service: those are the files the manifest reports on. Five: write a real page. Add apps/admin/app/_dashboard/reports/page.tsx that uses useBooks() to show total stock value by category, with a chart. Notice you are writing ordinary React against typed hooks, and that this was never going to be a resource definition. Your turn Count the lines in your customised index.tsx . Then estimate what the same screen would have cost hand-written: a table with server-side pagination, sorting, search, filters, selection, a modal form with
pages.title: What you get without asking

headings: The rule the layering exists for
Organised by layer, not by feature
Can you refactor to something else?
pages.text: You have the project. This chapter is the map: how the code is arranged, which layer is allowed to call which, and why those rules exist. Get this and everything in part five is predictable. A modular monolith with a layered API and an in-process event bus. One binary, one database, about fifty internal packages. That is the headline and it is slightly misleading, because no real system is one style. A Grit project runs six at once, each where it earns its keep: Modular monolith The whole API: one deployment, one transaction boundary Layered (n-tier) routes, handlers, services, models Event-driven internal/events : a write emits once, subscribers react Transactional outbox internal/outbox : durable delivery of those events Orchestration internal/saga : multi-step work that can half fail Microkernel The framework itself: grit plugin add If you know JavaScript Coming from Next.js, the mental shift is that there is one process rather than a function per route. State can live in memory, a connection pool is warm, a background worker runs, and nothing is cold-started. The cost is that you deploy and scale one thing, which for most products is a relief rather than a limitation. Follow one request all the way down. This is the shape every generated resource has. Each layer talks only to the one below it. A handler never touches the database; a model never calls a service. Handlers are thin on purpose , and the reason is not tidiness. Read the request, call one method, write the answer. Every rule lives one layer down, in the service. The payoff: a rule enforced in the service is enforced everywhere . The background job uses it. The CSV import uses it. The CLI command uses it. The test uses it. A rule written in a handler holds until the first time something other than a browser does the same thing, and then it silently does not. That signature is the whole architecture in one line. context.Context rather than *gin.Context means the service has no idea it is being called over HTTP, so a job can call it with context.Background() . Watch out The context carries more than cancellation here. It holds the organisation the multitenant plugin resolved and the actor that per-record ownership is scoped by. That is why passing the request's context down matters rather than creating a fresh one: a context.Background() in the middle of a request loses the caller's identity, and the query comes back unscoped. When a background job genuinely needs to act as nobody, there is an explicit way to say so rather than an accident. Open any generated service and you find three things above the methods: These are the answer to chapter twenty two's warning that a column name cannot be a placeholder. The client sends ?sort=name , and name is checked against a map the generator wrote, rather than being interpolated into SQL. If you know JavaScript This is the difference between an ORM protecting you and a convention protecting you. Prisma builds the query so the column is validated by its schema. Here the query is yours, so the whitelist is explicit and sitting at the top of the file where a reviewer sees it. A write emits once, and the systems that care subscribe. The audit log, outbound webhooks and realtime clients are subscribers , not calls the handler has to remember. Adding a fourth consumer does not mean editing every handler. Three delivery modes, and choosing correctly matters: Sync Runs inline, before the response. For the audit record, which must be written before the caller is told the write succeeded. A slow Sync subscriber is a slow endpoint Async Runs on a worker pool after the handler returns. For anything with a network call: a webhook that takes four seconds must not make the API take four seconds Durable Through the transactional outbox: at least once, retried, surviving a restart. For work another module depends on Durable is the one worth understanding, because it is the difference between an event system and a reliable one. The event is written *in the same database transaction as the data*, so a crash between the commit and the HTTP call loses nothing. A relay then delivers it, claiming messages with a lease so another replica takes over if one dies. If you know JavaScript The naive version is a POST at the end of the handler. It works in the demo and loses events in production: the commit succeeded, the HTTP call did not, and nothing records that anything was owed. The outbox is the standard fix and it is already wired, which is B13 from chapter twenty six. Four, each with a reason rather than a dismissal: Not microservices. One binary by design. A split is worth paying for when teams need to release independently, and until then it buys network failures and a deployment pipeline in exchange for nothing. Not CQRS or event sourcing. Both earn their complexity in a hot spot, not across a codebase. The read path is already separate enough to point at another store when one query needs it. Not hexagonal. The generated service talks to GORM directly rather than through a port. Less indirection to read, at the cost of swapping the ORM being real work. That is a trade, stated as one. Not serverless. Jobs, a scheduler, realtime connections and a warm pool all assume a process that stays up. A fair question, since package-by-feature is what many Go teams land on: why is it models/ , services/ , handlers/ rather than invoice/ , customer/ ? What feature folders buy is real: a feature is a folder, you can delete one by deleting a directory, and the root stops growing. At forty resources Grit's services/ is forty files and the directory stops telling you which three form a subsystem. What the layered layout buys back is the entity graph . A business application has thirty entities pointing at each other: invoice to customer to organisation and back. Go forbids import cycles , so with feature folders the moment customer refers to invoice you need an event or an interface dance to express what is really a forei
pages.title: The short answer

headings: Four layers on the sign-in form
Ownership is the one that bites
Multitenancy is the same idea one level up
What is not solved for you
pages.text: B1 was "can different people see different things", and it is the question clients ask first. The answer has three layers that people routinely confuse, so this chapter separates them before showing what is generated. Authentication Who are you? Produces an identity, or a 401 Authorization May people like you do this? Roles and permissions, or a 403 Ownership May you do it to this record ? Per-row, or a 404 Most teams build the first, assume the second is the whole of the problem, and discover the third when a salesperson can open another salesperson's accounts by changing a number in the URL. If you know JavaScript That third one has a name: insecure direct object reference , and it is perennially near the top of the OWASP list. It is not an exotic attack. It is changing /invoices/41 to /invoices/42 , and an application that checks only the role will serve it happily, because the role was right. A new project already has: registration, login, logout, password reset, email verification, refresh tokens, server-side sessions, account lockout, optional two-factor, and OAuth and SAML behind flags. Three roles exist by default, ADMIN , EDITOR and USER , and you can add more. None of this is a plugin you enable. B2's answer is present before you write a line, for the reason chapter twenty seven gave: an opt-in security feature is a security feature most projects do not have. A JWT alone cannot be revoked: it is valid until it expires, so "log this device out" is not expressible. Every refresh token here is backed by a sessions row, stored as a SHA-256 hash rather than the token itself. That buys four things a bare JWT cannot: revoke one device, from the account page detect replay: a refresh token used twice means it was stolen, and the whole session chain is killed idle and absolute timeouts a password change signs out every device Watch out Storing only the hash matters. A database read, a leaked backup or an over-broad log should not hand someone a usable token. The same reasoning as password hashing, applied to the thing that is just as good as a password. The refresh cookie is also scoped to /api/auth , so it is not sent to every endpoint. The consequence to know: a handler outside that path cannot see the refresh cookie, so it cannot identify the session , only the user. The login endpoint is the most attacked route in any application, and it carries four defences: A rate limit on the route A lockout on the account after repeated failures A growing delay on repeated failure A locked account answers exactly like a wrong password The fourth is the one that gets missed, and it is the interesting one. If a locked account says "this account is locked" and an unknown one says "no such user", you have built an oracle for discovering who has an account. Combined with a breach list, that is a targeted attack. The polite, helpful error message is the vulnerability. Watch out The same trap hides in the timing. If the locked path returns instantly while the real check spends eighty milliseconds hashing a password, an attacker reads the clock instead of the message and learns the same thing. So the delay has to be on both paths. This is the kind of detail that is obvious once stated and absent from almost every hand-rolled login, and it is a decent argument for not hand-rolling one. That updates seven places: the Go constants, the Zod schema, the TypeScript union, the sidebar visibility, the form options and the seeded permissions. Doing it by hand means finding all seven, and the one you miss is usually the frontend, where the role exists but nothing shows for it. Protecting a route: And in a service, where it also holds for jobs and imports: Roles say "editors may delete invoices". Ownership says "this editor may delete this invoice". That adds a UserID column and, more importantly, scopes every generated query by the actor in the context. Listing returns only yours. Fetching someone else's returns 404, not 403, for the reason chapter thirty three gave. The scoping lives in the service rather than the handler, so it applies to the CSV import, the export, the background job and the CLI, which is the whole argument of chapter thirty two meeting the problem it was written for. Watch out This is why threading the request's context matters so much. A context.Background() created halfway through a request has no actor, so the scope cannot be applied, and the query returns everybody's rows. The failure is silent and it is a data breach rather than an error. When a background job genuinely must see everything, there is an explicit way to say so, and the explicitness is the point: an unscoped query should be a sentence someone wrote deliberately. B9 asked "can two of our clients use one system". Ownership scopes to a user; multitenancy scopes to an organisation, through the same context. The property to hold onto: *isolation is not a feature you add, it is something every query must have*. One forgotten WHERE in one place, in a background job or an export rather than a route, and one client sees another's data. That is why it travels in the context rather than being a parameter each method remembers to apply. A parameter can be forgotten at one call site. A context that carries the organisation is applied by the layer that builds the query. Two honest limits. Permission design is yours. The framework gives roles, permissions and per-record ownership. Deciding that a regional manager sees their region, and what happens when someone moves region, is domain modelling and nothing generates it. Approval workflows are not authorization. "An invoice over ten thousand needs a second approver" is a business rule that lives in a service, possibly a saga. It looks like permissions and it is not, and modelling it as a role produces a mess. Project 32: prove the isolation holds The only way to trust ownership scoping is to try to break it. One: two users. Register Ada and Grace through the API and keep both tokens. Two:

pages.text: Thirty one field types ship. This chapter is not a reference, it is an argument about why a field type is the right place to put a decision. When you write total:money , you are not choosing a storage format. You are making five decisions at once: Database an integer column in minor units, never a float a money.Amount , with arithmetic that cannot drift Validation a Zod rule that accepts 12.34 and rejects 12.345 Form a money input with a currency prefix and two decimal places Table right aligned, formatted for the locale Say float instead and all five change, each in a direction that is slightly wrong, and the one that costs you is the first. 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in any language with IEEE floats, and an invoice total that is out by a penny is found by an accountant rather than by a test. If you know JavaScript You already wrote this fix by hand in chapter nineteen, implementing MarshalJSON on a Money int64 . That was the right instinct. The difference here is that the correct decision is the default , applied in five places consistently, rather than something each developer remembers or does not. Most are unsurprising. The ones worth knowing properly are below. string , text and richtext differ in the column type and the input: string A varchar, a single line input. Names, codes, references text A text column, a textarea. Descriptions, notes richtext A text column holding HTML, and an editor in the form richtext is the one with a hidden cost: it stores HTML that a user supplied, so it has to be sanitised on the way in or you have shipped stored cross-site scripting. The generated service does that, which is the reason to use the field type rather than a text plus an editor you wire yourself. select , radio and check all constrain a value to a set, and differ only in the control: The values before the = go in the database; the labels after it go on the screen. This produces a constraint, a Go constant set, a Zod enum and a dropdown, from one string. Watch out Use select for one choice from many, radio when there are three or fewer and the user should see them all at once, and check for several choices at once, which stores a string_array . The trap is choosing string and validating in your head. A free status column collects open , Open , OPEN and opened within a year, and no report ever agrees again. Three, and they are the field types that save the most work. belongs_to is one word that produces a foreign key column with a constraint, a preloaded struct field, a nested TypeScript type, and a searchable dropdown in the form that shows the related record's label column rather than a UUID. one_to_one is the same with a uniqueness constraint. many_to_many creates the join table and a multi-select picker. If you know JavaScript The dropdown showing a name rather than an ID is the detail worth noticing, because it is the canonical hand-written bug. It happens because the frontend has no way to know which column is the human label, so it falls back to the primary key. The generator knows, because belongs_to told it to look. slug derives a URL-safe string from another field and keeps it unique, which is three decisions people usually get wrong separately: how to slugify, when to regenerate, and what to do about collisions. file and files store an upload reference rather than bytes in a column, and wire the upload pipeline from chapter forty two: resize, re-encode, strip EXIF, generate a thumbnail. Writing photo:file is how B8 gets answered. email , url , domain , tel and country are all strings with a format. They look cosmetic and are not: each produces a matching rule in Go and in Zod, so the browser and the API agree about what is valid. Watch out The point is the agreement, not the validation. Validating only in the frontend is a user-experience feature, not a security control, because anybody can post directly to your API. Validating only in the backend means the user discovers the problem after a round trip. One field type produces both, from one definition, which is D3 again. int , uint and float are the raw ones. percent , rating and money are numbers that carry their own rules: a range, a step, a format. Prefer the specific one, because the constraint travels with it. json stores arbitrary structure. Use it for genuinely unstructured data such as a webhook payload, and resist using it to avoid designing a schema, because nothing can query it well and nothing validates it. date is a calendar day with no time and no zone: a birthday, an invoice due date. datetime is an instant, stored UTC. time is a clock time with no date, for opening hours. Watch out Using datetime for a birthday is a real bug, not a style preference. Store it as an instant and somebody in a different timezone sees the day before. The rule: *if the answer should be the same everywhere in the world, it is a date .* Money money , never float A fixed set select , never string A calendar day date , never datetime A relationship belongs_to , never an int you join by hand An upload file , never a string holding a path An email email , so both sides validate it Unstructured json , and only when it really is Every row of that table is a decision that is cheap now and expensive in six months, which is the whole case for field types being a type system rather than a convenience. Project 27: one resource with every interesting type Generate a resource that exercises the types that carry decisions, then look at what each produced. Then check each claim rather than taking it on trust. The money column. Open models/property.go and find price . What Go type, and what does the GORM tag say? Then open the admin form and type 12.345 into it. Then post {"price": 12.345} directly to the API with curl. Both should refuse, and that is the agreement this chapter is about. The date against the time. Find available_from and viewing_time in the generated TypeScript. They are different types, because one is a day and one is a clock reading. The

headings: grit.json, and the seeding that matters
pages.text: One command, and the answers to most of chapter twenty six are already in your directory. This chapter is a tour of what arrives, so that nothing in part five is a surprise. It asks a few questions, or you can answer them up front: The architecture decides how many frontends you get. It is a word this framework uses in a specific way, and it is worth pinning down now because it is not the same thing as an architecture style: triple Web app, admin panel and API, as three applications double Web app and API, with admin as role-protected routes in the web app single One binary serving an embedded SPA api The Go API alone mobile API plus an Expo application Watch out In Grit, architecture means that choice and nothing else. The arrangement of the code inside, the modular monolith with its layers, is called the architecture style , and the two are documented separately for exactly this reason. When someone asks "which architecture does Grit use", find out which question they are asking. The Go side is where this book's attention goes: Five commands rather than one. cmd/restore existing beside cmd/backup is B5 from the last chapter answered honestly: a backup you have never restored is a rumour, so the restore is a first-class command rather than a runbook. Around fifty, and the names tell you what has already been decided for you. Grouped by what they answer: Your layers models , services , handlers , routes , policies Identity authz , password , totp , access , crypto Data database , migrate , paginate , concurrency , money , ids Work jobs , cron , outbox , saga , workflow , events Outside storage , files , media , mail , sms , webhooks , safefetch Operations audit , appendonly , backup , health , tracing , flags Compliance erasure , gdpr -adjacent pieces, settings Delivery respond , sanitize , imports , export , pdf , realtime , sync You will not read all of these. The point of listing them is that each one is a thing you did not write, and most of them correspond to a lettered problem from chapter twenty six. grit start brings up the API, the frontends and the infrastructure at once, which is D2 gone. What is now listening: :8080 The Go API :3000 The web app :3001 The admin panel /studio A database browser: tables, queries, the ERD /docs The API reference, generated from the registered routes /pulse Latency, query counts, profiles /sentinel Errors, with the request attached The second group is the interesting one. /studio is D6, /docs is D7 and /pulse is D5, and all three are paths that were already there rather than tools you installed. If you know JavaScript /docs deserves a note because it is the kind of thing that is usually a lie. It is assembled from the routes actually registered at runtime, not from comments or a hand-written specification. It cannot drift, because there is no second description to drift from. That is the only way an API document stays true, and it is why Grit generates one rather than asking you to maintain one. grit.json records what the project is: its architecture, its module toggles, its name. The CLI reads it so that later commands know the shape of the thing they are editing. The seed is worth insisting on, because it is the habit people skip: Fifty thousand rows is where you discover whether the list page works. At ten rows the sort is instant, pagination has one page, and an N+1 costs ten queries instead of ten thousand. That is D9, and the seeder is built as the pipeline from chapter fourteen: rows built in chunks, written in batches, with the number in flight bounded by a channel, so a million rows runs in about a minute with the heap flat. Eleven subsystems are toggles rather than permanent fixtures: Set one to false in .env and that subsystem does not start. Delete its package and the rest still builds. This is the "batteries included, individually removable" claim, and it is checkable: the packages are separate and the seams are real. Watch out The default project is the hardened one. Auth, sessions, the audit chain, backups and the upload pipeline are present before you write a line, rather than being plugins you remember to enable. That is deliberate and it is worth stating as a principle: an opt-in security feature is a security feature most projects do not have. The cost is a bigger project on day one, which is a real cost and the trade this framework makes on purpose. Open apps/api/internal/services/user.go . It is a struct with a *gorm.DB field and methods on it. Open a handler: it reads a request, calls one service method and writes a response. There is no framework type in your code and nothing to learn before you can read it. That is the whole dependency. If Grit disappeared tonight, this project compiles tomorrow, because there is nothing of Grit inside it. Everything you learned in parts one to three applies directly, which was the reason for putting those parts first. Project 24: make a project and look around No code to write. Make one and read it, because the rest of part four assumes you have seen these files. Then answer these by reading, not by searching the documentation. One. Open apps/api/internal/handlers/user.go and find where it calls the service. How many lines of that handler are about HTTP, and how many are about users? That ratio is the thin-handler rule from chapter eleven, enforced by the generator. Two. Open apps/api/internal/services/user.go and find paginate.Config . It lists which columns a client may search, sort and filter by. Why is that a whitelist rather than passing the client's column name through? The answer is in chapter twenty two, under placeholders. Three. Visit /studio and look at the tables. Then visit /docs and find the route for listing users. Compare the parameters it documents with the paginate.Config you just read: they are the same list, because one is derived from the other. Four. Count the entries in apps/api/go.mod . Then count what a comparable Express project needs in package.json . Neither num
