headings: Status codes, and the ones that matter
The 409, and a number that must not be a string
Validation, in two places that agree
pages.text: A handler's job is small and the contract it serves is not. This chapter is about the envelope every endpoint returns, why it is the same shape everywhere, and the two status codes that are worth understanding properly. Four lines of work. Parse the query against the whitelist, call one service method, hand any error to the boundary, write the answer. The h.ctx(c) is chapter thirty two's point: it converts the Gin context into a context.Context carrying the actor and the organisation, which is what makes the service's queries scoped. Every successful response has the same shape. A single item: A list: And every failure: If you know JavaScript The value of a fixed envelope is on the client side. One fetch wrapper knows how to find the data, one error handler knows how to find the message, and meta is always where pagination lives. Without it, every endpoint is a small negotiation and the frontend accumulates special cases. This is why the generated React hooks are so short: they can assume the shape. 200 201 Created. A POST that made something returns this, with the thing 400 The request was malformed. Bad JSON, a missing parameter 401 Not authenticated. You have no identity 403 Authenticated, and not allowed. You have one, it is insufficient 404 No such thing, or none you may see 409 Conflict. Covered below 422 Well formed, and the values are wrong. The validation case 429 Rate limited 500 We broke Two distinctions people get wrong. 400 against 422. A 400 means the request could not be understood: invalid JSON, a parameter that is not a number. A 422 means it was understood perfectly and the values are unacceptable: an empty name, an email without an @ . The frontend treats them differently, because only one of them can point at a field. 401 against 403. A 401 says "I do not know who you are", and the client should log in. A 403 says "I know exactly who you are and the answer is no", and logging in again will not help. Returning 401 for a permissions failure sends users into a login loop. A deliberate choice worth stating: when you ask for a record you are not allowed to see, you get 404, not 403 . A 403 confirms the record exists. That is an information leak: an attacker can enumerate IDs and learn which invoices, users or documents are real, even without reading them. Answering 404 for both "absent" and "not yours" gives nothing away. Watch out This surprises developers during integration, because a record they can see in the database returns 404 through the API. The cause is almost always ownership scoping doing its job: the query is filtered by the actor in the context, so the row is genuinely not in the result set. The fix is not to loosen the scope. It is to check who the request is authenticated as. Optimistic locking is the Version column from chapter thirty one. A client sends the version it is editing, and the server refuses if it has moved: That response is doing something more useful than reporting a failure: it is telling the interface enough to act . With the current version the client can offer to reload, show the difference, or retry. A bare "conflict" leaves the frontend with nowhere to go but an alert box. Watch out "current_version": 9 , not "9" . It shipped as a quoted string once. Every client that compared versions was comparing text, so "10" < "9" was true and the comparison was silently wrong in exactly the cases that matter. The general lesson: a number that crosses a wire as a string will be compared as a string by somebody, and the failure is silent. This is the same family of bug as omitempty on a bool from chapter nineteen. The respond package is the boundary from chapter eleven, made concrete. respond.Fail is the one to use by default. It walks the error chain with errors.Is and errors.As , finds the sentinel or typed error, and chooses the status and code. The handler does not decide; the error already knows. There are 119 distinct error codes, which sounds excessive until you consider what a frontend does with them. EMAIL_EXISTS can focus the email field. ACCOUNT_LOCKED can show a different screen from INVALID_CREDENTIALS . CSRF_INVALID can retry after refreshing the token. A single VALIDATION_ERROR for all of them makes every one of those a string match on the message. If you know JavaScript A Coded interface lets an error carry its own wire shape: So a package can define an error that knows it is a 409 called STOCK_INSUFFICIENT , and respond.Fail needs no case for it. That is chapter ten's consumer-declared interface in the framework's own code. A generated handler binds the request into a struct with tags: A binding failure becomes a 422 with per-field details, which is where the details object in the envelope comes from. The matching Zod schema in packages/shared was generated from the same field definitions, so the browser refuses the same values for the same reasons. Neither is trusted: the frontend validation is for the user, and the backend validation is the control. Adding an endpoint is ordinary Gin, and it should stay thin: Then register it in the routes file, next to the generated ones. Watch out Resist the urge to put the rule here because the data is already to hand. The check for "already paid" belongs in the service, as it was written in chapter thirty two, so that the CSV importer and the CLI obey it too. The test for whether a line belongs in a handler: *would it still need to be true if this were called by a background job?* If yes, it belongs one layer down. Project 30: exercise the whole contract Use the bookshop and drive every branch of the envelope from the command line, so the contract stops being documentation. The happy paths. Note the 201 and the message , and that meta on the list has four keys. 400 against 422. Send broken JSON, then valid JSON with a bad value: The second should carry details naming the field. That object is what lets a form highlight the right input rather than showing a banner. 401 against 403. Call a prote

headings: Seeding, and why it is not optional
A million rows, with the heap flat
Backups, and the half that counts
pages.text: D10 from chapter twenty six was "changing the schema is the scary part: the migration that half ran, with no way back". This chapter is how that is answered, and it is more interesting than it sounds, because the usual answer is a lie. A generated model is a struct with tags: Three of those fields are the framework's rather than yours. Version is optimistic locking, and chapter thirty three explains the 409 it produces. DeletedAt is soft delete: a DELETE sets the timestamp and every query excludes it automatically, which is how the Trash page works. CreatedAt and UpdatedAt are maintained by GORM. Watch out Soft delete has a consequence people meet late: a uniqueIndex on a column still applies to deleted rows. Delete a user with the email ada@example.com and you cannot create another with that email, because the old row is still there. The usual fix is a composite unique index including deleted_at , so the same value can exist once among live rows and many times among deleted ones. It is worth knowing before a user reports it. It reads your models and makes the database match. No migration files to write. That convenience has a well-known cost and this is where most frameworks are quiet: GORM's AutoMigrate has no down scripts . It can add a column. It cannot tell you what it added last Tuesday, and it cannot undo it. So the answer here is not a pretend rollback. It is a record: Each run writes down what it actually added. --down reads that record and drops exactly those things. It is not a general rollback, it is an undo of recorded runs, and the distinction matters: a change made by someone typing SQL into a console was never recorded, so it cannot be undone this way. If you know JavaScript Prisma and Rails generate a migration file per change, with an explicit up and down , which is more ceremony and gives you a reviewable artifact. This trades the file for automatic detection plus a recorded history. Neither is free. The file-based approach costs a step per change and gives you a precise diff in code review. This approach costs you reviewability and gives you speed. Know which you are using, and never assume a framework that offers --down can undo something it did not do. Dropping a column destroys data. The command asks, and a non-interactive run needs --yes , deliberately, so a CI pipeline cannot quietly delete a column because somebody renamed a struct field. A rename is the case to understand. Changing Name to FullName in a struct is not a rename to AutoMigrate: it is an unknown column appearing and a known one no longer being mentioned. The safe sequence is to add the new column, backfill it, then remove the old one in a later change, which is the same expand-and-contract dance every schema tool requires. D9 was "nothing to develop against". The generator writes a factory per resource that produces realistic values for each field type: a real-looking name for string , a valid address for email , an amount in range for money . At ten rows everything works. The sort is instant, pagination has one page, and an N+1 costs ten queries instead of ten thousand. Every list-page bug you have is invisible until the data arrives, which is why the habit is to seed before you look at a screen rather than after a user complains. The seeder is the pipeline from chapter fourteen, in production: Measured on a laptop: *999,800 rows in 59 seconds, with the heap flat at 10 MB the whole time*. The number that matters is the third one. Sixteen thousand rows a second is a fine figure and it is not the point. The point is that memory is a property of the pipeline rather than of how many rows you asked for: the channel holds a fixed number of batches in flight, so ten thousand rows and ten million look the same to the heap. Watch out The naive versions both fail, in opposite directions. One row per INSERT keeps memory perfect and takes an afternoon, because you pay query parsing, a transaction and a round trip a million times. Building all million rows into a slice first is fast until the process is holding a million structs plus the driver's copy, and then it swaps or is killed. Batching the writes is the win, not the goroutines. Going from one insert per row to one insert per batch moves the number by an order of magnitude. Parallelism on top is worth perhaps five times more. Parallelism without batching is worth almost nothing, because a million round trips is a million round trips however many goroutines are waiting on them. The seeder is also resumable : it counts what is in the table and inserts only the difference. Run it twice and the second run does nothing. Kill it halfway through a million rows and run it again, and it continues. cmd/restore existing beside cmd/backup is the point. B5 asked "is any of this backed up", and the honest reading of that question is "has anyone ever restored one". A backup you have never restored is a rumour. The archive carries a row count per table, so a restore can be checked rather than assumed, and the restore is a command rather than a runbook page nobody has followed. Project 28: break a migration on purpose The point of this project is to experience the failure modes while they are cheap. One: watch a run get recorded. Note what the last run says it changed. Two: add a column and undo it. Check in /studio that the column really left. Three: the rename trap. Edit models/product.go by hand and change SKU to Code . Run grit migrate --status after migrating and look carefully: a column was added, and the old one is still there with the data in it. Nothing was renamed, because nothing could know that was your intention. Now do it properly: add the new field, write a tiny cmd/ program that copies the values across, and only then remove the old one. That is expand-and-contract, and doing it once by hand is worth more than reading about it. Four: the scale that matters. Watch the progress line report rows per second and the heap. Then open the admin Products page, sor

headings: The two whitelists are the chapter
Where a rule does not belong in a service
pages.text: The thin-handler rule has come up three times now. This chapter is the one that justifies it properly and shows what a generated service actually contains. *Every database read and write for a resource lives in that resource's service. The handler reads the request, calls one method, and writes the answer.* The reason is not tidiness. It is this: That signature takes a context.Context , not a *gin.Context . The service has no idea it is being called over HTTP. So the same method serves: the HTTP route a background job a CLI command in cmd/ the CSV importer a test, with no server running A rule enforced here is enforced in all five. A rule written in the handler holds until the first time something other than a browser does the same thing, and then it silently does not. That is the whole argument, and it is why "put the validation in the handler, it is right there" is the most expensive shortcut in a web codebase. If you know JavaScript In an Express app the equivalent discipline is a service module that never imports req or res . Most teams intend this and drift, because the handler is where the data already is. Go makes the drift visible: the moment a service needs *gin.Context it must import Gin, and that import is a review comment waiting to happen. Four things, in this order. The struct, with one dependency. The list configuration, which is a security boundary: The writable set, which is the other one: The methods: List , GetByID , Create , Update , Patch , Delete , Bulk , BulkCreate , BulkEdit , Export . Chapter twenty two said a value can be a placeholder and a column name cannot. These maps are the consequence. A client sends ?sort=name&filter[group_id]=3 . Those strings end up in SQL as identifiers , which no placeholder can protect. So each is checked against a map the generator wrote: writableContact is the same defence for writes, and it closes a different hole. A PATCH that merged the client's JSON straight into the model would let anybody set id , created_at , version , or on a user record, role . That is mass assignment, and it is how a normal user becomes an administrator. Watch out When you add a field by hand rather than with grit generate field , *you must add it to these maps yourself*. The symptom of forgetting is not an error: sorting by the new column silently falls back, and patching it silently does nothing. This is the main reason to use grit generate field rather than editing the struct: the command updates the model, the migration, the two maps, the Zod schema, the type and the admin form together. That looks trivial and is not. The context carries the organisation the multitenant plugin resolved and the actor that per-record ownership is scoped by, and the scoping is applied through the context rather than by each method remembering to add a WHERE . So a service method that uses s.db(ctx) is automatically scoped, and one that reaches for s.DB directly is not. Watch out This is the strongest argument for threading the request's context all the way down rather than creating a fresh one in the middle. A context.Background() halfway through a request does not merely lose cancellation, it loses the caller's identity, and the query comes back unscoped: every organisation's rows, not just this one's. When a background job genuinely must act as nobody, there is an explicit way to say so. The explicitness is the point: an unscoped query should be a sentence someone wrote on purpose. The service returns the sentinels and typed errors from chapter eleven: Note what it does not do: it does not know about status codes, and it does not log. It returns, and the boundary decides. That is chapter eleven's "handle an error once" as a structural rule rather than advice. This is the part people worry about. The generated service is a starting point, and adding to it is ordinary Go: Three things worth copying from that. It reuses GetByID rather than writing another query. It returns a sentinel for the business rule, so the handler can map it to 409. And it emits an event rather than calling the audit log, the webhook sender and the realtime pusher by hand. Watch out Put it in the same file as the generated methods, not a separate one. The manifest from chapter twenty nine hashes generated files, so an edited file is reported on a re-run rather than silently overwritten. That protection only applies to the file it knows about. A method in invoice_custom.go is invisible to that machinery, and the next person to regenerate will not be warned about anything. Two exceptions worth naming. A rule about the shape of a request belongs in the validation layer: "email must look like an email" is a Zod rule and a binding tag, not a service method. A rule that spans resources may belong in a saga rather than in either service, because neither owns the sequence. Marking an invoice paid, adjusting stock and sending a receipt is three services and a failure mode in the middle, which is what internal/saga exists for. Project 29: add a business rule properly Take the bookshop from chapter twenty seven and add a real rule: a book cannot be discounted below its cost price. Then add the method to services/book.go , below the generated ones: Now prove the rule holds in more than one place, which is the point of the chapter. Write a test that calls it directly, with no HTTP: That test runs with context.Background() and no server, which only works because the rule lives in the service. Move the check into a handler and try to write the same test: you now need a request, a recorder and a router, and the CSV importer bypasses your rule entirely. Finally, write a four-line cmd/discount/main.go that calls the same method from the command line, and watch the rule apply there too, for free. Your turn Add the discount field to the admin by hand instead of with grit generate field : edit only the model. Then try to sort the Books table by it and patch it through the API. Both fail silently, because the two maps

headings: Why three, and what each one is for
nullable against optional, which is not pedantry
grit sync, and exactly what it does
The admin resource is updated, not overwritten
pages.text: D3 was "the same type exists four times". A Blog is a Go struct, a database column list, a TypeScript interface and a validation schema, and nothing makes them agree except the person who remembers to change all four. This chapter is about the place where three of those four stop being separate things, and about the one command that keeps them that way. It is a workspace package rather than a published one, so there is no build step and no version to bump. The frontends import it by subpath: you get types/blog.ts : and schemas/blog.ts , which is three schemas rather than one: BlogSchema The row as the API returns it. Every field, including the ones the server assigns CreateBlogSchema What a POST accepts. No id , no timestamps, and required where the Go binding tag said so UpdateBlogSchema The create schema, .partial() . A PATCH sends the fields that changed and nothing else id , created_at , updated_at and deleted_at are dropped from the create schema automatically. They are assigned by the server, so a form that offers them is a form that can lie. If you know JavaScript This is the shape you would have built by hand in a Next.js project, and the part that goes wrong by hand is UpdateSchema . People reuse the create schema for editing, so every PATCH has to send every field, so an edit form that was missing one input quietly blanks that column. .partial() is the fix, and having it generated means you cannot forget it on the eleventh resource. image is z.string().nullable() in the row schema and z.string() .optional() in the create schema, and the difference is the difference between two states that look the same in a form: nullable : the server will send "image": null . The key is there, the value is empty. optional : the client may leave the key out entirely, and the server applies its default. A Go pointer field ( *string , *time.Time ) becomes nullable, because a pointer is how Go says "this may be absent". A non-required field becomes optional on create. Get these the wrong way round by hand and you get a form that refuses to submit because a column the user cannot see is null . It parses every file in apps/api/internal/models/ with Go's own parser, not a regular expression, and for each struct it writes: types/<name>.ts The interface, overwritten schemas/<name>.ts The three schemas, overwritten the admin resource New fields added to the generated section only The name is kebab-cased from the struct: BlogPost becomes blog-post.ts . User is skipped. It has hand-written schemas covering login, registration, password reset and profile updates, which are not derivable from the struct, and regenerating them would throw away work the framework cannot reproduce. The mapping, for the types you will actually hit: TypeScript Zod string string z.string() int , int64 number z.number().int() uint number z.number().int().nonnegative() float64 number z.number() bool boolean z.boolean() time.Time string z.string() *time.Time string | null z.string().nullable() Times cross as strings, because JSON has no date type. Chapter nineteen covers the format; the thing to hold onto here is that the TypeScript type says string and means RFC 3339, and the parsing is the frontend's job. Watch out * grit sync overwrites those two files completely.* There is no merge and no manifest conflict: the generated type and the generated schema are outputs, and an output is rewritten. So a refinement you add inside schemas/blog.ts , a .refine() for a cross-field rule or a stricter message, is gone the next time somebody adds a column. Put it in a file beside it and compose: The rule for the whole framework, stated once: *edit the inputs, extend the outputs*. The model is an input. The shared schema is an output. The third thing sync touches is the admin resource definition, and it is treated differently because it is yours. The generated file carries markers around the section the generator owns. New model fields are added inside those markers, to the columns and the form. Anything you customised, a renamed label, a render function, a reordered column, sits outside them and survives. So the usual loop after changing a model is two commands: and the admin has the new field in the table and the form without you opening the file. sync keeps three things in step: the type, the schema, and the admin resource. It does not update the generated mobile forms or the desktop columns, because those have no marker scheme yet. It says so rather than pretending: That warning exists because the failure without it is miserable to diagnose: a correct API, a correct type, a correct admin screen, and a mobile create form frozen at the three fields the resource was generated with. The field is in the response and absent from the form, and nothing is broken enough to show an error. Watch out Treat that warning as a task, not as noise. The fix is to open the named screen and add the field by hand, which is five minutes, or to regenerate the screen if you have not customised it. A framework that quietly half-synced would be worse than one that does not sync at all, because you would trust the half. The schemas are not decoration. They are the validation layer of every generated form: The inferred input type comes from the same schema: so renaming a field in the Go model and running grit sync makes the editor underline every place the old name is used, before anything runs. That is the actual payoff of D3: not that the four definitions exist in one place, but that disagreeing with them is a compile error rather than a support ticket. The error codes travel the same way. types/errors.ts is generated from the Go error catalogue, so a frontend can match on a code rather than on a message: Three smaller files, each solving a small duplication that gets annoying at the third app: constants/ holds the API route paths, so a URL typo is a type error rather than a 404 at runtime. themes.ts holds the palette, read by the admin, the web app and the desktop c
pages.title: What is in it

headings: Two lists, and they belong to different people
Why these survive a decade of excellent libraries
The question a framework has to answer
What this means for the rest of the book
pages.text: You can now write Go. You have built a CLI, an HTTP service, a database layer and a deployable binary with no framework at all. So the fair question before part four is: why would you add one? The answer is not "to write less code". It is that every project runs into the same list of problems, the list is longer than people admit, and most of it has nothing to do with the product you were hired to build. The problems split in two, and the split matters because the two halves are paid for by different people at different times. The developer's twelve cost you the first two weeks. You feel them immediately and you can name them from memory. The client's fourteen are questions asked before anybody mentions your actual feature. They decide whether there is a project at all, and they are always promised for later. The copy-paste start. Auth, storage and email lifted from the last repository, bugs included Wiring the monorepo: workspaces, ports, env files, Docker, before anything runs The same type written twice, or four times: Go, TypeScript, the validation schema, the mobile client The same UI for every table. Twenty tables, twenty slightly different list pages Testing performance is its own project, so it waits for a quiet week that does not come No window into the database without installing one more tool The API nobody wrote down. Hand-written OpenAPI is accurate for one afternoon Import and export are always a ticket, and always a week rather than an afternoon Nothing to develop against: empty tables, and mail you cannot read D10 Changing the schema is the scary part: the migration that half ran, with no way back D11 The frontend is somebody else's job, and there is nobody else D12 Generating it with a model costs money every time, and none of it compounds Most of these you have met in this book. You wrote the error boundary in chapter eleven, the middleware in twenty one, the config validation in twenty four. None of it was hard. All of it was time, and none of it was the product. If you know JavaScript D11 deserves a sentence, because it is the reason many readers picked this book up. You are fluent in React and now also in Go, which makes you the rare person who can do both. The cost is that you are now the person who does both, for every project, forever. A generated admin panel is not about disliking frontend work; it is about not rebuilding the same table for the twentieth time. These arrive as questions, usually in the first meeting, before anybody has described the actual product. Can different people see different things? What happens if we get hacked? Does it work without internet? How will we know when it breaks? Is any of this backed up? What if it gets busy? Who changed this? Our users photograph things on their phones Can two of our clients use one system? B10 Does the screen update by itself? B11 Can we switch this on for one customer only? B12 What if two people edit the same record? B13 Does it talk to our other systems? B14 Someone has asked us to delete their data The honest answer to every one of them is "yes, in about three weeks", and the client hears that as a no. Notice what they have in common: each is real work with no demo attached . You cannot show a stakeholder an audit log. So each gets promised for phase two, and offline, audit and observability are the three that never arrive. Go's ecosystem is superb at solving one problem each. A router, a queue, a migration tool, an image decoder, all excellent. So why is the list still here? Libraries solve one problem each. Nobody hands you the shape. A router solves routing. Nothing solves "what does an application made of these look like", so the shape is hand-carved on every project, slightly differently. A template rots the day you clone it. A boilerplate repository freezes the bugs of the day you started. The fix you make on project five never reaches projects one to four, and you cannot tell which repository has which. This is D1 with extra steps. The client's fourteen are always phase two. Expensive, invisible, always cut. Which is a precise definition of what belongs in a framework. Watch out D12 is the newest and it is worth stating carefully, because the obvious version of the argument is wrong. An agent will write this scaffold for you. A Grit project measures about 74,500 lines, which is roughly three quarters of a million output tokens: at current frontier pricing, tens of dollars. That is cheap for two weeks of work and anybody who tells you the cost alone is the objection is overselling. The objection is the other three properties. You pay it again on the next project. The model writes something different each time, so the auth it gives you in March and in June are different code with different bugs. And because they are different, a fix you make in one project has nowhere to go. That is D1, the copy-paste start, with a bill attached. So the question is not which library . It is: #block(width: 92%, inset: 10pt, radius: 3pt, fill: rgb("#f6f7f9"), stroke: 0.5pt + rgb("#e3e6ea"))[ #set text(size: 11pt, style: "italic") Can the shape of an application be generated, owned outright by the team that generated it, and still improve after they own it? ] Three clauses, and they fight each other. Generated is easy. Plenty of tools generate code. Generated and owned is harder, and is where most scaffolders stop: they hand you a repository and walk away. Generated, owned, and still improving is the actual problem, because the moment code is yours, nobody can fix it but you. That third clause is what grit upgrade exists for, and chapter 29 is about how the line between "yours" and "the framework's" is drawn. Part four explains Grit's answer to that question: what grit new produces, how the architecture is laid out, why the resource is the unit of generation, and how the generated code stays plain Go that you can read with everything you learned in parts one to three. Part five builds real applications with it. Two pr
pages.title: Two lists, and they belong to different people

headings: Why one description is the point
A field type is a decision made once
It is still your code afterwards
pages.text: This is the idea the framework rests on. If you disagree with it, the rest of part four is wrong, so it gets a chapter of its own. *A resource is the only thing that spans the whole stack, so it is the thing worth generating.* Not a file. Not a layer. The invoice, from the database column to the form field. Consider what "add invoices to this application" actually requires: Database a table, columns, indexes, a foreign key a model, a service with the rules, a handler, routes Contract a validation schema, a TypeScript type Frontend a data hook, a list page, a form, a detail view Thirteen or so files. A scaffolder that generates a model has automated the easy part, because the model was never the expensive bit. The expense is that one concept, "invoice", has to be spelled correctly in thirteen places, and kept correct as it changes. If you know JavaScript This is D3 from chapter twenty six, and you have felt it. The Go struct, the Zod schema, the TypeScript type and the mobile client are four descriptions of one thing, kept in step by memory. Nothing fails to compile when they drift. You find out in the browser, from a user, as a blank column or a wrong total. Four field types. One of them is a relationship. That is the entire input. What it writes, by name: Plus the routes registered, the model added to the migration list, and the resource added to the admin's navigation. Watch out Note index.tsx in the resource folder. The generator writes it once and then never regenerates it , because that is where your custom cells and forms go. The distinction between "regenerated" and "written once" runs through the whole system, and chapter thirty one is about where that line sits. The thirteen files are not the achievement. The achievement is that they come from one description , so they cannot disagree. Add a field later: That reaches the model, the migration, the Zod schema, the TypeScript type, the admin table and the admin form in one step. There is no version of this where the backend has paid_at and the frontend does not, because there is no second place to update. That is the real answer to D3. Not "less typing": no drift . Thirty one field types ship. The important ones are not the obvious ones. Take money . Writing total:money decides a column type, a Go type, a Zod rule, an input mask and how the number is formatted in a table cell. Say float instead and you have shipped a rounding bug that will surface in a total months later, found by an accountant. This is the lesson from chapter nineteen, where you implemented MarshalJSON for exactly this. The difference is that here it is a type rather than advice, so the correct decision is the default rather than something you must remember. Take belongs_to . One word, and you get: a ClientID foreign key column, with a constraint a Client field on the struct, preloaded on read a nested type in the generated TypeScript a searchable dropdown in the admin form that shows the client's name rather than a UUID If you know JavaScript In a hand-written stack each of those is a separate decision someone makes slightly differently. The dropdown showing a UUID instead of a name is the canonical example: it is nobody's bug, everybody has shipped it, and it happens because the frontend had no way to know which column is the human label. Here the generator knows, because belongs_to told it. Open the generated service. It is a struct with a *gorm.DB and methods, with comments explaining why rather than what: One dependency, and it is GORM. You can edit any of it. The generated code is the starting point, not a sealed artifact. Watch out Re-running grit generate resource on an existing resource does not silently overwrite your edits. Every generated file is hashed into a manifest when written, and a file whose hash has moved is reported rather than replaced. This behaviour exists because the opposite happened: an early version rewrote the model, service and handler on a re-run, printing a green tick for each, and everything hand-written in them was gone. No prompt, no backup, and the documentation had promised that the service was where your business logic goes. A newcomer lost a BeforeSave rule and a service method in their first week. The lesson generalises past this framework: a generator that overwrites without asking is a generator you cannot trust with a file you have edited. Worth saying plainly, because the demo makes it look like magic. It generates the shape . It does not generate the rule that an invoice cannot be billed twice, the report the client asks for every month, or the pricing logic that is the reason they hired you. That is still yours, it is still the hard part, and it is still where the value is. What has gone is the two weeks before you got to any of it. Project 26: generate a resource and read every file In the project from chapter twenty seven: Then open every file it named, in this order, and answer one question about each. * models/book.go .* Find the money field. What Go type is it, and what does the GORM tag say the column is? Why is that not a float64 ? * services/book.go .* Find paginate.Config . Which columns can a client sort by, and which cannot? Now try ?sort=price and ?sort=secret against the running API. * handlers/book.go .* Count the lines that are about HTTP. Find the one call into the service per endpoint. * packages/shared/schemas/book.ts .* Find the Zod rule for price and compare it to the Go validation. They came from the same word in your command. * packages/shared/types/book.ts .* Compare the TypeScript type to the Go struct field by field. *The admin panel at :3001 .* Find the Books page. Sort by title, search, open the form. Notice the price input: it is a money input, not a number input, because of one word in your command. headings: Wrapping: adding context without losing the original
pages.text: This is the chapter that decides whether you get on with Go. Error handling is where the language is most unlike JavaScript, it is the thing newcomers complain about loudest, and the complaint is half right. Let us do the mechanics first and the argument second. Things you have not met yet Code here uses a few things this book has not covered yet: structs in chapter 5, slices in chapter 6, interfaces in chapter 10, errors.Is in chapter 11 and defer in chapter 12. You are not missing anything. Read them as the shapes they look like, and each one gets its own chapter. The type comes after the name, which reads backwards for about a day and then stops mattering. The reason is that it makes complicated declarations read left to right instead of spiralling outwards, which anyone who has read a C function pointer declaration will appreciate. Functions are values, so the things you do in JavaScript still work: If you know JavaScript That apply is Array.prototype.map , written by hand. Go had no generics until 1.18 and still has no map , filter or reduce in the standard library for slices. You write the loop. Go's argument is that a three-line loop needs no explanation and a chain of five callbacks sometimes does. You are allowed to find this annoying. A Go function can return several values, and this is not a curiosity: it is the foundation of the error system. The caller gets both: The convention is absolute, across the standard library and every package you will use: the error is the last return value, and you check it immediately . If you know JavaScript JavaScript has one return value, so a function that can fail either throws or returns something like { data, error } . Go makes the second shape the language default. If you have written Go-style error handling in TypeScript with a Result type, or used Rust, you already have the mental model. There is nothing magic about errors. error is an interface with one method: Anything with an Error() string method is an error. That means you can make your own, carrying whatever fields you want: A bare error from deep in a call stack is useless on its own. fmt.Errorf with the %w verb wraps one error inside another, keeping both. The message becomes a trail that reads from the outside in: Use %w , not %v . %v formats the error as text and throws the original away, and then both of the checks below stop working. Two functions read a wrapped chain. errors.Is asks "is this error, anywhere in the chain, that specific one": errors.As asks "is there an error of this type in the chain", and gives it to you with its fields intact: Watch out err != nil is the only check that matters, and comparing an error to nil has one notorious trap. A function returning a concrete error type rather than the error interface can produce an error value that is not nil even when it holds nothing: The fix is a rule: *always declare the return type as error , and return a literal nil , never a typed nil variable.* This catches experienced people and it is worth reading twice. Here is the complaint, stated fairly. This: The Go is twice as long. That is not a matter of opinion. What you get for it is that every failure point is visible at the point it can fail. In the JavaScript, which of the three awaited calls threw? You cannot tell from the code, and the catch block treats all three identically whether or not that is what you wanted. In the Go, each failure is a separate decision, and you could handle the migration failure differently from the connection failure by changing one block. The honest summary: try / catch is better when you want to treat a whole region of code as one unit that either works or does not. Explicit returns are better when failures deserve individual handling. Most real backend code is the second kind more often than people expect, and Go bet the language on it. What you lose, and should know about In JavaScript an uncaught exception unwinds to the nearest handler, so a forgotten catch still surfaces somewhere. In Go a forgotten error check silently continues with a zero value. Nothing warns you. This is a real hazard and the tooling answers it: errcheck , bundled into golangci-lint , fails the build on an unchecked error. Install it early. It is the one linter that is not optional. A function can name its return values, which is occasionally useful and frequently overused: Use naked returns only in short functions. In a long one, a bare return forces the reader to scroll up to learn what is being returned. Named returns do earn their place with defer , which schedules a call to run when the surrounding function exits, no matter how it exits: defer f.Close() immediately after a successful open is one of the most common patterns in Go, and it is how the language avoids the cleanup bugs that try / finally exists to solve. Watch out Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order, and their arguments are evaluated immediately, not at exit: And a defer inside a loop does not run at the end of each iteration, it runs when the function returns. Opening a thousand files in a loop with defer f.Close() keeps all thousand open until the function ends. Put the body in its own function if you need per-iteration cleanup. Project 3: a word counter that handles failure Write a program that takes a filename, counts the words in it, and reports errors properly rather than crashing. Run it on a real file, then on one that does not exist, and read the wrapped message. Notice os.Exit(1) and writing to os.Stderr : a command line tool that reports failure on stdout with exit code zero is a tool that breaks every script that uses it. strings.Fields splits on any run of whitespace, which is the right behaviour here and is worth remembering: it is not the same as strings.Split(s, " ") , which gives empty strings between consecutive spaces. Your turn Add a check that reports a clearer message when the path is a directory rather than a file. os.ReadFile returns an error you can inspe

headings: Capital letters are the access modifier
The commands you will actually use
pages.text: This chapter gets Go on your machine, gets a program running, and introduces the toolchain. If you have ever set up a Node project you will find this shorter than you expect, because most of the steps you are used to do not exist. Go to #link("https://go.dev/dl/")[go.dev/dl] and download the installer for your platform. There is no version manager to install first, no equivalent of nvm , and for most people there never needs to be. Go's compatibility promise means a program written for Go 1.0 in 2012 still compiles today, so "which version" is rarely a question that costs you an afternoon. Check it worked: You should see something like go version go1.25.0 windows/amd64 . If the command is not found, the installer did not put Go on your PATH ; restart your terminal first, because that fixes it more often than anything else. If you know JavaScript There is no nvm , no .nvmrc , and no per-project runtime. One Go installation builds every project on your machine. When a project needs a specific version, it says so in one line of go.mod and the toolchain downloads that compiler itself. Make a directory and put one file in it. Run it: Four things in that tiny file deserve explanation, because each is a rule you will meet constantly. package main declares which package this file belongs to. Every Go file starts with a package declaration. The name main is special: it means this package builds into a runnable program rather than a library. import "fmt" pulls in the formatting package from the standard library. Note there is no npm install . fmt ships with Go, as does an HTTP server, a JSON encoder, a test runner, a crypto suite and a templating engine. func main() is the entry point. A program starts here. There is exactly one main function in a program. fmt.Println prints a line. Capital P matters enormously, and it is the next section. This is the first genuinely surprising rule in Go, and it catches everybody. *An identifier starting with a capital letter is exported. One starting with a lowercase letter is private to its package.* That is the entire visibility system. There is no public , no private , no export keyword. If you know JavaScript In JavaScript you choose what leaves a module with export . In Go the name itself decides. fmt.Println works because Println is capitalised inside package fmt ; if it were println you could not reach it. This applies to functions, types, struct fields, constants and variables alike. Watch out This bites hardest with struct fields and JSON. A lowercase field is invisible to the JSON encoder, because the encoder lives in another package and genuinely cannot see it. A struct whose fields are all lowercase encodes to {} , with no error and no warning. Chapter sixteen covers this properly, but remember the symptom now: empty JSON usually means lowercase fields. A single file is fine for a demo. A real project is a module . Initialise one: That writes go.mod : That is the whole file. Compare it to a package.json for an equivalent project and notice what is missing: no scripts , no devDependencies , no main , no type: module . The module path doubles as the import path, which is why it looks like a URL: if you push this to GitHub, anybody can import it at exactly that address with no registry publish step. Add a dependency and go.mod grows a line: If you know JavaScript go.sum is your lockfile, equivalent to package-lock.json . Commit it. There is no node_modules : downloaded packages go to a shared module cache outside your project, and the compiler links what it needs directly into the binary. Deleting a project directory does not take 300MB of dependencies with it, because they were never there. Six commands cover almost everything. go run . Compile and run the current package, without keeping the binary go build Compile to an executable in the current directory go test ./... Run every test in this module go mod tidy Add what is imported, remove what is not. Run it often gofmt -w . Format every file. Your editor probably does this on save go vet ./... Report suspicious code the compiler allows The ./... pattern means "this directory and everything under it", and you will type it constantly. This is the part that sells Go to people who have deployed Node. You now have one executable file. It contains your code, every dependency, and the Go runtime. The target machine needs nothing installed. You can also build for a platform you are not on: That produces a Linux binary from a Mac or Windows laptop, with no container, no cross-compilation toolchain and no configuration. Copy it to a Linux server and it runs. Project 1: a greeting with arguments Write a program that takes a name as a command line argument and greets it, falling back to "world" when none is given. You need os.Args , which is a slice of strings where os.Args[0] is the program name itself. Build it, run ./hello Ada , then run it with no argument. Then break it deliberately: change len(os.Args) > 1 to len(os.Args) > 0 and run it with no argument to see what a real Go panic looks like. Reading panics early is worth more than avoiding them. Your turn Extend the greeting to accept several names and greet each on its own line. You will need a for loop over a slice, which looks like for _, n := range os.Args[1:] { ... } . The next chapter explains every piece of that line, so guessing now is fine and the compiler will tell you when you are wrong. Commit your work with the message Hello Go - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. A module, a program, and a binary you can hand to somebody. One. In part1-language/02-hello , run go mod init , write a program that prints a greeting, and run it with go run . . Two. Add a second file in the same package with one exported and one unexported function. Call both from main . Then try to call the unexported one from a different package and keep the compiler error in a comment. Three. Build a real binary and commit its size, not the b

headings: Missing keys return the zero value
Structs as values, and the thing you cannot do
Maps are not safe for concurrent use
pages.text: A Go map is a hash table with typed keys and typed values. It is the closest thing Go has to a JavaScript object used as a dictionary, and it differs in four ways that each cause a specific bug the first time you meet them. Things you have not met yet The concurrency-safe example at the end uses sync.Mutex (chapter 15) and defer (chapter 12). Skip it on a first read if you like: the map itself is the chapter. The type is map[KeyType]ValueType . Keys must be comparable, so strings, ints, booleans and structs of those are fine; slices, maps and functions are not. Watch out A nil map is readable but not writable , and this is the first map bug everyone hits: Always create one before writing: m := map[string]int{} or m := make(map[string]int) . The same trap hides inside structs, where a map field is nil until you assign one, so a constructor that forgets it produces a struct that panics on first write. Reading a key that is not there is not an error. You get the zero value of the value type. That last line is why counting in Go is so tidy: no "if the key exists, add one, otherwise set it to one". To tell "absent" from "present but zero", use the two-value form: ok is a bool. This is the comma ok idiom, and you will see the same shape for type assertions and channel receives. If you know JavaScript In JavaScript, obj.missing gives undefined , and you distinguish absent from set-to-undefined with in or hasOwnProperty . Go's v, ok := is the same idea with better ergonomics, because the check and the read are one operation and you cannot forget which you did. Run that twice and the order differs. This is not an implementation accident that might settle down: the runtime randomises the starting point on purpose, so that code which accidentally depends on order fails immediately and loudly rather than in production two years later when the table grows. To iterate in a stable order, sort the keys: If you know JavaScript JavaScript objects do have an order: integer-like keys ascending, then string keys in insertion order. Plenty of code quietly relies on it. Go removes the temptation. If your output needs an order, you must say what that order is, which is usually an improvement to the code anyway. Passing a map to a function does not copy it. The function can modify the caller's map. This is unlike a struct and unlike an array, and like a slice's elements. There is no const map and no way to pass one read-only. If a function must not modify a map, the only guards are a copy ( maps.Clone ) or a comment. A map of structs has one sharp edge: The map returns a copy of the struct, so incrementing it would modify something about to be discarded, and Go refuses rather than letting you write code that does nothing. Two fixes: The second is usually what you want when the values are large or frequently updated. The first is fine for small structs and avoids a layer of indirection. Go has no set type. The idiom is a map with an empty struct value: struct{} is a struct with no fields and it occupies zero bytes, so the map stores only keys. Using map[string]bool is also common and slightly more readable at the cost of one byte per entry; both are accepted Go. If you know JavaScript JavaScript has a real Set with .has() and .add() . Go's version is wordier, and that struct{}{} reads as line noise until you have seen it a dozen times. Read it as: the type struct{} , then an empty literal of it. Two goroutines writing to the same map at the same time will crash the program with a runtime error, deliberately. Go detects it and stops rather than corrupting the table silently. The answer is usually a mutex, which is chapter fifteen: If you know JavaScript This has no JavaScript equivalent, because the event loop means two pieces of your code never run at literally the same instant. In Go they do. Any value shared between goroutines needs protection, and a map is the one where forgetting is immediately fatal rather than subtly wrong, which is mercifully the better failure. Project 6: a word index with line numbers Extend the frequency counter into something genuinely useful: for each word, record every line it appears on. This is a map[string][]int , a map whose values are slices, and it is a shape you will use often. The line that rewards attention is index[w] = append(index[w], line) . If w is not in the map, index[w] is a nil slice, and appending to a nil slice is legal and returns a one-element slice. So the "create the entry if missing" branch that you would write in most languages simply does not exist here. Two zero-value rules, slices and maps, combining to delete a line of code. Also note bufio.Scanner : it reads line by line without loading the file into memory, so this works on a file larger than your RAM, unlike the os.ReadFile in the last project. And scanner.Err() must be checked, because the loop ends identically on end-of-file and on a read error. Your turn Change the value type to a small struct holding both the line numbers and a total count, and watch the compiler stop you from writing index[w].Count++ . Fix it both ways described above, then decide which you prefer and why. That decision, made consciously once, is the difference between copying Go idioms and understanding them. Commit your work with the message Maps - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. A word counter, which is the smallest program that forces every map lesson. In part1-language/07-maps , read a text file and report the ten most common words. One. Count with a map[string]int , using the fact that a missing key reads as zero rather than checking first. Two. Sort the results before printing, and say in a comment why printing straight from the map would make the output differ between runs. Three. Group with a map[string][]string : words by first letter. Note what happens when you append to a key that does not exist yet. Four. Try to assign to a field of a struct stored in a map, keep the compiler err

headings: The import path is the module path plus the directory
internal/ is a real access rule
Major versions are in the path
init, and why to avoid it
pages.text: You have been writing single-file programs. Real projects are many files, and Go's rules for organising them are stricter and simpler than what you are used to. This chapter is the one that makes a Go repository stop looking strange. Things you have not met yet errors.Is appears in one example and is properly chapter 11. Every .go file belongs to a package, declared on its first line. *Every file in a directory must declare the same package name*, and a directory is exactly one package. That is the whole rule. Files in store/ can see each other's identifiers with no import at all, even the lowercase ones. There is no equivalent of importing between files in the same folder, because they are already the same package. If you know JavaScript This is the biggest structural difference from JavaScript. In a Next.js project every file is its own module, and you import between them constantly. In Go, store/store.go and store/user.go share a namespace: a function declared in one is callable from the other with no ceremony. You import across directories , never within one. You refer to things by the package name , which is the last element of the path by convention but is really whatever the files declare. store.New , not New . The grouping above is conventional: standard library first, then third party, then your own module, separated by blank lines. gofmt sorts within groups and goimports adds and removes imports as you type. Watch out An unused import is a compile error, exactly like an unused variable. This is why goimports in your editor is not optional: without it you will spend real time adding and removing import lines by hand. The escape hatch, for a package imported only for its side effects, is the blank identifier: There is no baseUrl , no paths mapping, no @/components alias, and no relative imports. import "./store" is not valid Go. If your module is github.com/you/myapp , then the directory store/ is imported as github.com/you/myapp/store . Always the full path. If you know JavaScript Verbose compared to @/store , and it buys one thing: an import path is globally unambiguous. You can paste it into a browser and often land on the source. There is no build-time configuration that has to agree with your editor, your bundler and your test runner, because there is no mapping at all. A directory named internal is enforced by the compiler: only code rooted at its parent may import it. If someone imports github.com/you/myapp/internal/db from a different module, the build fails. This is how a library publishes a small surface while keeping the rest private, and it is why nearly every serious Go project puts most of its code under internal/ . If you know JavaScript The nearest npm equivalent is the exports field in package.json , which controls what consumers can reach. Go's version is a directory name, needs no configuration and cannot be worked around. Package names are short, lowercase, single words. No underscores, no camelCase, no plurals. The identifier is read with the package name, which leads to the most quoted style rule in Go: Watch out Avoid util , helpers , common and shared . They are not packages, they are places things go to hide, and they grow into a dependency that everything imports and nobody understands. If a function does not belong anywhere, that usually means the thing it operates on wants a package of its own. A module is a tree of packages with one go.mod at the root. You saw it in chapter two; here is what the rest of it means. The second require block is indirect dependencies: things your dependencies need. go mod tidy manages both blocks, adding what is imported and removing what is not. Run it before every commit. If you know JavaScript go.sum is the lockfile and must be committed. Unlike package-lock.json it is not a full dependency tree: it is a list of cryptographic hashes. Go uses minimal version selection , meaning it picks the lowest version that satisfies everyone, so builds are reproducible from go.mod alone and the sum file exists to verify integrity rather than to pin. There is also no devDependencies . A tool you use at development time is either run with go run or tracked in a tools.go file. Upgrading is explicit: This surprises everyone. From v2 onward, the major version is part of the It looks strange and it solves a real problem: two major versions of the same library can coexist in one build, because as far as the compiler is concerned they are different packages. You will see this in Grit itself, which imports as github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/v3 . A package can declare func init() , which runs automatically before main . Use it rarely. It makes startup order implicit, it cannot return an error, and it runs even when a test only wanted one function from the package. Explicit setup called from main is almost always better. Project 8: split the inventory into packages Take the inventory from chapter seven and give it a real project layout. The point is to feel the import rules rather than to add features. internal/inventory/item.go : internal/inventory/store.go : main.go : Now run three experiments. Call inv.low(5) from main.go and read the error: lowercase means package-private, and the compiler enforces it. Move the whole internal directory to pkg and confirm it still builds, then put it back. And try import "./internal/inventory" to see that relative imports genuinely do not exist. Your turn Add a second package, internal/report , with a function that takes a *inventory.Store and prints a summary. You will hit a design question immediately: report needs to read every item, but Store.items is unexported. Solve it by adding an exported method to inventory rather than by exporting the field, and notice that the package boundary just forced you into a better API than you would have written in one file. Commit your work with the message Packages - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Take one of your earlier programs apar

headings: Everything in Go is passed by value
nil, and the panic you will meet
When not to use a pointer
The loop variable, and a trap that Go fixed
pages.text: Pointers have a reputation they do not deserve, earned in languages where you can do arithmetic on them and walk off the end of memory. Go's pointers cannot do that. There is no pointer arithmetic, and the garbage collector means you never free anything. What is left is a small, useful idea: *a pointer is the address of a value rather than a copy of it*. You have already been using them. This chapter names what was happening. Things you have not met yet A couple of examples borrow from later chapters: errors.Is is chapter 11, goroutines are chapter 13, and the json tags are chapter 19. They are there because pointers are what those chapters trip over. This is the single sentence that explains pointers, and it is worth reading twice because it is the opposite of your JavaScript instinct. When you pass anything to a function, Go copies it. An int, a struct, a slice header, all copied. So a function cannot change what you passed: If you know JavaScript In JavaScript, objects are passed by reference to the same object , so a function that sets user.name changes the caller's object. Primitives are copied. Go removes the distinction: everything is copied, every time, and when you want the other behaviour you ask for it explicitly with a pointer. Less to remember, more to type. &x means "the address of x". *T in a type means "pointer to T". *p as an expression means "the value at p". Now the function that works: Watch out You almost never write (*u).Name . Go dereferences automatically for field access and method calls, so u.Name works whether u is a User or a *User . This is a deliberate convenience and it means pointer-ness mostly disappears from the code that uses the value. The place it reappears is nil . A pointer's zero value is nil . Using a field on a nil pointer crashes: If you know JavaScript TypeScript's strictNullChecks would make this a compile error. Go has no equivalent: a *User might be nil and the compiler will not stop you. This is the one area where TypeScript's type system is genuinely ahead, and it is worth saying rather than glossing over. Your defences in Go are: return values rather than pointers where you can, check at the boundary, and let the panic happen in development rather than coding defensively everywhere. Three reasons, and nothing else. One: you need to modify the caller's value. This is the common case, and it is why methods that change state take pointer receivers. Two: the struct is large and copied often. A struct with twenty fields copied in a tight loop is real work. For a three-field struct it does not matter, and chasing this before measuring is how code gets uglier for no gain. Three: nil is a meaningful value. A *string field distinguishes "the user did not supply this" from "the user supplied an empty string". You met this in chapter three as the limit of zero values. This is the fix. That is how a PATCH endpoint tells "clear this field" apart from "do not touch this field", and you will write it for real in part four. Slices, maps and channels already hold an internal pointer. Passing *[]int or *map[string]int is almost always wrong and marks code as written by someone still finding their feet. The slice version returns the new slice, which is the convention append itself follows. The pointer version works and reads badly. Small structs you only read are also better by value. A Point{X, Y int} is sixteen bytes; copying it is cheaper than following a pointer. For years this was the most common Go bug in existence: The loop variable was reused across iterations, so all the goroutines shared one variable and usually printed the last element several times. Go 1.22 changed this. Loop variables are now per-iteration, and the code above does what it looks like it does. Watch out You will still find the old workaround everywhere in blog posts and older codebases: It is harmless on modern Go and no longer needed. But check your go.mod : the new behaviour only applies if the go directive says 1.22 or higher. A module that still says go 1.21 gets the old semantics *even on a new toolchain*, which is a subtle and genuinely nasty way to inherit this bug. You can take the address of a field, and of a slice element, which is how the contact book in chapter five worked: What you cannot take the address of is a map entry, because the map may move its contents when it grows: This is the same restriction that stopped m["a"].Name++ in chapter seven, and it has the same two fixes: read-modify-write, or store *User in the map. Project 7: an inventory with adjustable stock Build something where the pointer decisions actually matter, and where getting one wrong is visible. Now do the experiment that teaches the chapter. Change the map to map[string]Item , holding values rather than pointers, and try to compile. The line it.Stock -= n will still compile, because it is now a copy, and the stock will never change. Run it and watch 10 left print after you took three. Then make it work by reading, modifying and writing back. That bug, with values where you meant pointers, is the single most common mistake newcomers make with Go collections, and having caused it once on purpose you will recognise it instantly. Your turn Add a Restock(sku string, n int) error method, then add a Low(threshold int) []*Item that returns every item below a stock level. Decide whether Low should return []*Item or []Item and be able to say why. One of them lets a caller change your inventory by accident, which might be exactly what you want or exactly what you do not. Commit your work with the message Pointers - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Three programs, each one line different. In part1-language/08-pointers : One. A Counter with Inc() on a value receiver. Call it ten times and print zero. Then change one character and print ten. Commit both, the broken one as value_receiver.go.txt so it does not compile into the build. Two. A function taking a struct by valu

headings: Arrays have a fixed length, in the type
Slices are a view onto an array
append, and the thing it does not promise
pages.text: Go has arrays and it has slices. You will use slices for essentially everything, and the distinction matters exactly twice: when you declare one, and when a surprising bug appears. This chapter covers both. Things you have not met yet One example counts words with a map. Maps are chapter 7; here it is just somewhere to put a count. The length is part of the type . [3]int and [4]int are different types, and a function taking [3]int will not accept [4]int . Arrays are also copied whole on assignment. This is almost never what you want, which is why arrays are rare in Go code. A slice is a small three-field value: a pointer to an underlying array, a length, and a capacity. That is the whole model, and understanding it explains every slice surprise you will ever hit. len(s) How many elements you can index right now cap(s) How many fit before the underlying array must be reallocated make([]T, len, cap) creates one with room reserved. When you know roughly how many elements are coming, say so: it avoids repeated reallocation. If you know JavaScript A JavaScript array handles all of this invisibly. push grows it and you never think about capacity. Go exposes the machinery, which costs you some attention and buys you control over allocation, which matters a great deal in a hot loop and not at all in a handler that runs once per request. append returns a slice. You must use the return value. The reason is that append may or may not allocate a new array. If there is spare capacity it writes in place and returns a slice with a longer length. If there is not, it allocates a bigger array, copies everything over, and returns a slice pointing at the new array. The caller's original slice still points at the old one. This is where the famous slice bug lives. Slicing does not copy. b is a window onto the same memory. Writing through one is visible through the other. Watch out It gets worse with append , because whether you corrupt the original depends on capacity, which depends on history: The fix, when you want a genuinely independent slice, is a three-index slice that caps capacity, or an explicit copy: This bug is rare in everyday handler code and vicious when it appears. The tell is "a value changed and nothing in my code assigned to it". range gives you a copy of each element. For ints that is irrelevant. For structs it is the bug from the previous chapter: modifying v changes nothing. Use the index when you need to write. If you know JavaScript Go has no map , filter , reduce , find or some for slices in the language. Since Go 1.21 the slices package covers some of it: For anything else, write the loop. A filter is four lines: A slice is cheap to pass: you are copying three words, not the data. That means a function can modify the caller's elements. But it cannot change the caller's length , because the slice header itself was copied: The convention, and the reason append works the way it does: a function that grows a slice returns it. The comparison function returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number, the same contract as JavaScript's Array.prototype.sort comparator. For stable sorting use slices.SortStableFunc . Project 5: word frequency, top ten Read a file, count how often each word appears, and print the ten most common. This uses slices, sorting and a map together, and it is a real tool you can point at a book. Three things worth noticing. make([]pair, 0, len(counts)) reserves capacity up front because we know exactly how many there will be. The tie-break on word makes the output deterministic, which matters because map iteration order is random and without it two runs would disagree. And min is a builtin since Go 1.21, so pairs[:min(10, len(pairs))] does not panic on a file with fewer than ten distinct words. Your turn Add a flag so the user can ask for a different number of results, for example freq book.txt 25 . Then add a stop-word list so "the", "a" and "and" are excluded, and decide whether a slice or a map is the better structure for holding those stop words. The next chapter will tell you whether you chose right. Commit your work with the message Slices - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Write the three helpers you miss from JavaScript, then prove the trap. In part1-language/06-slices : One. Filter , Chunk and Dedupe over []string , each with a table-driven test. You will write these generically in chapter seventeen, so keep them. Two. Reproduce the aliasing bug on purpose. Take a slice of a slice, append to it, and show the original changing. Then fix it with a copy, and write the one-line rule in a comment. Three. Sort a slice of structs by two keys, falling back to the second when the first ties. Four. In NOTES.md , state in one sentence what append does not promise. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.
pages.title: Arrays have a fixed length, in the type

pages.text: A JavaScript object is a bag of keys you can add to at any time. A Go struct is a fixed set of named fields with fixed types, decided when you declare the type and never changing. Everything else in this chapter follows from that one difference. Things you have not met yet Two things appear before their chapters: the & in front of a struct is a pointer, which chapter 8 is about, and the slices in these examples come in chapter 6. Neither matters for understanding a struct. There are four ways to make one, and you will see all four in real code. Notice what is missing from the first example: Admin was not set, so it is false . There is no undefined . Every field always has a value, and a struct you create is immediately complete. If you know JavaScript The closest JavaScript equivalent is a class with a constructor that sets every property. The difference is that you cannot add a field later. u.Age = 36 on a User with no Age field is a compile error, not a new property. This is the whole point: the shape of your data is checked, everywhere, for free. Go has no classes. You attach behaviour to a type by declaring a function with a receiver , the parameter in parentheses before the name. u User is the receiver. It behaves like a parameter, because that is exactly what it is: u.DisplayName() is sugar for passing u as the first argument. If you know JavaScript There is no this , and that removes an entire class of JavaScript bug. The receiver is a normal named parameter, bound at the call site, and it cannot be rebound by how the function was called. No .bind(this) , no arrow function workaround, no const self = this . This is the first thing in Go that genuinely trips people up, and it is worth getting right now rather than debugging later. A value receiver gets a copy. Changes to it do not affect the original. A pointer receiver gets the address, so changes stick. You do not write (&u).Rename(...) . Go inserts the address-of automatically when the method needs a pointer and you have an addressable value. Watch out The rule in practice: *if a method modifies the receiver, it must be a pointer receiver.* A value receiver that assigns to a field compiles happily and silently does nothing, which is one of the few truly quiet bugs in Go. The second rule: be consistent within a type. If any method on User takes a pointer, give them all pointers. Mixing the two is legal and makes the rules about which calls are addressable surface at the worst moment. A practical reason to prefer pointer receivers even when not mutating: a value receiver copies the whole struct on every call. For a struct with twenty fields called in a loop, that is real work for no benefit. Go has no extends . It has embedding , which looks similar and behaves differently in one important way. The embedded type's fields and methods are promoted to the outer type. If Timestamps had a method Age() , then p.Age() would work. If you know JavaScript This resembles class Post extends Timestamps , and the difference matters: there is no polymorphism here. A Post is not a Timestamps and cannot be passed where one is expected. Embedding is a convenience for forwarding fields and methods, not a type relationship. In Go, the thing that lets one type stand in for another is an interface, which is chapter ten. A field can carry a string of metadata, used by libraries through reflection. You will meet this constantly, because it is how Go does JSON. Without tags, json.Marshal uses the Go field names, so you get {"ID":1, "Name":"Ada"} . With them you get the lowercase JSON your frontend expects. Watch out Those backticks are a raw string literal, and the format inside is strict: json:"name" with no space after the colon. json: "name" silently does nothing, the tag is ignored, and the field encodes as Name . There is no error. If a field is coming out with the wrong key, check for that space first. Go has no constructor keyword. The convention is a package-level function named New or NewThing that returns the type. Returning *User rather than User is the usual choice, because the caller almost always wants to pass it around without copying, and because it lets you return nil on failure. If you know JavaScript A JavaScript constructor cannot fail cleanly: it either throws or returns a half-built object. A Go constructor is an ordinary function, so it returns an error like everything else, and you cannot get a *User back unless it succeeded. Structs are comparable with == when all their fields are, and the comparison is by value, field by field. That is deep equality for free, and it is a genuine surprise if you are used to a === b on objects being an identity check. Watch out It stops working the moment a struct contains a slice, a map or a function, because those are not comparable. The compiler tells you. For those, use reflect.DeepEqual , or in tests google/go-cmp , which prints a readable diff instead of just false . Project 4: a contact book in memory Build a small type with behaviour, and exercise value and pointer receivers. The subtle line is return &b.contacts[i], true . Ranging with for _, c := range b.contacts would give you a copy of each contact, and tagging that copy would change nothing. Indexing with i and taking the address reaches the real element. Change it to the copying version and watch the tag vanish: that is the lesson of this chapter in one experiment. Your turn Add a Remove(email string) bool method to Book . You will need to build a new slice or use the slices.Delete helper from the standard library. Then add a Count() method and decide, with a reason you can say out loud, whether it takes a value or a pointer receiver. Commit your work with the message Structs - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Model something real, with the receiver choice made deliberately. In part1-language/05-structs , build an Invoice with a Customer , a slice of Line items, and a Status . One. A constructor Ne
