headings: The types you will actually use
Zero values: there is no undefined
Strings are bytes, and that matters
pages.text: This is the chapter where Go feels most foreign, and it is worth knowing why in advance. In JavaScript, a variable is a box that holds anything and can hold something else tomorrow. In Go, a variable has one type forever, decided when it is created, and the compiler refuses to build your program if you break that promise. That refusal is the feature. Work with it for a week and you will notice a whole category of bug has stopped happening to you. Go has two ways to make a variable, and you will use one of them ninety percent of the time. The := operator is the one you want. It declares a new variable and infers its type from the value on the right. It only works inside a function, which is why package level variables use var . If you know JavaScript := is closest to let in that it creates a new binding. There is no equivalent of const for variables created with := . Go's const exists, but it is only for values known at compile time: numbers, strings, booleans. You cannot declare a constant struct or slice. If you want "do not reassign this", Go's answer is to write a small enough function that it is obvious. An unused variable is a compile error , not a warning. If you know JavaScript JavaScript coerces almost anything: "3" * 2 is 6 , [] + {} is a string, and 0.1 + 0.2 is famously not 0.3 . Go does none of this. There is no implicit conversion between any two types, not even int and int64 . Every conversion is written out, which is more typing and removes an entire family of surprise. Every type in Go has a zero value , and a declared variable always has it. There is no undefined , and no uninitialised memory. string int , float64 bool false pointers, slices, maps, interfaces, functions nil This is genuinely useful. A struct you create is immediately valid, with every field at a sensible default, and you never check whether a field "exists". Watch out It is also the one place zero values hurt: you cannot tell "the caller set this to zero" apart from "the caller did not set it". If that distinction matters, for example a form field where empty and absent mean different things, you need a pointer ( *int , where nil means absent) or a dedicated type. Chapter eight covers pointers properly. This problem is real, and it is the usual reason you see *string in a struct. An if in Go takes a bool . Not a value that is bool-ish. A bool . More characters, and no memorising which values are falsy. There is no == and === distinction either, because there is only one == and it does not coerce. A Go string is a read-only slice of bytes holding UTF-8. Indexing it gives you a byte. To work with characters, range over the string, which decodes runes: if and for are almost familiar, with two differences worth stating. There are no parentheses around the condition, and braces are mandatory even for one line. for is the only loop keyword. It covers every case JavaScript spreads across for , while and for...of . An if can carry a statement before the condition, scoped to the if . You will see this constantly in real code: Project 2: a temperature table Write a program that prints a table converting Celsius to Fahrenheit from minus 40 to 100 in steps of 20. The formula is f = c*9/5 + 32 . Two things to notice. float64(c) is required: without it you get integer division and wrong answers for anything not divisible by five, which is the bug this chapter exists to prevent. And %8.1f means "right align in eight columns, one decimal place", which is how Go does string formatting. Now break it on purpose: remove the float64(...) conversion and read the error. Then change it to c*9/5 with c still an int and see that it compiles but produces wrong numbers. The compiler catches the type error. It cannot catch the maths error, and knowing which is which is the skill. Your turn Add a third column showing Kelvin ( k = c + 273.15 ), and right align the header over it. Then make the step size a variable at the top of main and confirm the table still lines up when you change it to 10. Commit your work with the message Variables - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Make the zero values concrete, because undefined is the habit that takes longest to drop. In part1-language/03-types , write a program that declares a variable of every type in this chapter's table, with no initial value, and prints each one with its type: One. Print the zero value of a string, an int, a float64, a bool, a slice, a map, a pointer and a struct. Note in a comment which of them you can use immediately and which panic if you write to them. Two. Write three lines that each fail to compile, and keep them commented out with the exact error: an int assigned to a float64, a string compared to a number, and an if on a non-boolean. Three. In NOTES.md , answer in two sentences: which of these would JavaScript have accepted, and what would it have done instead? Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer. Commit your work with the message Variables - Assignment Two , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Strings are bytes, and the day that matters is the day somebody types their own name into your form. In part1-language/03-types/strings : One. Take a string with characters outside ASCII in it, your own name or a word with an accent on it, and print len(s) next to utf8.RuneCountInString(s) . Explain the difference in a comment. Two. Index it with s[0] and print what comes back. It is a number, and the type is the explanation. Three. Loop over it twice, once with an index loop over bytes and once with range , printing each item. Only one of them produces characters. Four. Reverse the string, correctly. The byte-wise reversal that works for "hello" will produce nonsense for your test string, and both versions belong in the commit. Five. headings: The shape of Go, in one page
What you give up, stated plainly
The one example that explains everything
pages.text: You already build and ship software. You know React, you know Next.js, and you can take an idea to production without asking anybody how. So the first question this book owes you is not "what is Go", it is "why would you spend a month learning a second language when the one you have works". Here is the honest answer, and then the honest list of what you give up. Most JavaScript developers do not come to Go out of curiosity. They come because something in their stack got painful in a specific way. Usually one of these four. The deployment got heavy. Your Next.js app needs Node on the server, a node_modules directory with a few hundred megabytes in it, and a build step that has to run somewhere. You want to copy one file onto a server and run it. A compiled Go program is one file. It has no runtime to install, no package directory, and no build step on the target machine. You build it on your laptop and the output is the thing that runs. The work stopped being request-and-respond. An API that answers a question in forty milliseconds is a perfect job for Node. A process that holds ten thousand open connections, or runs a job queue, or chews through a large file while staying responsive, is where the single-threaded event loop stops being an elegance and starts being a constraint you work around. You wanted the errors earlier. In JavaScript, a renamed field is found by a user. TypeScript helps enormously and you should keep using it, but it is a layer on top of a language that does not have types, and it disappears at runtime. In Go the types are the language. A program that compiles has already had a whole class of mistake removed from it. Somebody said the word "backend" and meant it. Payment handling, a scheduler, an audit trail, something that must still be correct at 3am when nobody is watching. Go was built by people who operate systems like that for a living, and it shows in what the language refuses to let you do. If you know JavaScript None of this makes Go better than JavaScript. It makes it different in ways that matter for one kind of work. You are not replacing React. In the second half of this book you will have a Go backend and a React frontend in the same project, talking to each other with types generated from one definition. That is the shape most people actually want. Before any syntax, here is the character of the language, because it explains every decision you are about to meet. Go is small on purpose . The entire specification is about one hundred pages. There are twenty five keywords. JavaScript has roughly double that and a standard library that has grown for thirty years. You can hold all of Go in your head, which is a design goal rather than an accident, and it is why Go teams onboard people in days rather than weeks. Go is explicit on purpose . There is no implicit type coercion, no this that changes meaning depending on how a function was called, no prototype chain to walk. When you read a line of Go, what happens is what is written. This is sometimes tedious and it is never surprising, and after a few weeks you will notice you have stopped debugging a category of problem entirely. Go is opinionated about formatting , which sounds trivial and is not. There is one correct way to format Go code, a tool called gofmt produces it, and every Go project on earth uses it. No Prettier config, no debate about semicolons, no .editorconfig . The argument is over because the language ended it. Go compiles fast . Not "fast for a compiled language", fast in absolute terms: a medium project builds in a couple of seconds. This matters more than it sounds, because it means the compile step never becomes a reason to avoid checking your work. A book that only lists advantages is marketing. Here is the other side, and you should weigh it before chapter two. You will write more lines. Go has no map , filter or reduce built into the language the way JavaScript does. Where you write one chained expression, you will often write a four-line loop. Go's position is that the loop is easier to read six months later. You may disagree, and you will still write the loop. Error handling is verbose. You are about to meet if err != nil and you will type it hundreds of times. There is no try / catch wrapping half a function. Every single operation that can fail says so, at the point it can fail. This is the single biggest adjustment coming from JavaScript, and chapter four is entirely about making peace with it. The ecosystem is smaller. npm has over two million packages. Go has far fewer. For web application work this matters less than you would think, because Go's standard library covers an enormous amount of what you would reach for a package to do in Node. But if you need an obscure SDK, check before you commit. No null safety. Go has nil , and a nil pointer dereference will crash your program at runtime exactly like reading a property of undefined crashes yours. Go's type system is simpler than TypeScript's, and in this one specific area TypeScript is genuinely ahead. Watch out If someone tells you Go is simply better than JavaScript, stop listening to them. The two languages were built for different jobs by people with different problems. Go's concurrency is better than the event loop for sustained work, and the event loop is a beautiful fit for a UI. Use both. Here is the same program in both languages: read three URLs, and print how long each took. It is worth studying before you understand any Go syntax, because the difference in shape is the whole argument. The JavaScript is shorter and, if you know JavaScript, clearer. Do not let anybody tell you otherwise. But look at what the Go version is doing. The word go in front of that function call starts a goroutine : an independent line of execution that the Go runtime schedules onto a real operating system thread. Three URLs here, but the same code with fifty thousand URLs would start fifty thousand goroutines, and Go would handle it, because

headings: Fail at startup, not on the first request
Flags, for tools rather than services
pages.text: A program that works on your laptop and nowhere else usually has its configuration hard-coded. This short chapter is how to avoid that, and how not to leak a database password into your git history on the way. os.Getenv returns "" for a variable that is unset, so you cannot tell unset from set-to-empty. When that matters: If you know JavaScript This is process.env.ADDR , with the same string-only limitation. There is no dotenv in the standard library, so a .env file needs a package, usually joho/godotenv . Many Go teams skip it entirely and export variables from a shell script or a compose file, because production almost never uses a .env file anyway. Scattered os.Getenv calls are the thing to avoid. Read everything at startup, validate it, and pass the result down. time.ParseDuration accepts "30s" , "5m" , "1h30m" , which is far better than an integer whose unit lives in a comment. Watch out Those helpers silently fall back to the default when parsing fails, so MAX_WORKERS=eight quietly becomes 4. For anything that matters, fail loudly instead: A typo in a deployment variable should stop the program at startup, not change its behaviour silently three weeks later. This is the single most valuable habit in this chapter. A missing variable should crash the container immediately, so the deploy fails visibly, rather than letting a half-configured process serve errors. Three rules, and the first one is the one people break. Never commit a secret. Not in a .env file, not in a test fixture, not "temporarily". Git keeps it forever, and a repository that goes public later publishes your history too. Commit a .env.example with the keys and no values, so a new developer knows what to set. Never log one. This is easy to do by accident: The defence is a String method that redacts: Because fmt looks for String() , this covers %v , %s and Println . It does not cover %+v on a struct that embeds yours, so the surer answer is a dedicated type: Now the only way to see the value is to call Reveal() , which is greppable in review. Never put one in a URL you log. postgres://user:pass@host/db is a secret in its entirety, which is why redact above hides the whole string rather than trying to mask the password portion. If you know JavaScript The mechanics are the same as Node: environment variables, a gitignored .env , a secret manager in production. The Go-specific part is that a compiled binary feels like a sealed box and is not: strings compiled into it are readable with the strings command. Never embed a key in source, even in a binary you only ship internally. For a CLI, flag is in the standard library: flag gives you -h for free, printing every flag with its default. It does not support subcommands or long-and-short pairs; for those, spf13/cobra is the near-universal choice and is what Grit's CLI is built on. The usual division: flags for tools, environment for services . A service configured by flags is awkward in a container, and a CLI configured by environment variables is awkward to use. Project 22: configure the shortener properly Take the URL shortener from the last chapter and give it a real configuration layer, with validation that fails at startup. And in main : Try it: The last two are the point. A deployment with a typo'd variable now fails immediately and says which variable and what it received, instead of starting up and generating two-character codes that collide constantly. Write the test too, since config is easy to test and almost nobody does: t.Setenv sets a variable for one test and restores it afterwards, and it refuses to run in a parallel test, because environment variables are process global and that would be a race. Your turn Add an API_KEY using a Secret type with a redacting String() , and prove with a test that fmt.Sprintf("%v", cfg) does not contain the value. Then add -config as a flag pointing at a JSON file, with environment variables taking precedence over the file and the file over the defaults. Getting that precedence order right, and writing a test for each layer, is most of what configuration libraries do for you. Commit your work with the message Config - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Make a program refuse to start rather than fail at midnight. Take your chapter twenty two API and give it real configuration. One. One Config struct, parsed once at startup, with defaults for everything that has a sensible one. Two. Validation that fails loudly: a missing database URL exits with a message naming the variable, before any connection is attempted. Three. A String() method that redacts secrets, and a startup log line that uses it. Then log the raw struct once to see what you would have leaked. Four. The same binary started twice with different environments, proving nothing is compiled in. The website's Config With Defaults and Validating Config at Start-up exercises are the compressed version. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.

headings: The pool is the important part
Writing, and what you get back
NULL, and why your struct fields lie
pages.text: Go's database/sql is not an ORM. It is a thin, driver-agnostic layer over SQL: you write the queries, it manages connections and scans rows into your variables. Coming from Prisma or Drizzle this feels primitive for about a day and then feels like relief, because nothing is hidden. The blank import registers the driver with database/sql . You never call the driver package directly, which is why it is imported as _ . Watch out * sql.Open does not connect.* It validates arguments and prepares a pool, lazily. A wrong password or a missing server is not reported until the first query. Always Ping at startup, or your service starts happily and fails on the first user request. *sql.DB is not a connection. It is a pool, safe for concurrent use, and you should create exactly one and pass it around. Watch out The default MaxOpenConns is unlimited . Under load, Go will happily open more connections than your database allows, and Postgres will start refusing them. Set it. A common starting point is 25, and the right number is something like (cores * 2) + effective spindles , measured rather than guessed. Set MaxIdleConns to the same value as MaxOpenConns . If idle is lower, connections are closed and reopened constantly under steady load, which is pure latency. Scan copies columns into the pointers you give it, in order. The number and order must match the SELECT . sql.ErrNoRows is the sentinel for "no row", and it is a normal outcome rather than a failure. Translating it into your own ErrNotFound , as above, is chapter eleven's design in practice: callers should not have to import database/sql to understand your errors. Three things are mandatory and two of them are easy to forget. * defer rows.Close() .* An unclosed Rows holds its connection. Leak enough and the pool is exhausted and every query blocks forever. *Check rows.Err() after the loop.* Exactly like scanner.Err() in chapter twenty, and for the same reason. *Check the Scan error inside the loop.* Watch out LastInsertId is not supported by Postgres. There you use RETURNING and treat the insert as a query: Note also the placeholders: SQLite and MySQL use ? , Postgres uses $1 , $2 . This is the main thing that is not portable between drivers, and it is why switching databases is never quite free. A placeholder sends the value separately from the statement, so it can never be parsed as SQL. String concatenation is SQL injection, and '; DROP TABLE users;-- is only the famous example rather than the dangerous one: the real attacks read data rather than destroy it. If you know JavaScript Prisma and Drizzle protect you by generating the SQL. Here you write the SQL and the protection is the placeholder. The rule is simple: *values are placeholders, always*. Table and column names cannot be placeholders, so if those are dynamic, validate them against an allowlist you control. Grit does exactly this, which is why its generated services carry a Sortable map of permitted columns rather than interpolating whatever the client sent. A NULL column cannot scan into a string . It fails at runtime: Three options, in order of preference: Since Go 1.22 there is also sql.Null[T] , the generic version: Most NULL problems are schema problems. If a column has no meaningful "absent" state, make it NOT NULL and the whole question disappears. defer tx.Rollback() right after BeginTx is the pattern. After a successful Commit the rollback does nothing, so one line covers every failure path including a panic. Watch out *Everything inside a transaction must use tx , not db .* A query on db inside a transaction takes a different connection from the pool, so it cannot see uncommitted changes and does not participate in the rollback. This compiles, passes casual testing, and corrupts data under concurrency. The usual defence is to pass something that could be either: Both *sql.DB and *sql.Tx satisfy it, so a function can be called inside or outside a transaction. This is chapter ten's consumer-declared interface, doing real work. The most common performance bug in any application, in any language: Fifty posts means fifty-one queries. Each is fast, so nothing looks slow, and the page takes two seconds. The fix is one more query, not fifty: Now swap this in behind the handlers from chapter twenty one and you have a persistent JSON API with two dependencies: the SQLite driver and nothing else. Two details worth dwelling on. RowsAffected() == 0 is how Delete knows the row was missing, because a DELETE that matches nothing is not an error in SQL. And SetMaxOpenConns(1) is correct for SQLite, which allows one writer: leaving it unlimited gives you database is locked errors under concurrency, which is the single most common SQLite complaint and is a configuration problem rather than a SQLite problem. Your turn Write a test using t.TempDir() for the database file, covering create, get, list and a Get that returns ErrNotFound . Then add an Update and give it a transaction that refuses to blank out the text, returning a validation error, and prove with a test that the row is unchanged after the failure. That last test is the one that proves you understand defer tx.Rollback() . Commit your work with the message Database - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Move the notes API onto a real database. In part3-standard-library/22-database , use SQLite through database/sql . One. A schema, an Open , and the pool settings configured rather than defaulted. Two. All four operations with placeholders. Then write one query by concatenating a string, put a quote in the input, and keep the result in NOTES.md as the reason you will not do it again. Three. A nullable column read into sql.NullString , and a decision about what the API returns for it. Four. A transaction that writes two rows and rolls back on the second failing, with a test that proves the first row is gone. Five. Create the N+1: list notes, then fetch each note's tags in a loop. headings: Middleware is a function that wraps a handler
Passing values down: context, not globals
pages.text: Go's standard library includes a production-grade HTTP server. Not a toy, not a reference implementation: the thing you actually deploy. This chapter builds a real one with no dependencies at all, because understanding this makes every framework afterwards, Gin and Grit included, read as a convenience rather than magic. No npm install , no framework, no config. That server handles concurrent requests across every core, because net/http starts a goroutine per request. If you know JavaScript Express needs npm install express and gives you app.get('/hello', (req, res) => res.send('hello')) . The shapes are similar. The differences: Go's server is in the standard library and versioned with the language, and it is concurrent by default rather than on one event loop. *http.Request is the incoming request: method, URL, headers, body, context. http.ResponseWriter is where you write the response. Note the asymmetry: the request is a pointer to a struct you read, the writer is an interface you call. Watch out Order matters and the compiler will not help you. Headers must be set before WriteHeader , and WriteHeader before Write . Writing the body first implicitly sends a 200, and your later WriteHeader(404) is ignored with a log line: The rule: set headers, then status, then body. Always that order. Since Go 1.22 the standard router handles methods and path parameters, which removed the main reason people reached for a third-party router. Path parameters come out by name: A request that matches the path but not the method gets a 405 automatically. If you know JavaScript This is app.get('/users/:id', ...) with req.params.id . Two differences: the method is part of the pattern string rather than the function name, and there is no next() , because middleware composes by wrapping rather than by calling through. http.ListenAndServe uses a default server with no timeouts at all . A single slow client can hold a connection open indefinitely, and enough of them exhaust your file descriptors. This is a real denial of service and it is the default. Watch out Set ReadHeaderTimeout at minimum. Without it, a client that opens a connection and sends one byte per minute occupies a goroutine and a file descriptor forever. This attack is called slowloris, it is twenty years old, and Go's defaults do not defend against it because the standard library cannot know your deployment. There is no middleware API. A middleware is a function taking a handler and returning a handler. Compose by nesting: The outermost runs first. Reading that line right to left gives you the request path, which is why many codebases add a small helper: If you know JavaScript Express middleware takes (req, res, next) and calls next() to continue. Go's takes a handler and returns one, so "continue" is calling next.ServeHTTP(w, r) and "stop" is simply not calling it: No next(err) , no forgetting to call next() and hanging the request. Middleware that authenticates a user needs to hand it to the handler. The mechanism is the request context from chapter sixteen. r.WithContext returns a copy of the request. Forgetting to pass the new one to next.ServeHTTP is a common bug: the value is set on a request nobody sees. Killing a server mid-request drops responses. Production code waits. Shutdown stops accepting new connections and waits for in-flight requests, up to the context's deadline. ListenAndServe returns http.ErrServerClosed when this happens, which is why that error is checked for and ignored. This matters for every container deployment: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits before SIGKILL , and a server without this drops every request in flight on each deploy. net/http/httptest runs a handler in memory. No port, no network, no cleanup, and it runs in microseconds. For testing a whole mux including middleware, httptest.NewServer starts a real one on a random port. Project 20: a complete HTTP service, no dependencies Everything above in one runnable file: routing, middleware, JSON, timeouts, graceful shutdown. Exercise it: Then press Ctrl+C and watch it log stopped cleanly rather than dying. Count the dependencies in go.mod : there are none. This is a concurrent, panic-resistant, gracefully shutting down JSON API with request logging and body size limits, in one file, with nothing installed. That is the baseline Go gives you, and it is why Go web frameworks are thin. Your turn Add GET /notes/{id} using r.PathValue("id") and strconv.Atoi , returning 404 when absent. Then write the handler test with httptest and no running server. Finally, remove ReadHeaderTimeout and leave a connection open with telnet localhost 8080 without sending anything, to see for yourself what the default costs you. Commit your work with the message HTTP Server - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. A JSON API with no framework at all, so you know what one is for. In part3-standard-library/21-http , build a notes API with net/http . One. GET /notes , POST /notes , GET /notes/{id} on a ServeMux , returning JSON with the right status codes. Two. A Server with read, write and idle timeouts set. Say in a comment what the default is and why it is a problem on the open internet. Three. Two middlewares, logging and a request ID, composed as functions that wrap a handler. Put the ID in the request context and log it from the handler. Four. Graceful shutdown on SIGINT , with an in-flight request finishing rather than being cut. Five. Tests with httptest , no port bound. These are the four steps a generated Grit handler performs, which is worth having done by hand once. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.

headings: io.Copy, and the pattern it enables
pages.text: Two interfaces carry most of Go's I/O, and you met them in chapter ten: One method each. Files, network connections, HTTP bodies, gzip streams, in-memory buffers, standard input and standard output all satisfy them, which means a function written against io.Reader works with every one of those without knowing which it has. When the file is small and you want it all: And writing: 0o644 is the Unix permission mode: owner read and write, everyone else read. On Windows it is mostly ignored. 0o600 for anything secret. Watch out os.ReadFile loads the entire file into memory. For a 2GB log file that is 2GB of RAM, and your process is killed. Use it for configuration and small documents; stream anything that could be large, which is the rest of this chapter. Memory stays constant regardless of file size. Watch out *You must check scanner.Err() .* The loop ends identically whether the file finished or the disk failed, and without the check a read error looks exactly like a successful end. This is the most commonly skipped error check in Go. Second trap: Scanner refuses lines longer than 64KB by default, returning bufio.Scanner: token too long . For long lines, enlarge the buffer: os.Open Read only. Fails if the file is missing os.Create Write only. Creates, or truncates an existing file to empty os.OpenFile Everything else: append, read-write, custom permissions os.Create truncating is worth remembering, because it means opening a file to "check something" with Create destroys it. To append: Every Write on a file is a system call. Writing a million lines one at a time is a million system calls. Watch out A buffered writer must be flushed. The last few kilobytes sit in memory until you do. defer w.Flush() immediately after creating it is the habit, and note the order: defer f.Close() was registered first so it runs last , which is correct, because flushing into a closed file fails. Better still, check the flush error, because a failed flush means data did not reach the disk: That one line downloads a file to disk, with constant memory: An HTTP response body is an io.Reader . A file is an io.Writer . Neither knows about the other. Useful companions: Watch out io.LimitReader on anything a user controls is a real defence. Without it, a request body or an uploaded file can be as large as the client wants, and reading it into memory is a denial of service that costs the attacker nothing. For HTTP specifically there is http.MaxBytesReader , which also returns a proper error. This is the practical payoff. A function that takes concrete types is hard to test: The same function over interfaces is trivial to test: No temp files, no cleanup, no filesystem. strings.NewReader and bytes.Buffer are the two types you will use most in tests. If you know JavaScript This is why Node's stream API exists, and Go's version is far smaller: one method per direction instead of an event emitter with data , end , error and backpressure semantics you have to learn. The tradeoff is that Go's streams are synchronous and blocking, which is fine because blocking a goroutine is cheap. Use filepath , not path , and never build a path with string concatenation. path is for URLs and always uses forward slashes; filepath adapts to the operating system. Watch out Never join a user-supplied name onto a directory without cleaning it: filepath.Join does call Clean , which resolves the .. , but the result can still point outside uploads . The check is explicit: Go 1.24 added os.Root for this, which opens a directory and refuses to escape it, and is the better answer where available. In tests, t.TempDir() does this and cleans up automatically: Project 19: a log analyser Bring together everything from Parts I and II: stream files that may be large, parse them, aggregate with maps, sort, and process several files concurrently. Make a test file and run it: Three design choices worth noticing. analyse takes an io.Reader , so the same function serves a file, standard input, and a strings.Reader in a test: write that test, it is four lines. Each goroutine builds its own stats and merges once at the end, so the lock is held briefly rather than on every line. And malformed lines are skipped rather than fatal, because a log analyser that dies on one bad line is useless against real logs. Your turn Write the test for analyse using strings.NewReader , covering a good line, a malformed line and an empty input. Then add a -json flag that emits the stats as JSON instead of text, which needs the capital-letter rule and struct tags from the last chapter. Finally, feed it a file with a 100KB single line and watch where the buffer limit bites if you remove the sc.Buffer call. Commit your work with the message Files - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Write wc , then make it testable without touching the disk. In part3-standard-library/20-io : One. Count lines, words and bytes in a file with bufio.Scanner . Handle the scanner's error, which is the line everybody forgets. Two. Change the signature to take an io.Reader rather than a filename, and have main pass the file. Now the test passes a strings.Reader and there are no fixtures. Three. Add a mode that copies input to output with io.Copy and reports the bytes moved, with the writes buffered and the buffer flushed in a defer . Four. Feed it a file with a very long single line and fix the scanner error you get. Record the fix in NOTES.md . Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.
pages.title: Reading a whole file

pages.text: This is the chapter that explains why people who deploy Node sound envious when Go comes up. Deployment is scp and ./app , and the rest of this chapter is the detail around that sentence. One file. It contains your code, every dependency, and the Go runtime. The target machine needs nothing: no Go, no package manager, no shared libraries. If you know JavaScript Deploying a Next.js app means Node of the right major version, a node_modules tree, a build step, and a process manager. Deploying this means copying one file. That is the whole difference, and it is the reason Go dominates CLI tools and containers. The default build includes debug symbols and a symbol table. -s drops the symbol table, -w the DWARF debug information. Expect roughly 25 to 30 percent off. The cost is that a stack trace from a panic loses some detail and the binary cannot be inspected with a debugger, so many teams ship unstripped and accept the size. For genuinely small, upx compresses further, at the cost of slower startup and antivirus software treating your binary with suspicion. Rarely worth it. A binary that cannot tell you which commit it is costs real time during an incident. -X sets a string variable at link time. It only works on string variables in the main package or a named package path, and only ones that are not constants. If you know JavaScript Grit does exactly this, which is why grit version reports a real version rather than "dev". Its release process bumps three places that must agree: the Go variable, the scaffolder's default, and the documentation site's constant. Chapter 47 covers why a version that disagrees with itself is worse than no version. Two environment variables, no toolchain to install. From any machine, to any target. This is not an exaggeration: a Windows laptop builds the Linux ARM binary that runs on your Raspberry Pi, with no container and no configuration. Watch out Cross compilation is free until you use cgo . Any package binding to a C library (the classic mattn/go-sqlite3 , some image codecs, some crypto) needs a C cross-compiler for the target, and the simplicity evaporates. The defence is to prefer pure Go packages. This is why the database chapter used modernc.org/sqlite rather than mattn/go-sqlite3 : the former is Go all the way down, so GOOS=linux go build works from anywhere. Check for cgo with: If that fails, something in your tree needs C. A multi-stage Dockerfile builds in one image and ships in a tiny one. The final image contains your binary, CA certificates and nothing else: no shell, no package manager, no libc. Typical size is your binary plus about two megabytes. CGO_ENABLED=0 is required for the static base, because there is no libc in it to dynamically link against. Watch out Copy go.mod and go.sum and run go mod download before copying your source. Docker caches layers, and if the source is copied first then every code change re-downloads every dependency. This one ordering decision is the difference between a ten second rebuild and a two minute one. go:embed puts files inside the executable, so your single-file deployment can still serve a frontend. The comment is the directive and must sit immediately above the variable with no blank line. embed.FS for a tree, string or []byte for one file. This is how a Go program ships a built React app inside itself: compile the frontend, embed dist/ , and deploy one file that serves both the API and the UI. Grit's single-binary architecture mode does precisely this. -trimpath removes absolute file paths from the binary, so a panic trace says main.go:42 rather than /home/you/projects/secret-name/main.go:42 . It also makes builds reproducible, which matters if you sign releases. Targets a newer x86 instruction set for a few percent. Only do this if you control the hardware, because the binary will not run on older CPUs. A tag-triggered workflow that cross compiles and attaches binaries: goreleaser reads a config file, builds every platform, writes checksums, generates release notes from commits and uploads everything. It is the standard tool, and it is what turns "I tagged v1.2.0" into binaries for six platforms without further thought. Project 23: ship the shortener Take the URL shortener and make it genuinely deployable: versioned, containerised and cross compiled. First, the version: Wire it into main before anything else happens: A Makefile , because the build command is now too long to retype: The Dockerfile : Build and check the results: Three things to notice. make release produces four binaries for four platforms from one machine, in seconds, with no cross-compilation toolchain, because nothing in this project uses cgo. The container has no shell at all, so docker exec -it ... sh fails: that is the point of distroless, and it is worth experiencing once so the tradeoff is a decision rather than a surprise. And the whole image is small enough that pulling it is not a deployment consideration. Compare the image size to a Node service doing the same job. That number is the argument of this chapter. Your turn Add go:embed for a small HTML page at / that posts to /shorten , so the single binary serves a usable interface as well as an API. Then add a /healthz that reports the version, and confirm with docker run that the version baked in by the build argument is what the endpoint reports. That round trip, from build flag to running container to HTTP response, is the whole deployment story in one check. Commit your work with the message Shipping - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Ship the shortener as if somebody else had to run it. One. Build with the version embedded, and have -version print it: Two. Cross compile for Linux, macOS and Windows, and record the three sizes in RELEASE.md . Three. A two-stage Dockerfile ending in a minimal image. Record the image size next to the binary sizes. Four. Embed the static files with embed , so one file is genuinely the whole program. Five. A

pages.text: Everything from Parts I to III in one finished program: an HTTP server, a database, concurrency, context, error design, tests. Around three hundred lines, no framework, and it is genuinely deployable. This chapter is one long project. Type it as you go. Plus: it refuses nonsense URLs, counts hits without slowing the redirect, and shuts down cleanly. Watch out crypto/rand , not math/rand . A short code generated from a predictable sequence can be guessed, which for a link shortener means enumerating everybody's private links. Use crypto/rand for anything a user should not be able to predict: codes, tokens, session IDs, password reset links. Watch out The scheme check is not optional. Without it, somebody shortens javascript:alert(document.cookie) and your redirect endpoint serves it. Any time user input ends up in an href or a Location header, allowlist the scheme. What this program demonstrates Walk back through it and name the chapter each decision came from. Error design (11). ErrNotFound and ErrInvalid are sentinels, wrapped with %w , and the handlers branch on errors.Is . No handler reads an error message. Pointers and nil (8). Lookup returns *Link , nil on failure, so a caller cannot accidentally use a half-built value. Goroutines and context (13, 16). The hit counter runs in its own goroutine with a fresh context, because r.Context() is cancelled the moment the redirect is written. Using the request context there would silently lose most of your statistics under load, and it is the kind of bug that never shows up in testing. Interfaces (10). writeJSON takes http.ResponseWriter , and the tests pass an httptest.ResponseRecorder instead. Nothing was designed for testability; it is testable because the standard library is built on small interfaces. The database chapter (22). defer rows.Close() , rows.Err() , placeholders, sql.ErrNoRows translated at the boundary. Security. crypto/rand for unguessable codes, a scheme allowlist against XSS, MaxBytesReader against oversized bodies, DisallowUnknownFields against typos, and timeouts on the server. Count the dependencies: one, the SQLite driver. Your turn Three extensions, in order of difficulty. Add an expiry column and a GET /{code} that returns 410 Gone for expired links. Add rate limiting to POST /shorten using a map of IP to a token bucket, protected by a mutex, which is chapter fifteen's material. Then add a custom alias ( {"url":..., "alias":"docs"} ), which forces you to handle a real UNIQUE constraint violation rather than the random collision retry, and that is a different error path entirely. Commit your work with the message URL Shortener - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Finish the project, then push it past the chapter. Build the shortener as written, in part3-standard-library/23-shortener , with the tests passing. Then add three things of your own. One. Expiry: a link that stops working after a given time, with the expiry checked on read rather than by a sweeper. Two. Hit counting that does not slow the redirect down. The redirect is the hot path, so the count should not be on it synchronously. Three. A custom alias ( /go/standup ) that refuses to overwrite an existing one, with the race between two creators handled by the database rather than by a check. Four. A README with the one command that builds it and the one that runs it. This is the first thing in the repository somebody else could use. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.

headings: Why the assignments are pushed rather than just done
Step three: join the Gopher League
The loop, for every chapter from here
There is more practice on the website
pages.text: Every chapter in this book ends with an assignment. You write it, you commit it with an exact message, and you push it. This chapter sets that up, and it takes about ten minutes. Do it now rather than at chapter four, because the habit is the point and a habit started late is usually not started. Three reasons, and the third is the one that matters. You will finish them. Work that leaves your machine gets finished. Work that stays in a scratch file gets abandoned at the interesting part, which is usually one step before the thing it was teaching. You will have something to show. By the end of this book your repository holds fifty-odd small Go programs, each one solving a named problem, each with a readable commit history. That is a more convincing portfolio than a single large project, because it shows range and it shows persistence. You are not doing it alone. The commits are scored on a leaderboard shared with everybody else working through this book, which is what the rest of this chapter is about. One repository for the whole book. Not one per chapter: the history is the record, and a single timeline is what makes the progression visible. Give it a structure that will still make sense at chapter fifty: Each assignment gets a directory with its own main.go , and where it needs one, its own go.mod : Watch out A separate go.mod per assignment keeps them independent, so an experiment in chapter twenty cannot break chapter three. The alternative, one module at the root with a package per chapter, also works and means one go.mod , but every go build ./... then compiles everything. For a learning repository, independent modules are the better trade. Use a Go workspace if you want go build ./... to still work across all of them: Write a README.md on day one, because you will not write it later: Then push it: Make the repository public . The leaderboard reads public activity, and a public learning repository has never cost anybody a job. Install Committed from the Play Store: Sign up with your GitHub account , which is how it sees your commits. There is nothing to configure after that. Open the app and join with the code: Or follow the link, which does the same thing: The group's description says what it is: #block(width: 92%, inset: 10pt, radius: 3pt, fill: rgb("#f6f7f9"), stroke: 0.5pt + rgb("#e3e6ea"))[ #set text(size: 10pt, style: "italic") Gopher League is a friendly leaderboard for developers learning Go together. Every commit, merged PR, review and closed issue earns points. Ship Go, climb the table, and get crowned weekly champion. ] Commits score. So do merged pull requests, reviews and closed issues, which is worth knowing: reviewing somebody else's assignment is worth points, and it is also one of the better ways to learn. Every assignment in this book carries an exact commit message, printed in its own box: Use the message exactly as printed. It is not decoration. The leaderboard matches on it, and a commit called "did the variables thing" earns nothing, which is a sad way to lose a week's points. The pattern is always the same: So the first few are Hello Go - Assignment One , Variables - Assignment One , Variables - Assignment Two , and so on. Watch out Commit per assignment , not once per chapter and not once per day. Partly because each one scores. Mostly because a commit that says exactly what it contains is the single most useful habit in this book, and a history of fifty precise commits is worth more to you in six months than fifty files in one commit called "work". Four commands, maybe fifteen minutes per chapter. The leaderboard updates on its own. The Grit documentation has a Go guide with forty six interactive exercises, which run in the browser with a solution to check against: They cover the same ground as Parts I to III and are shorter than this book's assignments, so they work well as a warm-up before a chapter or as revision after it. Where one lines up with a chapter, that chapter's assignment says so. The division worth knowing: *the website exercises are for practising a concept, and this book's assignments are for building something and pushing it*. Do both if you have time, and if you only do one, do the assignment, because that is the one that leaves your machine. Commit your work with the message Setup - Repository , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Set up everything above, and prove it works. One. Create the go-journey repository, public, with the directory structure and the README. Two. Install Committed, sign up with GitHub, and join Gopher League with the code 5TCLJ27Z . Three. Add a file part1-language/00-setup/notes.md answering the question from the end of chapter one in two sentences: what is the specific thing in your current stack that made you pick this book up? You will want that answer again at chapter twenty six. Four. Commit and push, then open the app and confirm your commit appears on the leaderboard. If it does not, the usual cause is that the repository is private or the email on the commit does not match your GitHub account: Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer. Your turn Open the leaderboard and find your position. It will be last, which is the correct place to start and the only time the number matters. Then look at who is near the top and how often they commit. Almost always the answer is "a little, most days" rather than "a lot, once". That pattern is the actual lesson of the leaderboard, and it applies to learning Go whether or not anybody is counting.

headings: A channel is a typed pipe
The nil channel, and why it is useful
pages.text: Goroutines run independently. Channels are how they talk. The slogan Go is famous for is *do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating*, which sounds like a fortune cookie until you have written both versions of the same program. Things you have not met yet sync.WaitGroup turns up in a couple of examples and is chapter 15. A channel can do the same job, less clearly, which is the comparison. The arrow always points in the direction the value travels. ch <- v puts a value in, <-ch takes one out. No time.Sleep this time. The receive blocks until the send happens, which is synchronisation and message passing in one operation. If you know JavaScript The closest JavaScript analogy is an async generator or a stream, with one crucial difference: a channel receive blocks the goroutine . There is no callback, no await , and no promise. The code reads top to bottom, and the runtime parks the goroutine while it waits. If you have used postMessage between workers, the mental model is closer: separate lines of execution passing values, except channels are typed and synchronous by default. An unbuffered channel has no room. A send blocks until a receiver is ready, and a receive blocks until a sender is ready. The two goroutines meet. Go detects when every goroutine is blocked and stops the program rather than hanging forever. This is a feature, and it is how you will find most channel bugs. A send blocks only when the buffer is full; a receive blocks only when it is empty. Watch out Buffering is not a performance trick to sprinkle on. The capacity is a design decision: it is how many items may be in flight before the producer must slow down. That back pressure is usually what you want, because an unbounded queue in front of a slow consumer is just a memory leak with extra steps. Choose zero when you want a handshake, and a specific number when you know how much slack the system should tolerate. "I made it 100 so it would not block" is how a queue silently grows to 100 and then blocks anyway. The sender closes a channel to say "no more values". Receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately. The two-value form tells you which happened: Watch out Three rules that cover every close-related bug: Only the sender closes. A receiver closing a channel causes the sender to panic on its next send. Closing twice panics. So does sending on a closed channel. You do not have to close. A channel that is garbage collected is fine. Close only to signal completion to a range or a select . Note chan<- int in that signature: a directional channel type, meaning send-only. <-chan int is receive-only. Using them in function parameters makes the data flow obvious and lets the compiler stop a receiver from closing. select blocks until one of its cases can proceed. If several are ready it picks one at random, which prevents one busy channel starving another. A default case makes it non-blocking: If you know JavaScript select is Promise.race , with two differences worth noting. It can wait on sends as well as receives. And the losing cases are not "cancelled", they simply were not chosen: the other channels still hold their values for the next receive. Promise.race leaves the losers running and their results are discarded, which is a frequent source of leaked work in JavaScript. time.After returns a channel that delivers a value after the duration. This is the idiomatic timeout, and it is three lines. Watch out time.After leaks until it fires. In a tight loop, creating one per iteration piles up timers for the full duration. For a loop, create a time.NewTimer once and reset it, or use a context deadline, which is the next chapter. A channel carrying no data, used only to signal, is a common shape: Closing is the broadcast mechanism: every goroutine blocked on <-done wakes up at once, because a closed channel always yields immediately. Sending a value would wake only one. This pattern is so common that the standard library wrapped it, and that wrapper is context , which is chapter sixteen. Understand the done channel first and context becomes obvious rather than magical. Sending or receiving on a nil channel blocks forever. That sounds like a pure bug and it has one real use: disabling a select case. Once in is nil its case can never be chosen, so the loop keeps serving done without spinning on a closed channel returning zeros forever. The canonical channel program: a fixed number of workers pulling from a jobs channel. The ordering is the whole lesson. Close jobs so the workers' range ends. Wait for the workers. Then close results , because closing it earlier would panic a worker still writing. If you know JavaScript Compare this to the semaphore from chapter thirteen. Both bound concurrency. The semaphore starts a goroutine per item and limits how many run; the worker pool starts a fixed number and feeds them. The pool is better when goroutine startup matters or when each worker holds an expensive resource, like a database connection. The semaphore is simpler and usually enough. Project 13: a pipeline with cancellation Build a three-stage pipeline where each stage is a goroutine connected by channels, and where the whole thing can be stopped early. This is the shape of a great deal of real Go. Run it and note the time: six lines at ten milliseconds each would be sixty milliseconds serially, and with three workers it is closer to twenty. Then do the experiment that proves the cancellation works. Change the loop in main to stop after the first two results: The defer close(done) fires, every stage's select takes the <-done case, and all the goroutines exit. Remove the done channel entirely and the producer blocks forever trying to send into a pipeline nobody is reading: a goroutine leak, which in a long-running server is a slow memory leak you will eventually have to find. Run the whole thing with -race as well. It is clean, because every value moves through a channel and nothing is shar

headings: The standard library already honours it
Values, and why to be sparing
pages.text: You will see ctx context.Context as the first parameter of almost every function in a Go codebase, and it looks like noise until you understand what it buys. It is the done channel from chapter fourteen, standardised so that every library in the ecosystem agrees on how to be cancelled. A user opens a page, your handler starts a database query, and the user closes the tab. Without cancellation the query runs to completion, the connection stays busy, and the result is thrown away. Multiply by a thousand users on a slow page and the database falls over serving nobody. Context is a signal that travels down the call stack so that work can stop. You rarely create a context from nothing. Two roots exist: TODO is for when you are threading context through an existing codebase and have not reached the caller yet. It behaves identically; it exists so that grep TODO finds the unfinished work. From a root you derive : Each returns a child and a cancel function. Watch out Always call cancel, even on the timeout versions. It is not optional: Not calling it leaks the timer and the goroutine watching it until the deadline passes. go vet catches the obvious cases and not all of them. Writing defer cancel() on the very next line is the habit to build. A context has a Done() channel that closes when the context is cancelled, and an Err() saying why. That is the shape: check between units of work, return promptly when told. For anything that blocks, put ctx.Done() in the select directly: If you know JavaScript This is AbortController and AbortSignal . You create a controller, pass signal to fetch , and call abort() . Go's version has two differences: the convention of passing it as the first parameter of every function is near-universal, so the whole ecosystem supports it, and contexts form a tree where cancelling a parent cancels every descendant. Nothing is killed. A context cancellation sets a flag and closes a channel; code that does not check it keeps running. There are no interrupts and no thread killing in Go. If a library does not take a context, it cannot be cancelled, and that is a reason to prefer libraries that do. This is where it pays off, because you mostly pass a context rather than check one: An incoming HTTP request already carries one, cancelled automatically when the client disconnects: So passing r.Context() into your service layer, which passes it to the database, gives you end-to-end cancellation for free. That is the single most valuable thing context does, and it requires no select anywhere in your code. A derived context cannot outlive its parent, which gives you sane behaviour without arithmetic. If the request's three seconds elapse first, the inner context is cancelled too, even though its own 500ms had not expired. A context can carry request-scoped values. Use an unexported custom key type, never a plain string, or two packages using "user" collide silently. Watch out Context values are the most abused part of the package. They are untyped, invisible in a function signature, and found at runtime or not at all. The rule from the standard library documentation: use them for *request-scoped data that crosses API boundaries*, such as a request ID, an authenticated user, or a trace span. Never for optional parameters. If a function needs a value to do its job, that value is a parameter: Four, and they are followed almost universally. *Context is the first parameter, named ctx .* func Get(ctx context.Context, id int) . Never store it in a struct. A context describes one call's lifetime; a struct outlives calls. The exception is http.Request , which has its own reasons. Never pass nil. Use context.TODO() if you have nothing better. Do not pass a context to something that outlives the request. Starting a background job with the request's context means the job is cancelled when the response is sent. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to keep the values and drop the cancellation. Project 15: a search that races two sources with a budget Query two backends at once, take whichever answers first, give up on both after a deadline, and never leak a goroutine. This is context, channels and select doing the job they exist for. Three things this program teaches. The buffered channel is a correctness requirement, not an optimisation. When first returns after the winner, the loser still sends. With no buffer that send blocks forever and the goroutine never exits. Change the 2 to a 0 , run with -race and then inspect goroutine counts, and you have reproduced one of the most common leaks in Go services. The defer cancel() is what makes the loser stop early rather than running its full three hundred milliseconds into a void. And errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) works through the %w wrap in search , which is chapter eleven's design paying off: the caller can tell a timeout from any other failure. Your turn Add a third source and make first return as soon as two of the three agree, rather than on the first answer. Then add a context.WithoutCancel branch that logs the losing results to an audit sink after the winner has been returned, and confirm that work still completes after first has returned. That is the pattern for "respond now, finish the bookkeeping afterwards", and getting the context wrong there is why audit records go missing under load. Commit your work with the message Context - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Make a cancellation actually reach the bottom of a call stack. In part2-ideas/16-context , write a handler that calls a service that calls a slow HTTP endpoint. One. Thread one context.Context from the handler to the request. Use http.NewRequestWithContext , not the plain one. Two. Give the handler a two second timeout and point it at a server that takes five. Show the error chain reporting the deadline. Three. Write a worker loop that honours cancellation with a select on ctx.Done() , and one that ignores it. Cancel both and time how long ea

headings: defer: cleanup that cannot be forgotten
defer can change the return value
panic: stop, this should not have happened
pages.text: Three keywords that look like finally , throw and catch and are not. The resemblance is close enough to mislead, which is why they get a chapter. Things you have not met yet One example defers inside a goroutine. Goroutines are chapter 13; the point here is only that defer belongs to the function it is written in, not to the one that started it. defer schedules a function call to run when the surrounding function returns, by any path. Write the defer immediately after the thing that needs cleaning up. That adjacency is the point: open and close are one line apart, so a reviewer can see the pair without scrolling. If you know JavaScript try { ... } finally { f.close() } does the same job by wrapping, which indents the body and separates the close from the open. defer keeps them together and costs no indentation. It also composes: ten resources means ten defer lines, not ten nested blocks. One: arguments are evaluated immediately, the call happens later. msg was read when the defer statement ran. To defer the evaluation , wrap it in a closure: Two: deferred calls run last in, first out. All the files stay open until processAll returns. With a thousand paths you run out of file descriptors. The fix is to give each iteration its own function, so there is a return for the defer to fire on: Extracting the loop body into a function is the standard answer, and it usually improves the code for other reasons too. A deferred closure can modify a named return value after the return statement has chosen it. This is the one legitimate use of named returns. Used sparingly this is tidy. Used often it makes a function's return value hard to trace, so prefer explicit wrapping at each return unless you have many of them. A deferred Close discards its error, which is usually fine for reading and sometimes wrong for writing: a failed Close on a file you wrote may mean the data never reached the disk. That is verbose and correct. For a read-only file, defer f.Close() is accepted practice and nobody will object. panic unwinds the stack, running deferred functions as it goes, and if it reaches the top of a goroutine the program crashes with a stack trace. Go panics on its own for a handful of runtime faults: nil pointer dereference, index out of range, division by zero, sending on a closed channel, and writing to a nil map. If you know JavaScript throw in JavaScript is for expected failures: a 404, a validation problem, a parse error. panic is not. Go's expected failures are returned values, and panic is reserved for "this program's assumptions are broken". If you find yourself panicking in a request handler because a user sent bad input, that is the JavaScript habit talking. Return an error. recover stops a panic, and it only works inside a deferred function . There are exactly two good reasons to use it. One: a server that must not die because one request was bad. A panic in one handler should return 500 for that request, not take down the process serving everybody else. Log the stack. A recovered panic with no stack trace is a bug you will never find. Every Go web framework ships this middleware, Gin included, and Grit wires it in for you. Two: a library turning an internal panic into an error at its edge. Some parsers panic internally to unwind out of deep recursion, then recover at the public function and return an error. The caller never sees a panic. This is legitimate and rare. Watch out recover only catches panics in its own goroutine . A panic in a goroutine you started is not caught by a recover in the function that started it: Every goroutine that could panic needs its own recover. This is the single most common way a Go server dies in production: a background worker with no recover, panicking on a nil map six hours after deployment. Project 11: a worker that survives bad input Build a small job runner where one bad job must not stop the rest, and where cleanup is guaranteed. This is the panic boundary in miniature. Three things to notice when you run it. The finished line prints for every job including the ones that panicked, because deferred calls run while the stack unwinds. That is what makes defer safe for cleanup in a way that a line at the end of the function is not. The two deferred functions run in reverse order, so finished prints before the recover's error is assembled. And the program exits normally with a count, rather than dying on job three. Delete the recover block and run it again: you get a stack trace and jobs four, five and six never run. That difference is the reason every server has this middleware. Your turn Move the recover from runOne up into runAll , wrapping the whole loop, and run it again. You will catch the first panic and then the loop stops, because the panic unwound past the loop. That experiment shows exactly what "a boundary" means: it has to be inside the unit of work you want to isolate, not outside it. Commit your work with the message Defer - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Copy a file correctly, which is harder than it looks. In part2-ideas/12-defer , write CopyFile(dst, src string) (err error) . One. Open both files, defer both closes, and copy with io.Copy . Two. Return the error from closing the destination, because a failed flush is a failed copy. Use the named return and the deferred assignment from this chapter. Three. Write the loop version that opens a hundred files and defers every close inside the loop. Watch the file descriptors, then fix it, and write the rule in a comment. Four. Add a recover boundary to a tiny handler, log the panic with the stack, and return a 500. Then panic on purpose and confirm the process survives. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.

headings: Three kinds of error, and when to use each
Wrap, but not at every level
Error strings are a contract, lowercase and unpunctuated
Do not return both a value and an error
pages.text: Chapter four covered the mechanics: if err != nil , wrapping with %w , errors.Is and errors.As . This chapter is about the decision those mechanics leave you with, which is harder and matters more: *when someone calls your function and it fails, what should they be able to do about it?* Get this right and the caller writes three lines. Get it wrong and they end up matching on error message strings, which is the clearest sign of an API that did not think about failure. Opaque. The caller can log it and give up. Nothing else. This is the default and it is correct far more often than people expect. If there is nothing useful a caller could do differently, do not invent a way for them to try. Sentinel. A specific, exported value the caller compares against. The caller: Use a sentinel when the condition is a fact with no detail : not found, already exists, timed out. The name is the entire payload. Typed. A struct implementing error , carrying fields. The caller: Use a typed error when the caller needs data from the failure, not just its identity. A validation failure needs the field name. A rate limit needs the retry-after. A conflict needs the version that is current. Opaque Caller logs and gives up. The default Sentinel Caller branches on identity. errors.Is Typed Caller needs fields out of it. errors.As Watch out A sentinel or an exported error type is part of your public API . Renaming ErrNotFound , or changing which conditions return it, breaks callers exactly like changing a function signature. Declare them deliberately and few. The corollary: do not export an error type just because you made one. If nothing outside the package uses errors.As on it, keep it unexported and return it as a plain error . %w preserves the chain, and the temptation is to wrap at every function boundary. Do not. The result is a message like: Every layer added a word and none added information. The rule worth following: *wrap when you add context the caller does not already have*. The database layer knows the query. The service layer knows the user ID. The handler knows the request. Each of those is worth one wrap. "I am a function and I called another function" is not context. If you know JavaScript This is the same discipline as a JavaScript stack trace, with one difference: Go errors have no stack trace by default, so the chain of wraps is your trace. That is why each one should earn its place. Some teams add stack traces with a library; the standard library deliberately does not, on the grounds that a well-wrapped error is more readable than sixty frames. Convention, followed throughout the standard library: The reason is composition. Errors get wrapped into sentences, and a capital in the middle reads badly: Also: do not end with a newline, and do not include the word "error". The reader knows. Pick one. A function that returns a partially filled struct and an error invites the caller to use the broken value. The exceptions are real but narrow: io.Reader returns a byte count with an error because a partial read is meaningful, and strconv.Atoi returns zero because it has nothing better to offer. If you are not implementing something in that shape, return nil. The most common error-handling bug in any language is doing two things with one failure: Now it is logged at every level, and the operator reading the logs sees the same failure five times and has to work out whether it happened once or five times. Choose: either handle it, or return it. The usual split is that libraries and services return, and the top layer, a handler or main , logs once and decides what the user sees. This is where the three kinds pay off. One place in your program turns errors into HTTP responses: Everything below this function returns errors and logs nothing. Everything above it gets a correct status code. That is the whole architecture of error handling in a Go service, and you will meet it again in part four, because it is exactly what Grit generates. If you know JavaScript In an Express app this is the error middleware, app.use((err, req, res, next) => ...) , and the design problem is identical: the middleware has to work out what kind of failure it received. JavaScript usually does it with err instanceof ValidationError or a code property. Go's errors.As is the same idea with the chain-walking built in, so it still works after the error has been wrapped three times. Go has panic , and it is not for expected failures. A panic unwinds the stack and, uncaught, kills the program. Use panic for programmer error that cannot be recovered from : an impossible state, a nil dependency at startup, a configuration that cannot be parsed before the server starts serving. The Must prefix is the convention: it means "this panics instead of returning an error, and you should only call it where failure means the program is broken", typically at package initialisation with a literal you wrote yourself. Never panic for a bad request, a missing row, or a failed network call. Those are expected, and expected failures are values. Project 10: a user store with a designed error surface Build a small store that uses all three error kinds deliberately, plus the boundary mapping. This is a miniature of the structure every Go service ends up with. Two things to prove to yourself. First, errors.Is(err, ErrConflict) returns true even though the error was wrapped with extra text, which is the entire reason to use %w rather than %v . Change that one verb to %v and watch the conflict case fall through to 500. Second, note that Create never logs. It returns. describe is the only function that decides what a failure means to the outside world, so moving this store behind an HTTP API means changing one function. Your turn Add an Update(id int, name string) error that can fail in three ways: the user is missing, the name is invalid, or the name is unchanged. Decide for each whether it is opaque, sentinel or typed, and be able to defend the choice. "Unchanged" is
