headings: The constraints you will actually use
What the standard library gives you
When to write your own, and when not to
Interfaces are still usually the answer
pages.text: Go got generics in 1.18, after a decade of arguing about whether it should. The result is deliberately less powerful than TypeScript's, and the community consensus is that you should use them rarely. This chapter covers enough to read other people's code and to recognise the handful of cases where writing your own is right. Type parameters go in square brackets before the arguments. T is a type parameter and any is its constraint , meaning "any type at all". Inference usually works, so you rarely write First[int](...) . Note var zero T . You cannot return nil for an arbitrary T , because T might be int . The zero value is the only thing you can produce without knowing the type, and this little declaration appears in almost every generic function. If you know JavaScript TypeScript's function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined is the same idea, with a much more capable type system behind it. TypeScript has conditional types, mapped types, template literal types and inference that borders on computation. Go has type parameters and constraints, and that is the lot. If you arrive expecting the TypeScript toolkit you will be disappointed, which is by design: the proposal was accepted on the promise that it would not make Go code hard to read. A constraint says what you may do with a value of that type. You must constrain T to types that support + . Constraints are written as interfaces containing type sets : The ~ means "any type whose underlying type is this", so a named type still qualifies: Without the tilde, Celsius would be rejected, which is almost never what you want. Write ~ unless you have a reason not to. Two come from the standard library and cover most cases. cmp.Ordered is every type supporting < , which is the numeric types and string . comparable is built in and means "supports == ", which is what map keys require: Types can take parameters too. Watch out Methods cannot introduce new type parameters. This compiles nowhere: If you want a Map that changes the element type, it has to be a package function, not a method: This single restriction is why Go will never have fluent chained collection methods like items.map(...).filter(...) . It was a deliberate choice to keep the type checker simple, and it is the main reason generics changed Go code far less than people expected. Since 1.21 there are generic helpers, and you should use these rather than write your own. Watch out maps.Keys returns an iterator ( iter.Seq[K] ), not a slice. To get a slice, collect it: This trips up anybody reading older blog posts, where an earlier experimental version did return a slice. The honest guidance, which matches what the Go team says: *write the concrete version first*. Write the generic version when you have written the same function for the third type and the bodies are identical. Good reasons: A container: a stack, a set, a typed cache. A function over any slice or map where the body does not care about the type. Removing an any and the type assertions that came with it. Bad reasons: "It might be reused later." It usually is not. To avoid writing a four-line loop. The loop is clearer. To model a hierarchy. Go has interfaces for that, and they are better at it. If you know JavaScript The decisive difference from TypeScript: TypeScript's generics are erased at runtime and cost nothing, so using them liberally is free. Go's are compiled, and a generic function is often slower than the concrete one because of how the compiler shares instantiations for pointer-shaped types. If you are reaching for generics for performance, measure. The usual answer is that the concrete function wins. The mistake to avoid is reaching for a type parameter where an interface does the job better. The rule of thumb: if the function's behaviour depends only on methods , use an interface. Use a type parameter when you need the actual type back out, which is what interfaces cannot do. Project 16: a typed result cache A small generic container that is a genuinely good use of type parameters: the body does not care what it stores, and the caller gets its type back with no assertion. Now prove the value. Rewrite Cache with map[any]any and no type parameters, then try u.ID+1 : you need u.(User).ID+1 , an assertion that can panic, and the compiler no longer checks that you put a User in and got a User out. That assertion, repeated at every call site, is exactly what generics removed. Then try to add a Map method that converts a Cache[K, V] into a Cache[K, W] and watch the compiler refuse, because methods cannot introduce type parameters. Make it a package function instead and notice how that constraint pushes Go code away from fluent chaining. Your turn Add a Keys() []K method, then write a package-level Filter[K comparable, V any](c *Cache[K, V], keep func(V) bool) []V . Then stop and ask whether either of them earns its place, or whether the caller ranging over a plain map would have been clearer. That question, asked honestly every time, is the whole discipline of generics in Go. Commit your work with the message Generics - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Write the generic versions of what you already wrote, then judge them. In part2-ideas/17-generics : One. Rewrite chapter six's Filter , Chunk and Dedupe to work for any element type. Dedupe needs comparable , which is the constraint doing real work. Two. A generic Set[T comparable] with Add , Has and Items . Three. A Map[T, U any] that changes the element type, and one use of it that would have needed any and a cast before. Four. Now the honest part. In NOTES.md , name one place in your own code where an interface is the better answer than a type parameter, and say why. A chapter on generics that does not leave you more careful has failed. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.

headings: Races, and the detector that finds them
Bounding how many run at once
When not to use a goroutine
pages.text: You already write concurrent code. Every await you have typed was concurrency. What you have not had is parallelism : two pieces of your own code running at the same instant on two cores. This chapter is about the difference, because it is the whole reason Go's model exists. Things you have not met yet This chapter starts goroutines and mostly waits for them crudely. Channels are chapter 14 and sync.WaitGroup and sync.Mutex are chapter 15. Those are the proper answers; this chapter is about what a goroutine is. Put go in front of a function call and it runs independently. That is the entire syntax. No async on the function, no await at the call, no promise returned. Any function can be a goroutine; nothing about its declaration changes. Watch out The time.Sleep is there because *when main returns, the program exits immediately*, killing every goroutine still running. Remove it and you will probably see only "from main". Sleeping is never the real answer. The real answers are sync.WaitGroup and channels, both below. But almost every Go tutorial starts with a sleep, and it is worth knowing that it is a placeholder for synchronisation rather than a technique. In Node, your JavaScript runs on one thread. The event loop interleaves work: while one request waits on the database, another gets a turn. That is excellent for I/O and useless for computation, because a function that spends two hundred milliseconds doing arithmetic blocks everything. Go runs goroutines on a pool of operating system threads, usually one per CPU core. Two goroutines can execute at literally the same moment. Node Unit Promise / task Goroutine Threads One for your code One per core, by default Waiting on I/O Excellent Excellent CPU work Blocks everything Uses every core Cost each Small object About 2 KB of stack Practical limit Many thousands Hundreds of thousands A goroutine starts with a two kilobyte stack that grows as needed. An operating system thread starts with one or two megabytes . That thousand-fold difference is why "start a goroutine per request" is a normal design in Go and "start a thread per request" was never viable in Java or C\#. If you know JavaScript The mental shift: in Node you structure code so it never blocks, because blocking is catastrophic. In Go you write straight-line blocking code, and the runtime moves the goroutine off the thread while it waits. There is no colour to functions, no async infecting every caller up the stack. A function that reads a file looks like a function that reads a file. A WaitGroup counts outstanding work. Three rules, and the bugs that come from breaking them: * wg.Add before the go , never inside it.* Inside, Wait may run before the goroutine starts and see a count of zero. * defer wg.Done() as the first line.* A panic or an early return otherwise leaves the count above zero and Wait blocks forever. *Pass the WaitGroup by pointer* if it crosses a function boundary. Copying one gives the callee its own counter, and the original never reaches zero. Since Go 1.25 there is a shorthand that removes the first two: Goroutines return nothing. A go call is a statement, not an expression, so there is no value to take. Write into a pre-sized slice, one index per goroutine. No lock is needed because no two goroutines touch the same element. If you know JavaScript This is Promise.all , with the ordering preserved the same way: by index rather than by completion. The difference is that an error in one goroutine does not reject the whole batch. Here every result carries its own error, which is usually what you wanted from Promise.allSettled anyway. Appending to a shared slice instead of indexing would be a data race, because append reads and writes the slice header. Index assignment to distinct elements is safe. Two goroutines touching the same variable, at least one of them writing, with no synchronisation, is a data race . The result is not "the wrong number", it is undefined. count++ is three operations: read, add, write. Two goroutines interleaving them lose updates. Go ships a race detector, and it is the most valuable tool in the toolchain: Watch out Run your tests with -race in CI. Always. A data race can run correctly ten million times and corrupt data on the ten-million-and-first, on a different machine, under load. The detector finds it the first time the racing access happens, which turns an unreproducible production mystery into a failing test. It costs roughly ten times the CPU and a few times the memory, so it is a CI and development tool rather than something you ship. The fix for the counter is a mutex: Or, for exactly this shape, an atomic: Unbounded goroutines are a real hazard. Ten thousand URLs means ten thousand simultaneous connections, which will exhaust file descriptors or get you blocked. A buffered channel used as a semaphore caps the concurrency: Channels are the next chapter. For now, read sem <- struct{}{} as "wait until there is room, then claim a slot". If you know JavaScript The JavaScript equivalent is a library like p-limit , because the language gives you nothing for it. Here it is two lines and a channel, which is a fair summary of the trade Go makes across the board: fewer batteries, better primitives. Starting one is cheap, which makes it tempting. Three cases where it is wrong: When the work is faster than the coordination. Spawning a goroutine to add two numbers costs more than adding them. When you do not wait for it. A goroutine whose result nobody collects, with no WaitGroup and no channel, is a leak. If main exits it is killed silently; if it blocks forever it holds its stack forever. When it needs ordering. Goroutines have no execution order. If step two must follow step one, write them in sequence. Project 12: a concurrent link checker Check a list of URLs in parallel, with a concurrency limit and a timeout, and report which are broken. This is a genuinely useful tool and it exercises everything in this chapter. Run it against a handfu

headings: The direction: interfaces belong to the consumer
pages.text: If you take one idea from this book, take this one. Go's interfaces look like TypeScript's and work backwards from them, and once that clicks a great deal of Go code stops looking odd and starts looking inevitable. Things you have not met yet Two examples look ahead: context.Context is chapter 16 and the test is chapter 18. Interfaces are what make both of them work, which is why they are here rather than there. An interface is a set of method signatures. Any type with those two methods is a Shape . You do not say so anywhere. This is structural typing , and it is called implicit interface satisfaction. If you know JavaScript TypeScript interfaces are structural too, so this much is familiar: an object with the right shape satisfies the interface. The difference is where the interface lives and who declares it, which is the next section and is the part that actually matters. In Java or C\#, the implementer declares what it implements: class Rect implements Shape . The interface is defined near the thing that provides it, and the provider must import it. In Go, the convention is the reverse. *The interface is declared by the package that consumes it, and lists only what that consumer needs.* Consider a function that writes a report somewhere. Now Generate accepts a file, a network connection, an HTTP response, an in-memory buffer, a gzip stream, or anything else with a Write method. None of those types know report exists. The dependency points from the consumer to nothing at all. If you know JavaScript In TypeScript you would often import a type from the module that provides it, or define a shared types.ts that both sides import. Go's version removes the shared file: the consumer owns a small interface, the provider owns a concrete type, and neither imports the other. That is the decoupling, and it is why Go codebases have surprisingly few imports between their own packages. That Writer above is the real one. io.Writer in the standard library is exactly those four words, and it is arguably the most successful interface ever designed: One method. Hundreds of types satisfy it. Everything composes. The proverb is the bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction . A one-method interface is satisfied by nearly anything and is easy to fake in a test. A ten-method interface is satisfied by one type and is a class declaration wearing a disguise. Watch out The beginner mistake, carried in from other languages, is to define an interface for every struct up front: One implementation and one interface that mirrors it exactly is pure ceremony: you have doubled the code and decoupled nothing. The Go advice is accept interfaces, return structs : return the concrete type from your constructor, and let whichever caller needs an abstraction declare the two methods it actually uses. An interface with no methods is satisfied by everything. any is Go's unknown , not its any . You cannot do anything with the value until you establish what it is. The tool is a type assertion : Or a type switch, which is the readable form when several types are possible: Watch out The single-value assertion s := x.(string) panics if the type is wrong. The two-value form s, ok := x.(string) never panics. Use the two-value form unless you genuinely want to crash, which in a server you almost never do. Reach for any rarely. It throws away everything the type system knows, and most uses of it in a new codebase are better served by an interface with one method or, since Go 1.18, by generics. This one catches experienced people and is worth the page. An interface value has two parts internally: a type and a value . It is nil only when both are nil. The returned interface holds type *MyError and value nil . The type is not nil, so the interface is not nil, so err != nil is true and your error handling runs for an error that is not there. If you know JavaScript There is no JavaScript equivalent because there is no such two-part value. The practical rule is the one from chapter four, and now you know why it exists: *declare the return type as error and return a literal nil *, never a typed nil variable. Four from the standard library carry an enormous amount of Go code. io.Reader io.Writer error Error() string . You met it in chapter four fmt.Stringer String() string . How a type prints itself Stringer is a quick win. Implement it and fmt.Println uses it: If you know JavaScript That is toString() , with one important difference: nothing is called implicitly during string concatenation, because Go has no implicit conversion. "x" + u does not compile. Only the fmt family looks for String() . The payoff arrives when you test. A function that takes an interface can be handed a fake with no mocking library and no dependency injection framework. The test: Six lines of fake, no library, no configuration. That is the whole argument for consumer-declared interfaces, and it only works because Mailer has one method rather than the fifteen a real mail client has. Project 9: a notifier with three backends Build something that uses an interface the way Go intends, then prove the decoupling by adding a backend without touching the code that uses it. Notice three things. WriterNotifier is constructed twice with completely different destinations, a string builder and standard output, because both satisfy io.Writer . CollectingNotifier uses a pointer receiver because it mutates, so the slice holds collector rather than CollectingNotifier{} , and putting the value in instead is a compile error worth seeing. And alertAll would work unchanged against an email sender, a Slack client or a test fake. Now add a fourth: a PrefixNotifier that wraps another Notifier and adds a prefix before delegating. That is the decorator pattern, in Go, in eight lines, with no base class: Your turn Give CollectingNotifier a String() string method so it satisfies fmt.Stringer , then print the collector directly with fmt.Println(collector) and watch the output change. Then wri

headings: omitempty, and what it actually means
Times, and the format you will meet
pages.text: JSON is where your Go backend meets your React frontend, so this chapter earns its place twice: once now, and again in part four when Grit generates the types on both sides of that boundary. Unmarshal takes a pointer, because it fills in the value you give it. Passing back instead of &back compiles and silently does nothing useful, which is the chapter's first trap. For readable output: This is the single most common Go and JSON bug, and you met the rule in chapter two. An empty object. No error, no warning. The encoding/json package lives in another package and literally cannot see unexported fields. Watch out *If your JSON comes out as {} , check for lowercase field names first.* It is the answer about nine times out of ten. The same applies on the way in: an unexported field is never populated by Unmarshal . json:"name" Use this key json:"-" Never encode or decode this field json:",omitempty" Omit when the value is the zero value json:",string" Encode a number or bool as a JSON string no tag Use the Go field name, capital included Watch out The tag syntax is unforgiving and silent. All of these are wrong and none produce an error: The field then encodes as Name . If one key in your JSON is capitalised and the rest are not, you have found a stray space. go vet catches malformed tags. Run it. omitempty omits the zero value , which is rarely what people assume. Active: false disappears from the output. If false is a meaningful value and not merely "unset", omitempty is wrong and will cause a real bug. The fix is a pointer, which is chapter eight's lesson in its natural habitat: If you know JavaScript JavaScript has no such ambiguity because undefined and false are different values. Go's zero values collapse them, so a *bool is how you get the distinction back. You will see *string and *bool all over the struct definitions of any API that supports partial updates, and now you know exactly why. Without a struct, JSON decodes into map[string]any : Every number becomes a float64 , which surprises everyone: Prefer a struct whenever you know the shape. The type system is the point. Two behaviours that catch people: Unknown fields are silently dropped. For an API that should reject nonsense, use a decoder: This turns a typo in a client's payload into a 400 instead of a silently ignored field, which is usually what you want for a write endpoint. For an HTTP body, do not read it all into memory first: Decoder reads from any io.Reader and Encoder writes to any io.Writer , which is chapter ten's small interfaces paying off again. time.Time marshals to RFC 3339: That parses directly with new Date(...) in JavaScript, so the default is the right one. A zero time encodes as "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z" , which looks alarming in output; use a *time.Time with omitempty when the field is genuinely optional. Implement MarshalJSON to control a type's representation: Note the receivers: MarshalJSON on the value, UnmarshalJSON on the pointer, because unmarshalling has to modify. Getting this backwards means your custom decoder is silently never called, which is the second-most-common JSON bug after lowercase fields. If you know JavaScript This is toJSON() and a reviver function, combined into an interface. Money is the classic case: a float64 cannot represent 0.10 exactly, so storing cents as an integer and formatting at the boundary is the correct design in any language. Grit has a money field type that does exactly this, and part four explains why it is a type rather than advice. Project 18: a JSON reformatting CLI Build jsonfmt : read JSON on standard input or from a file, validate it, pretty print it, and optionally extract one field. This is a tool you will actually use, and it exercises streaming, unknown shapes and error handling. Build it and try it: Two details worth understanding. dec.UseNumber() stops every number becoming a float64 , so a large integer ID survives the round trip instead of losing precision: without it, {"id": 12345678901234567} comes back subtly wrong. And doc is declared as any rather than map[string]any , so a top-level JSON array works too. The ...any in fail is a variadic parameter, Go's rest argument. Passing it on to Fprintf with args... spreads it again, which is the Go equivalent of ...args in both directions. Your turn Add a -keys flag that prints the top-level keys one per line, sorted. You will need a type switch on doc , because the document might be an object or an array, and the two cases want different answers. Then add DisallowUnknownFields behind a -strict flag and find out what it does to a document with no struct to compare against. The answer tells you something real about what that option is actually for. Commit your work with the message JSON - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Round-trip something awkward, because the easy cases never bite. In part2-ideas/19-json : One. Marshal your chapter five Invoice , then unmarshal it back and compare. Any field that does not survive is a missing tag or a lowercase name. Two. The omitempty trap: a bool field that is deliberately false . Show it disappearing, then fix it with a pointer, and write in a comment which choice you would make in an API. Three. Decode into map[string]any for a payload whose shape you do not control, and pull one nested value out with a type assertion that does not panic on the wrong type. Four. A custom MarshalJSON for a type that must serialise as a date rather than a timestamp, with a test for both directions. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.

headings: Mutex: one goroutine at a time
sync.Once: exactly once, no matter who asks
sync.Map, and why you probably do not want it
pages.text: The previous chapter sold channels. This one is the correction: *channels are not always the answer*, and reaching for one where a mutex belongs produces code that is slower and harder to read. The Go team's own guidance, from the wiki: use a channel to pass ownership of data or to distribute work; use a mutex to protect shared state. The rest of this chapter is what that means in practice. Lock blocks until no other goroutine holds the lock. defer c.mu.Unlock() on the line after is the pattern: a path that returns early without unlocking deadlocks the whole program. Watch out Four rules, each the source of a real bug: The zero value works. var mu sync.Mutex is ready. Never mu := sync.Mutex{} then copy it around. Never copy a struct containing a mutex. Copying duplicates the lock, so two copies protect nothing. This is why Inc has a pointer receiver. go vet catches most of these. Lock the reads too. A read racing with a write is still a data race, and the race detector will say so. Reading an int is not atomic in any sense you can rely on. Keep the critical section small. Never do I/O, call an unknown function, or send on a channel while holding a lock. That is how a lock becomes a queue and then a deadlock. Common style, and it reads well: The cost is that Lock and Unlock become part of the type's public API, so callers can lock your struct. Keep the mutex a named field when the type is exported from a package. When reads vastly outnumber writes, sync.RWMutex lets readers run concurrently. Watch out RWMutex is not automatically faster. It has more bookkeeping than a plain Mutex , so for short critical sections with moderate contention a Mutex often wins. Use RWMutex when reads are frequent and the critical section is long enough to matter, and confirm with a benchmark rather than a feeling. Also: never upgrade an RLock to a Lock while holding it. That deadlocks. Release, acquire the write lock, and re-check the condition, because things may have changed in between. Do runs the function once, ever. Concurrent callers block until the first one finishes, so nobody sees a half-built value. If you know JavaScript This is the lazy singleton you would write in JavaScript as a module-level let instance with an if (!instance) check. That check is a race in Go, because two goroutines can both see nil. sync.Once is the correct version and is shorter anyway. For a counter or a flag, a lock is heavier than necessary. The typed atomics ( atomic.Int64 , atomic.Bool , atomic.Pointer[T] ) arrived in Go 1.19 and are much nicer than the old function forms. They cannot be copied, which the compiler enforces. Use atomics only for a single value. The moment two values must change together, you need a mutex, because two atomic operations are not one atomic operation: There is a concurrent map in the standard library. It is specialised, and the documentation says so plainly: it is optimised for two cases, where a key is written once and read many times, or where goroutines work on disjoint key sets. For everything else, a plain map with a mutex is faster and far more readable, because sync.Map has no type safety: everything is any and you assert on the way out. Reach for sync.Map after measuring, not before. Channel Passing ownership of a value, distributing work, signalling an event Mutex Protecting state that several goroutines read and write in place RWMutex The same, when reads dominate and the section is long atomic One number or flag, nothing else Once Lazy initialisation WaitGroup Waiting for a known set of goroutines to finish The counter from chapter thirteen makes the point. With a channel: That is a goroutine, two channels, a select loop that never exits, and a lifetime you now have to manage. Against: The channel version is the one that looks clever and the atomic is the one you want. Sharing a number is not communication. Project 14: an in-memory cache with expiry Build something with real shared state: a cache with per-entry expiry and a background cleaner. It needs a mutex, a Once , an atomic and a goroutine, and the combination is typical of real service code. Run it with -race . It must be clean. Then break it three ways, one at a time, and run with -race after each. Change hits from an atomic.Int64 to a plain int64 and watch the detector fire. Change RLock to no lock at all in Get , same result. Finally remove the sync.Once from Close and call it twice: the second close(c.done) panics, which is the "closing twice" rule from the last chapter meeting a real program. One design note worth absorbing: Get releases the read lock before checking expiry and updating counters. The counters are atomic so they need no lock, and holding a lock while doing work you do not have to is the habit that turns a cache into a bottleneck. Your turn Add a Len() int method and decide which lock it takes. Then add a maximum size, evicting the entry closest to expiry when the cache is full. That second one is harder than it looks: finding the minimum requires scanning under the write lock, which makes Set O(n). Think about what you would need to make it fast, and notice you are now designing an LRU, which is why real cache libraries exist. Commit your work with the message Sync - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Build a cache, then find out which lock it wanted. In part2-ideas/15-sync , write a concurrent cache with Get and Set . One. A sync.Mutex version with the mutex embedded, and a test that hits it from fifty goroutines under -race . Two. A sync.RWMutex version. Benchmark both at ninety percent reads: Commit the numbers in NOTES.md and say which you would ship. Three. A sync.Once that loads the cache the first time anybody asks, no matter how many ask at once. Four. Replace the counter inside it with atomic.Int64 and note what you gave up by doing so. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answe

headings: Error messages are the whole skill
Comparing things that are not numbers
pages.text: Go ships a test runner, an assertion-free testing philosophy, a benchmark harness, a coverage tool, a fuzzer and a race detector. There is nothing to install and nothing to configure. After a JavaScript project's testing setup, this takes some adjusting to, mostly because you keep looking for the config file. A test file ends in _test.go , sits beside the code it tests, and contains functions named TestXxx taking *testing.T . If you know JavaScript No describe , no it , no expect . A test is a function, and it fails by calling t.Errorf . There is no assertion library in the standard library, and this is deliberate: the Go team's position is that if got != want is clearer than learning which of toBe , toEqual and toStrictEqual you wanted. You will still meet testify in real codebases, which adds assert.Equal(t, want, got) . It is popular and it is fine. Start without it. A failing test must tell you what happened without opening the source. The convention is got, want : That line names the input, the result and the expectation. Compare it to t.Error("failed") , which tells you nothing you did not already know. t.Errorf records a failure and keeps going . t.Fatalf records it and stops the test function immediately. Use Fatalf when continuing would panic or produce noise. Use Errorf when you want to see every failure in one run. This is the dominant Go testing idiom. One test function, a slice of cases. t.Run creates a subtest with its own name, so output identifies the case: You can run one case directly: If you know JavaScript This replaces describe.each and test.each . The advantage over both is that the cases are an ordinary slice of an ordinary struct, so adding a field to the table is a normal code change and the compiler checks every row. == works on structs of comparable fields. For slices, maps and nested structs, use reflect.DeepEqual or, much better, go-cmp : A readable diff instead of false . This is the one testing dependency worth adding on day one. A helper that reports failures should call t.Helper() so the line number points at the caller : Without it, every failure points at the line inside mustLoad , which is useless when ten tests call it. t.Cleanup registers work to run when the test finishes, including on failure. For package-wide setup, TestMain : If you know JavaScript t.Cleanup is afterEach , scoped to one test and registered where the resource is created rather than in a separate block. TestMain is globalSetup and globalTeardown . There is no beforeEach : you call a helper at the top of each test, which is more typing and means a reader can see what a test depends on without scrolling. Tests in different packages already run in parallel. t.Parallel() marks tests within a package as safe to interleave. Watch out A parallel test must not share mutable state with another test. Writing to the same database table, the same temp file or the same package-level variable will fail intermittently, which is worse than failing reliably. Combine t.Parallel() with -race so that a shared-state mistake is reported rather than merely flaky. Test the kind , not the message. Message text is not a contract. And always test that an error is returned when you expect one: The second opens a browser showing every line in green or red. It is the fastest way to find the branch nobody tested. Watch out Coverage measures lines executed, not behaviour verified. A test that calls every function and asserts nothing reports high coverage and proves nothing. Use it to find what you missed , never as a target to hit. Operations per second, nanoseconds each, bytes allocated and allocation count. b.Loop() replaced the older for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ in Go 1.24 and is harder to get wrong, because it stops the compiler optimising your work away. Project 17: test the user store properly Take the store from chapter eleven and give it a real test suite: table driven, testing error kinds rather than messages, with a helper and cleanup. Run it four ways and notice what each tells you. go test ./... gives you pass or fail. go test -v ./... names every subtest, which is how you confirm the table ran every row rather than silently skipping. go test -race ./... would catch the shared-state bug if newStore returned a package-level store instead of a fresh one, which is the mistake t.Parallel() makes dangerous. And go test -cover ./... tells you which branch of Create you forgot. The important design point is in TestCreateDuplicateEmail : it asserts errors.Is(err, ErrConflict) and never looks at the message. Change the wording of that error and the test still passes, which is correct, because the wording was never the promise. Your turn Add a benchmark for Create and run it with -benchmem . Then change the duplicate-email check from a linear scan to a second map keyed by email, and run the benchmark again with a thousand existing users. The allocation count and the nanoseconds per operation will both move, and seeing a design change show up as a number is the habit this chapter is really teaching. Commit your work with the message Testing - Assignment One , exactly as written, so the leaderboard can score it. Go back and test something you already wrote. Take your chapter eleven store package and bring it to a state you would defend in review. One. Table-driven tests for every exported function, including the error cases, with the table naming each case. Two. A failure message that says what it wanted and what it got. Break one test on purpose and check the output names the case. Three. A t.Helper() assertion helper, and t.Cleanup for anything the test created. Four. Coverage, recorded rather than chased: Five. One benchmark, with -benchmem , and one sentence on whether the allocations surprised you. Work it through yourself first. The chapter above has everything you need, and the leaderboard scores the commit, not the answer.

headings: Database Mastery with GORM: Models, Migrations & Queries
pages.text: Every application stores data. The question is how elegantly you interact with it. GORM lets you work with databases using Go structs instead of raw SQL. In this course, you ll master models, migrations, relationships, advanced queries, scopes, hooks, and performance optimization , everything you need to build data-heavy applications with Grit. Reference docs: Models & Database → Databases speak SQL. Go speaks structs. An ORM bridges the gap , it translates between your Go code and the database, so you can create, read, update, and delete records using familiar Go syntax instead of writing SQL strings. Here s the same operation in raw SQL vs GORM: What are 3 advantages of using an ORM like GORM over writing raw SQL? Think about readability, safety, and portability. Can you think of a situation where raw SQL would be better than an ORM? A GORM model is a Go struct that represents a database table. Each field becomes a column. You control column behavior with struct tags , constraints, indexes, defaults, and JSON serialization names. Common field types and their database column types: Define a GORM model for a Blog Post with these fields: Title (required string), Slug (unique string), Content (long text), Published (boolean, defaults to false), AuthorID (foreign key to User). Don t forget to embed gorm.Model . Once you define a model, you need to create the corresponding database table. GORM s auto-migration reads your struct and creates (or updates) the table to match. No manual SQL needed. In a Grit project, you run migrations with: What auto-migration does: • Creates tables that don t exist • Adds columns that are missing • Creates indexes and constraints • Does NOT delete columns (to prevent data loss) • Does NOT change column types Add a new Stock int field to your Product model. Run grit migrate . Open GORM Studio and check the products table. Did the new column appear? What s its default value? CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update, Delete , the four fundamental database operations. GORM provides clean methods for each one. Let s see them all: Using GORM Studio, perform these operations: (1) Create 3 products with different names and prices, (2) Query all products, (3) Update one product s price, (4) Soft-delete a product, (5) Query all products again , is the deleted one still visible? (6) Use db.Unscoped().Find(&products) to see all products including deleted ones. Real applications have related data. A product belongs to a category. A category has many products. A post has many tags, and a tag has many posts. GORM handles all three relationship types: belongs_to, has_many, and many_to_many. Create a Category model with a Name field. Add a CategoryID and Category field to your Product model. Run grit migrate . Then: (1) Create a category called Electronics , (2) Create 5 products in that category, (3) Query products with db.Preload( Category ).Find(&products) . Does the category name appear on each product? GORM s query builder lets you chain conditions to build complex queries. It s like writing SQL, but in Go , type-safe, composable, and readable. Write these queries using GORM s query builder: (1) Find the 5 most expensive active products, ordered by price descending, (2) Count the total number of products per category, (3) Find all products whose name contains Pro and cost more than $50, (4) Get the average price of all active products. When you find yourself writing the same Where clause in multiple places, it s time to create a scope. A scope is a reusable query function that you can chain onto any query. Create a Published scope for blog posts that filters to only published posts ( published = true ). Create a Recent scope that orders by created_at DESC and limits to 10. Use them together: db.Scopes(Published, Recent).Find(&posts) . Does it return the 10 most recent published posts? Sometimes you need code to run automatically before or after a database operation. For example, auto-generating a slug from the title when creating a blog post, or sending a welcome email after creating a user. GORM hooks let you do this. Add a BeforeCreate hook to your Blog model that auto-generates a slug from the title. My First Post should become my-first-post . Test it: create a blog post with only a title, then check if the slug was set automatically. Also add a BeforeSave hook that ensures the title is not empty. GORM s query builder handles 90% of your database needs. But sometimes you need the full power of SQL , complex aggregations, window functions, database-specific features, or performance-critical queries. GORM lets you run raw SQL when needed. Write a raw SQL query that returns: (1) the average price per category, (2) the total number of products per category, and (3) the most expensive product in each category. Define a result struct to hold the data. Run it and check the results in GORM Studio. A slow database is a slow application. Here are the most impactful performance optimizations you can apply to your GORM queries: 1. Use Indexes , An index is like a book s table of contents. Without it, the database scans every row to find matches. With it, lookups are nearly instant. 2. Avoid N+1 Queries , The most common performance killer. If you load 100 products and each one triggers a separate query to load its category, that s 101 queries. Use Preload to load everything in 2 queries. 3. Paginate Large Results , Never load all records at once. Always use Offset and Limit . 4. Select Only Needed Columns , If you only need the name and price, don t load the entire row. Review your product queries from the previous challenges. For each one, check: (1) Are you using Preload for relationships (avoiding N+1)? (2) Are you paginating large result sets? (3) Are you using Select to load only needed columns? (4) Do your frequently-filtered columns have indexes? Fix any issues you find. You ve mastered GORM , from basic models to advanced query optimization: Models , Go structs with GORM tags d

headings: GORM Studio: The Visual Database Browser
pages.text: Your database holds all your application s data, but most of the time it s a black box. You send API requests and trust the data is there, but you cannot see it directly. GORM Studio changes that , it s a visual database browser embedded in every Grit project. Browse tables, edit records, run SQL, export data, and generate Go models , all from your browser at /studio . Reference docs: Database & GORM Studio → GORM Studio is a database browser built specifically for GORM (Go s most popular ORM). It s embedded in every Grit project and available at /studio . You do not need to install anything , it s part of your API. What makes GORM Studio different from tools like pgAdmin, DBeaver, or TablePlus: • Zero installation , runs inside your Grit API, accessible in the browser • GORM-aware , understands GORM conventions (soft delete, relationships, auto-migrate) • Go model generation , can generate Go struct code from existing tables • Multi-format export , SQL, JSON, CSV, XLSX, YAML, DBML, ERD diagrams • Password-protected , secured with its own credentials, separate from your app s auth Start your Grit API and open http://localhost:8080/studio in your browser. Log in with the default credentials: username admin , password studio . What do you see? How many tables are listed? When you open GORM Studio, the left sidebar shows all tables in your database. Click any table name to see its records displayed in a data grid on the right. The table view shows: • Column headers , with the column name and data type (varchar, integer, boolean, timestamp) • Records as rows , each row is one record in the table • Pagination , for tables with many records, navigate between pages • Row count , total number of records in the table Find the users table in GORM Studio. How many columns does it have? What are their data types? Click through the other tables , which table has the most records? Which has the most columns? Click on any row in the table view to see the full record details. The detail view shows every field with its value, including fields that might be truncated in the table view (like long text fields or JSON columns). For records with relationships, the detail view can show related data. For example, clicking on a blog post might show: • The post s own fields (title, content, published, created_at) • The category_id foreign key , and which category it points to • The user_id , the author of the post This is especially useful for debugging. When a frontend shows wrong data, you can check GORM Studio to see exactly what s in the database , is it a frontend bug (wrong display) or a backend bug (wrong data)? Find a specific user in the users table by scrolling or using the search. Click on the row to see the full detail view. What fields can you see? Is the password field visible? (Hint: the password is stored as a bcrypt hash , you should see a long string starting with $2a$ .) GORM Studio lets you edit records directly. Click on a cell in the table view to enter edit mode. Change the value, then save. The change is written directly to the database. This is incredibly useful for: • Debugging , quickly change a value to test how the frontend handles it • Fixing data , correct a typo or wrong value without writing a migration • Testing roles , change a user s role from USER to ADMIN to test admin features • Seeding data , quickly add test data without writing API requests Find a user with the USER role in GORM Studio. Edit their role field to ADMIN and save. Now log in as that user in your application. Can they access admin features? Change it back to USER when you are done. Click the New button to create a new record. GORM Studio shows a form with a field for each column. Fill in the values and save to insert a new row directly into the database. Some fields are auto-populated and you can leave them empty: • ID , auto-incremented by the database • CreatedAt , set automatically by GORM • UpdatedAt , set automatically by GORM • DeletedAt , null for active records Use GORM Studio to create a new record in a non-user table (e.g., categories or blogs). Fill in the required fields and save. Can you see the new record in the table view? Can you also see it through the API (e.g., GET /api/categories )? Select one or more rows in the table view and click Delete. But here s the important question: is the record actually gone? When you delete through the API, GORM performs a soft delete. The record s DeletedAt field is set to the current timestamp. It disappears from GET /api/resources but remains in the database. In GORM Studio, you can see soft-deleted records , they show a non-null DeletedAt value. You can also perform a hard delete (permanent removal) if needed. Delete a record through the API (e.g., DELETE /api/categories/1 ). Then open GORM Studio and look at the categories table. Can you still see the deleted record? What value does DeletedAt have? Is the record visible through GET /api/categories ? GORM Studio includes a SQL editor where you can write and execute any SQL query directly against your database. This is the most powerful feature , it gives you the full expressiveness of SQL for data exploration, reporting, and debugging. Some useful queries to try: Open the SQL editor in GORM Studio. Write a query that counts users by role. Your result should show something like: ADMIN: 1, EDITOR: 2, USER: 10. Try a second query: find the 5 most recently created records across any table. GORM Studio can export your complete database schema in multiple formats: The SQL export is especially useful for documentation and database migrations. It produces the exact CREATE TABLE statements that reproduce your schema: Find the schema export feature in GORM Studio. Export your schema as SQL. Open the file , can you read the CREATE TABLE statements? How many tables are in the export? Do the column types match what you defined in your GORM models? Beyond schema export, GORM Studio can export and import the actual data i
pages.title: GORM Studio: The Visual Database Browser

pages.text: 5 self-paced courses that take you from zero to a distributable desktop app. Each course is ~30 minutes with hands-on challenges you complete yourself. No videos, no lectures , just concepts, examples, and practice.
pages.title: Building Desktop Applications with Grit

pages.text: In this final course, you will compile your desktop app into a native binary, learn about platform targets, customize the app icon, optimize the file size, and understand how to distribute your app to users. Reference docs: Building & Distribution → Until now, you ve been running your app in development mode with grit start . Development mode includes tools that help you build the app but are not needed by end users: To compile your app into a production binary, run: Or use the Wails command directly: Here is what happens during the build: 1. Vite builds React , bundles, minifies, and optimizes all JavaScript, CSS, and assets 2. Go embeds the frontend , the built React files are embedded into the Go binary using go:embed 3. Go compiles to native code , the entire application (backend + embedded frontend) becomes a single executable The output binary is placed in the build/bin/ directory: Run grit compile in your project directory. How long does it take? Where is the output file? What is the file size? Try double-clicking the binary , does the app open? Wails can build for different operating systems and architectures: Build for your current platform with grit compile . Find the output binary in build/bin/ . Run it directly (double-click on Windows, ./myapp on macOS/Linux). Does it work the same as dev mode? Every desktop app needs an icon , it appears in the taskbar, dock, file explorer, and the window title bar. Wails uses icon files in the build/ directory: To change the icon: 1. Create a 1024x1024 pixel PNG image for your app icon 2. Replace build/appicon.png with your new image 3. Rebuild with grit compile , Wails converts it to platform-specific formats Find the default app icon file in the build/ directory. Replace it with a custom PNG (1024x1024). Rebuild and check , does the new icon appear in the taskbar and window title? The wails.json file controls how the production window appears: The name field is what appears in the operating system s task manager and window list. The size settings define the default dimensions and minimum size. Change the default window size to 1200x800 in wails.json . Rebuild with grit compile and run the binary. Is the window larger? Try resizing it below the minimum dimensions , does it stop at the minimum? A typical Grit desktop app binary is 15-30 MB . This includes the entire Go backend, all React code, CSS, and embedded assets. For comparison, an Electron app with similar features would be 100-200 MB. You can reduce the binary size by stripping debug symbols: For even smaller binaries, you can use UPX compression (a tool that compresses executables): Typical size reduction: Build your app normally and note the file size. Then rebuild with wails build -ldflags -s -w . How much smaller is it? If you have UPX installed, compress it further. What s the final size? Once your app is compiled, you need to get it to your users. There are several distribution methods: The simplest method , upload the binary to your website, GitHub Releases, or a file hosting service. Users download the file and run it. No installer needed. Wails can generate an NSIS installer for Windows. This creates a .exe installer that adds your app to the Start Menu, creates desktop shortcuts, and supports uninstallation: On macOS, Wails builds a .app bundle. You can package it into a .dmg disk image for distribution , the standard macOS app distribution format. For Linux, you can package the binary as an AppImage , a single executable that works on most Linux distributions without installation. • Windows , requires a code signing certificate ($200-400/year) from a Certificate Authority • macOS , requires an Apple Developer account ($99/year) and notarization through Apple s servers • Linux , code signing is optional; most Linux users install from package managers or trust direct downloads If you re on Windows, try building with wails build -nsis to generate an installer. Run the installer , does it create a Start Menu entry and desktop shortcut? Can you uninstall it from Settings? The most common way to distribute desktop apps for open-source projects is GitHub Releases. You build for each platform and upload the binaries: Users visit your GitHub repository s Releases page and download the binary for their platform. Build your app for your current platform. Create a CHANGELOG.md file documenting what your app does. If you have a GitHub repository, create a release and upload the binary. The difference between development builds and production builds How to compile your app with grit compile or wails build Platform targets , building for Windows, macOS, and Linux How to customize the app icon Window configuration in wails.json Optimizing binary size with -ldflags -s -w and UPX Distribution methods , direct download, NSIS installer, DMG, AppImage What code signing is and when you need it Build your notes app for your current platform. Test the binary , create some data, export to PDF, verify everything works the same as dev mode. Check the file size. Change the window title in wails.json . Replace the app icon with a custom one. Rebuild with -ldflags -s -w . Compare the file size to the previous build. Does the new title and icon appear? Send the compiled binary to a friend (or test on a different computer). Does it run without installing Go, Node, or Wails? Does the SQLite database get created automatically on first launch? This is the power of a native binary , zero dependencies for the end user. Congratulations , you ve completed the entire Grit Desktop course track. You now know how to: • Scaffold a desktop app with grit new-desktop • Generate full CRUD resources with Wails bindings • Customize the UI with frameless windows, themes, and shadcn/ui • Export data to PDF, Excel, and CSV • Compile and distribute a native binary Next steps: build something real. A personal finance tracker, a note-taking app, a project management tool, a CRM for your business , the possibilities are endles

pages.text: In this course, you will learn how CRUD operations work in desktop apps, generate resources with the Grit code generator, understand Wails bindings in depth, and work with SQLite through GORM. Reference docs: Desktop Resource Generation → In web apps , React calls REST APIs over HTTP. You use fetch() or axios to send requests to endpoints like GET /api/blogs . In desktop apps , React calls Go functions directly via Wails bindings , no REST endpoints to define and no fetch() calls to write by hand. (Under the hood, Grit runs an embedded Gin API bound to 127.0.0.1:34999 that the bindings talk to, but you never touch the HTTP layer yourself.) From your React code it s just function calls: This is simpler and faster , no hand-written serialization, no CORS configuration to manage. Your React code just calls Go functions and gets results back; the Wails bindings and the embedded local API handle the plumbing. The grit generate resource command works for desktop projects too , same syntax, same workflow, but different output. For desktop, it generates Wails bindings instead of HTTP handlers, and TanStack Router routes instead of Next.js pages: This creates everything you need for a full Task CRUD: Run grit generate resource Task --fields title:string,description:text,done:bool,priority:int in your desktop project. List the files that were created. Did the sidebar update with a new Tasks entry? When you generate a resource, Grit adds methods to app.go that become the bridge between Go and React: On the React side, Wails automatically generates TypeScript wrappers. You import and call them like any other function: After generating the Task resource, look in wailsjs/go/main/App.ts (this file is generated when you run wails dev ). What functions are available? Do they match the Go methods in app.go ? Desktop models use the same GORM patterns as web projects, but with the SQLite driver instead of PostgreSQL: Open the Task model at internal/models/task.go . Compare it to a web project model if you have one. What s the same? The struct tags, the GORM model embedding, and the JSON tags should all look familiar. Desktop apps use TanStack Router with hash history for Wails compatibility. The route files live in frontend/src/routes/ : The $id prefix means a dynamic parameter , TanStack Router extracts the value from the URL and makes it available in your component. So /tasks/42/edit gives you id = 42 . Find the route files for your generated Task resource in frontend/src/routes/tasks/ . What URL patterns do they follow? Open index.tsx , can you see where it calls GetTasks() ? Services contain all business logic. The App methods in app.go call services, and services call GORM. This is the same pattern used in web projects , keeping logic separate from the transport layer: Open the task service at internal/service/task.go . Read the List() method. What GORM query does it use? What order does it sort by? When you define fields in grit generate resource , each type maps through three layers: Without looking at the table: What SQLite type does a float64 become? What about *time.Time ? What Go type does bool map to? Check your answers against the table above. You can create related resources using the belongs_to field type. For example, a Note that belongs to a Category: This creates a CategoryID foreign key on the Note model and sets up the GORM relationship. The generated UI includes a dropdown to select the category when creating or editing a note. Generate a Category resource with a name field, then generate a Note resource with title:string,content:text,category:belongs_to:Category . Create 3 categories and 5 notes. Does the note form show a category dropdown? Made a mistake? The grit remove resource command cleanly removes everything that was generated: This removes the model file, service file, types file, route files, the sidebar entry, and the bindings in app.go . It s a clean undo of grit generate resource . Remove the Task resource with grit remove resource Task . Verify: is the model file gone? Are the route files gone? Is the sidebar entry removed? Now generate it again with different fields: grit generate resource Task --fields title:string,due_date:date,status:string,done:bool . GORM auto-migrates your models when the app starts. When you add a new field to a model, restart the app and GORM adds the column to the SQLite database automatically. Add a new field to your Task model manually: . Restart the app. Open GORM Studio , is the new column there? Create a task with notes to confirm it works. How desktop CRUD differs from web CRUD , direct function calls vs HTTP How to generate resources with grit generate resource for desktop How Wails bindings work , Go methods become TypeScript functions GORM models with SQLite , same patterns, minor differences TanStack Router file-based routing for desktop apps The service layer pattern , business logic separated from bindings Data type mappings from Grit types to Go, SQLite, and TypeScript How to remove resources cleanly with grit remove resource Starting from a fresh desktop project, generate two resources: Category --fields name:string:unique and Note --fields title:string,content:richtext,category:belongs_to:Category,pinned:bool,color:string:optional . Create 3 categories and 10 notes across those categories. Open GORM Studio with grit studio . Browse the notes table. Can you see the category_id foreign key? Filter notes by category. Export the data if Studio supports it. Create a note, edit it (change the title and category), then delete it. Verify each operation in GORM Studio. Does the note count on the dashboard update after each operation?
pages.title: Desktop CRUD & Data

pages.text: In this course, you will learn how to customize the look and feel of your desktop app. Frameless windows, custom title bars, sidebar navigation, dark theme CSS variables, shadcn/ui components, and resizable panels. Reference docs: Desktop Overview → Grit desktop apps use frameless windows by default. The setting lives in wails.json : When frameless is true , the OS title bar disappears entirely. Your React app fills the entire window. This means you need to build your own title bar with window controls. Open wails.json in your desktop project. Find the frameless setting. What are the width and height values? Try changing frameless to false , restart the app, and see what happens , you ll get the default OS title bar. Since there s no OS title bar, Grit scaffolds a custom one with React. It includes the app name and window control buttons (minimize, maximize, close). These buttons call Wails runtime functions: The Wails runtime provides these functions: • WindowMinimise() , minimize the window to the taskbar • WindowToggleMaximise() , toggle between maximized and normal size • WindowClose() , close the application • WindowSetTitle(title) , change the window title programmatically Find the title bar component in your project (look in frontend/src/components/ ). What Wails runtime functions does it import? Click each window control button , do minimize, maximize, and close all work? Without the OS title bar, users cannot drag the window to move it. Wails solves this with a CSS property: --wails-draggable . Any element with this property set to drag becomes a drag handle: The title bar uses --wails-draggable: drag so you can grab it and move the window. The window control buttons use --wails-draggable: no-drag so clicking them triggers the button action instead of starting a drag. Try dragging the window by the title bar area , it should move. Now try dragging by the main content area , it should not move. Can you identify the exact CSS property that makes this work? The sidebar is auto-generated from your resources. When you run grit generate resource , a new sidebar entry is injected automatically with an appropriate icon: The sidebar is collapsible , it can shrink to just icons, giving more space to the main content. Grit picks Lucide icons based on the resource name (e.g., Task gets a check icon, Note gets a sticky note icon). Generate 3 new resources (e.g., Project, Invoice, Report). Restart the app. Does the sidebar show 3 new entries with icons? Check the sidebar component to see how the entries are defined. Grit desktop apps use a premium dark theme defined with CSS custom properties (variables). These variables are used by all shadcn/ui components and your custom components: You use these variables through Tailwind CSS classes: • bg-background , the darkest background (#0a0a0f) • bg-bg-elevated , card and panel surfaces (#22222e) • text-foreground , primary white text (#e8e8f0) • text-accent , accent purple (#6c5ce7) • border-border , subtle borders (#2a2a3a) Find the CSS file with theme variables (look in frontend/src/ ). Change the --primary color from #6c5ce7 to #3b82f6 (blue). Save and check , does the entire app s accent color update? Grit desktop apps use the same shadcn/ui components as web projects. These are unstyled, accessible React components that you can customize: All components live in frontend/src/components/ui/ and are imported like: Search your project for imports from @/components/ui/ . Find at least 5 different shadcn/ui components used in the app. Which component is used most frequently? Grit desktop apps can include resizable split panels, similar to IDE-style interfaces where you can drag a divider between the sidebar and main content to adjust their widths: The ResizableHandle is the draggable divider between panels. Users can grab it and drag to resize. The minSize and maxSize props prevent panels from becoming too small or too large. If your app has resizable panels, try dragging the divider between the sidebar and main content. The sidebar should resize smoothly. What are the minimum and maximum sizes? The wails.json file controls window appearance and behavior: Change the window size to 1200x800 in wails.json . Set the minimum size to 900x650. Restart the app , is the window larger? Try resizing it below the minimum , does it stop? How frameless windows work , hiding the OS title bar for a custom look Building a custom title bar with Wails runtime window controls Making windows draggable with --wails-draggable CSS property Auto-generated sidebar navigation from resources The dark theme system with CSS custom properties Using shadcn/ui components in desktop apps Resizable panels for IDE-style layouts Window configuration in wails.json Customize your app in four ways: (1) Change the accent color from purple to a color of your choice. (2) Modify the title bar text to show your app s name. (3) Add a new icon to the sidebar for a section called Settings . (4) Adjust the default window size to 1280x720 in wails.json. Create a second theme by duplicating the CSS variables with different colors (e.g., a light theme or a blue-tinted dark theme). Add a button in the title bar that toggles between themes by swapping CSS classes on the root element. Does the entire app update?
pages.title: Custom UI & Theming

pages.text: In this course, you will learn how to export data from your desktop app into PDF documents, Excel spreadsheets, and CSV files. You ll understand the export service, the download flow, and how to customize report templates. Reference docs: DataTable & Export → Users need to get data out of your application. Common use cases include: • Invoices , generate a PDF invoice to email or print for a client • Reports , export monthly data summaries for management • Data backups , export all records to CSV for archiving or migration • Spreadsheets , export data to Excel for further analysis in tools like Google Sheets Grit desktop apps include a built-in export service in Go with three main methods. The service lives in the internal/service/ directory: Each method queries the database, formats the data, writes it to a temporary file, and returns the file path. The React frontend then uses this path to trigger a download. Open the export service file in your project (look in internal/service/ ). What methods does it have? What Go libraries does it import for PDF and Excel generation? The PDF export creates a formatted document with a title, headers, and a data table. The Go code uses a PDF library to build the document programmatically: The generated PDF includes proper formatting: bold headers, alternating row colors, page numbers, and timestamps. Make sure you have at least 5 blog posts in your app. Find the export button in the blog list page and click it to generate a PDF. Does the file download? Open it , are all your blog posts listed? Excel exports create .xlsx files with proper sheets, headers, and data rows. The Go code uses the excelize library: The Excel file includes styled headers, proper column widths, and typed cells (numbers stay as numbers, dates as dates). Export your blog data to Excel. Open the .xlsx file in Excel, Google Sheets, or LibreOffice. Does it have proper column headers? Are the dates formatted correctly? CSV is the simplest format and works everywhere. The output looks like this: Export your blog data to CSV. Open the file in a text editor (not a spreadsheet app). Can you read the raw data? Each line should be one blog post with comma-separated values. The export flow in a desktop app works differently from a web app. There is no browser download dialog , instead, Go generates the file on disk and the React frontend opens it: 1. React calls the Go export method via Wails binding 2. Go queries the database and generates the file in a temp directory 3. Go returns the file path to React 4. React uses the Wails runtime to open the file or show a save dialog On the Go side, the bound method looks like: On the React side: Click an export button in the UI. Where does the file save? Check your system s temp directory. Can you find the exported file there? Try opening it directly from that location. Export your blog data to all three formats: PDF, Excel, and CSV. Open each file. Compare them , which format is best for printing? Which is best for editing? Which is best for importing into another app? You can customize the PDF layout to match your brand. Common customizations include: • Header , add your app name, logo, or company information • Footer , page numbers, generation date, confidentiality notice • Colors , match your brand s accent color for headers and borders • Layout , landscape vs portrait, margins, font sizes Open the export service and modify the PDF generation code. Add a custom header with your app s name and today s date. Change the header color to match your theme. Export again , does the new header appear? Why export matters , invoices, reports, data backups, spreadsheets The export service with GeneratePDF, GenerateExcel, and GenerateCSV methods How PDF generation works , headers, tables, formatting with Go libraries How Excel generation works , workbooks, sheets, styled headers, typed cells How CSV export works , the simplest, most universal data format The desktop download flow , Go generates file, returns path, React opens it How to customize PDF templates with headers, footers, and brand colors Generate an Invoice resource with fields: customer:string,amount:float,date:date,status:string,paid:bool . Add 10 invoices with different customers and amounts. Export your invoices to PDF, Excel, and CSV. The PDF should look like a real invoice report. The Excel file should have proper number formatting. The CSV should be importable into Google Sheets. Open all three exported files side by side. Which format preserves the formatting best (PDF)? Which is easiest to edit (Excel)? Which is the smallest file size (CSV)? When would you use each one?
pages.title: PDF & Excel Export

pages.text: In this course, you will install Wails, scaffold a desktop application with Grit, understand how Go functions are called directly from React, and run your app in dev mode. By the end, you will have a working desktop app with authentication, blog CRUD, and a SQLite database. Reference docs: Your First Desktop App → Desktop apps are different from web apps in several important ways: • They run locally , no browser needed, no internet required (unless your app needs it) • They can access the filesystem , read and write files on the user s computer • They feel faster , no network latency between the UI and backend • They are distributed as a single file , users download one executable and run it Grit uses Wails to build desktop apps. You write Go for the backend and React for the UI , the same languages you already know from Grit web. Wails works by embedding a webview (a lightweight browser engine) inside a native window. Your React app runs in this webview, and Wails creates a bridge so JavaScript can call Go functions directly: • Go side: You write normal Go methods like GetUsers() or CreateBlog(input) • React side: You import and call them as if they were local functions , • No HTTP layer: No REST endpoints, no fetch(), no axios , direct function calls over an internal bridge Learn more at wails.io . Wails supports Windows, macOS, and Linux from a single codebase. Open wails.io in your browser. What platforms does Wails support? Find the Getting Started section , does it mention Go as a requirement? You need the same tools as Grit web (Go, Node.js, pnpm) plus one more , the Wails CLI: Install the Wails CLI with: After installation, verify everything is working: The wails doctor command checks your system for all required dependencies (Go, Node, npm/pnpm, platform-specific build tools) and reports any issues. Run go install github.com/wailsapp/wails/v2/cmd/wails@latest to install the Wails CLI. Then run wails doctor . Does it pass all checks? If any checks fail, follow the instructions to fix them. The command for desktop apps is grit new-desktop , this is different from grit new which creates a web monorepo: After running the command, Grit creates a complete desktop project with authentication, blog CRUD, contact CRUD, a dark theme, and a SQLite database , all wired up and ready to run. Run grit new-desktop notes-app . Look at the folder structure that was created. How many Go files are in the root directory? How many folders are there? A Grit desktop project has a flat, simple structure: Compare this to a Grit web project which has apps/api , apps/web , apps/admin , and packages/shared . A desktop project is much simpler , everything is in one place. The key file is app.go , this is where all your Go methods that React can call are defined. Every public method on the App struct becomes available in the frontend: Open app.go in your notes-app project. What methods are available? These are the functions React can call. Count how many public methods the App struct has. Start your desktop app with either command: Or use the Wails command directly: When you run grit start , a native desktop window opens with your app. The frontend dev server runs at localhost:34115 (you can also open it in a browser for debugging). Run grit start in your notes-app directory. The app should open as a desktop window. Try the login page , can you see the registration form? Desktop apps use SQLite instead of PostgreSQL because users should not need to install a database server. The database file travels with the app , it s just a file on disk: When the app starts, GORM automatically creates the .db file and runs migrations. You can browse the database with GORM Studio: After running the app and registering an account, find the .db file in your project folder. Open GORM Studio with grit studio and browse the tables. Can you see the user you just registered? Your scaffolded desktop app comes with everything you need to start building: • Login and Register pages , local authentication with bcrypt password hashing • Dashboard , stats cards showing total blogs, contacts, and recent activity • Blog CRUD , create, read, update, and delete blog posts • Contact CRUD , manage a contacts list with full CRUD operations • Sidebar navigation , collapsible sidebar with icons for every section • Dark theme , premium dark UI using Grit s design system Register an account in your app. Create 3 blog posts with different titles and content. Create 2 contacts with names and emails. Visit the dashboard , do the stats update to show your new data? Desktop apps have a simpler .env file compared to web projects , no database URLs, no Redis, no S3 storage: • APP_NAME , your application name, shown in the title bar • JWT_SECRET , secret key for signing authentication tokens • DB_PATH , path to the SQLite database file • TOTP_ISSUER , name shown in authenticator apps for two-factor auth Open the .env file in your project. What is the database file name? What is the JWT_SECRET set to? Here are the commands you ll use every day when building desktop apps: Run grit routes in your project folder. How many routes does the desktop app have? Can you identify which ones handle blogs and which handle contacts? Run grit studio . Browse the tables in your SQLite database. Can you see the blogs and contacts you created earlier? Try editing a record directly in Studio. What desktop apps are and how they differ from web apps What Wails is , Go + React desktop framework with direct function calls How to install the Wails CLI and verify with wails doctor How to scaffold a desktop app with grit new-desktop The flat project structure (main.go, app.go, internal/, frontend/) How Wails bindings work , Go methods callable from React How to run in dev mode with grit start and hot reload SQLite as the database , file-based, no server required The essential CLI commands for desktop development Create a brand new desktop app called todo-app with grit new-desktop to
