headings: Build an Invoice Generator: Desktop App with Wails
pages.text: In this course, you will build a real, useful desktop application , an invoice generator. Create clients, generate invoices with line items, export professional PDF invoices, and track payment status. Everything runs offline with SQLite, no internet required. Reference docs: Desktop Apps → An invoice generator is one of the most practical apps a freelancer or small business can use. Instead of paying $20/month for a SaaS tool, you build your own , and it runs entirely on your computer with no subscription: • Client management , store client names, emails, addresses, companies • Invoice creation , auto-numbered invoices with line items, tax calculation • PDF export , professional invoices ready to email to clients • Payment tracking , Draft, Sent, Paid, Overdue status workflow • Excel export , export all invoices for accounting and tax filing • Dashboard , total revenue, outstanding balance, overdue count Everything is stored locally in SQLite. No server, no cloud, no account needed. Open the app and start invoicing. List 5 features an invoice generator needs beyond what s listed above. Think about: recurring invoices, multiple currencies, late fees, payment reminders, client portal. Which would you prioritize? Use Grit s desktop scaffold command to create the project: This creates a Wails v2 project with Go backend, React + TypeScript frontend, local auth, SQLite database, and export capabilities (PDF + Excel). Start the development server: The app opens as a native window. You should see the login page , create an account and explore the default dashboard. This is your starting point. Scaffold the project and run grit start . Create an account and log in. Explore the default pages , dashboard, blog, contacts. These are the starter templates you will customize into an invoice app. The invoice app needs three resources. Notice how they relate to each other: a Client has many Invoices, and an Invoice has many LineItems. The relationships work like this: • Client , standalone entity. Has name, email, optional phone/address/company. • Invoice , belongs to a Client. Has dates, status, financial totals. • LineItem , belongs to an Invoice. Each line is one product/service with qty and price. Generate all three resources. Check the Go models , are the belongs_to foreign keys correct? Can you see the relationships in the model structs? Every invoice needs a unique, sequential number. Instead of making the user type one, auto-generate it. Add this method to the Invoice service: This counts existing invoices and generates the next number: INV-001 , INV-002 , INV-003 , and so on. The %03d format pads with leading zeros up to 3 digits. Call this method when creating a new invoice. The Wails binding exposes it to the frontend, so you can pre-fill the invoice number field automatically. Add the NextNumber() method to your invoice service. Create 3 invoices , are they numbered INV-001 , INV-002 , INV-003 ? Delete the second one and create another , what number does it get? The client list is your first custom page. It shows all clients in a searchable, sortable DataTable , the same component Grit s desktop scaffold provides: The client list is the foundation. Every invoice needs a client, so build this page first. Add a New Client button that opens the FormBuilder with fields for name, email, company, phone, and address. Build the client list page and the create client form. Add 5 clients with different companies. Can you search by name? Sort by company? Edit a client s email? The invoice form is the most complex page in the app. It has multiple steps and dynamic line items that calculate totals automatically: Step 1: Invoice Details • Select client from dropdown (populated from your client list) • Invoice number (auto-filled, but editable) • Issue date (defaults to today) • Due date (defaults to 30 days from today) Step 2: Line Items • Dynamic rows: description, quantity, unit price • Line total auto-calculated: quantity x unit price • Add Line Item button to add more rows • Remove button on each row Step 3: Review • Subtotal (sum of all line totals) • Tax rate input (percentage, e.g., 10%) • Tax amount (subtotal x tax rate) • Grand total (subtotal + tax) • Optional notes field Build the invoice form. Create an invoice with 4 line items (e.g., Web Design , 40 hours at $75 , Logo Design , 1 at $500 , etc.). Verify: Are the line totals correct? Is the subtotal the sum of all lines? Does the tax calculate properly? The invoice detail page shows a complete, formatted view of an invoice. This is what the user sees when they click on an invoice from the list: • Header , invoice number, status badge, issue date, due date • Client info , name, company, email, address • Line items table , description, quantity, unit price, line total • Totals section , subtotal, tax, grand total • Status badge , color-coded: Draft (gray), Sent (blue), Paid (green), Overdue (red) • Action buttons , Export PDF, Mark as Sent, Mark as Paid, Edit, Delete Build the invoice detail page. Navigate to one of your invoices. Is all the information displayed correctly , client name, line items, totals? Does the status badge use the right color? The killer feature of an invoice app: generating a professional PDF that you can email to clients. Grit s desktop scaffold includes an export service that generates PDFs from Go: The PDF should include: • Company header , your business name, address, logo (optional) • Invoice number and dates , prominently displayed • Bill To section , client name, company, address • Line items table , with headers, alternating row colors • Totals , subtotal, tax, grand total (bold) • Payment terms , Payment due within 30 days • Notes , any additional notes from the invoice Add a Export PDF button to the invoice detail page. Generate a PDF for one of your invoices. Open the PDF , does it look professional? Is all the data correct: client info, line items, totals? Invoices follow a status workflow. Each transition rep
pages.title: Build an Invoice Generator: Desktop App with Wails

headings: The health check loop is not optional
Gate on errors, not on latency
pages.text: A load test you remember to run is a load test you run twice. The value is in running it on every pull request, so the regression is attributed to the change that caused it rather than discovered three weeks later with forty commits to bisect. Smoke first, as its own step. When the average load step fails you want the summary to say which one broke, and a green smoke step means the script and the deployment are fine and the finding is real. go run returns as soon as the process starts, not when it is serving. Without the loop, k6 begins while the API is still connecting to Postgres and running migrations, and you get a run of connection refused that looks exactly like a system that cannot handle two users. Poll /api/health , not /health . The unversioned health route is /api/health and the versioned one is /api/v1/health ; a bare /health 404s, and curl -sf treats a 404 as a failure, so the loop runs its full sixty seconds and then starts k6 anyway. This is the part people get wrong, and the project's own CI already says why about benchmarks: timing a shared runner tells you about the runner. A GitHub hosted runner is a noisy neighbour environment, and its p95 varies by more between two identical runs than most real regressions do. An error rate is a property of your code. A p95 on a shared runner is a property of whoever else is on the machine. Gate the merge on the first, and keep the tight latency threshold for the runs you do on known hardware. Nine minutes on every pull request is a real cost. If that is too much, shorten the hold rather than dropping the test: two minutes at a hundred users still catches an N+1 that was not there yesterday. Keep the k6 summary as an artifact with --summary-export=summary.json and upload it. A regression is much easier to argue about when you can diff this week's numbers against the merge that caused them. One. Add the workflow above to your project and push it on a branch. Confirm both k6 steps run green. Two. Break it on purpose: add a time.Sleep(3 * time.Second) to a handler the journey hits, and push. Confirm the workflow fails and read which threshold it names. Three. Remove the sleep. Then delete the health check loop and push. Note what the failure looks like now, and how long it takes to understand it. In step three, read the k6 output rather than the step name. The distinction worth seeing is between a request that was answered slowly and a request that was never answered. Step two fails on http_req_duration with a p95 in the seconds, and the summary points straight at the endpoint. That is the regression gate working. Step three fails on http_req_failed at 100% with connection refused, which reads as a total outage and is actually a race in the workflow. Both are red; only one is about your code. Knowing the difference on sight is most of what makes a CI load test worth having rather than something people start ignoring.
pages.title: The workflow

headings: One: the connection pool, and the surprise in it
Three: a cache that is cold, or absent
Four: GC pauses, which are usually not the problem
pages.text: Load tests in a Grit API find the same handful of things, over and over. Knowing the shortlist does not replace measuring, but it tells you where to point the measurement, and it stops you optimising the handler when the problem is the pool in front of it. This is the most common one and the least intuitive, so it is worth real numbers. Grit sizes the pool in internal/database/database.go : Idle defaulting to open is the part that matters. When the idle limit is lower than the open limit, a request past the idle limit returns its connection to a full pool, so the connection is closed , and the next request opens a new one, which makes Postgres fork a backend process. Under concurrency that is a connection storm. Measured with k6 at 50 VUs, 4 CPUs per container, single row reads: Three times the throughput from one number, and note where the cost showed up: as database CPU. Nothing in the application looked wrong, which is why this is the bottleneck people profile around for a week. Bigger is not automatically better. The total across processes is what the server sees: every replica opens a pool, and Sentinel opens a second one in each, all against max_connections , which is 100 on a default Postgres. Size it as (max_connections - reserve) / replicas - SENTINEL_DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS . The defaults, 25 and 5, are that sum for three replicas with ten left over for migrations and psql. One query for the list, then one per row for a relation. At a request a second it is invisible. At 100 virtual users it is the whole problem, because a 20 item page is 21 round trips and every one of them holds a connection from the pool above. You do not have to spot these by reading. Pulse counts queries per request and flags the pattern, which is the difference between knowing a route is slow and knowing it issued 43 queries. Two different faults that look the same in a graph. A cold cache gives you a slow first minute and a fast rest of the run, which is why the ramp stage is excluded from the baseline. A missing cache gives you a flat, uniformly mediocre line that never improves. The one to watch for is the cache that is evicted under load. If the working set no longer fits, the hit rate falls exactly when traffic rises, and latency goes up faster than load does. The signature is a p95 that climbs non linearly with virtual users. Go's collector is concurrent, and pauses are typically well under a millisecond. They are worth suspecting only when p99 is bad while p50 is fine and allocation rate is high: a handler allocating a large slice per request, JSON encoding a big response, reading a whole file into memory. The fix is almost never tuning GOGC . It is allocating less, and the next course finds out where with a heap profile. The third line is the one people skip. Latency with no CPU anywhere is the system waiting, and waiting does not show up in a CPU profile at all. One. Run the average load test against a list endpoint with a relation and watch Pulse's queries per request for that route. Two. Set DB_MAX_IDLE_CONNS=2 in .env , restart, and run the same test. Compare throughput and database CPU. Three. Put it back. Then classify your own system against the four line list above. In step two, watch where the cost lands. The interesting part is not that it got slower, it is which process got busier. Step one usually produces a bigger number than people expect the first time they look. A query count of 21 on a 20 row page is the classic, and Preload takes it to 2. Step two reproduces the measurement above: throughput falls, and database CPU rises while the API gets less busy. That is the signature worth memorising, because every instinct says to look at the application and the application is not the problem.
pages.title: One: the connection pool, and the surprise in it

headings: Same test, same data, same machine
k6 says what moved. Pulse says why
Write the result down, including the failures
pages.text: Finding the bottleneck is the easy half. The hard half is the discipline after it: one change, re-measured the same way, kept or reverted on the number rather than on how clever it felt. Step three is where most performance work goes wrong. Two changes at once gives you one number and no attribution, and the usual outcome is that both get kept: the one that helped, and the one that made things slightly worse and is now load bearing for no reason. A comparison is only a comparison if everything else held still. The things that move without anybody deciding to move them: The data. A load test writes rows. The second run starts with a bigger table than the first, so a "15% regression" can be nothing but the table growing. Reset the database between runs, or use read only journeys for comparisons. The machine. A laptop that was idle for run one and compiling for run two produces a number about the compiler. Close the other work, and watch the load generator's own CPU. The stage. Comparing a p95 over the whole run against a p95 over the hold is comparing two different questions. Pick one and write it down. Warmth. First run after a restart has cold caches and an empty pool. Discard it, or always discard it, but be consistent. Run the before measurement twice before you change anything. The gap between those two runs is your noise floor, and no improvement smaller than that gap is an improvement. People skip this and then celebrate 4% on a benchmark that varies by 9%. k6 is outside the process. It can tell you p95 went from 40ms to 310ms, and it has no way to tell you which function those 310ms were in. Pulse is inside the process, and the two are meant to be read together. That is grit generate perf , which writes a k6 script that calls Pulse at the start and end of the run. Three things come out of it that k6 cannot measure: Traffic per route before, during and after, from the API's own rollups rather than from k6's view of its own requests. Queries per request, and N+1 findings, in each window. An N+1 that is invisible at one request a second is exactly what falls over at 500 VUs. A CPU profile captured over the run, so you get the flame graph of the slow window rather than of an idle process afterwards. The second entry is the one worth keeping. A change that did nothing is a fact about your system, and without the note somebody tries it again in three months, including you. One. Run the average load test twice without changing anything. The difference between the two p95s is your noise floor. Write it down. Two. Make one change you believe will help, from last lesson's shortlist. Re-run. Record whether the change is larger than the noise floor. Three. Revert it and run again. Confirm the number goes back. Step three is the one everybody skips and the only one that proves causation. If the number does not return, something else changed between your runs and step two proved nothing. Noise floors on a laptop are commonly 5 to 15% and on a quiet CI runner 2 to 5%. Knowing yours converts "it feels faster" into a decision rule you can apply in ten seconds. If step three does not restore the original number, the honest conclusion is that the experiment was invalid, not that the revert was also an improvement. Reset the data, close the other work and start again.
pages.title: The loop

headings: Failed is not the same as wrong
Throughput, and why it is a result and not a target
pages.text: k6 prints about twenty numbers at the end of a run. Four of them answer questions you have, and the rest are context. This lesson is the four, and the one number everybody quotes that should be ignored. iteration_duration catches people out: it includes the think time in the journey, so it is about 2 seconds whatever your API does. It measures the script, not the system. The number that measures the system is http_req_duration . The average is the one number almost every report leads with, and it is the least informative thing in the summary. An average of 50ms is consistent with every request taking 50ms, and equally consistent with 95% taking 10ms and 5% taking a second. p50, the median. The typical experience. Useful for "did my change make the common case faster", and useless for finding problems, because problems are not typical. p95. The usual SLO number. One request in twenty is worse than this. On a page that makes ten API calls, p95 per request means roughly half of page loads contain at least one slow call, which is why p95 matters more than it sounds. p99. Where the pathologies live: GC pauses, cache misses, lock contention, a connection being opened. It is also the noisiest, and it needs volume. At 60 requests, p99 is one request and tells you nothing. At 60,000 it is the most interesting line in the summary. Never average percentiles, and never compare a p95 computed over a whole run against one computed over a steady state. Both are arithmetic that looks reasonable and produces a number that describes nothing. Report the percentile from the hold stage, and say which stage it came from. http_req_failed counts responses that were not 2xx or 3xx. checks counts your own assertions. They answer different questions, and a gap between them is informative: The third line is the one worth having checks for. An endpoint that returns 200 with an empty list because a query timed out and the error was swallowed is invisible to http_req_failed and completely visible to a check that asserts the shape of the body. Which is why the check has to be specific. The suite Grit shipped until v3.432.0 checked r.body && r.body.length > 0 , which an error envelope passes. It reported a successful check on a 500 for months. The replacement asserts Array.isArray(r.json('data')) . http_reqs per second is a function of your virtual user count and your think time, not of how fast the system is. A hundred VUs with a 1 to 3 second sleep produce about 50 requests a second whatever your API does, until the API becomes slow enough to be the limiting factor. Throughput only becomes a measurement of the system at the point where latency starts rising, and that point is what the breakpoint test finds. One. Run the average load test and record avg, p50, p95 and p99 for http_req_duration . Two. Work out the ratio p99 divided by p50. Write it down. Three. Add a deliberate stall to one handler, time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond) behind a 1 in 20 condition. Re-run and recompute the ratio. Watch what the average does in step three compared with what p95 does. One of them notices. A p99 to p50 ratio under about 3 is a system doing the same amount of work for every request. Above 10 there is a second population in there: a cache that misses sometimes, a code path taken occasionally, a lock. In step three the average moves by roughly 25ms, which looks like noise and would survive any review. p95 moves to over 500ms, because one request in twenty is exactly what p95 measures. That is the entire argument for percentiles in one experiment.
pages.title: The summary, annotated

headings: VUs vs. iterations , the mental model
Adding auth , a more realistic test
pages.text: Time to write a real k6 test. We'll hit your local Grit API's /api/health endpoint with 10 virtual users for 30 seconds, then read the output. Write it to tests/k6/hello.js . Grit already scaffolds a six test suite into that directory, and the next chapter is about those; this one is a scratch file so you can see every part of a k6 script in one screen before reading somebody else's. Three sections, each non-negotiable: options , how many VUs, for how long, with what thresholds. The default function , what each VU does repeatedly until time runs out. check , assertions on the response. Failed checks count toward checks metric. Four metrics matter on a smoke test: checks , 100% means every response was healthy. http_req_duration , latency. The p(95) tells you the 95th-percentile latency , the bar most teams set SLOs against. http_req_failed , error rate. Anything > 0% on a healthy smoke test is a red flag. http_reqs , total + rate. Useful for capacity planning. At the bottom of the output: ✓ means the threshold held. ✗ means a breach , and k6 exits with non-zero status. That's how CI knows your PR regressed the API. VUs are virtual users , independent loops running your default function. With 10 VUs, ten copies of the function are running concurrently. Each VU loops until the duration ends. An iteration is one trip through the default function. With sleep(1) and a 30s duration, each VU does about 30 iterations, so 10 VUs × 30 iterations = ~300 total. That lines up with what we saw above. setup() runs once before VUs start; its return value is passed to every iteration as data . Use it for: log in once, share the token; create a fixture user, share the ID. Smoke-test your real API: Save the smoke.js script from this lesson. Boot your local API: cd apps/api && go run cmd/server/main.go . Run k6: k6 run tests/k6/hello.js . Capture the p(95) for http_req_duration. Paste in notes.md . Now write a SECOND script for /api/profile (requires auth). Use the setup pattern from this lesson. Run it. Compare p(95) to the smoke test. You should see /api/health at single-digit ms and the authed endpoint higher, because it runs the auth middleware and reads a row. That delta is the cost of auth plus a database call, and it is worth knowing before you go looking for it somewhere else. Chapter 2, the test types . Grit scaffolds six of them into tests/k6/ : smoke, average load, stress, spike, soak and breakpoint, each with the thresholds that suit it.
pages.title: The script

headings: Docker , if you don't want to install
The k6 binary on its own
pages.text: k6 is a single Go binary. No Node. No Python. No dependencies. Three install methods covered here , pick the one that matches your OS. The -i pipes your local script into the container. Useful in CI; clunky in dev. Native install is usually nicer. Any 0.50+ works. Most APIs in this course assume features from 0.49 or later. k6 has no UI. It's pure CLI. You write a JavaScript file (k6 has its own JS runtime, NOT Node), then run k6 run script.js . Output goes to your terminal. That's the entire mental model. Tests live with code. Same repo, version-controlled. Anyone can run them. Confirm installation: Install k6 via the method for your OS. Run k6 version and capture the output. Make a folder tests/k6/ in your Grit project , we'll put real scripts there next lesson. Paste the version output into notes.md . That's it. Next lesson we'll write a 20-line script that hits your local API. Next , Your first k6 script . A real test against your running Grit API.
pages.title: macOS , Homebrew

pages.text: Load testing means deliberately hammering your API to find out what happens when traffic spikes. Most teams discover their bottleneck on launch day from a screaming Slack channel. This course is the alternative: find it on Tuesday afternoon, with coffee, and fix it. How many concurrent users can my API handle? 50? 5000? You should be able to answer this with a number. Where does it break? DB CPU, connection pool, app CPU, memory, downstream service? What does the user experience look like under load? p95 = 200ms? 2s? 20s? The difference matters. Does my change make things WORSE? Run before + after; the numbers tell you. Smoke : 2 VUs for 30 seconds. "Does this basically work, and is my script right?" Run on every PR, and run it before every other type. Average load : ramp to 100 VUs, hold 5 minutes. "Does it hold up at planned scale?" This is the baseline every other run is compared against. Stress : 4x normal, held. "How does it behave past its limits: gracefully, or not?" Spike : 50 to 1000 VUs in ten seconds. "Does a marketing email crash us, and does p95 come back afterwards?" Soak : 100 VUs for four hours. "Do we leak memory or connections over time?" Breakpoint : a slow climb that aborts on the first breached threshold. "What is our actual capacity number?" Load testing has a cost: time to write, infrastructure to run, signal to interpret. Skip it if: You have <100 daily active users. Your DB isn't the bottleneck , feature velocity is. Build first. You haven't shipped anything. "What if a million users come?" is a great problem to have later. Don't pre-optimise. The endpoint is rarely called. A quarterly-reporting endpoint doesn't need to handle 1000 rps. Test the hot paths, ignore the cold ones. A k6 suite in tests/k6/ with one script per scenario type. Thresholds that fail the build on regression. A workflow that runs k6 on every PR via GitHub Actions. One real measured optimisation against your own API. Most performance work is vibes-based: "feels faster", "should be quicker". Load testing is the discipline of replacing vibes with numbers. You make a change, you run the test, the number went down , or it didn't. The graph is brutal honest. That's the whole point. Next lesson , Install k6 . One binary, no Node, no deps. We'll have you running a test by the end of the next 3 minutes.
pages.title: What load testing answers

headings: What a passing smoke run looks like
Point it at something that costs money
pages.text: Grit scaffolds six load tests into tests/k6/ . They all run the same user journey from lib/common.js and differ only in their stages, which is the shape of the load over time. This lesson is the first two, and they are the two you will actually run most weeks. Two virtual users for thirty seconds. That is not a load test, and it is not meant to be: Run it before every other type. A stress test that fails tells you nothing until you know the script itself works, because the two look identical from the outside: requests failing, thresholds breached, a red summary. Smoke separates "the system broke" from "my test was never right". This is not hypothetical. The suite Grit shipped until v3.432.0 asked for /health , a path no Grit API has ever served, and /api/blogs , which only a project with a Blog resource serves. Every request 404d, every threshold breached, and all six tests reported a broken system before measuring anything about it. Nobody noticed, because nobody ran smoke first and asked why a two user test was failing. Two numbers are worth noting now. 62 requests, not 60: the two extra are the sign-in in setup() , which runs once and is not part of any iteration. And p99 is twenty times p95 on a run this small, because one request was the first to touch a cold code path. At 60 requests, p99 is a single request. It becomes a number worth reading at thousands. The hold is the point. A ramp measures a system that is still filling its connection pool, warming its caches and compiling nothing in particular; the five minutes at a hundred users is the only part that describes normal operation. Report p95 from the hold, not from the whole run. The thresholds are the same ones smoke uses, and they are what turns this into a regression check rather than a number you write down: A breached threshold makes k6 exit non-zero, which is the whole reason these two tests belong in CI and the other four do not. The journey reads /api/health and /api/profile . Both are cheap, and a journey made of cheap requests reports a system faster than yours is. Name one of your own resources: A resource generated by grit generate resource needs ADMIN or its own permission. The throwaway user the journey registers is a USER, so without LOADTEST_EMAIL you get a run of 403s: fast, consistent and completely meaningless. One. Run k6 run tests/k6/smoke.js against your local API. Write down p95 and the request count. Two. Run it again with -e RESOURCE= set to one of your resources. Write down p95 again. Three. Run the average load test. Compare its p95 to the smoke run's, and account for the difference. Between steps two and three the only thing that changed is how many users are doing it at once. Anything the difference cannot be explained by concurrency is worth a second look. Step two is almost always slower than step one, by more than people expect: a list endpoint is a query plus serialisation plus whatever your handler does, where health is a map lookup. That delta is the cost of the work, and it is the number worth tracking. Step three should be slower again, but not proportionally. If p95 at 100 users is roughly p95 at 2 users, you have headroom. If it is twenty times worse, you have found something to profile, and the next chapter is about which something.
pages.title: Smoke: does the test work?

headings: Soak: a hundred users for four hours
pages.text: Every test so far finishes in under ten minutes, and there is a whole category of fault that ten minutes cannot see. A goroutine that leaks one per request, a slice that is appended to and never reset, a connection that is opened and not returned: at ten minutes they are invisible, and at four hours they are the outage. The load is deliberately ordinary. A soak test is not about pressure, it is about duration: the same hundred users doing the same thing for long enough that anything accumulating has time to accumulate. Run it overnight, or on a CI runner, before a release that matters. The tilt is the whole finding. Any single ten minute window inside that graph looks healthy, and that is exactly why the leak reached production: it passed every test anyone was willing to wait for. Open /pulse/ui/ in another tab for the duration. k6 tells you latency drifted. Pulse tells you heap in use climbed with it, or that goroutine count never came back down, which is the difference between knowing something is wrong and knowing what. Goroutines. The common shape is a goroutine waiting on a channel nobody will write to again, one per request. It costs a few kilobytes each, which is nothing until it is four hours of traffic. Database connections. Rows that are never closed, or a transaction that neither commits nor rolls back on an error path. The pool fills, and the symptom is latency, because every request is now waiting for a connection. Caches with no bound. A map keyed by something unbounded, such as a user id or a URL, with no eviction. It is not a leak in the strict sense; it behaves exactly like one. Nothing at all. Latency that drifts upward with a flat heap is usually the database: a table growing through the run, an index no longer fitting in cache, autovacuum falling behind. The suite has one more script, and it answers a question the other five do not: not "does it hold at 400" but "at what number does it stop holding". abortOnFail is what makes this different from a stress test. The run stops at the first breach, and the virtual user count at that moment is your capacity number: the one to put in a launch plan, divide by your expected concurrency, and use to decide how many replicas to pay for. One. Start the soak test with -e RESOURCE= set, and note p95 at the fifteen minute mark. Two. Leave it running and check p95 every thirty minutes. Four hours is the script's default; one hour is enough to see a tilt if there is one. Three. Separately, run the breakpoint test and record the VU count at the abort. Divide by your expected peak concurrency and write down the headroom. For step two, compare each reading against the fifteen minute one rather than against the previous reading. A drift of a few percent per half hour is invisible step by step and obvious end to end. A flat line over an hour is a real result: write it down, since the value of a soak test is mostly in the runs that find nothing. A line that has climbed 20% by the end is a leak, and Pulse's heap and goroutine graphs over the same window narrow it to one of the four causes above in a minute. The breakpoint number is the one to be careful with. It is capacity for this journey on this hardware with this data volume. It is not a property of your application, and it moves when any of those three do.
pages.title: Soak: a hundred users for four hours

headings: The thing you are actually looking for
Spike: the surge, and the recovery
pages.text: Smoke and average load ask whether the system works. Stress and spike ask what it does when it stops working, which is a different question and usually a more useful one, because every system stops working eventually and only some of them do it gracefully. Four times is a convention, not a law. Pick the multiple that represents your worst realistic day: the Monday after a launch, the hour after an email goes out, Black Friday. The two minutes at normal load first are there so you have a before to compare against, in the same run and on the same machine. A stress test is supposed to hurt. With the normal thresholds it would breach in the first thirty seconds and the run would report failure, which tells you only what you already intended. The looser set lets the run finish so you can watch how it degrades. Rising latency with a flat error rate is a queue doing its job: requests wait, and they are served. Rising latency and rising errors means something is giving up: a connection pool timeout, a context deadline, an out of memory kill. The second is the one that wakes you up, and it is invisible in any single number. Watch the API's own memory and the database's CPU during the run, not just k6's output. A system that collapses at 4x almost never does so because of the API process: it runs out of database connections, or the database runs out of CPU. Most people read this script as the 10 second ramp to a thousand users. The important stage is the last minute, back at fifty. A system that survives a spike and returns to its baseline latency has absorbed it. A system whose p95 is still elevated a minute after the surge has not: something is still draining. A retry storm, a queue that filled and is being worked off, a cache that was evicted and is being rebuilt one request at a time. That is the finding, and it only exists in the recovery window. A thousand virtual users from one laptop is usually a test of your laptop. If CPU on the k6 machine saturates, every number it reports includes its own queueing. Watch the load generator as carefully as the system under test, and move k6 to a bigger box before concluding anything about the system. One. Run the stress test with -e RESOURCE= set to your heaviest list endpoint. Record p95 at the two minute mark and at the seven minute mark. Two. Record the error rate at the same two points. Classify the system: graceful or collapsing. Three. Run the spike test. Record p95 during the hold, and again in the last thirty seconds of the recovery window. For step three, compare the recovery p95 against the first minute's baseline, not against the spike. The question is whether it came back, not whether it was bad while the spike was on. Step two is the classification that matters. Latency up, errors flat is a system under pressure and working. Latency up, errors up is a system failing, and the error response tells you where: a 503 from your own middleware, a 500 from a pool timeout and a connection reset are three different problems. In step three, a recovery p95 within noise of the baseline means the spike cost you nothing after it ended. Anything elevated by more than about 20% a minute later is a system still working something off, and the next chapter is how to find out what.
pages.title: Stress: four times normal, held

headings: Build a Fitness App: Go API + Expo React Native
pages.text: Build a fitness tracking app with a Go backend and Expo React Native frontend. You ll design a data model for workouts and exercises, generate API resources, build mobile screens with React Native, and create a workout logger you can use on your actual phone. Reference docs: Mobile Apps → We re building a fitness tracking app , the kind of app people actually use every day. The Go API stores all the data (exercises, workouts, sets, reps, weight). The Expo app runs on your phone and lets you log workouts, browse exercises, and view your history. The app has 4 core screens: • Exercise Library , browse all exercises grouped by muscle group (chest, back, legs, shoulders, arms) • Workout Logger , create a workout, add exercises, log sets/reps/weight in real-time • Workout History , see past workouts with total volume and duration • Dashboard , weekly summary, workout streak, total volume lifted On paper or a whiteboard, sketch 4 screens for a fitness app: Exercise Library, Workout Logger, Workout History, and Dashboard. For each screen, write down what data it needs to display. What actions can the user take on each screen? Grit s --mobile flag scaffolds a monorepo with a Go API and an Expo React Native app: This creates a monorepo with three parts: The key difference from a web project: instead of apps/web (Next.js), you get apps/expo (Expo React Native). The Go API is identical , the mobile app consumes the same REST endpoints. Run grit new fitness --mobile . Open the project in your editor. Compare the folder structure to a web project ( grit new myapp ). What s the same? What s different? How many files are in apps/expo/ ? Before writing code, let s design the data model. A fitness app needs three core entities: Our three resources: The relationship is: a Workout contains many WorkoutExercises , and each WorkoutExercise references an Exercise . This is a classic many-to-many relationship through a join table (WorkoutExercise). After generating, restart the API. GORM will auto-migrate the new tables. Generate all 3 resources using the commands above. Restart the API. Open GORM Studio at /studio and verify that the exercises , workouts , and workout_exercises tables exist. How many columns does the workout_exercises table have? An empty exercise library is useless. Let s populate it with real exercises. You can do this through GORM Studio s inline editing or through the API. Here are the exercises to create, organized by muscle group: Create at least 10 exercises across 4 different muscle groups (Chest, Back, Legs, Shoulders). Use the API docs or GORM Studio. After creating them, call GET /api/exercises and verify all 10 are returned. Try filtering with ?muscle_group=Chest , does it work? With the API running and seed data loaded, it s time to start the Expo mobile app. You ll need two terminals , one for the API and one for Expo. Expo will show a QR code in the terminal. To open the app on your phone: • iPhone , install Expo Go from the App Store, scan the QR code with your camera • Android , install Expo Go from Google Play, scan the QR code from the Expo Go app • Emulator , press i for iOS Simulator or a for Android Emulator Start both the API and Expo. Open the app on your phone or emulator. You should see the default Grit mobile app with login/register screens. Register a user, log in, and confirm you see the main app screen. Is the API responding to requests from the mobile app? The exercise list is the first screen users see. It fetches exercises from the API and displays them in a scrollable list, grouped by muscle group. Here s how to fetch and display exercises: The pattern is straightforward: useQuery fetches the data, we group it by muscle group using reduce , and FlatList renders each group with its exercises. Create the exercise list screen. Display exercises grouped by muscle group. Each exercise should show its name and description. Verify that all the exercises you seeded appear. How many muscle groups are displayed? The workout logger is the core feature of the app. Users create a workout, add exercises to it, and log sets with reps and weight for each exercise. This involves creating a Workout record and then creating WorkoutExercise records linked to it. The flow is: The workout form combines API calls with local state. The workout itself is created on the server first (so we get an ID), then each exercise entry is posted as the user logs it: Build the workout logger screen. Create a workout called Push Day. Add 4 exercises (e.g., Bench Press, Incline Dumbbell Press, Cable Fly, Overhead Press). For each exercise, log sets, reps, and weight. When you re done, verify the data exists in the API by calling GET /api/workout-exercises?workout_id=1 . The history screen shows all past workouts with summary data: name, date, duration, and total volume. Volume is the key metric in fitness tracking , it s the total weight lifted in a workout. The calculateVolume function sums sets * reps * weight for every exercise in the workout. This gives users a clear, numeric measure of how hard they trained. Create the history screen. Log at least 5 workouts over a week (you can backdate them by setting different dates in the API). Display them in reverse chronological order (newest first). Each entry should show: workout name, date, duration, number of exercises, and total volume. Which workout had the highest volume? Mobile users expect to pull down on a list to refresh it. This is a standard mobile pattern that React Native supports natively through the RefreshControl component. TanStack Query makes this trivial. The refetch function triggers a fresh API call, and isRefetching tracks whether the refetch is in progress. Wire these into RefreshControl and you re done. Add RefreshControl to both the Exercise List and Workout History screens. Pull down on each list , does the spinner appear? Does the data reload? Test it by adding a new exercise through the API docs and pulling to refresh on t
