Result stored in database: $2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy Open the auth service code in your project. Find where bcrypt hashes the password during registration and where it compares during login. What cost factor is used? What would happen if you changed it to 14? (Hint: each increment doubles the time.) After verifying a password, Grit issues two tokens: an access token (short-lived, 15 minutes) and a refresh token (long-lived, 7 days). This dual-token approach limits the damage if a token is stolen. Why two tokens? If an access token is intercepted by an attacker, it only works for 15 minutes. The refresh token is stored in an HTTP-only cookie (inaccessible to JavaScript), so XSS attacks cannot steal it. When the access token expires, the frontend silently uses the refresh token to get a new one. The auth middleware runs on every protected route. It extracts the JWT from the Authorization header, verifies the signature, checks the expiration, and attaches the user information to the request context. Login to your Grit API and copy the access token. Go to jwt.io and paste it. What information is in the payload? What algorithm is used for signing? What is the expiration time (exp claim)? Authentication answers who are you? Authorization answers what are you allowed to do? Grit uses role-based access control (RBAC) with three built-in roles: The RequireRole middleware enforces access control at the route level: Log in as a user with the USER role. Try to access an ADMIN-only endpoint like GET /api/admin/users . What HTTP status code do you get? What does the error message say? Now log in as an ADMIN and try the same endpoint. Passwords can be stolen through phishing, keyloggers, or data breaches. Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second layer: something you know (password) plus something you have (your phone). Even if an attacker has your password, they cannot log in without your phone. The 2FA setup flow in Grit: 1. Generate secret. The API creates a random TOTP secret and returns it as a QR code URL. 2. Scan QR code. The user scans the QR code with their authenticator app, which stores the secret. 3. Verify code. The user enters the current 6-digit code from their app to prove it s working. 4. 2FA enabled. The secret is saved to the database. Future logins require both password and TOTP code. Enable two-factor authentication on your account using Google Authenticator, Authy, or any TOTP-compatible app. Follow the setup flow: generate the secret, scan the QR code, enter the verification code. Then log out and log back in , you should be prompted for a 6-digit code. What happens if you lose your phone? Without backup codes, you re locked out of your account forever. Grit generates 10 one-time backup codes when 2FA is enabled. Each code can be used exactly once as a substitute for the TOTP code. Backup codes are: • 10 codes generated when 2FA is enabled • One-time use , each code is invalidated after use • bcrypt-hashed in the database , if the database is compromised, the raw codes are not exposed • Shown once , the user sees the plain text codes only at generation time and must save them With 2FA enabled, use a backup code to log in instead of your authenticator app. Then try the same backup code again. What happens? How many backup codes do you have remaining? Entering a 2FA code every time you log in on the same computer gets annoying fast. Trusted devices solve this: after you verify 2FA once, the server sets a 30-day cookie on your browser. On subsequent logins from that device, the 2FA step is skipped. The trusted device cookie is: • Secure , only sent over HTTPS (in production) • HTTP-only , JavaScript cannot read it (XSS protection) • 30-day expiry , after 30 days, you ll need to enter a 2FA code again • Per-device , trusting you
pages.title: Security Deep Dive: Auth, 2FA, WAF & Rate Limiting

headings: Permissions: the catalogue, not a string
Policies: the rule that needs the row
The ceiling: the one people forget
pages.text: The last lesson fixed one IDOR by hand. Doing that in every handler is how the second one gets forgotten, so Grit puts the answer in one package: internal/authz . This lesson is a tour of what is in it and, more usefully, which of the four questions each part answers. Most arguments about access control are really people answering different questions with the same word. Separate them and the package stops looking like a grab bag: May this user touch widgets at all? That is a permission , it comes from the route's middleware, and it never looks at a row. Is this their row? That is ownership , and it is a column. Is this row in a state where that is allowed? A draft may be edited and a published post may not. That is a policy , and it needs the row and the user together. Can this admin grant a permission they do not hold? That is the ceiling , and forgetting it is how a junior admin promotes themselves. A rule that cannot be expressed as one of those four is usually two rules wearing a coat. Split it before you write it. The ownership helpers load the row and check the owner in one call. Note the status code: MustOwn answers a failure with 404, not 403 . That is deliberate, and it is the part people change back without thinking. A 403 says "this row exists and is not yours", which is a yes/no oracle: an attacker walks the id space and learns exactly which records exist before they ever break in. A 404 says nothing. Same code, same user experience for the legitimate caller, and no free map of your database. The variants exist because admin screens call the same endpoints: MustOwn , strict ownership. MustOwnUnlessAdmin , the same check with an ADMIN bypass. Without it an administrator opening the admin panel sees only the rows they personally created, which reads as a bug and gets fixed by removing the check entirely. ScopeOwned(ctx, query, column) , for lists. It adds the owner filter to a query rather than checking one row. ScopeOwned returns q.Where(...) , a statement clause. That matters: a clause is carried into Find , Scan and Rows alike. Scoping implemented as a GORM callback instead is easy to get wrong, because Scan does not go through the query callback. Permissions are generated into a catalogue rather than typed as strings at each call site, because a typo in a permission string fails open: Can(db, user, "psots.delete") is simply false for everyone, including the people who should be denied loudly. Neither a permission nor an owner column can say "a post may be edited while it is a draft and not after it is published". That is a policy: a named ability with a rule that receives the actor and the record. Then authz.Allows(ctx, "post.edit", &post) at the call site, or Inspect when you want the reason to put in the response. The reason is worth having: "forbidden" teaches a user nothing, and "a published post is not editable" stops a support ticket. An admin screen that lets somebody assign permissions must stop them assigning permissions they do not themselves hold. Otherwise the lowest-privileged admin account is a route to the highest, in two clicks and with a full audit trail showing it was allowed. Privilege escalation almost never looks like an attack in the logs. It looks like an administrator using an administration screen exactly as designed, which is why the check has to be in the code rather than in the reviewer's head. Take one endpoint in your project that lists rows and one that updates a single row. One. Put ScopeOwned on the list and MustOwn on the update. Two. Sign in as a second user and request the first user's row by id. Write down the status code you get. Three. Change MustOwn to return 403 instead, repeat, and explain in one sentence what an attacker now learns that they did not before. For step three, think about what you can discover by trying ids you have no access to, without ever succeeding at anything. Step two gives 404 . Step three gives 403 , and the difference is an existence oracle: 403 means the row is there, 404 means it may or may not be. Walking the id space against a 403 produces a list of every record in the table, which is useful on its own and is the reconnaissance for the next attack. Put it back to 404.
pages.title: Authorization is four different questions

headings: The pattern for ALL access control
Defense in depth , the SQL filter
pages.text: IDOR , Insecure Direct Object Reference , is the most common security bug in shipped APIs. It's also the easiest to fix. This lesson: how it happens, how to exploit it on your own endpoint, then ship the fix in three lines. Three problems in this code: The handler reads c.Param("id") without scoping by the authed user. The handler updates the row whose id matches the URL, regardless of ownership. The handler doesn't even check whether the row exists before updating. Five steps. Two minutes. B never had access to A's account but rewrote their data. This is IDOR. Three lines of fix: Load the note first. Compare note.UserID to the authed user. Return ErrForbidden if they don't match. Re-run the exploit , B gets 403. A still gets 200. Vulnerability closed. Load the resource by ID. Check authorisation. Compare owner/tenant/role to the authed actor. Act if allowed. Update / delete / return. Every CRUD endpoint that operates on a single resource follows this. Memorise it. grit generate resource emits this pattern by default , the bug only appears when humans write handlers and forget step 2. Belt-and-suspenders: scope the QUERY ITSELF by user_id, not just check after loading: Now even if the post-load check is removed by a future refactor, the query can't return another user's note. Two layers; both should fail to leak data. Now if a future refactor accidentally removes the check, this test fails and CI blocks the merge. Find and fix an IDOR in your own code: Search your handlers for any c.Param("id") that's used in a DB query without a corresponding user_id check. Pick one and write the exploit as curl commands (like this lesson's). Confirm you can read or modify another user's data. Move the DB call into the service (if not already there). Add the ownership check. Re-run the exploit. Should now return 403. Write a unit test that fails if the check is removed. Commit the fix + test in one commit. Reference the threat from SECURITY.md. You've eliminated the most common API vulnerability from at least one endpoint. Now do every other endpoint with the same pattern. This is what mature teams call "authz hardening" and it's 80% of the work. Next lesson , The authz package . Grit ships an internal/authz helper that centralises this pattern so you write it once, apply it everywhere.
pages.title: The attack, in one diagram

headings: The access token cannot be revoked, so make it short
alg: none, and why the key is named
pages.text: JWTs are easy to issue and hard to take back. Most of the trouble comes from that one sentence. This lesson covers the mistakes that show up in real audits, and what Grit already does about each. It is signed. Anyone holding one can read every claim in it, because the payload is base64, not ciphertext. Paste one into any decoder and it reads back in full. So a claim is public. An email address in a token is an email address in the browser's storage, in your logs, and in every proxy the request passed through. Put an id in and look the rest up. Signature verification is the whole check. The server does not ask a database whether the token is still good, which is exactly why JWTs scale and exactly why "log this user out everywhere" does not work on its own. A stolen access token is valid until it expires, and nothing you do in the meantime changes that. The answer is not a longer-lived token with a revocation list, which is a session with extra steps. It is a short access token and a refresh token that is backed by a row: Two decisions worth copying even outside Grit: Only the hash is stored. Somebody who reads the sessions table gets 64 hex characters, not a key to the account. The previous hash is kept on purpose. A refresh token is used once and replaced. If the old one turns up again, two parties hold it, which means it was stolen. The right response is to end the session, not to issue a fresh token to whoever asked last. That is the difference between detecting theft and merely surviving it. Rotation alone means the thief and the user take turns. Replay detection means the second use gives the theft away. If JavaScript can read it, any script on the page can take it, and that includes whatever arrives through a dependency you did not audit. Grit puts tokens in HttpOnly cookies, so there is no Authorization header and nothing for a script to steal. That choice buys an XSS defence and brings a CSRF obligation with it: a cookie is sent automatically, including on a request another site made. That is the next lesson, and it is why middleware.CSRF() exists. The original JWT disaster was libraries that trusted the alg header. Send alg: none , drop the signature, and a naive verifier accepts it. Modern libraries refuse, but the lesson underneath still applies: never let the token decide how it is verified . Grit decides from configuration rather than from the token. HS256 on the shared secret by default, RS256 when a private key is configured, with the public half derived from the private key rather than configured separately, so the two cannot disagree. Tokens name their key so a rotation can verify the previous one while new tokens are signed with the current. On HS256 the signing key and the verifying key are the same string. Anything that can verify a token can mint one. If a second service needs to verify your tokens, that is the argument for RS256, where it gets the public half only. One. Sign in to your project and copy the access token out of the cookie jar. Decode the payload with base64 -d . Write down every field in it and ask of each one: would I publish this? Two. Refresh the session, then replay the old refresh token. Record the status and what happened to the session. Three. In one sentence, say why answering that replay with a fresh token would be worse than failing. For step three: if two parties hold the same refresh token, what does handing out a new one to the one that asked accomplish? The payload decodes without a key, which is the point of step one: anything in there is effectively public. The replay fails and the whole session is revoked, so the real user is signed out too. That is the correct outcome. A used refresh token presented a second time means two parties have it, and there is no way to tell from the request which one is the thief. Issuing a fresh token would hand the session to whoever asked last and leave the theft undetected. Ending it costs one sign-in and closes the hole.
pages.title: A JWT is not encrypted

headings: What a good secret looks like
pages.text: Secrets leak through boring routes. Not clever attacks: a committed .env , a stack trace in a log aggregator, a database backup on a laptop. This lesson is about the boring routes, because that is where they actually go. Grit gitignores .env and ships .env.example with the shape and no values. Every generated secret, including the Studio password and the dashboard credentials, is produced per scaffold rather than shared, so two projects never have the same one. The thing worth internalising: a commit cannot be taken back. Removing a secret in a later commit leaves it in the history, and on any fork, clone or CI cache that pulled before you noticed. The only correct response to a committed credential is to rotate it. Cleaning the history is tidying, not remediation. If you are deciding whether a leak was "really exposed", you have already spent longer than rotating it would have taken. Rotate first and investigate afterwards. Logs travel. They go to a file, an aggregator, a vendor, a laptop during an incident, and they are retained long after the data they describe. Anything printed is effectively published to a wider audience than your database has. %+v on a struct is the common one. It prints whatever fields exist today, including the one somebody adds next year. Log the identifier and the outcome, never the payload. A backup is a copy of your data with weaker access control, kept somewhere else, often for years. Two things in Grit assume that: Passwords are hashed, not encrypted. Different words for different things. Encryption is reversible by design; hashing is not. There is no circumstance in which an application needs to recover a user's password, so it must not be able to. Refresh tokens are stored as SHA-256. The sessions table holds 64 hex characters. Somebody who reads it cannot replay a session. For data you do need back, Grit has field-level encryption: a column marked as encrypted is ciphertext at rest and plaintext in your Go code, so a dump is useless without FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY . The key must not live in the same place as the backup. Encrypting a column and then storing the key in a .env that goes into the same snapshot buys nothing: whoever has one has both. Length matters less than entropy. A long memorable phrase is a password; a signing key wants bytes from a CSPRNG. And a secret that is shared between environments is one secret: staging credentials get copied to laptops, pasted into tickets and reused in demos, so if staging shares production's key then production's key is in a ticket. One. Run git log -p -- .env in your project. If anything comes back, list what would need rotating. Two. Add log.Printf("login: %+v", req) to your login handler, sign in, and read the log line. Three. Remove it and write the version you would actually ship. For step three: what do you need from that line at three in the morning, and what is merely everything the struct happened to hold? Step two prints the password in plaintext, to wherever your logs go. That is the entire point of the exercise: it took one plausible line, and nobody reviewing it would call it a security change. The shippable version logs the outcome and an identifier, with no payload: Enough to find the user and understand the failure, with nothing in it you would mind a vendor retaining for a year.
pages.title: Three questions, in order

headings: A log an attacker can edit is not evidence
Reads are the half people forget
pages.text: Every other lesson in this course tries to stop something. This one assumes it already happened. The question an audit log answers is the one you cannot answer from your application database: what did they do while they were in? An ordinary table will not do. Somebody with database access can delete the row that records what they did, and nothing about the table will look wrong afterwards: no gap, no error, just a shorter list. Grit chains the entries. Each one's hash includes the hash before it, so an entry cannot be changed or removed without breaking every hash after it: This is tamper evidence , not tamper prevention. Somebody with write access can still rewrite the whole chain from the point they touched. What they cannot do is change one entry quietly, and that is the difference between a log that is worth reading after an incident and one that is not. Shipping the chain to somewhere the application cannot write, even a nightly copy, turns evidence into prevention. The attacker would have to reach two systems instead of one. Writes get logged because they change something. The question after a breach is almost always about reads: not "what did they edit" but "what did they see ". Without read entries the honest answer is "we cannot tell", and under most breach-notification rules that means assuming the worst about every record they could have reached. Grit generates this for a resource created with --audit-reads . Turning it on for everything would be expensive and useless: a read entry per page view on a public catalog is noise that buries the entry you needed. Decide per resource, and the rule of thumb is whether you would have to notify somebody if the data leaked. What does not go in: the values themselves. An audit log holding copies of the records is a second database with the same sensitivity and usually weaker access control, which makes the log the easier target. Record that the row was read and let the reader go and look at the row. One. Generate a resource with --audit-reads , create a few rows, and read one through the API. Find the entry. Two. Edit one earlier entry directly in the database: change a single character of its payload. Run the chain verification. Three. Now delete that entry entirely and verify again. Write down which entry the failure points at, and why it is not the one you deleted. Each entry's hash is computed from the one before it. Which entry is the first whose stored hash stops matching a recomputation? Both the edit and the deletion are caught, and in both cases the failure is reported at the entry after the one you touched: that is the first whose stored hash no longer matches what recomputing from its predecessor gives. So the break tells you where the tampering happened, not what was in the missing entry. The chain proves the log is not original; it does not recover what was removed. That is the argument for copying the chain somewhere the application cannot write.
pages.title: A log an attacker can edit is not evidence

headings: Why cookies make CSRF your problem
The defence, and why it works
The CORS failure nobody can see
pages.text: CSRF and CORS get discussed together, confused constantly, and solve different problems in opposite directions. Getting them straight is most of the work. The sentence that resolves most confusion: CORS does not stop the request being sent. A cross-site form post reaches your handler whatever your CORS policy says. CORS only governs whether the attacking page is allowed to read the answer , and for a write that does damage, the attacker does not care about the answer. Grit puts tokens in HttpOnly cookies, which removes an XSS risk and creates this one. A cookie is attached by the browser to any request to your domain, including one triggered by a page the user merely visited: No JavaScript of yours runs, no token is stolen, and the browser sends the session cookie because that is what cookies do. If the endpoint acts on it, the account is gone. Grit's middleware.CSRF() sets a grit_csrf cookie on safe requests, and requires unsafe methods to echo it back in an X-CSRF-Token header: The reason this works is worth saying out loud, because it is not that the value is secret. The attacking page can guess, but it cannot read your cookie to copy it into a header, since reading across origins is what the same-origin policy forbids. And a plain HTML form cannot set a custom header at all. So requiring a header that must match a cookie is a requirement only a page on your own origin can satisfy. SameSite=Strict on the cookie is the second layer: the browser declines to send it on a cross-site request in the first place. Two independent mechanisms, because SameSite handling has varied across browsers and is not something to rely on alone. This one costs more hours than the attacks do. A request from an origin outside your allow list gets a preflight with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin , which is the correct answer and a completely invisible one: Moving the admin panel to a different port is enough to produce it. Grit logs a line, once per origin, when it turns one away, which converts a silent dead button into something you can grep for. The fix is CORS_ORIGINS in .env . Never answer with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on an API that uses cookies. The browser refuses to combine the wildcard with credentials, so it will not work, and reaching for it is usually a sign somebody is about to echo back whatever Origin arrived, which is the same as having no policy. One. Save an HTML file to your desktop with a form that POSTs to one of your authenticated endpoints. Open it in the browser where you are signed in and submit it. Two. Note whether the request reached your handler, and what the response was. Three. Now start your web app on a port that is not in CORS_ORIGINS and try to sign in. Watch the network tab, then your API log, and write down what each one tells you. In step three, look for which request is missing from the server side rather than which failed. The form POST arrives , with cookies attached, and is rejected by the CSRF middleware for having no X-CSRF-Token header. The important half is that it arrived: CORS never stopped it, because CORS was never about stopping it. In step three the browser shows a failed preflight and your API log shows the refused-origin line and no handler. That gap, where the client reports failure and the server reports nothing at all, is the signature of a CORS problem, and knowing it saves an afternoon.
pages.title: They point opposite ways

headings: The mistake that makes it do nothing
Development limits, and why they are separate
pages.text: A login endpoint with no rate limit is a password guessing service you host for free. Rate limiting is the cheapest security control there is, and the one most often configured in a way that quietly does nothing. Grit mounts Sentinel with a global per-IP limit and a tighter per-route limit on the endpoints worth attacking: The numbers are not arbitrary. 30 logins in five minutes is more than any human needs and far less than a guessing attack wants. Registration is tighter because the cost of a false negative is an inbox full of signups rather than a locked-out user. totp/verify is on the list because a six-digit code is a million guesses, and without a limit that is an afternoon. Read the comment Grit carries at the mount point. It is there because it already happened: The limits were configured. The dashboard showed them. The paths were wrong by one version segment, so nothing ever matched, and the failure mode of a rate limit that does not match is silence . No error, no warning, and a login endpoint with no limit on it. A rate limit is one of the few controls whose failure looks exactly like success: traffic flows, nothing is blocked, everybody is happy. The only way to know it works is to exceed it on purpose and watch for the 429. The same function returns relaxed numbers when APP_ENV=development : 100 requests a minute instead of 30 in five, so nobody is locked out while testing a login form. This is worth doing deliberately rather than by disabling the middleware in development, because a control that is off in development is a control nobody exercises until production. Relaxed and present beats absent. A distributed attack. Per-IP limits assume the attacker has few addresses. A botnet has thousands, each staying under your limit. That is what Sentinel's auth shield and anomaly detection are for: they look at the account and the pattern rather than the address. A correct password. Rate limiting buys time against guessing; it does nothing against a credential already leaked elsewhere. That is what the breach check and 2FA are for. Expensive single requests. One report query that scans ten million rows is within every limit you have. Body size caps and statement timeouts cover that, not request counts. Counters have to be shared or they are per-process, and a limit of 30 across four replicas is a limit of 120. Grit configures Sentinel storage explicitly for that reason, falling back to a local SQLite file only when nothing else is set: One. With the API running in production mode, post wrong credentials to your login endpoint in a loop. Record which attempt first returns 429. Two. Change one route limit key to a path that does not exist, such as dropping the version segment. Restart and repeat the loop. Three. Write down what, if anything, told you the limit had stopped working. For step three, check the startup output, the Sentinel dashboard and the API log, and be precise about which of them mentions it. Step one gives a 429 on attempt 31 within the window. Step two runs the loop to completion with no limiting at all. Step three is the point: nothing tells you. The configuration is still valid, the dashboard still lists the rule, and a rule that matches no requests is indistinguishable from a rule nobody has hit. This is why the only honest test of a rate limit is to exceed it and look for the 429, and why that check belongs in your test suite rather than in a runbook.
pages.title: Two limits, doing different jobs

headings: The ordinary path is already safe
Where it actually gets in: identifiers
pages.text: Go and GORM make SQL injection hard to write by accident. They do not make it impossible, and the places it still gets in are specific and worth memorising, because they are the places where a parameter is not allowed and people reach for string concatenation instead. Every value you pass through a placeholder is sent to the database separately from the statement. The driver never builds one string out of both, so there is nothing for a quote to break out of: So Raw is not the villain. Concatenation is. The two get conflated, and the result is teams that ban Raw and then build strings somewhere else. fmt.Sprintf next to SQL is the single highest-signal thing to grep for in a Go codebase. It is almost never the right way to put a value into a query. A placeholder works for values. It does not work for column names, table names, or the direction of a sort, because those are part of the statement's structure rather than its data. The database will not accept ORDER BY ? . Which means any feature that lets the caller choose a sort column or a filter field has to build SQL from input. That is the real injection surface in a modern Go app, and it is in almost every list endpoint ever written: The fix is not escaping. It is an allow list, because you know the complete set of sortable columns and the caller does not get to invent one: Note what makes this safe: the strings that reach the query are yours . The caller's input is only ever used to pick one. An allow list fails closed, and it also gives you a stable public name for a column you may want to rename later. Grit's generated list endpoints already do this, with the sortable set derived from the resource definition. The risk is in the endpoint you hand-write next to them, where the habit of the generated code does not automatically follow. LIKE. Where("title LIKE ?", "%"+q+"%") is parameterised and safe from injection, but % and _ in the input are still wildcards. A search for % matches everything, which is a performance problem rather than a breach. IN with a slice. Where("id IN ?", ids) is safe. Building the list by joining strings is not. Migrations and admin tooling. The code that genuinely needs dynamic identifiers. It usually runs with the widest database privileges in the system, so it is the worst place to take a shortcut. One. Add a sort parameter to a list endpoint the unsafe way, passing c.Query("sort") straight to Order . Two. Call it with ?sort=(CASE WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users) > 0 THEN title ELSE id END) . It is a legal expression, so it sorts. Confirm it does, and note that you just ran a subquery the endpoint never offered. Three. Replace it with an allow list. Try the same input and confirm it falls back to the default. Step two is a demonstration, not an exploit: if an arbitrary expression runs at all, the boundary is already gone, and whether it can be weaponised depends only on the database and the driver. The unsafe version sorts without complaint, which is the whole finding: the caller supplied a SQL expression and the database evaluated it. From there the usual next step is a boolean oracle, flipping the sort on a condition to read data one bit at a time. With the allow list the lookup misses, the default applies, and there is nothing to probe. Escaping would have been the wrong fix: you cannot escape an identifier into safety, and you do not need to when you already know the valid set.
pages.title: The ordinary path is already safe

headings: Why it is worse than it sounds
What it actually blocks, and when
The part a library cannot do for you
pages.text: Server-Side Request Forgery is the bug where your server fetches a URL somebody else chose. It looks like a feature, because it is one: "import from URL", "fetch the image", "send this webhook", "render that page as a PDF". The server makes the request, so the request comes from inside your network. Your laptop cannot reach your database. Your server can. An attacker who makes your server fetch a URL has borrowed its position on the network, and that position is the whole point of a firewall. 169.254.169.254 is the cloud metadata service on AWS, GCP and Azure. It answers without authentication, because it assumes that anything able to reach it is already the machine. It hands out IAM credentials. That one address is why SSRF is rated the way it is. The other targets are less famous and just as useful: your Redis on 127.0.0.1:6379 , an internal admin panel on 10.0.x.x , a Kubernetes API, a health endpoint that leaks configuration. Grit ships internal/safefetch . Use it for every request to a URL the caller chose, and never http.Get : The interesting part is when . A naive guard parses the URL, resolves the hostname, checks the address against a block list, and then calls http.Get . That is a race: the attacker controls the DNS record, so the name can resolve to a harmless address for your check and to 169.254.169.254 a millisecond later for the real request. It is called DNS rebinding and it defeats every check that happens before the dial. safefetch puts the check in the dialer's Control function, which runs after the address is resolved and before the socket connects. There is no gap to race: A redirect is a second request to an address you never checked. Anything that follows redirects has to re-check every hop, which is the other half of why this belongs in a shared client rather than in each handler. The timeouts are short deliberately. A fetch that can be made to hang is an amplification vector: a few hundred requests to a URL that never answers will exhaust your connection pool without anything looking like an attack. safefetch stops your server reaching somewhere it should not. It cannot decide whether the response is safe to show the caller. Echoing a fetched body straight back turns a blocked request into an information leak the moment some future address is allowed, so return what the feature needs and not the raw body. Add an endpoint that takes a URL and reports the response status and content type. Nothing else. One. Write it with http.Get first. Point it at http://169.254.169.254/ and at http://127.0.0.1:6379/ . Note what happens. Two. Switch to safefetch.Get and repeat both. Three. Explain in one sentence why resolving the hostname yourself and checking it before calling http.Get would not be a fix. For step three: who controls what that hostname resolves to, and how many times is it resolved? With http.Get both reach something. On a cloud host the metadata address answers immediately; locally, Redis accepts the connection and complains about the protocol, which still tells you it is there. With safefetch both come back as ErrBlocked at connect time. Checking first is not a fix because the attacker owns the DNS record. It can answer with a safe address for your lookup and the metadata address for the one the HTTP client makes a moment later: two resolutions, two answers, and your check validated the wrong one.
pages.title: Why it is worse than it sounds

headings: What this course covers, by chapter
pages.text: The OWASP Top 10 is the closest thing the security community has to a standard reading list. This lesson is the speedrun tour , one sentence per category, in plain English, mapped to real Grit endpoints. Later chapters attack each one hands-on. What: User A can read or modify User B's data because the endpoint didn't check ownership. In Grit: Forgetting WHERE user_id = ? on a list, or skipping the if note.UserID != userID check on an update. The most common bug in shipped APIs. Chapter 2 is entirely this. What: Passwords stored unhashed, secrets committed to git, weak algorithms, no TLS on production. In Grit: bcrypt is wired by default for passwords. JWT uses HS256 with a strong secret. Your job: don't commit .env ; use real TLS in production. What: User input executed as code. SQL injection, command injection, HTML injection (XSS). In Grit: GORM parameterises by default , unless you fmt.Sprintf user input into a query. Templates auto-escape, unless you mark them as raw. Chapter 3. What: The system architecture itself is vulnerable , auth flow allows account takeover, password reset emails the token to the wrong address, etc. In Grit: Architectural review at threat-model time catches most of these. Chapter 4 covers JWT pitfalls, which are usually A04. What: Defaults left enabled (debug mode in prod, admin endpoints exposed, overly permissive CORS, no security headers). In Grit: The defaults are reasonable. Your job: confirm GIN_MODE=release in prod, set explicit CORS origins, verify CSP headers are emitted. Chapter 5. What: Old dependencies with known CVEs. In Grit: Grit's CI runs govulncheck and Dependabot is wired into the starter. Your job: don't ignore the alerts. What: Brute force allowed, weak passwords permitted, sessions never expire, no MFA. In Grit: Sentinel rate-limits login attempts. Password min-length is configurable. JWT expiry defaults to 15 min. TOTP MFA is included if you enable it. What: Trusting unverified updates, signed artefacts that aren't verified, supply chain attacks via compromised dependencies. In Grit: Modules are pinned in go.sum and frontend deps via pnpm-lock . If you blindly run install scripts from a stranger's package, that's on you. What: No way to detect an attack. No way to replay what happened after it. In Grit: Pulse provides request logging + timing per endpoint. Sensitive actions go through the audit log. Chapter 5 covers wiring this. What: Your server fetches a URL the attacker supplies, hitting internal services (metadata endpoints, admin panels, AWS IMDS) the attacker can't reach directly. In Grit: The safefetch package blocks private IP ranges by default. Every URL you fetch from user input should go through it. Chapter 3. Ch.1 (here): Mindset , threat model + OWASP tour. Ch.2: Broken Access Control , A01 , IDOR hands-on. Ch.3: Injection + SSRF , A03 + A10. Ch.4: Auth + Secrets , A02 + A04 + A07. Ch.5: The Grit defensive stack , A05 + A06 + A09. Chapter 2 , Broken Access Control . We'll write a deliberately-broken IDOR, exploit it, then ship the fix. The first hands-on attack of the course.
pages.title: A01 , Broken Access Control

pages.text: Before you defend against anything, write down what you're protecting, from whom, and how badly each thing matters. That is a threat model. It takes 15 minutes, costs nothing, and is the single highest-leverage security activity for a small team. What are we protecting? User data? Payment info? Source code? IP? From whom? Script kiddies? Competitors? Disgruntled employees? Nation-states? What are we willing to spend? A hobby project and a fintech have very different budgets. What's the worst case? A data leak embarrasses you; a payment leak ends you. For each endpoint in your API, ask: which letters apply? Most endpoints have a few. A login endpoint cares about S, I, D. A notes endpoint cares about T, I, E. Knowing which letter applies focuses your defence. A threat model doesn't need to be a 50-page Word doc. Yours can be a single Markdown file. Three sections: User accounts (email, password hash, profile) Tenant data (orders, notes, files) Payment info (last 4, never the full card) Admin access Service availability Anonymous user (public internet) Authenticated regular user (logged in) Authenticated user trying to access another user's data Compromised admin account Insider (developer, employee) One line per threat. Be specific. Map each to STRIDE. T1 (I, T): A logged-in user PATCHes another user's note by guessing the ID. (IDOR) T2 (S): An attacker uses a leaked JWT secret to forge tokens for any user. T3 (D): Bot floods /api/auth/login with brute force; password reset queue grows; legit users locked out. T4 (E): SQL injection on a search endpoint exfiltrates the users table. T5 (I): Public bucket lets anyone download customer uploads. Rate each threat 1-5 on likelihood and 1-5 on impact. Multiply. Sort. Spend your time on the top half. Ignore the bottom half for now. Don't obsess over precision. The point is forcing yourself to compare threats so you don't spend a week on a 1×1 threat while a 5×5 sits unhandled. For a small team / solo founder, a useful threat model fits on one page: 5 assets 5 actors 10 threats, ranked The top 3 actively being mitigated Anything more is overkill until you have customer/regulatory pressure for one. You launched a major feature (new endpoints, new data). You added a new third-party service (more attack surface). You had a security incident or scare. It's been > 6 months and you haven't looked. Write a threat model for your own Grit API: Create SECURITY.md at your repo root. List 5 assets you protect (be specific to YOUR product). List 5 actors. List 10 threats , one per STRIDE category at minimum. Rate likelihood (1-5) × impact (1-5). Sort. Underline the top 3. For each of the top 3, write 1 sentence on the planned mitigation. You should have a 1-page document that the next person to join your team could read in 5 minutes and instantly know what matters. That document drives the rest of the course. Next lesson , OWASP Top 10 tour . One sentence per category, mapped to real Grit endpoints. Then we attack IDOR in chapter 2.
pages.title: What a threat model answers

pages.text: Every SaaS needs payments. Stripe is the industry standard , it handles credit cards, subscriptions, invoices, and compliance so you don t have to. In this course, you ll integrate Stripe into your Grit app: create checkout sessions, manage subscription plans, handle webhooks, and build a complete billing system with a customer portal. Reference docs: Webhooks → Accepting payments on the internet is surprisingly complex. You need to securely collect credit card numbers, comply with PCI-DSS regulations, handle failed charges, manage refunds, send invoices, and deal with subscriptions. Stripe does all of this for you. You never see or store a credit card number , Stripe handles the sensitive parts. The payment flow with Stripe: Go to stripe.com and create a free account. Once logged in, find the Dashboard. Switch to Test Mode (toggle in the top bar). Find your test API keys under Developers → API Keys. You should see a Publishable key (starts with pk_test_ ) and a Secret key (starts with sk_test_ ). Never share the secret key. The grit-stripe plugin wraps Stripe s Go SDK with opinionated helpers designed for SaaS applications. It provides checkout session creation, subscription management, customer portal access, and webhook handling , all pre-configured for the common SaaS billing patterns. What the plugin provides: • CreateCheckoutSession , Redirect users to Stripe s hosted payment page • CreatePortalSession , Let users manage their subscription (change plan, update card, cancel) • HandleWebhook , Process Stripe events (payment succeeded, subscription cancelled, etc.) • GetSubscription , Check a customer s current subscription status • CancelSubscription , Cancel at period end or immediately Install the grit-stripe plugin in your Grit project by running go get github.com/MUKE-coder/grit-plugins/grit-stripe from your apps/api/ directory. Verify it appears in your go.mod and go.sum files. Stripe uses API keys for authentication. You need three keys in your .env file: the secret key (for server-side API calls), the publishable key (for client-side Stripe.js), and the webhook secret (for verifying webhook signatures). Initialize the plugin in your API: Add your Stripe test keys to your .env file. Initialize the grit-stripe plugin in your config. Start your API and verify there are no errors related to Stripe initialization. The secret key starts with sk_test_ , if it starts with sk_live_ , you re using production keys (switch to test mode in the Stripe Dashboard). When a user clicks Subscribe on your pricing page, your API creates a Checkout Session , a temporary URL that takes the user to Stripe s hosted payment page. The user enters their card on Stripe s page, and Stripe redirects them back to your app after payment. On the frontend, when the user clicks a plan s Subscribe button: Add a POST /api/billing/checkout endpoint to your API. It should accept a price_id in the request body and return a Stripe Checkout URL. Test it with a tool like curl or Postman. Copy the returned URL and open it in your browser , do you see Stripe s payment page? Use test card 4242 4242 4242 4242 to complete payment. Before you can charge customers, you need to create Products and Prices in your Stripe Dashboard. A Product represents what you re selling (e.g., Pro Plan ). A Price represents how much it costs and how often (e.g., $20/month ). A typical SaaS has 3 tiers: Create these in the Stripe Dashboard: 1. Go to Products in the Stripe Dashboard 2. Click Add Product 3. Name: Pro Plan , Pricing: Recurring, Amount: $20.00, Billing period: Monthly 4. Save , Stripe generates a Price ID (starts with price_ ) 5. Repeat for Team Plan ($50/month) In your Stripe Dashboard (test mode), create 2 products: Pro Plan at $20/month and Team Plan at $50/month. Copy the Price IDs (they start with price_ ). Add them to your .env file as STRIPE_PRO_PRICE_ID and STRIPE_TEAM_PRICE_ID . Here s the problem: the user pays on Stripe s page and gets redirected to your success URL. But what if they close the browser before the redirect? What if the network drops? You can t rely on the redirect to activate their subscription. Instead, Stripe sends webhooks , HTTP POST requests to your API , for every important event. Register the webhook route (no auth middleware , Stripe needs to access it): For a SaaS application, list 5 Stripe webhook events you should handle and describe what your API should do for each one. Think about: successful payments, failed payments, cancellations, plan changes, and trial expirations. Which event is the most critical and why? Users need to manage their subscription: update their credit card, change plans, view invoices, or cancel. Building all of this yourself is weeks of work. Stripe s Customer Portal gives you a hosted page where users can do all of this , with zero UI code from you. The Customer Portal lets users: • Update payment method , change credit card, add backup card • View invoices , download PDF invoices for each billing period • Change plan , upgrade or downgrade (with prorated billing) • Cancel subscription , cancel at end of billing period Add a POST /api/billing/portal endpoint. After completing a test checkout (from challenge 4), use the Stripe customer ID to create a portal session. Open the returned URL. Can you see the subscription? Can you update the payment method? Can you cancel? The pricing page is where users decide which plan to buy. It typically shows 3 plan cards side by side, with features listed for each plan and a Subscribe button that creates a checkout session. Design tips for an effective pricing page: • Highlight the recommended plan with a border, badge ( Most Popular ), or different background • Show savings for yearly billing , add a toggle (Monthly/Yearly) with a Save 20% badge on yearly • Use checkmarks for features , green checkmarks for included, gray X or dash for excluded • Keep it simple , 3 plans maximum, clear differentiation between each tier Build a pricing pa
pages.title: Stripe Payments & Subscriptions for SaaS

headings: Testing Your Grit App: Go, Vitest & Playwright
pages.text: Untested code is broken code , you just don t know it yet. In this course, you ll learn to test every layer of a Grit application: Go unit tests for your API, component tests for your React frontend, and end-to-end tests that simulate real users clicking through your app. Grit scaffolds test files for you. Your job is to understand them and write more. Reference docs: Testing → Every application has bugs. The question is whether you find them before or after your users do. Testing is how you catch bugs automatically, before they reach production. There are three main types of tests, and they form a pyramid: The testing pyramid: many unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a small number of E2E tests at the top. This gives you fast feedback (unit tests run in milliseconds) and high confidence (E2E tests prove the whole system works). Think about an application with no tests at all. Name 3 specific things that can go wrong when a developer pushes new code. For each one, explain how a test would have caught the problem before it reached production. Go has testing built into the language. No external framework needed. Test files end with _test.go , and test functions start with Test followed by a capital letter. The go test command finds and runs them automatically. Run all tests in a project with: Write a test function called TestIsValidEmail that tests the IsValidEmail function. Test at least 4 cases: a valid email, an email without @, an email without a dot in the domain, and an empty string. Use t.Errorf for failures. Go s built-in testing works, but the assertions are verbose. Writing if result != expected for every check gets tedious. The testify library gives you clean, readable assertions. Write a test using assert.Equal and assert.NotEmpty for a blog post creation function. Check that the title, slug (auto-generated from title), author_id, and created_at fields are set correctly. The slug for My First Post should be my-first-post . When you run grit new myapp , Grit scaffolds test files automatically. You don t start from scratch. Here s what you get: • auth_test.go , 6 tests covering registration (success, validation, duplicate email), login (success, wrong password, unknown email) • user_test.go , 4 tests covering auth guard (unauthenticated access blocked), admin list users, user not found (404), get user by ID • bench_test.go , benchmarks for health check, auth login, and auth register endpoints All scaffolded tests use SQLite in-memory databases. This means no Docker, no PostgreSQL, no setup , tests run instantly on any machine. Navigate to apps/api/ in your Grit project. Find the test files (they end with _test.go ). Run go test -v ./... and observe the output. How many tests pass? How many are there total? Authentication is the most critical part of your API. If auth is broken, everything is broken. Grit s scaffolded auth_test.go tests 6 scenarios: 1. Register success , valid name, email, password returns 201 + access token 2. Register validation , missing fields return 422 with error details 3. Register duplicate , same email twice returns 409 conflict 4. Login success , correct credentials return 200 + tokens 5. Login wrong password , returns 401 unauthorized 6. Login unknown email , returns 401 unauthorized (same error as wrong password for security) Open auth_test.go in your scaffolded project. Read through all 6 test functions. For each one, write down: (1) what HTTP method and path it calls, (2) what request body it sends, and (3) what status code and response body it asserts. After running grit generate resource Product name:string price:float active:bool , you get CRUD endpoints. Every endpoint needs tests. Here s the pattern for testing a generated resource: Generate a Product resource with grit generate resource Product name:string price:float active:bool category:string . Then write 5 tests: Create (valid data returns 201), List (5 products with pagination), GetByID (correct product), Update (fields change), Delete (returns 200, subsequent GET returns 404). Tests tell you if your code is correct. Benchmarks tell you if your code is fast. Go has built-in benchmarking , functions named BenchmarkXxx that measure how many operations per second your code can handle. Run benchmarks with: Typical output looks like: Reading benchmark output: 50000 is how many times the function ran. 24350 ns/op is nanoseconds per operation (lower is faster). Health check is fast (~24 microseconds), login is moderate (~2.3 milliseconds because of password verification), and bcrypt hashing is intentionally slow (~210 milliseconds). Navigate to your API directory. Run go test -bench=. -benchmem ./... . Look at the results. Which endpoint is fastest? Which is slowest? Why is BenchmarkHashPassword so much slower than the others? (Hint: it s by design.) Your Go API is tested. Now let s test the React frontend. Grit uses Vitest , a fast test runner built on Vite , combined with React Testing Library for rendering components. Grit scaffolds test files in apps/web/__tests__/ and apps/admin/__tests__/ . Run them with: Navigate to apps/web/ and apps/admin/ . Find the test files in the __tests__ directories. Run pnpm test in each. How many component tests does Grit scaffold? What components are tested? Unit tests check individual pieces. Integration tests check pieces together. But neither tells you if the whole application works from a user s perspective. That s what Playwright does , it opens a real browser, clicks buttons, fills forms, and verifies results. Grit scaffolds E2E tests in the e2e/ directory with auth.spec.ts and admin.spec.ts . Run them with: Find the Playwright configuration file in your project ( playwright.config.ts ). What base URL is it configured to use? What browsers does it test against? Start your app with grit start , then run pnpm test:e2e . Do the tests pass? So far, we ve written tests for existing code. TDD flips this around: you write the test
pages.title: Testing Your Grit App: Go, Vitest & Playwright

pages.text: The DataTable rendered by defineResource() handles sort, filter, pagination, search, row selection, and per-column cell rendering , all from the column config. This lesson tours the knobs. From the previous lesson's minimal config you got: Sortable column headers (click to sort) Pagination at the bottom (20 rows / page default) Search bar (searches columns with searchable: true ) Row action menu (Edit / Delete / View) Bulk selection checkboxes Loading + empty + error states out of the box Each filter appears in the toolbar. Selected values become URL query params, so a filtered view is shareable / bookmarkable / back-button-friendly. format is the quick-and-clean shortcut. cell is the escape hatch for custom JSX. Bulk actions appear in a toolbar that slides up when rows are selected. The handler gets the array of selected IDs + refresh() . Every filter, sort, page number, and search query syncs to the URL: A user can bookmark a filtered view, send the URL to a teammate, or hit the back button to undo a filter. No work on your part. Row actions live in the "..." menu at the end of each row. Default: Edit, Delete, View. Bulk actions appear above the table when rows are selected. Use for "archive 50 things" type workflows. Extend your products admin with two improvements: Make the name column searchable. Add a select filter for an is_active: boolean column (you may need to add this field to the Product model + grit migrate + grit sync). Add a bulk action "Mark as inactive" that flips is_active to false on selected rows. Test that the URL changes when you filter/search. Paste the URL of a filtered+searched+sorted state in notes.md . A filtered URL looks like: All state in the URL , bookmark-friendly, back-button-friendly. Last lesson of this chapter , FormBuilder . The forms behind New / Edit, with all 8 field types in action.
pages.title: The default surface

pages.text: defineResource() is the Grit admin's killer primitive. One call gives you list + create + edit + delete pages , DataTable, FormBuilder, routing, everything. This lesson covers the shape; next two lessons cover the components it renders. That's the whole admin page. List page + create form + edit form + delete confirmation , all generated. model: 'products' maps to your API's /api/products/* CRUD endpoints. Grit's code generator (covered in the Concepts course) already wired these when you ran grit generate resource Product . Convention: model name is the plural form used in API routes. Four pages from one function call. Each column's format tells the DataTable how to render the value: Add custom formatters by passing a function: . Each override slots into the generated page where you'd expect , actions go in the top-right toolbar, filters in the filter bar, bulk actions appear when rows are selected. Build a working products admin page: Ensure Product is generated and migrated (Concepts course ch.4). Create apps/admin/app/resources/products/page.tsx with defineResource . Visit localhost:3001/resources/products . Create three products via the New button. Edit one; delete one. Paste the list view (with your three products) in notes.md . You should see a working list page with three rows, each with a row-action menu (Edit / Delete). That's ~20 lines of code for what would otherwise be hundreds of lines of CRUD HTML. Next two lessons go deeper on the rendered components: DataTable (sort, filter, paginate) then FormBuilder (the field types in action).
pages.title: The call

headings: The eight field types in action
pages.text: FormBuilder is the Create / Edit half of the resource. Eight field types, automatic validation via the shared Zod schema, file uploads through Grit storage. This lesson covers the field types and the customisation patterns. Use the shared Zod schema as the source of truth. FormBuilder reads it automatically: Every error message in the schema becomes the inline error message in the form. Centralised validation; web, admin, mobile, AND the API all enforce the same rules. On submit, FormBuilder: Validates with the Zod schema (client-side) Uploads any files via the storage handler POSTs / PUTs to the API Shows a toast on success, navigates back to the list On error, surfaces field-level errors from the API's 422 response For chapter 4's assignment, extend the Product form with at least 6 of the 8 field types: name (text, required) description (textarea) price (money) stock (number) is_featured (switch) image (file, image/*, max 2MB) Create a product via the form, edit it, delete it. Paste the created product's admin /edit URL in notes.md . The /edit URL looks like: You've built a full CRUD admin page with 6 field types and file uploads in 30 lines of TypeScript. Filament-style. Final chapter , Tenants + Roles . Multi-tenant SaaS, role-based UI gates, the invitation flow.
pages.title: The eight field types in action

pages.text: Logged-in user landing surface. Three sections: stat cards across the top, a chart in the middle, an activity feed on the side. The Grit scaffold ships these as starter widgets , this lesson covers how they wire up. Server component , fetches stats on the server, passes to the client widgets that need interactivity (chart hover, feed polling). Pure server component. No JS shipped to the browser for the cards. Recharts is the practical pick , small bundle, declarative, composable. Charts are inherently interactive so they live in client components. Polls every 30 seconds for new events. For real-time, swap polling for the Grit WebSocket plugin (covered in the plugins course). For chapter 3's assignment, build the dashboard: Sign up a new user (from last lesson). Add 3 stat cards backed by real API endpoints. Add the activity feed pulling from /api/activity . Screenshot the dashboard. Paste it in notes.md . Should look like: Chapter 4 , The Admin Panel . Filament-style CRUD pages built from one defineResource() call.
pages.title: The dashboard shell

headings: What the dashboard looks like now
Three pieces of data per resource
Why the sparkline ignores the DateFilter
pages.text: The dashboard widgets lesson covered the dashboard shell , stat cards, charts, activity feed , wired by hand. That pattern doesn't scale: every new resource you generate deserves its own snapshot on the dashboard, but copy-pasting a stat card per resource is a chore. Per-resource dashboard widgets (shipped in v3.31.44 ) make that automatic: every registered resource gets a Total + 30-day sparkline tile and a Latest N preview, all scoped by the dashboard's DateFilter. Below the existing Quick Access section a new By resource band renders one row per registered resource. Each row is two widgets: a stat card on the left (Total + 30-day sparkline) and a Latest 5 list on the right (the resource's most recent rows, columns auto-picked). A single DateFilter at the top of the dashboard scopes every row in lockstep. One endpoint per resource, dispatched server-side. The web widget calls GET /api/admin/dashboard/resource-stats/:resource with whichever date params the DateFilter is active for. The handler delegates to a service function that switches on the resource name and calls a single reflective helper: The dispatcher is also the security boundary: only resources registered here are reachable. A compromised admin token can't dump arbitrary tables by guessing resource names in the URL , anything not in the switch returns a 400. The helper computes three things in one round-trip: Total , row count within the active date range. No range = all-time count. 30-day sparkline , one bucket per calendar day for the last 30 days. Always 30 days regardless of the active filter (see next section for why). Latest N , up to 10 newest rows in the active range. Returned via JSON round-trip so json:"-" tags are honoured , PasswordHash on User never reaches the response. The first instinct is "everything should scope to the filter." The Total + Latest list do , but the sparkline is fixed at 30 days on purpose. Under the "Today" preset a filter-scoped sparkline would collapse to a single bar with no trend information. The sparkline is meant to answer "is this resource growing?" not "what's inside the filter?" , those are different questions, and one widget shouldn't pretend to answer both. Most resources are worth showing on the dashboard. A few aren't , internal-only tables, audit-log rows, sync scratch data. Hide a resource's widgets by setting dashboard.enabled = false in the resource definition: Default is enabled , a newly generated resource gets the widgets without any extra config. The flag is opt-out , not opt-in, because the cost of forgetting to opt in is higher than the cost of occasionally opting out: a brand-new resource not showing up on the dashboard looks like a bug, while an extra row on the dashboard is easily ignored. The Latest widget shows at most three columns per row , it's a glance, not a full data table. The column picker prefers name , title , subject , email , status , and price in that order, then falls back to the first non-id text columns from the resource's table.columns config. Resources with no recognisable columns fall through to showing the row id in a monospace font. Pre-v3.31.44 projects don't have the new dispatch file, the handler, or the marker. The generator detects this and prints a one-line warning per generate instead of failing , the dashboard widget for that resource will render "not registered" until the file is added. To upgrade an existing project: Copy apps/api/internal/services/resource_stats_dispatch.go and apps/api/internal/handlers/resource_stats.go from a fresh scaffold (or the framework repo's internal/scaffold/api_resource_stats_files.go ). Register the handler + route in your routes file: resourceStatsHandler := &handlers.ResourceStatsHandler{` `} and admin.GET("/admin/dashboard/resource-stats/:resource", resourceStatsHandler.Get) . Copy apps/admin/components/dashboard/*.tsx and the By resource section in the dashboard page. Re-run grit generate on each existing resource (or hand-add cases to ComputeResourceStats ). In the project from the last exercise, see the new widgets end-to-end: Open the admin dashboard. Scroll past Quick Access , you should see the By resource band with one row per resource. Hover the sparkline; the tooltip should show "N new" per day. Toggle the dashboard DateFilter to "Last 7 days". The Total numbers should update; the sparkline should not. Confirm in the Network tab: resource-stats/products?created_since=7d fires per resource. In the admin, create one new Category. Wait the React Query refetch interval (60 s) or hard-refresh. Both the Total and the Latest list for Category should update. Add {`dashboard: `} to one resource definition. Reload the dashboard , that resource's row should disappear from the band. Screenshot the dashboard with the "By resource" band visible and paste it into notes.md . The widget request keys are and . Changing the DateFilter rewrites params (via dateRangeToQueryParams ) and both keys invalidate, triggering a refetch in lockstep. Opting out by setting {`dashboard: `} filters the resource out of the band at render time: . The data endpoint still works (the server-side dispatch case is untouched) , only the widget is hidden from the dashboard. The dashboard now scales linearly with your resource count , every new grit generate adds one row to the By resource band automatically. The next lesson ( web-nextjs/admin-panel/define-resource ) goes deeper on the resource definition itself, including the table + form halves and how they feed back into both the resource page and the dashboard widgets you just saw.
pages.title: What the dashboard looks like now

headings: The server action that hits your Go API
The login form is the same, simpler
pages.text: Signup + login are the two most important forms in your app. This lesson covers the Grit pattern: server action for submit, Zod for validation, secure HTTP-only cookie for the session. Server action runs in the Next.js server process, talks to your Go API, then sets HTTP-only cookies. JS in the browser never sees the token , XSS can't steal it. For server components / route handlers that fetch your Go API, wrap the fetch in an interceptor that refreshes when the access cookie is expired: Server components call apiFetch . Refresh is transparent; the user's session feels infinite. Same pattern, calls /api/auth/login instead of /api/auth/register . Same cookie setting. Same redirect on success. Wire signup end-to-end on your scaffolded project: Add the form + server action. Visit localhost:3000/signup . Submit. Verify (a) the API created a user (check localhost:8080/studio ), (b) cookies set in DevTools, (c) you land on /dashboard . Paste the cookies (just names + types, not values) in notes.md . You should see two cookies: Both HttpOnly. Neither readable by browser JS. That's the difference from localStorage. User is signed up + signed in. Last lesson of this chapter , what do they see? Dashboard widgets .
pages.title: The signup form

headings: The hero , server component, no JS needed
Run your retail business from one place
Why server components win for landing pages
pages.text: The landing page is the first thing a customer sees. Three sections, a clear value prop, a CTA. This lesson is about shipping a respectable landing page in 30 minutes , not perfecting it. Hero , headline, sub-headline, primary CTA Social proof , logos, testimonials, stats Features grid , three to six benefit-led items Pricing / final CTA Footer , links, social, copyright Server component by default. No "use client" at the top. HTML ships pre-rendered; bundle stays tiny. No hydration cost. The user gets HTML; the JS bundle is minimal. Lighthouse loves it. SEO-friendly out of the box. Bots see the content directly. Can fetch at request time. Stats, latest testimonials , fetch in a server component, render to HTML. Pull the hero into components/hero.tsx so other marketing pages (about, pricing, blog index) can reuse it. Pass {` `} as props. Build a real landing page on your scaffolded project: Replace apps/web/app/(marketing)/page.tsx with hero + features grid + final CTA. Add at least three feature items, real product-y copy. Open localhost:3000 , verify it looks like a product page, not a default Next template. Run Lighthouse on it (Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse → Performance). Aim for ≥90. Paste your Lighthouse score in notes.md . A healthy landing page scores: Anything below 90 on Performance means there's either too much client JS or unoptimised images. Last lesson of this chapter , SEO + Open Graph . Make your page discoverable and shareable.
pages.title: The standard parts

pages.text: SEO is "how do search engines find you"; OG is "how does your link preview when shared". Both are metadata. Next.js makes them one-liner additions. This lesson is the checklist. Next.js renders these into <meta> tags at build / request time. No work beyond declaring the object. 1200 × 630 PNG. Shows when someone shares your link in Slack / Twitter / WhatsApp. Build it once with Figma + export PNG. Or generate dynamically with next/og : Now https://acme.com/og renders a dynamic OG image , useful when you want page-specific previews (blog post titles, user profiles). Available at /sitemap.xml . Google reads it to discover every public URL. For dynamic blog posts, fetch from your API and map each post to an entry. Tells crawlers what to index. Always disallow /dashboard and similar logged-in surfaces , they'd 404 for the bot anyway. apps/admin should NEVER be indexed. Add a global robots meta in its root layout: For chapter 2's assignment, complete the SEO + OG pass on your scaffolded web app: Add a metadata object to apps/web/app/(marketing)/page.tsx . Add app/sitemap.ts + app/robots.ts . Add a static OG image (or generate via next/og ). Deploy to a public URL (Vercel, your VPS) and run the OG tester. Run Lighthouse , SEO score should be 100. Paste the OG preview + Lighthouse SEO in notes.md . A healthy Slack preview looks like: Title Description 1200 × 630 image Site name + URL If all four show, your metadata is right. Lighthouse SEO 100 is easy if your metadata is complete and you have a sitemap. Chapter 3 , The User Dashboard . Signup, login, the logged-in surface. The customer's home base.
pages.title: The page metadata object

pages.text: Welcome to Building Web with Next.js + Go API . We're using the triple kit , three apps in one monorepo (web, admin, api). By the end of this lesson, you'll have scaffolded a SaaS-shaped project ready for the rest of the course. Pick "Next.js" when prompted for the frontend framework (or use --next to skip the prompt). You'll end up with apps/web , apps/admin , and apps/api all wired together. apps/web , your customers. Marketing pages (public) + dashboard (logged-in). apps/admin , your staff. Different auth scope, different look, behind its own subdomain in prod. apps/api , same Go API serves both. Same code, different route groups for different roles. Three URLs come up: http://localhost:3000 (web), http://localhost:3001 (admin), http://localhost:8080 (API). Scaffold and run the full triple stack: grit new saas --triple --next cd saas && docker compose up -d pnpm install grit migrate && grit seed grit start Open all three URLs in different browser tabs. Paste each tab's title bar text in notes.md . Three browser titles to paste: Three apps running. Next lesson , tour each app's file structure so you know where to put new code.
pages.title: The command

headings: Why not just publish to npm?
What NOT to put in shared
pages.text: packages/shared is the glue. Zod schemas, generated TS types, route constants , anything web and admin both need. One source of truth; the two apps stay aligned forever. Importing from @workspace/shared uses pnpm's workspace symlinks. TypeScript follows the symlink and resolves types correctly. No build step needed. Reminder from earlier courses: when you change a Go struct, run grit sync to regenerate packages/shared/src/types/ . Both apps pick up the new types instantly. You could. But the workspace pattern means changes propagate instantly without a publish cycle. Edit a schema; both apps see it on next reload. For internal types this is ideal. When you graduate to public types (SDK for third parties), THEN publish to npm , but for internal monorepo work, workspaces win. React components , they belong in apps/web/components/ or apps/admin/components/ (or a separate packages/ui if you want a design system). App-specific business logic , that should stay in the relevant app. Anything that imports from apps/* , would create circular dependencies. Add a formatCurrency() helper to packages/shared : Create packages/shared/src/utils/currency.ts exporting formatCurrency(amount: number): string . Import it into apps/web/app/(app)/dashboard/page.tsx and use it to render a price. Import the same function into one admin page. In notes.md , paste both import statements + where you used it. That completes chapter 1's assignment. Both apps now have a single, consistent way to format money. Chapter 2 , The Public Site . Landing page, marketing pages, SEO + Open Graph. The customer-facing surface.
pages.title: What lives in it

headings: What's the same across both apps
pages.text: Tour all three apps. We already covered apps/api in the Go API course; this lesson focuses on apps/web and apps/admin , what's the same, what's different. Three route groups: (marketing) , (auth) , (app) . Each has its own layout. The parens don't appear in URLs. The killer file is app/resources/ x /page.tsx , we cover defineResource() in chapter 4. Almost every admin page is one of these. Both use Next.js 14 App Router (no Pages Router) Both import types from @workspace/shared Both use React Query for data Both use shadcn/ui + Tailwind CSS Auth scope , web cookies are scoped to customer-token ; admin to staff-token . One can't accidentally log into the other. Layout , web is marketing-shaped (header / hero / footer); admin is dashboard-shaped (sidebar / topbar). Robots , admin has noindex,nofollow on every page. In your scaffolded project, open both apps/web/app/layout.tsx and apps/admin/app/layout.tsx . In notes.md , write: What providers does each app wrap children in? What's in each app's root metadata (title, OG, etc.)? What one component or import is DIFFERENT between them? You should find: Both: QueryClient + ThemeProvider + ToastProvider Web layout: marketing header + footer; admin: sidebar + topbar Different cookie name in the AuthProvider Last lesson of the chapter , packages/shared , the glue between the three apps.
pages.title: apps/web , the public Next.js site

headings: You finished Building Web with Next.js + Go API 🎉
pages.text: Team invitations: admin types an email + role, system emails a one-time link, recipient clicks, sets a password, lands in your tenant with the right role. Grit ships this end-to-end. This lesson covers what's wired and the extension points. Single-use (set AcceptedAt on accept; reject if already set), time-bound (default 7 days), bound to email + role + tenant. Show context , "Join Acme as Staff" , so the recipient knows what they're accepting. Then a password form. Submit creates the user atomically with the right tenant + role. Sensible affordances: Re-send , generate a new token + email. The old one is invalidated. Revoke , delete the invitation. Even if the recipient still has the email, the link returns 404. Expired view , show pending invitations in the admin so admins can clean up stale ones. User already exists , if alex@example.com is already in the system (different tenant), how do you handle joining a second tenant? Usually: create a tenant-membership row, let the user switch between tenants. Email mismatch on accept , invitation says alex@example.com ; recipient is logged in as a different account. Force them to log out first. Email goes to spam , show admins a "Copy invite link" button as a fallback. For chapter 5's final assignment, end-to-end invitation: As an admin user, POST to /api/invitations with another email + role=staff . Check Mailhog ( localhost:8025 ) , the invitation email should be there. Click the accept link. Fill in the password form. Verify you land signed in as the new user, with the staff role, in the inviting admin's tenant. As that staff user, visit a page that gates on admin role , should be hidden (from previous lesson). The captured email looks like: Click → password form → signed in as a real user. Multi- tenant SaaS shape end-to-end. Chapter 5 done. Five chapters, 13 lessons. You can now scaffold the triple kit, build a marketing landing page with proper SEO, wire signup + dashboard widgets, customise an admin panel via defineResource() , and handle multi-tenancy + roles + invitations cleanly. From here: try Building Web + Desktop + Mobile to add native surfaces, or go deeper on the API with the Grit plugins (Stripe, WebSockets, OAuth).
pages.title: The flow

pages.text: Role-based UI: hide buttons the user can't use. Two layers , the UI hides actions for clean UX, the API rejects unauthorized requests for security. Both matter; neither replaces the other. Hierarchical: admin includes staff includes user . Owner gets billing + admin actions. Use it anywhere: For pages a role shouldn't see at all (e.g., /admin/billing for non-owners), redirect in the server component: Same outcome as <Can> but lets you use the boolean in JS logic (disabled state, conditional styling, etc.). For server actions / route handlers, check the role too: And the Go API has its own RequireRoles middleware (from the Go API course ch.3). Defence in depth: web hides, server action checks, API rejects. Add role gating to your scaffolded project: In apps/admin/app/resources/customers/page.tsx , wrap the Delete action in <Can role="admin"> . Promote one of your test users to staff (not admin). Log in as them. The Delete button should be hidden. Open DevTools, manually click the API endpoint that deletes (curl or fetch). Confirm the API rejects with 404 , that's Grit's RequireRoles middleware. Paste the curl response in notes.md . The expected curl response: 404 not 403 , leaks no info about whether the route exists. That's the convention from the Defender's Handbook page. Last lesson , the invitation flow . Inviting a teammate by email, completing signup, role + tenant assigned atomically.
pages.title: The roles you ship with

headings: The Tenant model on the web side
pages.text: Multi-tenant SaaS = many isolated customers in one DB. Each tenant sees only their own data. Done right, it's invisible; done wrong, you leak customer A's data to customer B. This lesson covers the Grit pattern. Two important pieces: a tenants table, and a TenantID column on every tenant-scoped row (orders, invoices, products , anything that "belongs to" a tenant). Every protected request gets tenant_id on its context from the authenticated user's tenant. Every read filters by tenant; every write forces the tenant from context, never from the request body. Never accept tenant_id in the request body , that'd let the user write to another tenant. Postgres supports row-level security (RLS) , DB-level filtering by a session var. If a handler forgets the filter, the DB itself rejects. Set up: Now even a buggy handler can't leak cross-tenant data. Worth the ~30 minutes to set up for high-stakes SaaS. On signup, create a tenant + assign the user as owner: Make one of your existing models tenant-scoped: Add TenantID uuid.UUID to the Product model. Run grit migrate .
