pages.text: One products table, four scenarios, one shared Postgres, identical container limits, and every framework on its own ecosystem's ORM: GORM, Eloquent, Prisma, Drizzle. Each framework was run head to head against Grit, back to back, three times, and each has a page showing exactly how to reproduce it. All six pairs below were measured back to back in one sitting on v3.134.0, and even so Grit's single-row read ranged from 4,536 req/s in the Bun pair to 8,509 in the Express pair, from an identical binary, because the machine drifts as write scenarios accumulate in Postgres. Within a pair both sides ran minutes apart under the same conditions, so the ratio survives; lining Bun's 2,717 up against Encore's 663 would imply a shared baseline that does not exist. Every table below is grouped by pair for that reason. 50 concurrent users, 30 seconds per run, 4 CPUs and 2 GB per app container. Every app shares one Postgres on 8 CPUs, deliberately more than any of them gets. Medians of three repetitions, never a best run. Measured before v3.134.0, when a generated write still sent seven statements to Postgres instead of one. This pair understates Grit and is being re-run. The Bun pair above is the corrected shape. A benchmark measures a request. This measures a Monday: how many of the things a real product needs are already running the first time you open the app. Every cell records how the capability arrives, not whether it exists, because a tick-or-cross matrix would be dishonest about frameworks whose answer here is genuinely good. Against Bun, two rows cannot be called. The paginated list and the mixed workload were measured four separate times. Mixed came out 0.91×, 1.21×, 1.19× and 0.91×, on both sides of even. Across seven repetitions Grit ranged from 329 to 643 req/s and Bun from 445 to 694. Any one of those numbers could be published as a result, which is exactly why none of them should be. The reason is in the CPU column. Postgres sits at 764-825% of its 800% allowance for both sides while Grit's own container idles at 125%. Neither framework is the limit; they are both waiting on the same database, so what moves between runs is database state rather than framework speed. Those two rows are marked within noise in the table above and no winner is claimed. The insert scenario used to be a real loss, and it is not any more. Bun was a quarter quicker at it. Postgres statement logging showed a single POST sending seven statements where Bun sent one: a transaction around an INSERT that Postgres already makes atomic, a SELECT re-reading the row just written, and an audit row written even for requests with no authenticated user. v3.134.0 fixed all three, inserts went from 2,686 to 4,959 req/s, and the scenario reversed from a 0.81× loss to a 2.23× win. A throughput number only means something when you know what stopped it. Where a framework's own container saturated, Laravel at 402-420% of its 400% allowance, Django at 398-408%, Next.js at 400-411%, Express at 416-434%, Bun at 399-411%. The figure is that framework's genuine ceiling on this hardware. Encore is the one exception: it never saturated anything, sitting at 142-195% with Postgres at 26-176%, so something else bounded it and its figures are a floor. The read-heavy rows are different. On list and mixed Grit used about 120-155% while Postgres sat near 900%: the database ran out first, not the framework. Those rows are a floor , and the real gap is wider than the ratio shows. Encore.ts is the mirror image: it never saturated anything, sitting at 155-211% with Postgres at 30-200%, so something else bounded it (most likely the Drizzle / node-postgres path rather than its Rust HTTP layer) and its numbers are a floor for Encore too. The list endpoint runs a COUNT(*) over the whole table on every request, on every framework. That is a fair comparison (they all do the same work) but at 50 concurrent users it is mostly a measurement of Postgres. For the cleanest read of framework overhead, look at show : one indexed lookup, one JSON encode, nothing else in the way. These runs predate v3.256.0, since when a Grit list reuses its total across pages until the table is written to, so a repeat of the list row would no longer count on every request. The first draft of these numbers was much worse, and the reason was Grit's fault every time. Building a benchmark you intend to publish is an unusually good way to find out your own defaults are wrong. The scaffold shipped SetMaxIdleConns(10) alongside SetMaxOpenConns(100) . Past ten concurrent requests, a connection handed back to a full idle pool is closed , and the next request makes Postgres fork a new backend. Under load that is a connection storm, and it shows up as database CPU rather than as anything you would think to look for in the application. Single-row reads went from ~810 to ~2,720 req/s on the one-line change. Idle now defaults to Open, tunable via DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS and DB_MAX_IDLE_CONNS . getEnv treated an empty value as unset and returned the default, so the asynq worker started anyway, failed to dial, and retried in a tight loop, burning CPU on reconnects with nothing in the logs but dial errors. Setting it empty now genuinely turns cache, jobs, worker and cron off, and says so once at boot. GORM re-sent and Postgres re-planned every query. PrepareStmt is now on by default, so a query that runs a thousand times is planned once per connection. Turn it off with DB_PREPARED_STATEMENTS=false if you run pgbouncer in transaction mode, where server-side prepared statements do not survive between requests. Re-running the Bun pair afterwards is what put a number on it. Inserts went from 1,568 to 2,686 req/s on the same hardware, which took Grit from 2.09× slower than Bun to 1.23×. Bun still wins that scenario, and the withdrawn figures are gone from this page rather than left standing because they flattered the fix. A benchmark is only worth publishing if the loser was given every reasonable advantage.
pages.title: Benchmarks: Grit vs Laravel, Django, Next.js, Express, Bun and Encore.ts

headings: Blueprints and examples are different things
pages.text: A blueprint is a whole application, in its own repository, built with Grit. Not something you install: something you clone and work from. A plugin adds a feature to your project; a blueprint is a project. Two reasons, and the second one is the one that matters to you even if you never open one. The first is a starting point. If you are building a storefront, starting from a storefront beats starting from an empty project and a tutorial. The second is that each blueprint is a load test for the framework. Building a real application finds things a test suite does not, and every gap a blueprint finds is fixed in Grit first, released, and then the blueprint runs grit upgrade into it. Its code stays Grit's own rather than drifting into a fork. The storefront alone found five framework bugs in one sitting, and those fixes shipped to everybody. What you open it for Announced, not built yet. Listed because "is there a Linear blueprint?" is better answered with "not yet" than with silence. One blueprint is , once, and it stays yours. A membership covers every paid blueprint, including the ones still on the list above, for as long as it runs. Access is a GitHub invitation. Checkout asks for your username and the invitation arrives within a minute; accepting it gives you read access to the repository, so you clone it like any other. A membership that ends takes that access back, and anything already cloned stays on your machine. A single purchase is never revoked. The same numbers are in the CLI, which is the point of printing them there: grit blueprint info instagram says what it costs and links to the page that sells it. The Grit repository also carries examples/ : complete applications checked into the repo and built on every CI run. Those are free and they are there to prove the framework works and to be read. A blueprint is a bigger, designed product in a repository of its own, kept current against new releases. Both are real applications; the difference is scope and where they live.
pages.title: Blueprints

pages.text: All notable changes to Grit are documented here. Each release includes new features, bug fixes, and any breaking changes you need to be aware of. releases. Every line links to its full entry below. Earlier weeks are in the entries below, newest first. It did not. The updater downloaded the release artifact and handed it straight to update.Apply with no checksum and no signature, while the release workflow had been publishing SHA256SUMS , a cosign signature over it and the certificate all along. Everything needed to check the download existed and nothing read it. This is the first command the README suggests after install. Now, before a byte is written over the running binary: the certificate chains to Fulcio's root, pinned in the binary rather than fetched, because a trust root you download at verification time is not one; its subject is this repository's release workflow on a tag , so a run from a branch cannot sign a release; its issuer extension is GitHub's OIDC provider; the signature over the checksums verifies; the artifact's SHA-256 is one of those checksums. What is not checked, said plainly because the alternative is implying more than is true: there is no Rekor inclusion proof, so there is no trusted timestamp for the signature. Adding sigstore-go would take this CLI from 56 modules to 129, which is a poor trade in the binary whose supply chain this protects, and the property that matters is held without it: forging a signature needs Fulcio's CA key or control of this repository's release workflow. Tested against the real artifacts of the real v3.448.0 release. A genuine release verifies; tampered checksums, a signature over other content, and a self-signed certificate claiming to be the release workflow are each refused with a reason. grit update refuses a release older than the one running, because moving backwards silently is how a fixed vulnerability comes back. --version 3.440.0 installs a named release, and --allow-downgrade is how you mean it. The refusal prints the exact command. Logout revoked the server-side session only when the grit_refresh cookie was there. A browser has one; a mobile or desktop client holding a bearer token does not, so its logout cleared nothing and answered "Logged out successfully" while the session stayed usable until the idle or absolute timeout. The access token already carried its session as the sid claim and Refresh already read it; the middleware simply never passed it on. It does now, and Logout falls back to it. Measured on a running project: GET /auth/me answers 200 before a bearer-only logout and 401 with the same token after it. The CSRF cookie set its Secure flag from c.Request.TLS alone while every auth cookie honoured X-Forwarded-Proto . Behind the usual TLS-terminating proxy that left the double-submit token as the one cookie without Secure . Four places, not the one reported. CORS now sets Vary: Origin , before the allow decision rather than inside it, because a refusal is also a response that varies by origin. That second one would have switched the URL cache off for every response at once, silently: shareableResponse refuses to store anything whose Vary names a header its key does not include, which is correct. It is safe to cache here for a specific reason, not a general one: a cache hit replays the status, the content type and the body and nothing else, so the origin-dependent header is written per request by middleware that runs ahead of the cache on a hit as well as a miss. The test asserts that replay stays header-free, and says to take the exception back out if it ever does not. SilenceUsage was set inside nine individual command bodies, which is too late for anything that fails before reaching the line. The sentence worth reading landed under twenty lines of flags. It is set on the root now, and a genuine usage error gets a one-line pointer after the message instead of the table before it. #141 . The multitenant plugin resolves the active organization from X-Organization-ID , and nothing in a generated client ever set it. A user who belongs to one organization is fine, because the middleware activates it automatically. A user who belongs to two had no way to choose, which is the case the plugin exists for. The admin gets a switcher now. It renders nothing at all below two organizations: a control offering one choice is furniture that implies a decision nobody has, and a single-tenant project looks exactly as it did. lib/active-org.ts and the api-core interceptor ship in every project, with or without the plugin, and send nothing until something sets a value. That split is deliberate: api-client.ts is rewritten by every upgrade, so a plugin that injected the header into it would make the file read as the developer's own edit. The injection would survive and the file would stop receiving the fixes that actually matter in it, which are CSRF, token refresh and the 401 retry. It is in api-core.ts specifically, which the admin and the web app share. One writer, two consumers. An invalidated query serves its old data while it refetches, and that data belongs to the organization being left: React Query would go on rendering one tenant's rows under another tenant's name. Showing a spinner is better. And a stored id for an organization the reader no longer belongs to is dropped when the list comes back without it. A membership can be revoked while the id sits in a browser; sending it then means every request carries an organization the API refuses, and the reader sees an app that is broken rather than one that moved them back. The hook called /organizations , and versionedPath only rewrites a path that starts with /api/ , so the request went to the host root and answered 404. It compiled, tsc --noEmit passed, and six new tests passed. The browser did not. There is a seventh test now. Verified end to end in a browser against a running project: the switcher appears with two organizations and not with one, switching changes the labe

pages.description: Understand Grit architecture: monorepo layout, Go API with handler-service-model pattern, Next.js frontend, shared types, and code generation.
pages.text: Grit is a full-stack monorepo that fuses a Go backend with Next.js frontends, a shared type package, and an admin panel. This page explains how all the layers fit together. Every Grit project is a Turborepo-powered monorepo managed by pnpm. The Go API lives alongside the Next.js frontends and a shared TypeScript package. This structure allows all apps to share validation schemas, types, and constants from a single source of truth. Turborepo handles parallel builds and caching across apps. The pnpm-workspace.yaml file links the frontend apps to the shared package, so importing @shared/schemas works without publishing to npm. The following diagram shows how the layers communicate. The browser talks to the Next.js frontends, which talk to the Go API over REST. The Go API manages the database, cache, file storage, job queue, and email. The backend is a Go application built with Gin (HTTP router) and GORM (ORM). It follows a layered architecture: routes register handlers, handlers call services, and services interact with the database through GORM models. Handlers are thin -- they parse HTTP requests, call a service method, and return a JSON response. All business logic, database queries, and validation live in the service layer. This separation makes code testable and reusable. Every request passes through a middleware chain before reaching a handler. Grit ships with four built-in middleware layers: The Go API organizes routes into three groups with different levels of authentication and authorization: When the code generator creates a new resource, it automatically injects CRUD routes into the protected group (list, get, create, update) and the delete route into the admin group. Both the web app and admin panel are Next.js 16+ applications using the App Router. They share the same data-fetching pattern: React Query hooks call the Go API through an Axios-based API client that automatically injects JWT tokens. The main customer-facing frontend. Ships with authentication pages (login, register, forgot-password), a protected dashboard layout with a sidebar, and React Query hooks for data fetching. Styled with Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui components. A Filament-inspired admin dashboard. Developers define resources in TypeScript (columns, form fields, filters, actions) and get full CRUD pages with data tables, forms, and dashboard widgets. The admin panel features: All API communication flows through React Query hooks. Components never call fetch or Axios directly. This ensures consistent caching, background refetching, loading states, and cache invalidation on mutations. The packages/shared directory is the bridge between the Go backend and the TypeScript frontends. It contains three categories of shared code: When you run grit generate resource or grit sync , these files are auto-generated from your Go models, keeping the frontend in sync with the backend. Here is the complete path of a typical authenticated API request, from the user clicking a button to the data appearing on screen: GORM Studio is a full-featured visual database browser and editor embedded directly into the Go API. It mounts at /studio and gives you a web UI to browse, query, import/export data, generate Go models, and inspect your database tables. All registered GORM models appear automatically. When you generate a new resource, the CLI automatically injects the model into the GORM Studio mount call using the marker. See the Database page for full GORM Studio documentation. All API endpoints follow a consistent JSON response format. This predictability allows React Query hooks and error handlers to work generically across every resource. Grit uses JWT (JSON Web Tokens) for authentication. The flow works as follows: Docker Compose provides all the infrastructure services needed for local development. In production, you can swap these for managed services (e.g., AWS RDS for PostgreSQL, ElastiCache for Redis, S3 for file storage).

pages.description: API-only architecture in Grit: pure Go backend with no frontend. All batteries included (auth, storage, email, jobs, AI). Perfect for mobile backends and microservices.
headings: API Only Architecture: Headless Go Backend
pages.text: Architecture Modes The leanest architecture Grit offers. Pure Go API with no frontend, no React, no Node.js. Your API docs page is the primary interface. The API-only architecture strips away everything except the Go backend. There is no React, no TypeScript, no Node.js, no pnpm, no Turborepo. You get a clean Go API that serves JSON endpoints and auto-generated API documentation at /docs . Test your endpoints with curl, Postman, or the built-in Scalar/Swagger UI. Despite being the smallest architecture, it still includes every backend battery: authentication (JWT + OAuth), file storage (S3), email (Resend), background jobs (asynq), cron scheduling, Redis caching, AI integration, and TOTP two-factor auth. You get the full Go API -- you just bring your own frontend. The project contains just the Go API inside apps/api/ plus root-level config files. No frontend directories, no packages directory, no TypeScript configuration. Three separate entry points for different operations. cmd/server/main.go starts the API server. cmd/migrate/main.go runs GORM AutoMigrate to apply schema changes. cmd/seed/main.go populates the database with initial data (admin user, sample records). Identical to every other Grit architecture. The handler-service-model pattern, middleware stack, mail templates, storage abstraction, job queue, cache layer, and AI integration are all present. The only difference is that no frontend code exists alongside it. The AI skill file is tailored for the API-only architecture. It contains no frontend rules, no React patterns, and no TypeScript conventions. This makes AI assistants more effective because they only see relevant Go patterns. No frontend key. The CLI knows to skip all frontend file generation when it reads this config. Running grit generate resource in an API-only project creates only Go files. No Zod schemas, no TypeScript types, no React hooks, no admin pages. Example: grit generate resource Post --fields "title:string,body:text,published:bool" creates 4 Go files (model, service, handler, and a <name>_import.go handler) and injects routes -- that's it. Every API-only project ships with these endpoints out of the box, before you generate any resources. With no frontend, the data flow is straightforward. Clients send HTTP requests directly to the Go API. Development is simpler than any other architecture -- just one terminal for the Go server. Deploy the Go binary with Docker or directly. No frontend build step needed. - Mobile app backends (iOS/Android consume your API) - Microservices in a larger system - Headless CMS or content API - Third-party integrations and webhooks - Frontend built by a different team or in a different repo - Projects that need an admin panel (use triple or double) - Full-stack apps where you want React scaffolded too - Teams that want shared TypeScript types from the same repo The Job Portal example built with the API-only architecture. Includes all endpoints, Docker setup, seed data, and API documentation.
pages.title: API Only Architecture: Headless Go Backend

pages.description: Streamlined Turborepo monorepo with 2 apps (web + API). Admin features live as role-protected routes in the web app. Best for blogs, portfolios, and simpler SaaS applications.
pages.text: Architecture Modes A streamlined Turborepo monorepo with two applications: a public-facing web app and a Go API. Admin features live inside the web app as role-protected routes instead of a separate application. Double architecture drops the separate admin application and gives you a two-app monorepo. The Go API handles all backend logic (authentication, CRUD, file uploads, jobs), and a single frontend serves both regular users and administrators. Admin functionality is implemented through role-protected routes within the web app , users with the ADMIN role see additional navigation items and have access to management pages. - Projects where admins and users share the same interface with extra privileges - Blogs, portfolios, and content sites where the author manages content inline - Simpler SaaS applications where admin features are minimal (user management, settings) - MERN/MEAN stack developers transitioning to Go who want a familiar two-app structure - Teams that want fewer apps to deploy and maintain - No apps/admin/ directory , the admin panel is a route group inside the web app instead, at /admin/dashboard , with its own layout and all the same screens (v3.235.0) - Resource definitions live in the web app , defineResource() files land in apps/web/admin-panel/resources/ , and the DataTable and FormBuilder work exactly as they do in a triple - One app to run and deploy , one Next.js process serves your pages and the panel. The panel guards itself: its layout redirects anybody who is not signed in, and sends a plain USER role to their profile rather than the dashboard - grit generate writes the admin screens too , the list and detail pages land at apps/web/app/admin/(dashboard)/resources/<name>/ and the resource appears in the sidebar, the same as in a triple - Either frontend , --next puts the panel in a route group at app/admin/ ; --vite puts it in the TanStack router at src/routes/admin/ , with its code behind @admin . Same screens, same URLs (v3.239.0) - Three layouts, one app , the root layout is the document alone. app/(marketing)/ is the public site with the navbar and footer, app/admin/ the panel with its sidebar, and app/(app)/ the signed-in customer area at /account. Route groups, so no URL changes (v3.237.0) - Simpler deployment , 2 apps instead of 3, fewer Docker images, less infrastructure This is the full tree generated by grit new myapp --double --vite . Compare it with the triple structure , the apps/admin/ directory is absent, and the web app gains role-protected admin routes. The root configuration is nearly identical to triple. The key difference is in grit.json which stores , telling the CLI to skip admin-specific file generation. Identical to the triple architecture. Contains Zod schemas, TypeScript types, and shared constants. The only difference is that there is one consumer (web) instead of two (web + admin). The marker comments and injection system work the same way. The Go API is identical to the triple architecture. It uses the same handler-service-model pattern, the same middleware stack, the same batteries (cache, storage, email, jobs, cron, AI). The only difference is that the CORS middleware is configured to allow a single frontend origin instead of two. In double architecture, the web app serves double duty. Public pages are accessible to everyone, while admin routes are protected by role checks. The navigation dynamically shows admin links (e.g., "Users", "Settings") only when the logged-in user has the ADMIN role. The backend also enforces role checks via the RequireRole("ADMIN") middleware on admin API routes, so the frontend check is for UX only , not a security boundary. The double architecture has a simpler data flow with a single frontend talking to the API. Admin and user requests follow the same path , the only difference is the role attached to the JWT token. In double architecture, grit generate creates fewer files compared to triple because there is no admin panel to scaffold into. The Go backend files and shared types are identical , the difference is the absence of admin resource definitions and admin pages. - internal/models/product.go , GORM model with struct tags, belongs_to relationship - internal/services/product_service.go , CRUD operations with pagination - internal/handlers/product.go , Gin handlers: Create, GetAll, GetByID, Update, Delete - schemas/product.ts , Zod schemas: CreateProductSchema , UpdateProductSchema - types/product.ts , TypeScript interface: Product - hooks/use-products.ts , React Query hooks: useProducts() , useProduct(id) , useCreateProduct() , useUpdateProduct() , useDeleteProduct() - resources/products.ts , No admin resource definition - app/(dashboard)/products/page.tsx , No auto-generated admin page with DataTable and FormBuilder To manage products as an admin in double architecture, you build the management UI yourself inside the src/routes/(admin)/ route group, using the generated React Query hooks and shared types. Double uses 5 marker injections instead of 6 (no admin resource marker). With one fewer frontend, the port layout is simpler. No port 3001 is occupied. Deploying double is simpler than triple , two containers instead of three, one frontend domain instead of two. The production Docker Compose file builds the Go API and the web app as optimized images. With only 2 app containers, resource usage is lower and the configuration is simpler. Works the same as triple , grit deploy reads the grit.json manifest to determine which apps to build and deploy. With double architecture, it skips the admin container entirely. Deploy the web app (Next.js) to Vercel and the Go API to a VPS. Simpler than triple because you only have one Vercel project to configure instead of two. Set NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL in Vercel to point to your API server. If you chose --vite , the web app builds to static files that can be served from any CDN (Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, S3 + CloudFront). The Go API is the only server-side compo

pages.description: Mobile architecture in Grit: Go API paired with Expo React Native in a Turborepo monorepo. SecureStore for tokens, Expo Router for navigation, shared types between backend and mobile.
headings: Mobile Architecture: API + Expo React Native
Working screens, then make them yours
pages.text: Architecture Modes Go API paired with an Expo React Native app in a Turborepo monorepo. Shared types between backend and mobile, with encrypted token storage and file-based navigation. The mobile architecture gives you a Go backend and an Expo React Native app inside a Turborepo monorepo. Types and schemas are shared through a packages/shared/ directory, just like the double and triple architectures. The mobile app uses Expo Router for file-based navigation (similar to Next.js App Router but for native screens) and SecureStore for encrypted token storage. The Go API is identical to every other architecture -- same handler-service-model pattern, same batteries, same code generation. The difference is on the client side: instead of a web browser, your users interact with a native iOS/Android app. A Turborepo monorepo with the Go API in apps/api/ , the Expo app in apps/expo/ , and shared types in packages/shared/ . Identical to every other Grit architecture. The full Go backend with Gin router, GORM models, handler-service-model pattern, and all batteries (auth, storage, email, jobs, cache, AI). The API does not know or care whether the client is a web browser or a mobile app -- it just serves JSON over REST. The Expo app uses the managed workflow with Expo Router for file-based navigation. Screens live in the app/ directory and follow the same conventions as Next.js App Router: _layout.tsx for layout wrappers, group folders like (tabs)/ for navigation groups, and regular .tsx files for individual screens. The tab group provides the main navigation structure. The _layout.tsx inside this folder defines the tab bar with icons. Each file becomes a tab: index.tsx is Home, profile.tsx is Profile, and settings.tsx is Settings. Zod schemas and TypeScript interfaces shared between the API types (via grit sync ) and the Expo app. Import with @shared/schemas or @shared/types from anywhere in the monorepo. On the web, JWT tokens are stored in localStorage . On mobile, this is insecure because any app with root access can read localStorage. Expo provides expo-secure-store , which uses the iOS Keychain and Android Keystore to encrypt tokens at rest. On the web, localhost:8080 works fine because the browser and the API are on the same machine. On a physical mobile device, localhost refers to the phone itself, not your development machine. You need to use your machine's local IP address instead. On the iOS simulator and Android emulator, you can use localhost (iOS) or 10.0.2.2 (Android emulator). But on a real device connected via USB or Wi-Fi, use the machine's local IP. Mobile apps use different UI patterns than web apps. Here are the key differences in the Expo scaffold. React Native doesn't have or . Data lists use FlatList which virtualizes rendering for performance -- only visible items are rendered. The tab bar is the primary navigation pattern on mobile. Expo Router makes this declarative with a (tabs)/ group folder. Expo Notifications provides a unified API for push notifications on both iOS and Android. Register the device's push token with your Go API, then send notifications from the backend using Expo's push service. This is useful for real-time alerts, chat messages, order updates, and marketing notifications. Running grit generate resource in a mobile project scaffolds the full stack , Go backend, shared TypeScript types, and a working set of Expo Router screens (list, detail, create, edit) plus a typed React Query hook and a form component. You get a functioning CRUD flow on the device immediately, then style it to taste. The generated Expo screens are real, navigable, and wired to the API through the typed hook , a full create/read/update/delete flow the moment you generate the resource. They're a starting point, not a cage: restyle the FlatList , swap components, or rework the form in resource-forms/posts-form.tsx , the shared types keep everything in sync with the backend. Expo provides two ways to distribute your app: EAS Build for full native builds (submitted to App Store / Google Play), and OTA updates for JavaScript-only changes that skip the app store review process. For JavaScript-only changes (bug fixes, UI tweaks, new screens), you can push updates directly to users without going through the app store review process. The Go API is deployed separately using Docker, the same as the API-only architecture. - Mobile-first products (social, delivery, fitness, etc.) - Cross-platform apps (one codebase for iOS + Android) - Apps that need push notifications, camera, GPS - Teams that know React and want to build native apps - Apps where the primary interface is a phone - Web-first apps (use double or triple instead) - Apps that need both web and mobile (add web to this scaffold later) - Games or heavy GPU apps (use Unity or native SDKs) - Projects that need an admin panel (add admin app separately) The Job Portal example built with the mobile architecture. Includes the Go API, Expo app with tab navigation, SecureStore auth, shared types, and EAS build config.

pages.description: Combine --desktop with other flags to scaffold a shared-API multi-client SaaS. One Go backend serving Expo mobile and Wails desktop, with optional web and admin. The Linear / Notion / Slack pattern.
headings: The command that started it all
2. Mobile + desktop with a marketing site
What Ships in the Desktop App
pages.text: Architecture Modes One Go API serving an Expo mobile app AND a Wails desktop app -- all in a single monorepo with shared types. The pattern real SaaS products use (Linear, Notion, Slack). Added in v3.9.0 via the --desktop flag. The multi-client pattern combines a Go API with two or more native clients (mobile via Expo, desktop via Wails, optionally web via Next.js or TanStack). All clients share the same packages/shared/ types and schemas, and all talk to the same API over HTTP. No code duplication across clients. This isn't a separate architecture mode -- it's a --desktop flag you combine with an existing architecture ( --mobile , --triple , --double , or --api ). Scaffolds: Go API + Next.js web + admin panel + Expo mobile + Wails desktop, all in one monorepo, all sharing types. Pick the multi-client pattern when you're building a product that needs to live in multiple places: Native apps AND a web presence -- e.g. a Slack-style team tool with desktop, mobile, and a browser fallback A mobile-first product that also needs a power-user desktop app -- e.g. a task manager like Things or Linear Any product where customers expect to pick up where they left off across phone and laptop -- e.g. chat apps, note-takers, calendars Enterprise tools where clients specifically request a native desktop installer instead of a browser tab Don't use this for simple SaaS apps where a browser-only experience is enough -- stick with --triple . Don't use it for offline-first desktop apps either -- use grit new-desktop instead (standalone Wails + embedded Go + local SQLite). These are two different desktop patterns. Pick the one that matches your product: The --desktop flag combines with every architecture mode except --single (single apps already bundle their own frontend). Here are the common setups: Scaffolds: apps/api , apps/web , apps/admin , apps/desktop , plus packages/shared . You get a web marketing site, an admin dashboard for ops, and a native desktop app -- all sharing one API. Scaffolds everything above PLUS apps/expo . This is the full Slack / Notion setup: every client surface. Scaffolds apps/api , apps/expo , apps/desktop . Good for products that are native-only (no marketing page yet). Scaffolds apps/api and apps/desktop . The leanest multi-client setup. Single-app architectures already bundle their own SPA into one Go binary. Adding a separate desktop client would be redundant. Use --triple or --api if you want a desktop app. The shape of grit new myapp --triple --next --desktop --mobile : The key insight: packages/shared is the glue. Change a Zod schema there and both the Expo app and the desktop app pick it up immediately. Change a Go model, run grit sync , and the TypeScript types regenerate for every client. With all apps running, you get live hot-reload across everything. One grit start runs them all, or start each app on its own: Or start a single app from anywhere in the project: The three client patterns (web, mobile, desktop) use the same primitives but with platform-appropriate adapters: The useAuth hook signature is identical across all three: useMe() , useLogin() , useRegister() , useLogout() . Only the adapter (where tokens get stored) differs. Copy a feature from web to desktop and the structure stays the same. The Wails desktop scaffold is intentionally minimal on the Go side and rich on the React side. Go handles only what the browser can't: window chrome, file dialogs, and OS keychain. Everything else lives in the React frontend and calls the API. main.go -- Wails bootstrap, frameless 1280x800 window (min 1000x700) app.go -- Native bindings: window controls, file dialogs, keychain, platform detection internal/keychain.go -- Cross-platform keychain via 99designs/keyring Custom title bar with platform-aware window controls (macOS traffic lights on the left, Windows/Linux controls on the right) Command palette ( Cmd+K / Ctrl+K ) with keyboard-first navigation Fixed 240px sidebar (not collapsible -- desktop windows are wide enough) Topbar with search, notifications, theme toggle, user menu Pre-built auth flow (login / register / forgot-password) using react-hook-form + zod Dashboard, Profile, Settings pages out of the box Global keyboard shortcuts via useShortcuts() Add your own with the useShortcuts() hook: Each client ships differently. The shared API is deployed once, and the clients point to it: Cross-compiles, uploads via SCP, configures systemd + Caddy with auto-TLS. Code-sign and notarize as needed (macOS) or sign with a certificate (Windows). Distribute as standalone binaries, via a download page, or through app stores. Set VITE_API_URL in the desktop frontend's env when deploying. In dev, Vite proxies /api to localhost:8080 , but once built, the frontend needs to know the full production URL. CORS matters again. Native clients don't enforce CORS the way browsers do, but your API still needs to allow the desktop origin if you proxy through one. Usually fine with Grit's default CORS middleware; check if you customize. Keep Wails bindings minimal. Resist the urge to expose CRUD methods as Wails bindings -- it creates a second API surface to maintain. Do data work over HTTP, use bindings only for window/file/keychain. Dev without Wails. You can run the desktop frontend in a regular browser with cd apps/desktop/frontend && pnpm dev (it falls back to HttpOnly cookies set by the dev API). Useful for quick UI iteration without launching the full Wails window. Tokens are never written to localStorage in either mode. Match platform expectations. macOS users expect traffic lights on the left; Windows/Linux users expect close/min/max on the right. The scaffold handles this automatically via getPlatform() . Read the style guide. GRIT_STYLE_GUIDE.md §14.5 covers desktop-specific patterns: no breadcrumbs, no collapsible sidebar, 32px content padding (vs web's 24px), tighter focus rings, OS keychain only -- never localStorage. Triple architecture -- the base you'll usually combine --des

pages.description: Single architecture in Grit: one Go binary serves both API and embedded React frontend via go:embed. Flat project structure, no monorepo, simplest deployment.
headings: Or the same thing with Next.js
pages.text: Architecture Modes One Go binary serves both the API and the frontend. No monorepo tooling, no separate deployments. Build it, ship one file, done. The single architecture is the most different from the other Grit modes. Instead of a Turborepo monorepo with separate apps, you get a flat project where a single Go binary serves both the REST API and the compiled React frontend using go:embed . Think of it like Laravel or an embedded Next.js app -- one deployment unit that handles everything. There is no Turborepo, no pnpm-workspace.yaml , no turbo.json . The Go module path is just myapp (not myapp/apps/api ). Schemas and types live directly in frontend/src/ -- there is no pnpm workspace, so no shared package. One SPA, four sections, each with a layout of its own: routes/_site is the public site with the navbar and footer, routes/admin the panel, routes/_auth the sign-in pages and routes/account the signed-in customer area. The names starting with an underscore are pathless, so none of this changes a URL. Run grit add web-auth to get the last two: login, registration, password reset, and an account dashboard behind them (v3.238.0). The admin panel is in there too, as a section of the same SPA at /admin/dashboard (v3.236.0). Same dashboard, resource CRUD, system hub, settings and account security a three-app project has: 35 screens, its own layout and sidebar, and the site's navbar steps aside for it. One binary still serves all of it. --single --next gives you everything on this page with Next.js in place of Vite, and it is one binary too. Next builds with output: "export" , the export is copied into api/web , and the binary embeds it exactly as it embeds the Vite build. One thing differs, and it is visible in the URLs. An export has to have a file for every address it serves, and a dynamic segment cannot be built: its values are rows in a database the build never sees. So a record is at /resources/users/view?id=... rather than /resources/users/123 . Same screen, same component, a URL the build can produce. The Vite single keeps path segments, because a SPA resolves them in the browser. There is also no middleware.ts : an export has no server to run one. The panel's own auth redirects a signed-out visitor, and every endpoint behind it is checked by the API, which is the check that matters. The entire project is flat. Go code lives in internal/ , The app owns the project root, the way a Vite or Next.js project is laid out anywhere else, and the Go API sits in api/ with its own go.mod. Open the folder and it is a web project with a Go API beside it, which is what it has always been. The root main.go file is where everything starts. It uses Go's embed package to bundle the compiled frontend into the Go binary. In production, this means you get a single executable that can serve both the API and the static frontend files. Need just the Go API? Use grit start server . The generated Makefile also exposes the same workflow if you prefer make : The Vite config proxies API requests so the frontend can call /api/users without worrying about CORS or port differences during development. Building for production is a two-step process: build the frontend, then build the Go binary. The Go compiler embeds the compiled frontend assets into the binary at compile time. No Node.js runtime needed on the production server. No npm install , no pnpm , no build tools. Just the binary and your environment variables. When you run grit generate resource in a single-architecture project, the CLI creates files in different locations compared to the monorepo architectures. With no packages/shared/ to publish to, the generated hook declares its own Post interface inline rather than importing one -- a single-binary app has exactly one consumer, so there is nothing to keep in sync. Deploying a single-architecture app is as simple as it gets. You only need to transfer two files to your server: the compiled binary and your .env file. - Solo developers who want the simplest deploy story - Laravel or Rails developers who like one-app-does-everything - Internal tools and admin dashboards - Microservices where each service has its own UI - Apps where SSR and SEO are not critical (SPA is fine) - SEO-heavy public sites that need server-side rendering - Large teams that need separate frontend and backend deploys - Teams that deploy the admin panel separately from the app, on its own domain or behind its own network rules (use triple) - Apps that share types with multiple frontend clients The Job Portal example built with the single architecture demonstrates all the patterns described above: go:embed, Vite proxy, TanStack Router, and production Dockerfile.
pages.title: Single Architecture: One Binary

pages.description: The default and most feature-rich Grit architecture. Turborepo monorepo with 3 apps (web, admin, API) sharing types via packages/shared. Best for SaaS, marketplaces, and content platforms.
headings: Step-by-step for a typical API call
Shared types keep everything in sync
pages.text: Architecture Modes The default and most feature-rich architecture mode. A Turborepo monorepo with three applications (web, admin, api) sharing types and validation through a shared package. Triple is the default architecture when you run grit new . It scaffolds a Turborepo monorepo containing three applications that communicate through a shared TypeScript package and a REST API. The Go backend serves as the single source of truth for data and authentication, while the two frontends serve distinct audiences: the web app faces your end users, and the admin panel provides a Filament-like dashboard for managing resources, viewing analytics, and configuring the system. - SaaS products with distinct admin operations (user management, billing, analytics) - Marketplaces where sellers/admins need a separate interface from buyers - Content platforms (CMS, LMS, blog networks) where editors manage content separately - Multi-tenant applications requiring tenant administration - Any project that benefits from a dedicated admin panel with DataTable, FormBuilder, and dashboard widgets This is the full, unabbreviated tree that grit new myapp --triple --next generates. Every file and directory is listed with its purpose. The monorepo root contains configuration files that apply to all applications. The grit.json manifest tells the CLI which architecture mode and frontend framework the project uses, so commands like grit generate know exactly which files to create. The shared package is the bridge between frontend applications. Both web and admin import from it to ensure consistent validation and types. When you run grit generate , new schemas and types are injected here automatically via marker comments. The Go API follows a strict handler-service-model pattern. Handlers are thin HTTP layers that parse requests and call services. Services contain business logic and GORM queries. Models define the database schema. This separation makes the codebase testable and maintainable. The web application is what your end users interact with. It consumes the Go API via React Query hooks and validates form inputs using the Zod schemas from the shared package. With Next.js, pages can be server-rendered for SEO. With TanStack Router (Vite), the app is a client-side SPA served as static files. The admin panel is a Filament-inspired dashboard with runtime resource definitions. It provides DataTable (sorting, filtering, pagination, row selection), FormBuilder (31 field types), multi-step forms, dashboard widgets, and system administration pages. Resources are defined declaratively using defineResource() and the admin automatically generates CRUD pages from those definitions. The single source of truth shared by the web app and the admin panel: TypeScript types, Zod validation schemas, shared theme tokens, and API route constants. When your Go structs change, grit sync regenerates the TypeScript types here, so both frontends stay in lock-step with the API , no drift, no hand-maintained duplicate interfaces. Every scaffolded project includes an AI skill file tailored to its architecture mode. The skill teaches Claude Code (or any LLM) the project conventions, folder structure, naming rules, available CLI commands, and code markers. This means AI assistants can generate correct Grit code without additional context. The following diagram shows how a typical request flows through the triple architecture, from the user's browser all the way to the database and back. User clicks "Save" in the admin panel form (or the web app) React Query mutation fires a POST request to /api/v3/products with the JWT in the Authorization header Gin router matches the route and passes the request through the middleware stack CORS middleware validates the origin. Rate limiter checks the IP. Auth middleware extracts and verifies the JWT, injecting the user into the Gin context. The CreateProduct handler parses the JSON body using Gin's binding tags for validation Handler calls productService.Create() which runs the GORM insert query Service returns the created product. Handler responds with 201 Created and the standard JSON envelope React Query invalidates the products list query, triggering a background refetch of the table data The Go model struct tags define the API contract. When you run grit generate , matching Zod schemas and TypeScript types are created in packages/shared/ . Both the web and admin apps import from the same package, so a type change in Go propagates to both frontends via grit sync . When you run a generate command, Grit creates files across all three applications and the shared package, then injects import statements and route registrations into existing files using marker comments. - internal/models/product.go , GORM model with struct tags, belongs_to relationship to Category - internal/services/product_service.go , CRUD operations with pagination, preloaded relationships - internal/handlers/product.go , Gin handlers: Create, GetAll, GetByID, Update, Delete - schemas/product.ts , Zod schemas: CreateProductSchema , UpdateProductSchema - types/product.ts , TypeScript interface: Product - resources/products.ts , Resource definition with columns, filters, search config, form fields - app/(dashboard)/products/page.tsx , Admin page with DataTable and FormBuilder, ready to use - hooks/use-products.ts , React Query hooks: useProducts() , useProduct(id) , useCreateProduct() , useUpdateProduct() , useDeleteProduct() In addition to creating new files, the generator injects code into 6 existing files using marker comments. This is how routes get registered, imports get added, and types get re-exported , without manual wiring. During development, all services run on different ports. The CORS middleware in the Go API is configured to allow requests from all frontend origins. Triple architecture supports multiple deployment strategies depending on your infrastructure preferences and scale requirements. The scaffolded docker-compose.prod.yml

pages.description: Which architecture style Grit is: a modular monolith with a layered Go API, an in-process event bus, a transactional outbox and sagas. Which styles it deliberately is not, and what it costs to refactor a Grit project from one style to another.
headings: The one rule the layering exists for
The whole wheel, segment by segment
Why Grit is organised by layer and not by feature
What feature folders buy, and Grit gives up
What Grit buys back: the entity graph
One thing worth taking from it either way
Can you refactor from one style to another?
The seams, if you are planning to split
What a heavy refactor costs you with the generator
If you are choosing a style for a new product
The same argument, in a talk
pages.text: Which of the named architecture styles Grit actually is, which ones it deliberately is not, and what it costs to move a Grit project from one to another. Written because both questions get asked in the same breath. A word with two jobs. In Grit, architecture normally means the project shape you pick with --architecture : single, double, triple, api or mobile. This page is about something else: the architecture style the code inside is written in. A modular monolith with a layered API and an in-process event bus. One binary, one database, around fifty internal packages, and a domain event bus that lets the audit log, outbound webhooks and realtime clients subscribe to a write rather than be called by it. That is the honest headline, and it is also slightly misleading, because no real system is one style. Styles compose. A Grit project is running six of them at once, each in the place where it earns its keep. Handlers are thin on purpose. A handler reads the request, calls one service method and writes the answer. Every database read and write for a resource lives in that resource's service, and every service method takes a context.Context rather than a *gin.Context . The payoff is not tidiness. It is that a rule enforced in the service is enforced in the background job, the CLI command, the import, the export and the test, not only on the HTTP route. A rule written in a handler is a rule that holds until the first time something other than a browser does the same thing. The question usually arrives with a chart attached: the one with twenty-seven styles arranged in a circle. Here is Grit's position on every segment of it, so whichever one you are pointing at has an answer. Three of the answers are partly , and that is the honest one more often than either of the others. Most styles are not a thing a system is or is not: they are a thing a system does in one place and not another. This is the question that follows the one above, and it is a better question. Package-by-feature, a folder per noun with that noun's model, rules and storage inside it, is the layout most Go teams land on, and it is taught as the end state of the tour for good reasons. Grit does not do it. Here is the trade, stated honestly, because it is a real one. ))} What feature folders buy, and Grit gives up A feature is a folder. Everything about an invoice is in one place and nothing else is, you can delete a feature by deleting a directory, and the root stops growing a package every time a new technology arrives. Grit pays for not having this: at forty resources, services/ is forty files and the directory no longer tells you which three of them form a subsystem. That cost is real and it arrives exactly when the codebase is big enough to need the help. The examples that make feature folders look obvious have two or three domains with a clean one-way reference. A business application has thirty entities with a dense graph: an invoice points at a customer, which points at an organisation, which points back at users who raised invoices. Go forbids import cycles. So the moment customer needs to refer back to invoice , feature folders force you into an event announcement or an interface dance to express what is really just a foreign key. That is the correct answer when two domains must stay independent, and it is a lot of machinery for invoice.customer_id . Grit's thirty-odd models are one flat package models . Any model can reference any other with no ceremony, which is the thing that lets client:belongs_to be a single word in a generate command rather than a design conversation. The layout is not laziness; it is what buys the generator its simplicity. The rule still bites in the other direction, and it is worth knowing before you go looking for it: models cannot import services , so a hook on a model calls the lower-level package directly rather than the service that wraps it. Feature folders are the better default for an application a team writes by hand, with a handful of genuinely independent domains. Layer folders are the better default for a generated application with a dense entity graph, because one command has to know where every file goes and the entities all point at each other. Those are different problems, and the layouts are not competing for the same job. If your application really is a few independent domains, package-by-feature is a good choice and Grit is the wrong tool, which is a better thing to find out now than in month three. The strongest idea in the feature-folder literature is not the folders. It is that a dependency should be declared by the code that uses it and named for what it needs, rather than taken whole: a two-method interface instead of somebody else's four-method one. That is right in every layout, Grit included. It is worth being precise about where it pays, because the obvious application of it here does not. A generated handler calls ten of its service's ten exported methods, so a "narrow" interface in front of that service would be a verbatim copy of the service: the same thing written twice, which is the cost the idea exists to avoid. Grit does not generate one, on purpose. Where it does pay is the weaker form of the same rule: do not reach around a thing to rebuild what it already knows. The blog list handler used to skip its service and query the database directly, re-typing the search clause the service already had, so the list and the stat cards above it held two definitions of the same search in two different files. Add a searchable column to one and they disagree. The service now states that search once and exposes it as CountQuery , which the handler asks for by name. Shipped in v3.403.0. The lesson generalises better than the interface does. Count how many methods the caller actually uses before you narrow something, and spend the effort instead on the places where a consumer has quietly grown its own copy of a rule. Package-by-feature is often called domain-driven, and the fo Styles in use: Modular monolith | The whole API: one binary, one deployment, around fifty internal packages. | One process removes every distributed-systems failure mode from a product that does not yet have the traffic to need them. // Layered (n-tier) | routes to handlers to services to models. | The service owns the rules and every database call, so a job, a CLI command and a test get the same rules as the HTTP route. // Event-driven, in process | internal/events. A write emits once; audit, webhooks and realtime subscribe. | The handler does not have to remember to call three systems, so adding a fourth does not mean editing every handler. // Transactional outbox | internal/outbox, behind the bus Durable delivery mode. | The event is queued in the same transaction as the write, so a crash between the commit and the HTTP call loses nothing. // Orchestration (saga) | internal/saga, for work that spans modules and can half fail. | The sequence and its compensation are readable in one place, which is the thing choreography gives up. // Microkernel / plug-in | The framework itself: grit plugin add. | Capabilities that only some projects want are not carried by the ones that do not. Not this: Microservices | A split is worth paying for when teams need to release independently. Until then it buys network failures, eventual consistency and a deployment pipeline, in exchange for nothing. // CQRS and event sourcing | Both earn their complexity in a hot spot, not across a codebase. The read path is already separate enough to point at another store when one query needs it. // Hexagonal / ports and adapters | The generated service talks to GORM directly rather than through a port. That is a deliberate trade: less indirection to read, at the cost of swapping the ORM being a real job. // Serverless | Background jobs, a scheduler, realtime connections and a warm connection pool all assume a process that stays up. Refactors: Add CQRS to one endpoint | Hours | Yes | good | The read path is already a separate whitelist of searchable, sortable and filterable columns. Point one list query at a denormalised table or a read replica and leave every other endpoint alone. This is the refactor that is almost always the right one, because it is local and reversible. // Extract one module into its own service | Weeks | Yes, with care | good | The service layer is the seam: it is already the only thing that touches the database for its resource, and it already takes a context rather than a request. Replace the in-process call with an HTTP client and give the new service its own schema. What makes it expensive is not the code, it is the foreign keys you have to cut. // Go fully hexagonal inside the monolith | Weeks, and it keeps costing | Possible, rarely worth it | warn | Putting a port in front of every service is mechanical. The ongoing cost is that the generator keeps writing the un-ported version, so every generate is followed by a hand edit and every upgrade reports a conflict. If you want this shape, the honest answer is that Grit is fighting you. // Split into microservices across the board | Months | Only with a reason | warn | The reason should be organisational: separate teams with separate release cadences, or one module whose scaling profile is nothing like the rest. "It will scale better" is not a reason on its own, and a modular monolith on one large machine outruns most products for years. // Move to event sourcing | A rewrite of the write path | No, not as a refactor | bad | Current state stops being a row and becomes a fold over events, which changes every read, every migration and every admin screen. The append-only audit log is not a head start on this: it records what happened for a reviewer, it is not the source the state is rebuilt from. // Collapse existing microservices into Grit | Weeks | Yes, and often the right direction | good | Easier than the reverse and more common than people admit. Each service becomes a package with its own services and models, cross-service HTTP calls become function calls, and the events between them become bus subscriptions. Layouts: By layer | What Grit generates | internal/ ├── models/ │ ├── invoice.go │ ├── customer.go │ └── ... 31 more, one package ├── services/ │ ├── invoice.go │ └── customer.go └── handlers/ ├── invoice.go └── customer.go // By feature | A folder per noun | internal/ ├── invoice/ │ ├── model.go │ ├── invoice.go │ └── stores/invoicesql/ ├── customer/ │ ├── model.go │ └── stores/customersql/ └── web/ └── handlers/

pages.description: Complete reference for Grit CLI commands: grit new, grit generate resource, grit sync, grit add role, grit start, and grit remove.
headings: The CLI across a project's life
pages.text: The Grit CLI is a single binary that scaffolds projects, generates full-stack resources, and syncs types between Go and TypeScript. Running grit new is interactive by default -- it walks you through architecture mode and frontend selection. Install it once and use it across all your Grit projects. Four commands carry a Grit project from empty folder to production. Everything else, meaning migrate , seed , sync , studio , slots in between these stages. Install the Grit CLI globally using Go: Install and remove plugins. A plugin generates code into your project, models, routes and pages, which you then own and can edit. Everything an install does is recorded in .grit/plugins.lock.json , and removal replays that record backwards, so uninstalling is exact rather than best-effort. Commit the lockfile. See Plugins for writing your own, and Multi-tenancy for the first-party one. Remove a previously generated resource. This deletes the Go model, service, handler, Zod schemas, TypeScript types, React hooks, resource definition, and admin page. It also cleans up all injection markers that were added when the resource was generated. The resource name should be the singular PascalCase name (e.g., Post , Product , BlogCategory ), the same name you used with grit generate resource . Add a new role to your project. This command updates all relevant files across the stack in one step: Go model constants, TypeScript types, Zod schemas, shared constants, and admin panel resource definitions (badge, filter, and form options). This single command updates 7 locations across your project: The role name is automatically uppercased. Multi-word roles use underscores: grit add role CONTENT_MANAGER Start development servers for your Grit project. Use subcommands to launch the frontend client apps or the Go API server individually. Runs pnpm dev from the project root, which starts all frontend apps (web, admin, expo, docs) via Turborepo. Runs go run cmd/server/main.go from the apps/api directory to start the Go API server. Both commands auto-detect the project root by looking for docker-compose.yml or turbo.json , so you can run them from any subdirectory within your project. Runs every test suite in the project: Go, the frontend suites, and with --e2e the Playwright tests, then prints one report. Which suites exist depends on the architecture you scaffolded, and this command works that out for you. A suite that cannot run is reported as SKIP with the reason , never dropped from the report. A runner that silently runs nothing looks exactly like one that passed, and that is the most expensive kind of green. End-to-end tests are opt-in because they need the API and frontends already running. Failing against a server that was never started tells you nothing about your code. The command exits non-zero if any suite fails, so it drops straight into CI. Parse all Go model files and regenerate the corresponding TypeScript types and Zod schemas in the shared package. Use this command whenever you manually modify a Go model and want the frontend types to stay in sync. Note: You do not need to run grit sync after using grit generate resource . The generator already creates the TypeScript types and Zod schemas for the new resource. Bring a project's framework files up to the CLI's version: admin components, the web app shell, Docker and root config, the migrate and seed tools. Your resource definitions, handlers, models and .env are not touched. Since v3.147.0 it also does not touch framework files you have edited. Grit records what it wrote and its hash in .grit/manifest.json , so an upgrade can tell a file nobody has opened from one you have customised. Untouched files are replaced. Edited ones are listed and left exactly as they are. Since v3.444.0 there are two more answers it can give, both from the same record. A file Grit has no record of writing , in a project that has a manifest, is not Grit's: if it differs from the template it is left alone under a heading that says so, because "you have edited this" is the wrong sentence for a file Grit never wrote. And a file Grit did write that is gone along with the directory it lived in is a feature the project removed, so it is not written back. One file deleted out of a directory that is still there still comes back, because that is how you reset a framework component. The directory is what tells the two apart: removing one is a bigger statement than removing a file, and the only one of the two that reads as "I do not want this". --force writes a removed directory back, and the upgrade lists what it left absent, so it is a decision rather than a silence. A screen you removed on purpose returning on every upgrade is what used to happen. This is also why there is grit add expo and grit add desktop . Copying an app in from another project gives it no records at all, and the first upgrade after a copy cannot tell a file you deleted from one this version has newly added, so a deleted screen comes back once. These commands write the app and record it, so the provenance is right from the first upgrade. It also raises the libraries every API mounts, Sentinel, GORM Studio and Pulse, to at least the versions this CLI was tested with. One below its floor is raised with go get and named, with the reason; one above it is left alone. It never lowers a version. --diff prints a unified diff of your version against the new one, so you can port the parts you want by hand. --force overwrites everything, which is what upgrade did unconditionally before this release. A project created before v3.147.0 has no manifest, so nothing can be said about what has been edited in it, and the first upgrade behaves exactly as it always did. That upgrade writes the manifest, and every one after it is protected. Commit .grit/manifest.json so the protection applies to everyone on the team. Update the Grit CLI itself to the latest version. It first checks GitHub for the newest release and exits immediately if you

pages.description: How Grit code generation works: generating full-stack resources with models, handlers, services, Zod schemas, TypeScript types, hooks, and admin pages.
headings: Add a field to an existing model
pages.text: The Grit code generator creates full-stack CRUD resources from a single command. It generates 9 new files and injects code into 10 existing files, wiring everything together automatically so your resource is immediately usable. When you run grit generate resource , the CLI goes through four stages: For a resource named "Post", the generator creates the following 9 files. Each file is complete, ready to use, and follows Grit's conventions. Here is what the generator produces for grit g resource Post --fields "title:string,content:text,published:bool" : In addition to creating new files, the generator injects code into existing files to wire everything together. Each injection uses a marker comment that was placed during project scaffolding. Grit uses special marker comments in scaffolded files to know where to inject new code. These markers are placed during project creation and should not be removed. The generator finds each marker and inserts new code on the line before it. Important: Never remove marker comments from your files. If a marker is missing, the generator will skip that injection and print a warning. You can safely add your own code above or below the markers. There are two injection modes used by the generator: Most markers use this mode. The generator finds the marker comment, then inserts the new code on the line immediately before it. This is used for model registration, route definitions, exports, and resource imports. The GORM Studio marker uses this mode. The generator inserts code directly before the marker on the same line. This produces clean output like: {`&models.Post , `} A long --fields string is a file you have not written yet. The same description in YAML goes in the repository, gets reviewed in a pull request like everything else, and regenerating the resource a year later is one command rather than archaeology through your shell history. A field is written either as the one-line spec the command line takes, or as the mapping of keys below. They can be mixed in one file: use a line for the fields that fit on one, and keys for the ones with more to say. A condition is if <field> == <value> on the one-line form, and an if: key on the mapping form. A file may also set owned_by , tree , public , append_only and tenant_owned ; a flag on the command adds to those and never removes one the file set. The mapping form gives you the properties below, and is what you want for a field with a default, a description or a long option list. Generated code is yours to edit , Grit scaffolds it once and never overwrites it. Two common follow-ups: One command. It writes the column into the Go model, both Zod schemas, the TypeScript type, and the admin table and form: No migration file is written, deliberately: the Go model is what describes the schema, and GORM adds the column from it. Scalar, select and toggle types are supported. Four types it declines: relationship, file, slug and array fields. Each writes more than a column , a foreign key and a preload, an upload pipeline, a hook that fills the value on save , and half-wiring those is worse than refusing. The command says so and points you at regenerating the resource instead: grit g resource Product --fields "...including the new one" . Its injections are idempotent, so existing routes and registrations are skipped. You can still edit the Go model by hand and run grit sync , which rewrites packages/shared from your structs and inserts the field between the // grit:cols:auto and // grit:fields:auto markers so hand-edited rows survive. Worth knowing, because it is the path for anything the command will not do. Note that the create and update handlers bind explicit request structs, so a hand-added field also has to be added there before the API will accept it , which is the step grit g field does for you. Every resource declares an icon , a Lucide icon name , at the top of its resource file. The generator guesses one from the resource name; change it to any icon you like: The name must exist in apps/admin/lib/icons.ts (the app's icon registry). Most common icons are already there; if you pick one that isn't, add it to that file's import, the iconMap , and the re-export, and it becomes available. System links (Roles, Security, System Hub) get their icons from the sidebar component ( components/chrome/CollapsibleSidebar ) rather than a resource file. Each Grit field type maps to specific types and behaviors across the entire stack. This table shows the full mapping from field type to Go, GORM, TypeScript, Zod, DataTable column format, and form field type. The generator automatically builds search queries based on your field types. All string and text fields are included in the search WHERE clause using PostgreSQL's ILIKE operator for case-insensitive matching.

pages.description: Every field type for grit generate resource --fields, with its Go type, TypeScript type, Zod schema, and default admin form control and table column. The single source of truth for field mapping.
headings: When is a field conditional, rather than just optional?
Modifiers, and the tags they add
pages.text: The complete set of field types you can pass to grit generate resource --fields . Each one drives the Go struct field, the shared TypeScript type, the Zod schema, and the default admin form control and table column , from one declaration. A field is name:type , with optional extra segments. Separate multiple fields with commas inside --fields . A type that takes an argument takes it in brackets, and a field that only applies sometimes says so in words. Read one left to right and it tells you everything about itself. Labels are derived from the values, so monthly renders as "Monthly" and in_progress as "In Progress". Give one explicitly only when it differs: [monthly, annually="Every year"] . Only some types take an argument: select , radio and check take their options, slug takes the field to slugify, belongs_to , one_to_one and many_to_many take the related model, file and files take what they accept, tel and country take a country code, and rating takes a number of stars. Every other type goes straight from its name to its modifiers, which are appended with colons: email:email:unique . Name the argument, even when it can be guessed. client:belongs_to infers the model from the field name and works; client:belongs_to[Client] says which model, and keeps saying it when somebody renames the field. The same goes for the upload types: photo:file[image] and gallery:files[image] declare what is accepted, where a bare file accepts anything. Every example in these docs is written out in full for that reason. Optional means the answer may be blank. Conditional means the question does not apply. The test: if you asked it about a record where the condition is false, would the answer be meaningless rather than merely empty? A billing cycle on a one-off project is meaningless, so it is conditional. A phone number nobody gave you is empty, so it is optional. Two things to get right in when=kind=recurring . The field name is a sibling on the same resource, written as it appears in the spec, and it must exist, or the command is refused. The value is the stored value, which for a select is the left-hand side of recurring=Recurring , not the label; it is compared as text, so case matters. It works on any field type, including a relationship: a plan that only applies to a recurring project is plan:belongs_to[Plan]:when=kind=recurring . For a condition that is more than one field equalling one value, write the predicate by hand in the resource definition and the rule in the service. What each type becomes in the database, and the thing about it that the Go type does not tell you. These are the tags the generator writes; a model you edit by hand keeps whatever you put there. The fields say what the resource holds. These say what it is for, and most of them change the generated code in more than one place at once. How each field type resolves across the stack. Source of truth: internal/generate/field.go . Primary keys are always UUID string (never uint ); a belongs_to FK column is a matching UUID string. Each type also picks a default form control and DataTable column format in the generated admin resource. You can override either in the resource definition. email, url, domain, tel, country, color, percent, rating, time and json are stored as plain columns with a known shape. The API checks and normalises them on every write that goes through a model: create, update, PATCH, bulk edit, CSV reads the format tag on the model field. A refused value is a 422 in the usual error shape, with the field named in details . The admin form checks the same rules before it sends, and shows the API's message if one gets through: Phone numbers are validated with libphonenumber's metadata on both sides: github.com/nyaruka/phonenumbers in the API and libphonenumber-js in the browser, so the form and the API agree about which numbers are valid. The Go module is added to a project the first time it generates a tel field, not before. The country picker, shared by tel and country, is a Base UI combobox: type a country's name, its code (UG) or its calling code (256), move with the arrow keys and press Enter. With --faker , every formatted field seeds values its own rule accepts, with the row number mixed in so a unique column seeds thousands of rows without a collision: valid mobile numbers from twenty countries, addresses such as ada.lovelace.12@example.com , ratings weighted towards four and five stars, and times in business hours. grit g field adds any of them to an existing resource except json, which needs gorm.io/datatypes in the model: regenerate the resource for that one. The Expo form uses the phone keyboard and checks E.164 for tel, and the matching keyboard for email, url and domain; the desktop forms use the browser's own email, url, tel, time and colour inputs.
