headings: The ordering, and why it is a string
pages.text: Boards, columns and cards in the admin, with dragging by pointer, by finger and by keyboard. It is also the plugin the authoring guide is written around, because a board is the smallest feature that needs every part of the plugin system at once. Boards then appears in the admin sidebar, under Content. A new board starts with To do, In progress and Done, because landing on an empty screen with one button is a worse first thirty seconds than landing on a board. Board , BoardColumn and BoardCard models, with migrations CRUD routes for all three, plus a move endpoint for cards and one for columns A boards list page and a board page in the admin, with React Query hooks An optional work-in-progress limit per column, enforced on the server A boards.card_moved event on the domain bus, so webhooks, the audit log and realtime subscribers all hear about it without the handler calling them Boards are visible to every signed-in user and record who created them. If boards need to be per-tenant, install the multitenant plugin , which scopes every model including these. This is the part worth reading even if you never install the plugin, because every ordered list has the same problem: a playlist, a priority queue, a sortable table. The obvious design is an integer position column. Moving a card then means: That rewrites every card below the drop. With one person on the board it works. With two, their rewrites interleave and the column ends up with duplicate or skipped positions, and on Postgres the two statements can deadlock outright because they touch the same rows in opposite orders. Gap numbering (100, 200, 300) only delays it: the gap closes after a few drags between the same pair and you are renumbering again. So a rank here is a string , compared lexicographically, and there is always a string strictly between any two others. A move is: One row. No renumbering, no transaction spanning cards somebody else is dragging, and no lock held while a user decides where to drop. The same ORDER BY works unchanged on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite, which matters because Grit targets all three and a scheme needing dialect-specific SQL is three bugs. Append three cards to an empty column and they get a0 , a1 , a2 . Drag the last one to the top and exactly one row changes: The keys stay short because a rank has an integer part that increments rather than a string that grows. Ten thousand appends leave the key four characters long. Only repeated insertion between the same two neighbours lengthens one, by a character at a time, and it never runs out of room. Two people who drop a card into the same slot at the same moment compute the same rank. That is a tie, not corruption. Every read orders by (rank, id) , so the tie breaks the same way for both of them and the board is stable. The move request names the two cards the dragged card was dropped between, not an index. An index is stale the instant anybody else moves a card, and a stale index silently puts the card in the wrong place. Neighbour ids survive that: if one of them has moved away, the server notices and appends rather than computing a position from a row that is no longer where the browser thought it was. Every card has a drag handle that is a real button , so it is in the tab order. Space picks a card up, the arrow keys move it within and between columns, Space drops it and Escape cancels. A live region announces the column by name: "Picked up Email the list from To do", "Over In progress", "Dropped Email the list in In progress". This is the entire reason the plugin takes a dependency on @dnd-kit rather than using HTML5 drag events. Those do not fire on touch devices and cannot be driven from the keyboard at all, so a hand-rolled board works in a demo and excludes two groups of people who are not in the room when it is demonstrated. A column can cap how many cards it holds. The limit is checked on the server, and a move that would exceed it is answered with 409 and the card goes back where it came from. Reordering inside a column that is already at its limit is allowed: a limit is about how much work is in progress, not about whether it can be rearranged. Removal replays the install backwards from the lockfile: the files it wrote are deleted, the lines it injected are taken back out, and the project compiles again. Your board data stays in the database until you drop the tables. Steps: Install it | grit plugin add kanban | Writes the three models, the service holding the ordering, the routes, the hooks and two admin pages, and adds Boards to the sidebar under Content. // Install the admin dependency and migrate | pnpm install cd apps/api && go run cmd/migrate/main.go | The dependency is @dnd-kit, which is what makes dragging work with a finger and a keyboard as well as a mouse. The migration creates boards, board_columns and board_cards. // Create a board | Open Boards in the admin and name one. It starts with To do, In progress and Done, because landing on an empty screen with a single button is a worse first thirty seconds than landing on a board. // Add some cards and drag one | Add a card from the foot of a column. Drag it with the pointer, or Tab to its handle, press Space, use the arrows and press Space again. The column name is announced as you cross it. // Set a work-in-progress limit | curl -X PATCH localhost:8080/api/v1/board-columns/ -d ' ' | A move that would push the column past its limit is refused with 409 and the card returns where it came from. Rearranging inside a full column is still allowed: a limit is about how much work is in progress, not whether it can be ordered. // React to a move from your own code | events.On("boards.card_moved", func(ctx context.Context, e events.Event) error ) | go | The handler emits on the domain bus, so webhooks, the audit log and realtime subscribers all hear about it without the move endpoint knowing they exist. Related: Multi-tenancy | /docs/plugins/multitenant | Boards become per-organisation as soon as the three models embed tenant.Owned, with no change to the board code. // Command palette | /docs/plugins/command-palette | The other keyboard-first surface in the admin, and the fastest way to reach a board. // Saved views | /docs/plugins/saved-views | If the work is better as a filtered table than as a board, this is the plugin that makes the table worth returning to.

pages.text: Plugins Every plugin, in three groups. All of them write ordinary code into your project, and all of them come back out with one command. Built into the CLI, maintained with the framework, tested on every release. Larger pieces that ship as Go modules from grit-plugins . Installed with go get rather than grit plugin add , because they are libraries your code imports rather than code generated into it. Written by other people and listed here on request. Listing is not endorsement The review is deliberately shallow: that the repository exists, that it installs and removes cleanly on a fresh project, and that it is not obviously hostile. Nobody audits the code for you. A plugin writes files into your project and patches existing ones, so read what it did with git diff , the same as any dependency. Installing one takes the repository directly. Grit names the source and confirms before cloning, and nothing from the repository is executed: it reads the manifest and writes the files that manifest names. grit plugin submit prints the checklist and the submission link. Three commands on a freshly scaffolded project, and the third is the one people skip: Removal replays the lockfile backwards, so it only works if every change the plugin made is one the lockfile recorded. A plugin that edits a file outside the injection mechanism installs fine and leaves wreckage when it is taken out. Official: kanban | Kanban boards | Boards, columns and cards, dragged with a pointer, a finger or the keyboard. | /docs/plugins/kanban | official | grit plugin add kanban // multitenant | Multi-tenancy | Organizations, per-org roles, and query scoping a forgotten WHERE cannot leak past. | /docs/plugins/multitenant | official | grit plugin add multitenant // impersonate | Impersonate | Sign in as another user to reproduce their bug, with an audit trail of every swap. | /docs/plugins/impersonate | official | grit plugin add impersonate // command-palette | Command palette | Ctrl+K to anywhere in the admin, built from the resource registry. | /docs/plugins/command-palette | official | grit plugin add command-palette // saved-views | Saved views | A table's filters, sort and search saved as a named view, per user. | /docs/plugins/saved-views | official | grit plugin add saved-views // device-pairing | Device pairing | Sign in a browser by scanning a code from a phone that is already signed in. | /docs/plugins/device-pairing | official | grit plugin add device-pairing // push | Push notifications | Notifications to the Expo app through Expo, so no certificates reach the API. | /docs/plugins/push | official | grit plugin add push // video | Video | Clips converted by ffmpeg to an MP4 and a poster every client can play. | /docs/plugins/video | official | grit plugin add video // stripe | Stripe | Checkout and billing, with webhooks that survive a redelivery. | /docs/plugins/stripe | official | grit plugin add stripe // webhooks | Webhooks | Outbound webhooks to headings: How the active organization is chosen
When there is no active organization
Single sign-on does not join an organization
An organization has roles of its own
What an organization's role may hold
pages.text: One user, many organizations, a different role in each, with query scoping that can't be forgotten. Most apps are single-tenant, and putting org_id on every table is a schema decision no framework should make for you. Install it when you need it. Embed tenant.Owned . That's what opts a table into isolation: Generated resources are shared until you do this. grit generate resource does not know this plugin is installed, so a model it writes has no OrgID and no scoping. That is the right default for a shared table like a country list, and the wrong one for anything belonging to a customer. Open the model and embed tenant.Owned for each resource that belongs to an organization, and remember it again after any --force regeneration. Scoping applies per model, so a table without OrgID is simply never filtered. Nothing warns you: the endpoint works, returns rows, and returns everyone's. Then just query normally: scoping is applied for you: A query against a tenant-owned model with no active organization returns an error. It does not quietly return every tenant's rows. Hand-written scoping fails the other way: forget one WHERE and you get a silent cross-tenant leak that no test catches, because the query returns more rows rather than failing. Platform admin screens and background sweeps need to see everything. Opt out explicitly, so each call is deliberate and greppable: From the X-Organization-ID header, or automatically when the user belongs to exactly one. No subdomains : they force DNS and TLS decisions on every deployment and make local development awkward. Membership is always verified against the database . Trusting the header alone would let any signed-in user read another tenant's data by editing one request header. Requesting an organization you don't belong to returns 404 , not 403 . A 403 confirms it exists and lets an attacker enumerate tenants. A tenant-owned row cannot be read or written without one, and the scoping callback fails closed rather than guessing. The caller is told so: 400 with the code NO_ORGANIZATION , which happens when they belong to no organization, or to several and named none. Until v3.233.0 this arrived as a 500 saying "Failed to fetch deals", because the error reached the generic handler and nothing knew what it meant. Membership carries a role, so somebody can be an editor in one organization and a viewer in another. It reuses the roles you already have, with no parallel permission system. The semantics, because they are a choice: an organization role adds permissions inside that organization. Platform roles, the ones assigned with PUT /users/:id/roles , stay global. So an organization can grant but cannot take away, and a project with no membership roles behaves exactly as it did. This is what v3.233.0 fixed: the membership role was stored, put on the request context, and read by nothing, so being an administrator of one organization meant being one in every organization you belonged to. A user provisioned by SSO or a social login belongs to no organization, so every tenant-owned endpoint answers NO_ORGANIZATION for them until somebody puts them in one. That is deliberate: which organization a new user joins is a policy the framework cannot guess, and guessing would be a cross-tenant bug rather than a convenience. Map it where you know it, from the email domain, the SSO connection, or a group the identity provider releases. grit doctor reminds you when both are present. grit new <name> --multitenant at scaffold time, or grit plugin add multitenant in a project that already exists. Both go through the same install, so they write the same project. Either way, nothing is scoped until you say which models are owned. Add tenant.Owned to a model, or generate it with --tenant-owned . That is deliberate: putting org_id on every table is a schema decision no framework should make for you, and a model that is shared on purpose (a currency table, a country list) would be the thing it broke. Clients send it as X-Organization-ID . A user who belongs to exactly one organization has it activated automatically and never sends the header at all. A user who belongs to two gets a switcher in the admin, which the plugin installs. It renders nothing below two organizations, so a single-tenant project looks as it did. Switching clears the React Query cache rather than invalidating it: an invalidated query serves its old data while it refetches, and that data belongs to the organization being left. The header itself is the framework's, in lib/active-org.ts and the api-core interceptor, and it is present in every project whether or not the plugin is. It sends nothing until something sets a value, so a single-tenant project carries a few inert lines and nothing else. A role's name is unique per owner, not across the platform, so two customers can each have an "Accountant" and an edit by one does not change the other's permissions. A role with an empty owner_org_id is the platform's; one carrying an organization's id belongs to that organization, is listed only through that organization's endpoint, and cannot be read, edited or handed out by anybody else. Who may author one: the organization's owner, a platform administrator, or a member holding orgroles.manage . Who may change the membership: the same three, with orgmembers.manage . Nothing grants either by default, so until the owner authors such a role only they can do these things, which is the safe default rather than the convenient one. Never * , and never the platform's own administration: users. , roles. , settings. , apikeys. , audit. and the rest. A membership role's grants are merged into every request made with that organization active, and the platform's routes check the permission key rather than who owns the role, so one of those in a customer's role is that customer reading everybody's data. Beyond that, the ceiling is the author's own grants, with one widening for the owner, who holds no role by default and would oth Steps: Install it | grit plugin add multitenant | Writes the Organization and OrganizationMember models, the tenant package holding the GORM callbacks, the organisation screens in the admin, and the switcher in the navbar. // Run the migration | cd apps/api && go run cmd/migrate/main.go | Creates the two tables. Nothing else in the project has changed shape yet. // Make a model tenant-owned | type Deal struct | go | Embedding tenant.Owned adds OrgID and brings the model under scoping. Until a model has it, it stays shared across organisations, which is the right default for a currency table and the wrong one for a deal. // Migrate again, and backfill | cd apps/api && go run cmd/migrate/main.go | The new org_id column starts empty on existing rows, and an empty org_id matches no organisation. Rows that predate this are invisible to every scoped query until you give them one, so backfill before anybody looks. // Tell the API which organisation is active | curl -H "X-Organization-ID: org_123" localhost:8080/api/v1/deals | The admin and web clients send this header automatically once an organisation is selected. Without it a scoped query fails closed with NO_ORGANIZATION rather than returning everything. // Opt one query out, visibly | // A platform-wide report, deliberately across organisations. var total int64 tenant.Unscoped(db).Model(&models.Deal ).Count(&total) | go | Scoping is automatic so that forgetting is impossible; the escape hatch is explicit so that crossing tenants shows up in review. Read internal/tenant/tenant.go before using it. Related: Impersonate | /docs/plugins/impersonate | Once data is per-organisation, the fastest way to answer "what does this member actually see" is to be them for a minute. // Kanban boards | /docs/plugins/kanban | Boards become per-organisation the moment Board, BoardColumn and BoardCard embed tenant.Owned. Nothing else changes. // Saved views | /docs/plugins/saved-views | Views are already per-user; with organisations in play they are the natural way to keep one team's filters apart from another's.

headings: Keeping a plugin up to date
pages.text: A Grit plugin generates real code into your repo , models, routes, pages, migrations , not a runtime dependency that hides in node_modules . And because every install is recorded, plugins do the one thing most plugin systems can't: cleanly uninstall. Most frameworks extend through packages: you install one, it lives in your dependency folder, and at runtime it reaches in and registers itself. That's fine until you want to see what it did or remove it , the code isn't yours, it's behind a version number. Grit plugins work the other way around. grit plugin add multitenant writes Go models, handlers, routes, admin pages and migrations directly into apps/api , apps/admin and the rest of your project. After it runs, the code is yours : read it, edit it, step through it in a debugger. There's no hidden runtime library deciding your app's behavior. This is the same idea as code generation : grit generate resource gives you a model, a service, a handler and an admin page you own. A plugin is that, bigger and reusable , a packaged code generation. When a plugin runs, Grit records everything it did , every file it created and every injection it made , into a lockfile: So removal isn't a second pile of code the author maintains , it's derived. grit plugin remove reads the lockfile and replays the install backwards: it deletes the files it added and reverts the injections, in reverse order. Commit the lockfile, and your plugins are as reversible as a git branch. A framework whose plugins publish migrations into your app can't cleanly reverse them , publishing is a one-way door. Grit's can, because the install is a recorded, replayable transaction. grit plugin add refuses to run with uncommitted changes, so the diff it produces is always clean and reviewable. Read the diff, commit it, and it's part of your app like anything else. A plugin gets fixes like everything else, and until grit plugin update those fixes reached nobody: add refuses once a plugin is installed, and remove then add loses your edits and re-inserts the patches at their markers, which moves them relative to code you have written since. That is not theory. Doing it to a shop built on Grit put the payment service below the code that constructs things from it, and the API stopped compiling. So an update rewrites only what it can prove nobody has touched. Every file is fingerprinted when the plugin writes it: one whose fingerprint still matches is replaced, one that differs is left exactly as it is and named. Files the plugin has gained simply arrive, which is what most plugin releases are, and a patch already in place is never applied twice or moved. Nothing is ever deleted. grit upgrade runs this for every installed plugin, because a command nobody runs fixes nobody's project. Two things it will not do quietly. A project installed before Grit recorded fingerprints cannot be vouched for at all, and there half an update is worse than none: the file a release adds is usually the one another file has to change to use, so the update stops, changes nothing, and tells you which files it cannot judge. And a file you have edited is never overwritten. Both are the same way out: A second set lives at github.com/MUKE-coder/grit-plugins . These are ordinary Go modules rather than code generators, so they install with go get and you wire them into your routes yourself. grit plugin list prints these too, under a separate heading, so the command is a complete picture of what is available rather than of what it can install itself. No overwrite. A plugin can't clobber a file that already exists , it creates, or it fails loudly. A missing marker is an error. If an injection's anchor isn't found, the install stops rather than silently doing nothing. No double install. Installing an already-installed plugin is refused. Requirements both ways. A plugin's dependencies must be present to install it, and can't be removed while it's still installed. The built-in catalog covers the big, opinionated pieces that don't belong in every app, and the small high-value features that the best admin ecosystems treat as add-ons. Want to build one? See Writing a plugin . Plugins are how Grit stays small at the core and still grows: the batteries every app needs are built in, and the bigger, opinionated pieces are plugins , real code, in your repo, that you can always take back out.
pages.title: Plugins

pages.text: Send a notification to a user's phone from Go, in one line. The API talks to Expo's push service, which relays to Apple and Google, so there is no APNs certificate or Firebase key to manage. Go sends in the background, so the request that caused it never waits on the push service. Every device the users registered gets it. Send does the same and waits, returning how many devices Expo accepted: for a background job that wants the result. apps/expo/lib/push.ts asks for permission, gets the device's token and registers it. Call it after sign-in and on every launch while signed in; unregister before signing out. Dead tokens clean themselves up. When an app is deleted or notifications are turned off, Expo answers DeviceNotRegistered for that token, and it is removed on the spot instead of being tried with every message from then on. A phone belongs to whoever signed in last. A token is unique, and registering it moves it to the current user, so a shared or handed-down phone stops getting the previous person's notifications. Batches of 100. Expo takes at most 100 messages a request; sending to more users makes as many requests as it needs. Ten devices a user. The oldest are dropped first, since a phone that was replaced stops re-registering. Real devices only. Simulators and the web cannot receive push; registerForPush returns null there and the app carries on. Store builds need an EAS project id; set EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN if the project uses enhanced push security. Checked against Expo's live service while building the WhatsApp blueprint: a message to someone with a registered token went out through Expo, and a token no device owned came back as not registered and was removed. Steps: Install it | grit plugin add push | Writes the token model and handlers, the services.Push sender, and apps/expo/lib/push.ts. It needs an Expo app in the project. // Run the migration | cd apps/api && go run cmd/migrate/main.go | Device tokens are rows against a user, so a phone that signs in as somebody else stops receiving the last user's notifications. // Register the device | import from "@/lib/push"; await registerForPush(); // asks permission, then POSTs the token | ts | Call it after sign-in. The matching unregister call belongs in your sign-out path, or the handset keeps receiving notifications meant for the previous account. // Send yourself a test | curl -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/push/test -b cookies.txt | Goes to every device registered to the signed-in user. If nothing arrives, the response says which token Expo rejected. // Send from your own code | services.Push.Go(ctx, []string , "Deal won", deal.Title, map[string]string ) | go | Sends in the background, 100 devices per request. Tokens Expo reports as no longer registered are deleted automatically, so the table does not fill with dead handsets. Related: Device pairing | /docs/plugins/device-pairing | The other half of treating devices as first-class: pairing starts a session, push reaches it. // Video | /docs/plugins/video | The other plugin that assumes an Expo app, for the clips a notification might point at.
pages.title: Push notifications

pages.text: Capture a table's filters, sort, search, and date range as a named view , then switch between them in one click. Per user, per resource. You keep re-applying the same filters and sort every time you open a table , "active users sorted by signup", "unpaid invoices this month". It's a small friction that repeats dozens of times a day. Saved views let you capture that arrangement once and reapply it instantly. In some admin ecosystems this exact feature ships as a paid "advanced tables" add-on. In Grit it's a plugin you install when you want it. Grit's resource tables already sync their entire state , filters, sort, search, date range , to the URL query string. So a saved view is nothing more than that query string, stored per user, per resource. Applying one is a navigation; the table restores itself from the URL. Nothing in the DataTable itself has to change. Because the table's state already lives in the URL, the plugin only needs to store and replay a query string. A SavedView model with fields id , user_id , resource (the resource slug), name , query (the raw URL query string), and created_at : A handler exposes three endpoints: Every query is scoped to the signed-in user's id, so a user only ever sees or deletes their own views , a crafted id can't touch someone else's. A SavedViews bar renders above every generic resource table, injected at a resource-page toolbar marker. It shows a chip per saved view plus a Save current view button. Saving captures the current URL query (minus transient params like an open create/edit drawer), prompts for a name, and POSTs it. Clicking a chip navigates to the resource with that saved query; each chip has a small × to delete it. The plugin works on the triple and full architectures , it needs an admin app to render the views bar. Because it adds a table, run migrations after installing: Open a resource, set some filters, sort, or search, then click Save current view and give it a name. It appears as a chip. Click the chip anytime to reapply that exact view; click the × on a chip to remove it. The saved-views bar appears on generated resources , which use the generic resource page. Built-in resources with fully custom pages may not show it, since they don't render the toolbar marker the bar injects into. Any filter-and-sort combination you return to is worth saving: Active users , status filter plus a sort by signup date. Unpaid invoices this month , a status filter and a date range, captured together. Published posts by date , the segment you review every morning, one click away. Views are per user , so yours don't affect other admins, and each person builds the set of segments that matches how they work. They're ideal for quickly toggling between different slices of the same table. Steps: Install it | grit plugin add saved-views | Writes the SavedView model and handlers, the hook, and the chips that appear above every resource table. // Run the migration | cd apps/api && go run cmd/migrate/main.go | One table, scoped to a user and a resource. // Filter a table the way you want it | Set the filters, the sort, the search and the date range on any resource. The table already keeps all of that in the URL. // Save it | Click Save view and name it. What is stored is the query string, which is why the tables themselves needed no changes: applying a view is a navigation. // Switch between them | The views appear as chips above the table. They are per user and per resource, so one person's Overdue, mine is not everyone's. Related: Command palette | /docs/plugins/command-palette | Reach the table in two keystrokes, then a saved view to reach the rows. // Multi-tenancy | /docs/plugins/multitenant | If views need to differ per organisation as well as per user, that is the plugin that adds the dimension.
pages.title: Saved views

headings: Start a payment from your own handler
pages.text: Take money for an order without trusting the browser with the price. Your server works out what is owed, Stripe's form takes the card, and the order is marked paid when Stripe says so, once, however many times Stripe says it. Then set the keys from the Stripe dashboard: STRIPE_SECRET_KEY and STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET for the API, NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY for the web app. Without a secret key the payment routes answer PAYMENTS_UNAVAILABLE rather than failing somewhere less obvious. On a project made before v3.311.0, run grit upgrade first. There is deliberately no route that starts a payment. Your checkout handler already knows the order, so it works out the total and asks for that amount. The browser receives a client secret that can confirm this one payment and nothing else. It runs inside the transaction that marks the payment succeeded. If it returns an error, neither change is kept, the webhook is recorded as failed, and replaying it from the admin runs both again. OnRefunded works the same way for refunds. Stripe's Payment Element, in the app's colours, with whatever payment methods are switched on in the dashboard. Card details go from the browser to Stripe and never reach the API. The plugin adds Stripe.js to the web app's Content-Security-Policy: its script, its frames and its API, each of which the browser otherwise refuses with nothing but a console message. A recurring charge brings card updates, failed renewals, dunning, proration, tax and cancellation with it, and every one of those is a screen somebody has to build and keep correct. So subscriptions go through Stripe's own hosted checkout and billing portal, which are already localised and already handle 3-D Secure. The only thing your app has to get right is what happens when access starts and stops. The browser asks for a checkout and goes where it is told. Your plan table holds the price ids you made in the Stripe dashboard; nothing about the plan is hard-coded in the plugin. Return URLs are built from SITE_URL and a path, never from a URL the caller sends, because a return URL the browser chooses is an open redirect with a payment attached. A subscription row says what somebody is entitled to. It says nothing about the money: what they paid, when, or whether this month went through. So every paid invoice is recorded as a Payment , the same row a one-off purchase writes, referenced subscription:<id> , and your OnSucceeded hook runs for it exactly as it does for a one-off. A receipt written once covers both. A renewal that failed is recorded too, with what the bank said, because that is the one somebody has to see. A redelivered invoice changes nothing, and a failure event arriving late cannot unpay an invoice that was paid. What this buys you is an app that can answer "what did we take this month" and "what did this customer pay" out of its own database, with no trip to the Stripe dashboard. An invoice whose subscription this app has never seen is recorded as a failed webhook rather than shrugged off: Stripe retries, by then the subscription event has usually arrived, and the retry runs. Money is not something to drop quietly. Stripe's word, never the browser's. A redirect back to your site proves nothing. A payment is marked paid by a signed webhook, or by the API reading the intent back from Stripe with the secret key, and only when the amount and currency Stripe reports are the ones the payment was for. At least once, in any order. Stripe retries and does not promise order. Every change is a conditional update from the states it may come from, so a second delivery changes nothing and a late processing cannot undo a succeeded . Retries do not charge twice. Each intent is created with the payment's own id as its idempotency key, and each refund with a key made of what has been refunded so far, so a double click makes one refund. A failed renewal does not lock anyone out on the first retry. past_due still counts as entitled, because Stripe spends the next couple of weeks retrying the card and most of those succeed. Access ends when Stripe gives up, at unpaid or canceled . Cancelling keeps the days already paid for. No SDK. Four REST calls with the API version pinned. stripe-go's webhook parser refuses any event whose API version differs from the library's, which breaks a working endpoint on the first upgrade; the signature check every Grit project already has does not care. Built for the storefront blueprint, and checked against a running API on a new project: a wrong signature was refused with 401, a redelivered event was skipped as a duplicate, a late processing left a paid payment paid, an intent reporting 1 cent against a payment of 1000 was recorded as a failed event with that reason and left unpaid, and a partial refund was recorded. The shipped tests run the rest against a fake Stripe. Testing webhooks locally: stripe listen --forward-to localhost:8080/webhooks/stripe prints the signing secret to use. Or skip it: the return page's refresh settles card payments on its own. Steps: Install it | grit plugin add stripe | Writes the checkout handlers, the webhook endpoint and the models behind them. // Put the keys in the environment | STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_... STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_... | Test keys to begin with. The webhook secret is not optional: without it the endpoint cannot tell a real Stripe event from anybody who found the URL. // Run the migration | cd apps/api && go run cmd/migrate/main.go | Payments and processed event ids are rows. The second table is what makes a redelivered webhook harmless. // Forward webhooks to your machine | stripe listen --forward-to localhost:8080/api/v1/stripe/webhook | Stripe cannot reach localhost on its own. Most of the time a checkout "works but nothing happens" in development, this is why. // Take a payment and then replay it | stripe trigger payment_intent.succeeded | Run it twice. The second delivery must change nothing: Stripe redelivers on its own schedule, and a handler that is not idempotent double-charges or double-ships the first time that happens in production. Related: Multi-tenancy | /docs/plugins/multitenant | If each organisation is billed separately, add it before the billing model hardens around one customer per app. // Webhooks | /docs/backend/webhooks | Outbound webhooks, to the Standard Webhooks spec, for telling other systems what you just charged for.

pages.text: Take a clip from a phone or a browser and turn it into something every client plays: one H.264 MP4 that starts before it has downloaded, a poster frame, and the size and length a feed needs to lay it out. ffmpeg does the work in the background, and the upload request never waits for it. The API's Docker image gets ffmpeg. To convert while developing, install it on your machine: winget install ffmpeg , brew install ffmpeg or apt install ffmpeg . Without it, uploaded videos wait and the log says why. Upload the file as usual with accepts=video , which allows up to 300 MB, then hand its key to POST /videos . The answer is 202 with the video, pending. The Expo app has the same pair, playing with expo-video , and useUploadVideo() takes a clip straight from expo-image-picker . The owner also hears video.ready or video.failed on their realtime channel, for an app that would rather listen than poll. One format, every client. H.264 and AAC in an MP4, capped at 720 on the short side, with the index at the front. Every browser, iOS and Android plays it, so there is no HLS to serve and no player to choose per platform. A portrait clip stays portrait. The table is the queue. A worker claims a pending video with a conditional update, so a conversion survives a restart, several replicas share the work without Redis, and a claim held by a replica that died is taken over after fifteen minutes. One conversion at a time per replica, because ffmpeg uses every core it is given. A crafted file cannot read the server. ffmpeg follows what a file says it is, and a playlist posing as a video can name other files for it to open. Only MP4, MOV and WebM are converted, each read with a forced demuxer and local files only, and a playlist is refused before ffmpeg sees it as input. Only your own uploads. A video is made from an upload by its storage key, and a key that is not yours answers as not found, so it never confirms that someone else's file exists. Failures say why. Too long, not a video, or a file that would not convert: the video is marked failed with a sentence for the person who uploaded it, and a failure that could be temporary is tried three times first. Limits are videoService.Options.MaxEdge and MaxDuration , set in routes.go : 720 and three minutes. Built for the Instagram blueprint, and checked end to end on a new project: a 1080p clip uploaded over HTTP came back as a 720p H.264 MP4 with a poster within a second, served from storage, and another user sending the same key was told it does not exist. Steps: Check ffmpeg is on the machine | ffmpeg -version | The conversion runs in your own worker, not a hosted service. Without ffmpeg the plugin installs and the conversion fails at runtime, which is a worse place to find out. // Install it | grit plugin add video | Writes the video model, the conversion job, and the endpoints to start one and read its status. // Run the migration | cd apps/api && go run cmd/migrate/main.go | A conversion is a row, so its progress survives a restart and a failed one can be retried rather than lost. // Upload, then convert | curl -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/videos -d ' ' | The upload goes through the storage you already have. The key must name an upload you own, so one account cannot queue work against another's file. // Play it | The conversion produces an MP4 and a poster image. Poll the video's status, or subscribe to the event, and render the MP4 once it is ready rather than the original. Related: Push notifications | /docs/plugins/push | The obvious thing to do when a conversion finishes is tell the person who uploaded it. // Kanban boards | /docs/plugins/kanban | If clips are work items rather than content, a board is often the better surface for them.

headings: Why the signature is shaped like that
pages.text: Tell other people's systems when something happened in yours. Signed to the Standard Webhooks spec, retried with backoff, and logged so you can prove what you sent. This is the outgoing direction. For verifying webhooks other people send you , which the core already handles, see receiving webhooks . One call, from anywhere a handler can reach. It does not block on the network: the dispatch is queued, and a consumer that takes nine seconds to answer is the queue's problem rather than your request's. The signed content is . . , not the body alone. Signing only the body produces a signature that stays valid for ever: anybody who captures one request can send it again tomorrow, and it verifies. With the id and timestamp inside the signature, a replay is a message the consumer has already seen, or one whose timestamp is outside its tolerance. Following the spec also means your consumers do not have to trust your crypto. They verify with any off-the-shelf Standard Webhooks library, in whatever language they use, and the integration instructions you owe them are one paragraph. Consumers go down. Each attempt is recorded with its status, retries back off exponentially with jitter so a recovering endpoint is not knocked over by everything at once, and a delivery that exhausts its budget lands in the dead letter rather than disappearing. The admin page lists them and resends in one click. That log is the part worth having before you need it. "We never got the callback" is unanswerable without it, and unarguable with it. Steps: Install it | grit plugin add webhooks | Writes the wiring into internal/handlers and the admin page. The runtime itself is the grit-webhooks Go module, so upgrades are go get rather than a regenerate. // Rebuild and restart the API | cd apps/api && go build ./... | The subscriptions and delivery_attempts tables are migrated on boot, so there is no separate migration to run. // Add a subscription | Admin, then System, then Webhooks. A subscription is a URL, the events it wants, and a generated secret that starts whsec_. Show the secret to the consumer once: it is theirs, not yours. // Dispatch an event from your own code | handlers.DispatchWebhook("invoice.paid", gin.H ) | go | Returns immediately. Delivery, retries and the log all happen behind it, so a slow consumer never slows your handler down. // Watch it arrive, then break it on purpose | The delivery log shows every attempt with its status. Point a subscription at a URL that 500s and watch the backoff, the dead letter when the budget runs out, and the resend button putting it back in the queue. Related: Stripe | /docs/plugins/stripe | The incoming direction. Stripe sends you webhooks; this plugin sends yours to other people. // Realtime | /docs/backend/realtime | For your own frontend, where a websocket beats an HTTP callback you then have to secure.

pages.description: Learn Docker fundamentals for running Grit infrastructure: containers, images, docker-compose, PostgreSQL, Redis, and MinIO.
pages.text: A practical guide to Docker for developers who want to use Grit. You don't need to be a Docker expert , just understand enough to start and stop the infrastructure services that power your Grit project. Think of Docker like a shipping container for software. Just as shipping containers let you move goods between ships, trucks, and warehouses without repacking, Docker containers let you run software on any computer without worrying about what's already installed there. Without Docker, setting up a database like PostgreSQL means downloading an installer, configuring paths, managing versions, and troubleshooting OS-specific quirks. With Docker, you run a single command and get a fully working database in seconds , identical on every developer's machine. This eliminates the "works on my machine" problem entirely. Every developer on your team gets the exact same PostgreSQL version, the exact same Redis configuration, and the exact same MinIO file storage , guaranteed. Docker runs your database (PostgreSQL), cache and job queue (Redis), file storage (MinIO), and email testing server (Mailhog). Your Go API and Next.js apps run natively on your machine for faster development , only the infrastructure services live in Docker containers. Docker Desktop is the easiest way to get started on Windows and macOS. It bundles the Docker engine, Docker Compose, and a graphical interface for managing containers. On Linux, you install Docker Engine and Docker Compose separately. macOS (Homebrew) Linux (Ubuntu/Debian) Verify your installation Docker must be installed and running before you run grit new . The scaffolded project includes a docker-compose.yml that requires Docker Compose V2 (the docker compose command without the hyphen). An image is a blueprint , a read-only template that contains everything needed to run a piece of software: the operating system, the application, its dependencies, and configuration. Think of it like a recipe. A container is a running instance of an image , the actual dish you cook from the recipe. You can run multiple containers from the same image, and each one is isolated from the others. When you stop a container, it's like throwing away the dish, but the recipe (image) remains for next time. Grit uses official images from Docker Hub: postgres:16-alpine for PostgreSQL, redis:7-alpine for Redis, minio/minio for file storage, and mailhog/mailhog for email testing. The "alpine" variants are smaller, lightweight images based on Alpine Linux. A Dockerfile is a text file with instructions for building a custom image. Each line is a step: choose a base image, copy files, install dependencies, and specify how to start the application. Here are the key instructions: FROM , Sets the base image (e.g., golang:1.21-alpine ) WORKDIR , Sets the working directory inside the container COPY , Copies files from your machine into the image RUN , Executes a command during the build (e.g., installing dependencies) EXPOSE , Documents which port the app listens on CMD , The command that runs when a container starts A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM statements. The first stage compiles your code with all build tools, then the final stage copies only the compiled binary into a tiny base image. This keeps production images small and secure. Grit scaffolds two Dockerfiles: apps/api/Dockerfile builds the Go binary using a multi-stage build (final image is under 20MB), and apps/web/Dockerfile builds the Next.js app with standalone output. These are used by the production compose file, not during everyday development. Running individual docker run commands for each service gets tedious fast. Docker Compose solves this by letting you define all your services in a single docker-compose.yml file. One command starts everything. A compose file defines services (containers to run), their images , port mappings, environment variables, volumes for data persistence, and dependencies between services. It's like a blueprint for your entire infrastructure. Every Grit project has a docker-compose.yml at the project root that defines all four infrastructure services. There's also a docker-compose.prod.yml for production that additionally builds and runs the Go API, web app, and admin panel as containers. When you scaffold a new Grit project, the generated docker-compose.yml includes four services. Here's what each one does and why it's there: Start all four services with docker compose up -d . They'll run in the background. Your Go API connects to them via localhost and the ports listed above. All connection strings are pre-configured in the .env file. You only need a handful of Docker commands for day-to-day Grit development. Here's your cheat sheet: In practice, you mainly need two commands: docker compose up -d to start your infrastructure at the beginning of a coding session, and docker compose down when you're done. Everything else is for troubleshooting. By default, when you stop and remove a container, all its data disappears. Volumes solve this by storing data outside the container on your machine's filesystem. When you restart the container, the volume is re-attached and all your data is still there. Docker supports two types of storage: named volumes (managed by Docker, recommended) and bind mounts (map a specific folder on your machine). Grit uses named volumes for all services because they're simpler and work the same on every operating system. Your PostgreSQL data persists across container restarts thanks to the postgres-data volume. If you need a completely fresh start (e.g., your schema is out of sync), run docker compose down -v to delete all volumes, then docker compose up -d to recreate everything from scratch. GORM will auto-migrate your tables on the next API startup. Containers run in their own isolated network. To access a service from your machine, you create a port mapping that connects a port on your computer (the host) to a port inside the container. The syntax is HOST:CONTAINER . For ex

pages.description: Learn Go fundamentals for building Grit backends: variables, structs, functions, error handling, interfaces, pointers, goroutines, Gin routing, GORM, middleware, and JWT authentication.
headings: This page, the book, and the course
WaitGroup , Waiting for Goroutines to Finish
pages.text: Everything you need to know about Go to work with Grit's backend. This guide assumes you know another language like JavaScript or Python and walks you through Go's key concepts as they apply to building full-stack applications with Grit. This page is the reference: enough Go to read a Grit project, on one page, in the order the code appears. It assumes you are in a hurry. If you are learning Go rather than looking something up, the Go Full course is the whole book as lessons: 59 of them, every one ending in a committed assignment that the leaderboard scores. Same material, taught from zero rather than summarised. Want to practice as you learn? Try the code examples in our interactive Go Playground. Go (often called Golang) is a statically typed, compiled language created at Google. It compiles to a single binary with no runtime dependencies, starts up in milliseconds, and handles concurrency natively. These qualities make it ideal for building API servers. Every Go file belongs to a package . The special package main is the entry point for executables. The func main() function inside package main is where your program starts. You import other packages using the import keyword. Go uses modules for dependency management. You initialize a module with go mod init and run your program with go run . Four things in that file are worth naming, because every Go program has them. The package line comes first. The import block lists what the file uses. func main() is where execution starts. Anything after // is a comment. Here is the same program with a little more in it , still no variables, which arrive in the next section. The entry point for every Grit backend is apps/api/cmd/server/main.go . This file initializes the database connection, sets up middleware, registers routes, and starts the Gin HTTP server. You rarely edit it directly -- the code generator handles injecting new routes and models automatically. Go is statically typed -- every variable has a fixed type determined at compile time. You can declare variables with var (explicit) or := (short assignment, which infers the type). The short form is used inside functions and is by far the most common style in Go code. The basic types you will encounter are string , int , bool , and float64 . Go also has uint (unsigned integer, used for database IDs), byte , and rune (for Unicode characters). Constants are declared with const and cannot be changed after assignment. Two things surprise people arriving from JavaScript or Python. Every type has a zero value , declare a variable without assigning one and it is 0 , "" , false or nil , never undefined. And Go never converts implicitly: adding an int to a float64 is a compile error until you convert one of them yourself. One thing in the next example runs ahead of itself. Turning a string into a number can fail, so strconv.Atoi hands back two values: the number and an error. Read if err != nil as "if something went wrong" for now , section 4 covers errors properly, and this is the only place before then that needs them. Go's fmt.Printf and fmt.Sprintf use format verbs to control how values are printed. You will use these constantly when logging, building strings, and debugging. Here are the ones you need to know: You will see := everywhere in handlers and services. Config values loaded from .env are stored in typed struct fields (like Port int , JWTSecret string ). Constants are used for role names ( RoleAdmin = "ADMIN" ) and error codes. Format specifiers are used in error wrapping ( fmt.Errorf("failed to create user: %w", err) ) and logging throughout the codebase. Go has three keywords for control flow and no more: if , for and switch . There is no while , the for keyword covers every loop shape , and no ternary operator, so a conditional value is written as an ordinary if . Two details catch people out. Parentheses around a condition are not used, but braces are always required, even for a single statement. And switch does not fall through: each case ends by itself, so there is no break to forget. break leaves a loop entirely and continue skips to the next iteration. An if can also carry a short statement before its condition, which is where most Go code puts the variable it is about to test , it keeps that variable scoped to the branch that uses it. The shape you will write most often is the guard clause: an if that checks one thing and returns early. Handlers are a stack of them , reject the bad request, reject the unauthorised user, then do the work , which keeps the happy path at the left margin instead of nested four levels deep. Go functions can return multiple values . This is fundamental to Go's error handling: instead of throwing exceptions, functions return an error value as the last return. If the error is nil , the operation succeeded. If not, you handle it immediately. The if err != nil pattern appears on nearly every line that calls another function. It may look verbose at first, but it makes error flow explicit and easy to trace. Use fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err) to wrap errors with additional context as they bubble up the call stack. Wrapping with %w is only half the pattern. The other half is asking what an error was , further up the stack. A sentinel is a package-level error value you compare with errors.Is ; a package-level error value you compare with errors.Is , and it sees through any number of %w wraps. That is what lets a handler map a failure raised deep in a service onto the right status code without ever reading the message. (Errors that also carry fields need a struct and a method, so they wait until after those sections.) Every service function in internal/services/ returns (result, error) . Handlers call services, check for errors, and return the appropriate HTTP response. For example, user, err := service.GetUserByID(id) followed by an if err != nil block that sends a 404 or 500 JSON response. pages.description: Learn Next.js fundamentals for building Grit frontends: App Router, server/client components, data fetching, routing, and React Query.
pages.text: Welcome back. Count: A focused guide to the React and Next.js concepts you need to build with Grit. If you know another language or framework but are new to the React ecosystem, this page covers everything from components and hooks to data fetching and validation -- the building blocks behind Grit's admin panel and web app. React components are JavaScript functions that return JSX -- a syntax that looks like HTML but compiles to JavaScript. Every piece of UI in a React app is a component. Components accept props (input data) and can render other components as children . You handle events with inline functions and conditionally render elements using JavaScript expressions like && and ternaries. Every file in app/ and components/ is a React component. Pages like page.tsx export a default component for the route. Reusable UI pieces live in components/ and are imported wherever needed. Grit generates both page components and shared components when you scaffold a project. TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, catching bugs at compile time instead of runtime. Use interface to describe object shapes and type for unions, intersections, and computed types. Generics let you write reusable typed code (like ). TypeScript infers types wherever possible, so you don't need to annotate everything -- but explicit types on function parameters and return values make your code self-documenting. All Grit code is TypeScript. Shared types live in packages/shared/types/ and are generated from your Go models by grit sync . Both the admin panel and web app import these types, ensuring your frontend always matches your backend data structures. React hooks are functions that let components have state and side effects. useState declares a piece of reactive state -- when you call the setter function, React re-renders the component with the new value. useEffect runs side effects like API calls, subscriptions, or timers. The dependency array controls when the effect re-runs, and the cleanup function handles teardown. Grit uses useState throughout the admin panel for local UI state (search filters, pagination, modal visibility) and in the web app for form inputs and toggles. You rarely need raw useEffect for data fetching because React Query handles that, but it's still used for things like keyboard shortcuts and resize listeners. Next.js uses file-based routing: folders inside app/ become URL routes automatically. A page.tsx file makes a route accessible, layout.tsx wraps child pages with shared UI (like a sidebar), and loading.tsx shows a loading state. Route groups with parentheses like (auth) organize routes without adding a URL segment. Dynamic routes use square brackets like [id] . Both apps/web and apps/admin use the App Router exclusively. The admin app uses a (dashboard) route group with a shared layout containing the sidebar and navbar. Auth pages sit in an (auth) group with a minimal layout. When you run grit generate resource , it creates new page files inside the appropriate route group. In the App Router, components are server components by default. They run on the server, can be async , and can fetch data directly -- but they cannot use hooks or browser APIs. Add "use client" at the top of a file to make it a client component , which runs in the browser and can use useState , useEffect , event handlers, and everything interactive. In Grit, page-level components are typically server components that render the page shell. Interactive parts like DataTable, FormBuilder, and any component using React Query hooks are marked "use client" . The general rule: keep server components for layout and structure, push interactivity down to the smallest client component possible. Tailwind CSS is a utility-first framework where you style elements by composing small CSS classes directly in your JSX. Instead of writing margin-top: 1rem in a CSS file, you write mt-4 on the element. Responsive design uses breakpoint prefixes ( sm: , md: , lg: ). shadcn/ui provides pre-built, accessible components (Button, Card, Dialog, Input) that use Tailwind under the hood and can be customized by editing the source files directly. All styling in Grit is Tailwind -- there are no custom CSS files except for the base globals.css which defines CSS variables for the dark theme. UI components come from shadcn/ui and are scaffolded into components/ui/ . You can customize any shadcn component by editing it directly since it's your own code, not a node_modules dependency. React Query is the data fetching layer in Grit. useQuery fetches and caches server data with automatic background refetching, stale-time management, and loading/error states. useMutation handles create, update, and delete operations with callbacks like onSuccess to invalidate caches. The QueryClientProvider at the root of the app provides the cache to all components. All data fetching in Grit goes through React Query hooks stored in hooks/ . When you run grit generate resource , it creates a complete hook file with useList , useGet , useCreate , useUpdate , and useDelete hooks. Components never call fetch or axios directly. Zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. You define the shape and constraints of your data with a fluent API, then use z.infer to extract the TypeScript type from the schema -- so your validation rules and types are always in sync. Zod supports strings, numbers, booleans, enums, arrays, nested objects, optional fields, and custom validation messages. Use safeParse for error handling without exceptions. Zod schemas live in packages/shared/schemas/ and are shared across the admin panel and web app. When you run grit generate resource , it creates Zod schemas matching your Go model fields. The grit sync command can regenerate schemas from Go types to keep everything aligned. React Hook Form manages form state, validation, and submission with minimal re-renders. The useForm hook returns register (connects inputs), handleSubmit (validates before ca

headings: Where does a Grit app start?
The same thing, in the admin panel
Deep pages, and the index they need
The order is the whole thing
pages.text: Ten stages, from one server to sharding. A Grit app starts at the far side of five of them, and the rule for the rest is the same as everywhere else: do not add a box until something is actually breaking, then add exactly one. Most scaling guides begin with work you have to do first: move config to environment variables, put database access behind one module, get uploads off the local disk, add a health endpoint. That is the whole of Stage 1, and a generated Grit project has all of it on the first commit. It goes further than that. Sessions are rows, not process memory. Cron is elected to a single instance, so the daily digest is sent once rather than once per replica. The server drains in-flight requests on SIGTERM . Jobs retry with backoff and there is a transactional outbox for the ones that must not be lost. Those are Stages 4 and 8, and they are there before you have a user. Point it at the deployment that is struggling. These numbers describe wherever they are measured, and a laptop under no load is always healthy. The admin panel shows the same report; see below . It names one thing, and most of the time that thing is nothing. A tool that lists six possible improvements has handed the hardest part of the job, choosing, back to you. grit scale answers it from a terminal. The admin's Observability page answers it for everyone else, at the top of the page, refreshed every minute: the verdict, and then all ten stages with the state of each on this deployment. Every line is read off the running deployment rather than off a list of features. A tick against Stage 4 means this app was observed keeping sessions in the database and uploads in object storage; it is not a claim about what the framework can do. The three measured stages, 5, 6 and 7, go amber on the same thresholds the verdict uses, so the panel cannot show green for the stage the verdict is calling out. Two things it will tell you about that are easy to miss until a second instance exists. STORAGE_DRIVER=local keeps uploads on one machine's disk, so the second instance serves 404s for half of them. And SQLite serialises writes, which makes every scaling question after Stage 1 have the same answer. A page-numbered list is LIMIT 25 OFFSET n , and OFFSET is not free: the database fetches every one of those n earlier rows from the table and throws them away. On 500,000 rows, page 1 is 9ms and page 20,000 is 1.6 seconds. Every "last page" click pays it, and an index on the sort column does not help, because the planner still visits the heap for each row it skips. Past an offset of 1,000, paginate.List fetches the page in two queries instead: the primary keys first, from the index alone, then the rows by key. Same page, same order, about a tenth of the time. You do not switch it on and there is nothing to configure. The gain depends on the key query being answerable from an index alone . Every generated list carries deleted_at IS NULL , so a plain index on the sort columns still visits the table to check it, and the two-query path buys nothing. The index has to cover that condition: Add one per list people actually page deeply through, matching the columns that list sorts and filters by. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on the key query should say Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0 ; if it says anything else, the index is not covering the query and the page will not get faster. The real fix for a list somebody pages through all day is not to make page 20,000 fast but to remove the need for it: a filter, a search, or cursor pagination, which has no offset at all. Send ?mode=cursor and follow meta.next_cursor . It cannot give you page numbers or a total, which is why the admin table does not use it, but for an API client walking a list it is the right shape. One environment variable, and no code changes: Reads go to the replicas from the next boot. Writes, and everything inside a transaction including its reads, stay on the primary. That last rule is the one that matters and the one hand-rolled splits get wrong: a balance check inside the transaction that debits the balance must not read a replica, and here it cannot, whatever the handler was written to do. For the reads whose answer decides a write, outside a transaction: The classic replica bug: you post, the feed loads from a replica that has not caught up, your own post is missing, and you post it again. Grit pins a person to the primary for five seconds after they write, using a cookie rather than a shared store: it travels with the person who wrote, costs no lookup, and cannot itself be stale. Generated list and detail handlers use it. Hand-written ones should too: Remember is cache-aside with the three things a hand-written version misses. A cache read failure falls through to the loader, so Redis being down makes the app slower rather than broken. TTLs are jittered, so ten thousand keys written by one deploy do not all expire in the same second. And when a hot key expires, one caller rebuilds it while the rest wait briefly and read the result, instead of every concurrent request running the same expensive query. Invalidate from the write that makes the value wrong, and keep the TTL as the safety net for the invalidation somebody forgets: Connection exhaustion is the only failure here that arrives as errors rather than slowness: the API returns 500s while every dashboard looks healthy. It is also pure arithmetic, so grit doctor does it: Tell it how many instances you run with APP_INSTANCES . That is the number people get wrong: a pool of 25 is comfortable on one machine and fatal on eight, and nothing else in the config mentions the other seven. Grit does nothing here, deliberately. Sharding is the most expensive tool in the box and most applications never need it. Before it: archive cold rows, use Postgres native partitioning, move analytics to a warehouse and search to a search engine, or let Citus or CockroachDB shard for you. If you genuinely outgrow one primary, the shard key is the de stages: 0 | Measure first | Request percentiles, connection use, slowest queries, cache hit rate, and a verdict. | Run grit scale against production. | free // 1 | One server, one database | Config from env, one database module, uploads in object storage, /health. A Grit app is born finished here. | Nothing. | free // 2 | Vertical scaling | Go uses every core in one process. There is no cluster module to add. | Buy a bigger machine. | free // 3 | Horizontal + load balancer | Stateless by construction, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM, a health endpoint the balancer can poll. | Set an instance count. The balancer is your platform's. | free // 4 | Stateless servers | Sessions in the database, uploads in object storage, cache invalidation across replicas, and cron elected to one instance. | Nothing. The three-emails bug cannot happen. | free // 5 | Connection pooling | pgbouncer already in docker-compose.prod.yml, per-instance pool limits, and a doctor check that does the arithmetic. | Point DATABASE_URL at the pooler. | flag // 6 | Indexes, then read replicas | Indexes on foreign keys as generated. Replica routing, read-your-own-writes, and a lag probe. | Set DATABASE_REPLICA_URLS. No code changes. | flag // 7 | Caching | cache.Remember: cache-aside with fallback, jittered TTLs, stampede protection and a hit rate. | Decide what may be stale. Nobody can decide that for you. | flag // 8 | Queues and background jobs | asynq workers, retries with backoff, a jobs dashboard, cron, and a transactional outbox. | Move slow work into a job. | free // 9 | Sharding | Nothing, deliberately. | Archive, partition, or move to Citus first. Almost nobody needs this. | yours
pages.title: Scaling a Grit app, one break at a time

pages.description: How Grit defends every category of the OWASP Top 10:2025 by default, broken access control / IDOR via authz.MustOwn, SSRF via the safefetch package, injection via parameterised GORM queries, XSS via React escaping + CSP, auth flaws via Sentinel rate-limiting + JWT algorithm pinning + TOTP, security misconfiguration via the SecurityHeaders middleware, supply-chain via Dependabot + govulncheck, and tamper-evident audit logging.
pages.text: internal/authz is the IDOR defence, and from v3.224.0 a generated resource applies it in its service rather than its handler, so every caller gets it: a route, a background job, a command, a test. A list and an export are scoped in SQL, a read by id is checked after loading, and somebody else's row is 404 rather than 403, so a wrong guess cannot be told from a right one. The caller travels on the context: a handler puts it there with authz.WithActor(c.Request.Context(), authz.ActorOf(c)) , and a job says who it acts for with authz.AsSystem or authz.WithActor . An owned resource with no caller on the context matches nothing, which is the safe way for a job that forgot to fail. In a handler you write yourself, authz.MustOwn does the same check in one call and writes the 404 for you. For tenant / team scoping use authz.CheckScope ; for admin-only routes use authz.RequireRoles("ADMIN") . SSRF (absorbed into A01 in 2025) is handled by the internal/safefetch package, see A05 below. What is guaranteed here and what stays yours is listed per subsystem on the stability matrix . The SecurityHeaders middleware sets all the OWASP-recommended headers by default: HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy, and a strict Content-Security-Policy that blocks inline script. Error responses use a generic shape ( code , message ) that never includes a stack trace in production. Sensitive defaults: in production mode Sentinel WAF runs in block rather than log mode. Every Grit project ships with .github/dependabot.yml configured for Go modules, npm, and GitHub Actions on a weekly schedule, plus .github/workflows/security.yml running: govulncheck , Go vulnerability scan against the Go vulnerability database. pnpm audit , high+ severity gate on the frontend. CodeQL , static analysis for both Go and JavaScript on every PR. These run on every push and pull-request, plus weekly so newly-disclosed CVEs surface even when nothing in your code changed. .github/workflows/ci.yml runs the API's tests and the frontend's lint (Biome), type-check, tests and build on every pull request too. Go modules are pinned in go.sum with checksum verification; once pnpm-lock.yaml is committed, CI installs with --frozen-lockfile . Three layers of defence ship by default: Passwords , bcrypt via golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt with the library default cost. Constant-time verify. Never SHA-256, never MD5, never reversible encryption. Transport , HSTS preload enforced via SecurityHeaders. Any HTTPS request locks browsers into HTTPS-only for 2 years. JWT signing , HS256 with a 32-character minimum JWT_SECRET enforced at startup. The auth middleware verifies the algorithm explicitly so the classic alg:none attack is closed. Field-level encryption , declare a model field as crypto.EncryptedString and it is transparently encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM. GORM stores ciphertext (tagged enc:v1: with a fresh nonce per write) and your code reads plaintext; the column is opaque to anyone with the database but no key. Secrets live in environment variables, never in source. .env is in .gitignore ; the scaffold ships only .env.example . Encrypting a column. Set FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY (base64, 32 bytes, from openssl rand -base64 32 ) and mark the field when you generate it: notes:text:encrypted in --fields , or grit generate field Patient notes:text:encrypted on an existing resource. The model, the request structs and the CSV importer all get the type, writes encrypt, reads decrypt, and JSON responses stay plaintext. Encrypted columns are left out of search, sorting and filters, since ciphertext can never match. One rule: because every write uses a fresh nonce the ciphertext is non-deterministic, so an encrypted column can't be queried by equality. Use it for data you store and display but never filter on , personal notes, tokens, contact details , not for keys or lookup columns like email. With no key set the type passes values through as plaintext, so a project can adopt encryption later without a migration. Keep the key backed up: lose it and the encrypted columns are unrecoverable. A trap the connection closes for you: GORM map-based updates ( Updates(map[string]any{` `}) ) skip a column's encoder unless the value is itself an EncryptedString , so a bare string stores plaintext. Generated update and PATCH handlers write exactly such maps, and until v3.212.0 the first edit to an encrypted column was stored in plaintext, invisibly, because reads pass an unprefixed value straight through. crypto.Install , called when the API connects, now wraps any string headed for an encrypted column, and a test that ships with every project checks the raw column after a map update. It needs the model to know the column: db.Model(&row).Updates is covered, raw SQL is not. SQLi is closed at the protocol level: GORM uses parameterised queries for every Where , First , Create , Update , etc. The Grit codebase never builds queries by string concatenation; if you must use db.Raw , pass arguments as parameters, not interpolated strings. XSS , the React SPA escapes by default. The CSP header (A02) adds a second layer: even if something slips through, the browser refuses to execute inline script. In a scaffolded project, pnpm lint (Biome) flags every dangerouslySetInnerHTML . The few places Grit uses it carry a biome-ignore comment that says why the HTML is safe. SSRF (folded into A01 in 2025) , use the internal/safefetch package for any HTTP request whose URL came from the caller (webhooks, image-from-URL, PDF render, OEmbed): safefetch blocks the standard SSRF targets , loopback (127.0.0.1, ::1), RFC1918 private ranges, link-local, CGNAT (100.64/10), AWS metadata (169.254.169.254 + IPv6 fd00:ec2::/32), and well-known cloud-metadata hostnames. It also re-validates the resolved IP at TCP-connect time via a custom dialer, closing the DNS-rebinding TOCTOU window. Grit's architecture is o Owasp 2025: a01 | A01 , Broken Access Control | Users acting beyond their permissions; now includes SSRF. Still #1. // a02 | A02 , Security Misconfiguration | Insecure defaults, open buckets, verbose errors. Up from #5. // a03 | A03 , Software Supply Chain Failures | NEW in 2025 , compromised dependencies, build systems, distribution. // a04 | A04 , Cryptographic Failures | Weak/missing encryption exposing sensitive data. // a05 | A05 , Injection | SQLi, command injection, XSS , hostile input executed. // a06 | A06 , Insecure Design | Flaws baked into the architecture, not the code. // a07 | A07 , Authentication Failures | Weak login, sessions, credential handling. // a08 | A08 , Software & Data Integrity Failures | Trusting unverified code/data updates. // a09 | A09 , Security Logging & Alerting Failures | Can't detect or respond to attacks. Now includes 'alerting'. // a10 | A10 , Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions | NEW in 2025 , bad error handling, 'failing open', edge cases.
